authors.profile: Translator of Gregory the Great's Dialogues into Old English (c. 890s), a work commissioned by Alfred and prefaced by him; the earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic text.
authors.style: Faithful, competent Mercian-flavoured prose, somewhat more literal than the other Alfredian translations.
authors.concerns: The transmission of Gregory's hagiographical and pastoral teaching to a vernacular audience.
authors.significance: A key figure of the Alfredian translation program; his Dialogues preserve a major stage in the development of Old English prose.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the attribution of the translation rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

authors.name: William Baldwin
authors.biography: Born about 1515; a scholar of Oxford who became corrector of the king's printing under Edward VI and a prolific editor and compiler. His Treatise of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1547; his prose satire Beware the Cat, written in 1552–53, was printed in 1561. He planned and partly compiled A Mirror for Magistrates, printed in 1559 after his death. He died about 1563.
authors.profile: The author of the first English work of sustained prose fiction and the begetter of A Mirror for Magistrates. Beware the Cat — a night-long exchange of stories about cats, set in a London printing house and framed as a fantastic listening experiment — is the first English novel in embryo, and its anti-Catholic satire made it dangerous enough to be suppressed. The Mirror, which he edited and contributed to, became one of the most influential books of the Elizabethan age.
authors.style: Framed narrative in the plain style; printer's-shop realism; satirical fable with a serious theological edge.
authors.concerns: Protestant polemic against the old religion; the uses of fiction for truth-telling; the moral instruction of magistrates through the falls of great men.
authors.significance: A founding figure of English prose fiction and of the complaint tradition; his Mirror for Magistrates supplied subjects and rhetoric to Spenser, Shakespeare, and the whole Elizabethan tragic imagination.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; the division of authorship within the Mirror is editorial.

authors.name: William Camden
authors.biography: Born 2 May 1551 in the Old Bailey, London. Educated at Christ's Hospital and St Paul's School, then at Magdalen and Christ Church, Oxford. He taught at Westminster School (1575–97), where his pupils included Ben Jonson, and ended his career as Clarenceux King of Arms (1597). He died on 9 November 1623 at Chislehurst, Kent.
authors.profile: Britannia (1586, in Latin; English translation by Philemon Holland, 1610), the chorographical description of Britain, and the Annales of the reign of Elizabeth I (1615–25).
authors.style: Exact, methodical, elegant Latin and an English style of grave plainness; the scholar's impartiality joined to patriotic purpose.
authors.concerns: The recovery of British antiquity; the writing of sober, documented history against legend; national identity through the past.
authors.significance: The father of English antiquarianism; his Britannia launched the great tradition of county and national history that runs through the seventeenth century and beyond.
authors.uncertainty: The accuracy of the Annales on some episodes is disputed by later historians.

authors.name: William Caxton
authors.biography: A Kentish mercer who spent three decades in the Low Countries, rising to governor of the English merchants at Bruges, where he learned printing at Cologne and produced the first book printed in English, his own Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (Bruges, c. 1473–74). In 1476 he set up the first English press at Westminster, printing some hundred books — Chaucer, Malory, Gower, Lydgate, the Golden Legend, and his own translations — before his death c. 1491.
authors.profile: Printer and translator: the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye (c. 1473–74), The Game and Playe of the Chesse (1474), the History of Reynard the Fox (1481), the Golden Legend (1483), and numerous prologues and epilogues that constitute a body of critical prose.
authors.style: Lucid, idiomatic translation from French sources; a merchant's plain style enriched by courtly vocabulary; the prologues' genial self-presentation as servant of the 'comyn wele'.
authors.concerns: The provision of good books in English; the standardization of the language ('ouer rude termes' and the dialect of Kent); the moral and chivalric education of the nobility and gentry.
authors.significance: The introducer of printing to England: his press fixed the form of the English classics, began the standardization of written English, and made the fifteenth century's literature the sixteenth century's inheritance.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; the exact site and date of his first printing remain debated.
themes: The education of princes and magistrates

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

sources: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne

authors.name: William Congreve
authors.identity: The greatest master of the comedy of manners; author of The Way of the World (1700), Love for Love (1695), and the tragedy The Mourning Bride (1697), whose flawless comic prose and brilliant repartee represent the summit of English wit comedy.
authors.biography: Born 24 January 1670 at Bardsey, Yorkshire, son of an army officer; raised in Ireland and educated at Kilkenny and Trinity College, Dublin. He came to London, studied law at the Middle Temple, and astonished the town with The Old Bachelor (1693), followed by The Double Dealer (1693), Love for Love (1695), and The Mourning Bride (1697, the most successful tragedy of the decade). His masterwork The Way of the World (1700) was coolly received, and, sensitive to criticism and enjoying a comfortable government sinecure and the friendship of the Whig Junto (and a long liaison with Henrietta Godolphin, Duchess of Marlborough), he wrote little after 1700. He died on 19 January 1729 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
authors.profile: The consummate artist of comic prose, whose plays achieve a perfection of wit, structure, and tone — 'the prose Shakespeare' — treating the negotiation of love, marriage, and money in a society of manners with ironic elegance.
authors.style: Brilliantly epigrammatic prose; the 'proviso' scene of negotiated marriage; balanced, ironic repartee; elegant plotting; and, in The Mourning Bride, sonorous blank-verse declamation.
authors.concerns: Wit and true wit; love, marriage, and money; hypocrisy, affectation, and scandal; the social code of the town; and the relation of art and manners.
authors.significance: The Way of the World is universally regarded as the finest comedy of manners in English; Congreve defined the genre, influenced Sheridan and Wilde, and his tragic lines ('Musick has charms to soothe a savage breast') became proverbial.
authors.uncertainty: Congreve's life is well documented; his early retirement from writing is explained by his finances, health, and sensitivity to criticism, though the reasons remain partly conjectural.

authors.name: William Dunbar
authors.biography: A graduate of St Andrews (MA 1479) and a Franciscan novice in his youth, he served from c. 1500 as a clerk and poet at the court of James IV, for whom he wrote the celebratory poems of the marriage to Margaret Tudor (1503); he received a royal pension from 1500. He disappears from record after the battle of Flodden (1513), and died c. 1520.
authors.profile: Author of some eighty poems preserved chiefly in the Bannatyne and Maitland manuscripts: the Lament for the Makaris (c. 1505), The Goldyn Targe, The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo (c. 1500–07), the flying with Kennedy, the dream allegories, and the great occasional verse of the court.
authors.style: The most technically virtuosic of the makars: aureate magnificence (The Goldyn Targe) alternating with scabrous colloquial satire (the Tretis); the refrain, the flying, the alliterative line, and the French formes fixes all mastered; a voice by turns celebratory, venomous, elegiac, and devout.
authors.concerns: The vanity of life and the power of death (Timor mortis conturbat me); the hypocrisies of court and clergy; the duties and pleasures of the royal court.
authors.significance: With Henryson, the greatest poet of medieval Scotland; the Lament for the Makaris is one of the supreme elegies in the language and gave the Scottish tradition its name.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; his clerical status and career details are conjectural.
themes: Order and degree: the body politic

works.title: The Tretis of the Tua Mariit Wemen and the Wedo

sources: The Cambridge Companion to Milton, 2nd edition

authors.name: William Langland
authors.birthplace: probably Cleobury Mortimer, Shropshire, or the Malvern Hills area
authors.biography: Almost everything known of him is inferred from Piers Plowman, whose dreamer 'Will' is a long-clothed clerk of the Malvern country, married, and living in London in poverty among the Cornhill folk; the poem's A-text (c. 1367–70), B-text (c. 1377–79), and C-text (c. 1386–88) show a career of continuous revision. He is commonly identified with the William Langland recorded at Oxford and in London in the 1390s, though the identification is uncertain.
authors.profile: Author of Piers Plowman, the greatest English allegorical poem: a sequence of dream visions in which Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest amid the estates of fourteenth-century England.
authors.style: Unrhymed alliterative long lines of extraordinary range — satiric, homiletic, apocalyptic, tender; the allegorical dream vision fused with estates satire and biblical exegesis; the personification of abstract virtues with concrete social observation.
authors.concerns: The reform of society and church through penance and truth; the theology of grace and merit; poverty, labour, and the social order.
authors.significance: With Chaucer and Gower, the third summit of Ricardian poetry; Piers Plowman became the rallying text of reformist and radical traditions (it was read by the rebels of 1381 and printed by the Tudor reformers) and one of the most studied poems in English.
authors.uncertainty: Biography almost entirely conjectural; the attribution of the poem rests on manuscript rubrics and internal evidence.
sources: The Poems of Andrew Marvell

authors.name: William Lily
authors.identity: grammarian; first High Master of St Paul's School
authors.biography: Born at Odiham about 1468; studied at Oxford and in Italy, where he learned Greek. Appointed by John Colet as the first High Master of St Paul's School in 1512, he wrote the Latin grammar that, revised by Colet and Erasmus, became the standard school grammar of England. He died in February 1522 (new style 1523).
authors.profile: Author of the grammar that schooled England for three centuries. The Short Introduction of Grammar ('Lily's Grammar'), with its English accidence and its Latin Brevissima Institutio, was prescribed by royal proclamation under Henry VIII and Edward VI and memorized by every grammar-school boy from Shakespeare to Johnson — who quotes it, and its misquotations, throughout the literature of the period.
authors.style: The schoolmaster's clarity: paradigms, rules in English for boys, Latin examples; a grammar written to be memorized.
authors.concerns: The reform of Latin teaching on humanist principles; the founding of a public grammar school; the union of Greek learning with Christian education.
authors.significance: The author of the most widely used textbook in English history; Lily's Grammar structured the linguistic formation of the entire literate class of early modern England.
authors.uncertainty: The exact division of the grammar's authorship among Lily, Colet, and Erasmus is editorial.

authors.name: William of Malmesbury
authors.biography: A monk and librarian of Malmesbury Abbey, where he spent his whole career, becoming precentor and, late in life, refusing the abbacy; he died c. 1143. The greatest English historian since Bede, he gathered his materials from libraries across England and corresponded with the learned of his day.
authors.profile: Author of the Gesta Regum Anglorum (first version 1125, revised to c. 1135), the Gesta Pontificum Anglorum (1125), the Historia Novella (c. 1140–43), and saints' lives including those of Wulfstan, Dunstan, and Aldhelm.
authors.style: Polished, allusive Latin modelled on classical historians; critical assessment of sources; a gift for anecdote and character; patriotic pride in English history tempered by Norman loyalties.
authors.concerns: The continuity of the English kingdom from the Anglo-Saxons to his own day; the moral exemplarity of history; the recovery of the English past after the Conquest.
authors.significance: The founder of critical English historiography after Bede; his Gesta Regum is the principal narrative source for Anglo-Norman history and the model for the century's chroniclers.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; his Anglo-Saxon sources were largely lost in the Reformation.

authors.name: William of Ockham
authors.identity: philosopher; logician; political theorist; Franciscan friar
authors.biography: A Franciscan who studied and taught at Oxford, where his teaching was denounced to the papal court at Avignon (1324); while awaiting judgement he became embroiled in the Franciscan poverty controversy, fled Avignon with Michael of Cesena in 1328, and spent the rest of his life under the protection of the emperor Louis of Bavaria at Munich, writing political works against the papacy until his death in 1347.
authors.profile: Author of the Summa Logicae (c. 1323), the Ordinationes on the Sentences, the Quodlibeta, and a series of political treatises on poverty and papal power.
authors.style: The 'razor' of terminist logic: relentless elimination of superfluous entities and distinctions; a new theory of signs and mental language; clear, devastating polemic in the political works.
authors.concerns: The foundations of logic and knowledge; universals and nominalism; the limits of papal power; apostolic poverty.
authors.significance: The most consequential English philosopher of the Middle Ages: his nominalism reshaped European philosophy and theology (via Buridan, the via moderna, and Luther), and his political theory laid groundwork for conciliarism and modern notions of sovereignty.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; the chronology of his early works rests on internal evidence.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world

authors.name: William Roper
authors.biography: Born about 1496; a lawyer of Lincoln's Inn who married Margaret, Thomas More's eldest daughter, in 1521, and lived in More's household at Chelsea for sixteen years. He wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More between about 1553 and 1558 from intimate memory; it circulated in manuscript and was first printed in 1626. He died on 4 January 1578.
authors.profile: Author of the first great English biography of a private man. The Life of Sir Thomas More — the portrait of the Chancellor at Chelsea: his prayers, his jests, his relations with his family, and his final refusal of the oath — is the classic of Tudor life-writing and the foundation of the More legend that Shakespeare's play and the later tradition inherited.
authors.style: Plain, affectionate, anecdotal prose; the vivid recalled dialogue of the Chelsea household; a son-in-law's reverence without hagiographical inflation.
authors.concerns: The memory and example of More; conscience against the state; the sanctity of the family and the household.
authors.significance: Established the English biographical tradition and supplied the human More to every later age; a primary source of the first importance for the English Reformation.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate.

works.title: The Life of Sir Thomas More

authors.name: William Shakespeare
authors.identity: Playwright, poet, and actor; the central figure of English literature, author of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and two narrative poems.
authors.biography: Baptized 26 April 1564 at Stratford-upon-Avon, son of the glover and alderman John Shakespeare; educated at the Stratford grammar school. He married Anne Hathaway in 1582 (children Susanna, and the twins Hamnet and Judith), and by 1592 was established in the London theatre (Greene's 'upstart crow' attack). He wrote for the Lord Chamberlain's Men (from 1594) and its successor the King's Men (from 1603), was a sharer in the Globe (1599) and Blackfriars, and prospered as actor, playwright, and investor, buying New Place in Stratford in 1597. The narrative poems Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594) were his first printed works; the Sonnets appeared in 1609. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there on 23 April 1616; the First Folio of his plays was published by Heminges and Condell in 1623.
authors.profile: The supreme dramatist of the language and its greatest poet of the human interior: his histories, comedies, tragedies, and romances transformed every genre they touched, and his sonnets reinvented the Petrarchan sequence as a meditation on love, time, and art.
authors.style: Unmatched range of register — from the euphuistic wit and sonneteering of the early plays to the metaphysical density of the great tragedies and the late romances' verse of reconciliation; mastery of blank verse, prose, and song; the invention of character through soliloquy.
authors.concerns: Kingship, legitimacy, and the body politic; love, jealousy, and self-deception; time, mortality, and the immortality of art; the theatre itself as the mirror of nature; conscience and the divided self.
authors.significance: The measure of English literature: his works constitute the largest single achievement of the language's canon, translated into every tongue and performed continuously since the 1590s.
authors.uncertainty: The chronology of the plays rests on printed dates, records of performance, and stylistic evidence; the authorship of several plays (Titus Andronicus, Pericles, Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen, Edward III, Sir Thomas More) is collaborative, and the biographical record between 1585 and 1592 is a blank.

authors.name: William Tyndale
authors.biography: Born in Gloucestershire about 1494; educated at Oxford (BA 1512, MA 1515) and Cambridge. Denied episcopal patronage for an English Bible, he left England in 1524 and worked in Germany and the Low Countries: his New Testament was printed at Worms in 1526 and smuggled into England; the Pentateuch followed in 1530 and a revised New Testament in 1534. Betrayed at Antwerp in 1535, he was strangled and burned at Vilvoorde on 6 October 1536.
authors.profile: The father of the English Bible. His translations — made from the Greek of Erasmus and the Hebrew — gave English scripture its enduring shape: the Authorized Version of 1611 retains perhaps ninety per cent of his New Testament phrasing. As a polemicist he wrote the most effective Reformation tracts in English: The Obedience of a Christian Man (1528), The Parable of the Wicked Mammon (1528), The Practice of Prelates (1530), and An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue (1531).
authors.style: The plain style at its greatest: short sentences, monosyllabic Saxon diction, and rhythms tuned for reading aloud; learned argument made colloquial and urgent.
authors.concerns: The authority of scripture over church and prince; justification by faith; the translation of the Word into every ploughboy's language; the duty of obedience and its limits.
authors.significance: The principal architect of English biblical prose and of the language of English devotion; his translation work shaped the King James Bible and, through it, the speech of the English-speaking world.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date approximate; details of his early Gloucestershire life rest on Foxe's Acts and Monuments.

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
The Obedience of a Christian Man
The Parable of the Wicked Mammon

authors.name: William Wycherley
authors.identity: Restoration dramatist; author of the two fiercest comedies of manners, The Country Wife (1675) and The Plain Dealer (1676), whose savage wit and moral seriousness about lust, hypocrisy, and jealousy set him apart from his more elegant contemporaries.
authors.biography: Born c. 1640–41 at Clive, Shropshire, educated at Queen's College, Oxford, the Middle Temple, and in France (where he briefly became a Catholic before reverting). He served at sea in the Second Dutch War and moved in court circles. His plays — Love in a Wood (1671), The Gentleman Dancing-Master (1672), The Country Wife (1675), and The Plain Dealer (1676) — won him fame but little money. A secret marriage to the Countess of Drogheda ruined him; he spent seven years in the Fleet for debt, was briefly reconciled to his father, and lived in obscurity and poverty until, in old age, he married a young heiress days before his death on 1 January 1716, leaving his manuscripts to the young Alexander Pope.
authors.profile: The most savage and morally earnest of the Restoration comic writers, whose comedies expose sexual appetite, jealousy, and hypocrisy with a harsh, near-Jacobean intensity beneath the manners-comedy surface.
authors.style: Biting, energetic dialogue; intrigue plotting drawn from Molière and the Spanish; sexual frankness and dark comedy; and a moral seriousness unusual in the comedy of manners.
authors.concerns: Lust, jealousy, and cuckoldry; social and sexual hypocrisy; the corruption of town and country; misanthropy and plain dealing; and the vanity of pretence.
authors.significance: The Country Wife and The Plain Dealer are among the greatest English comedies; Wycherley's moral ferocity influenced Congreve and later satirists, and his late-life friendship with Pope linked Restoration and Augustan letters.
authors.uncertainty: Wycherley's birth year is uncertain (c. 1640–41) and much of his biography, especially his marriages and debts, is recorded only in anecdotal sources.

works.title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park

authors.name: Wulfstan
authors.biography: Bishop of London 996–1002, bishop of Worcester 1002–1016, and archbishop of York 1002–1023; the principal counselor and draftsman of law under kings Æthelred II and Cnut.
authors.profile: Author of the Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (1014), the most famous Old English sermon, preached in the crisis of the Danish invasions; the Institutes of Polity (a treatise on the orders of Christian society); the Canons of Edgar; the law codes of Æthelred and Cnut; and a series of eschatological homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis) warning of the approaching end.
authors.style: A distinctive, urgent rhythm built on two-stress phrases, alliteration, intensifying repetition, and cumulative word-pairs; the most recognizable idiolect in Old English prose.
authors.concerns: National repentance; social order and the duties of each estate; the coming of Antichrist; the law of God as the foundation of earthly law.
authors.significance: With Ælfric, the last great writer of Old English prose; his homilies and law codes shaped the response of the English church and state to the conquest of 1016.
authors.uncertainty: Birth date and early career unknown; the canon of his writings rests on stylistic analysis.

works.title: Wulfstan's Eschatological Homilies (De Antichristo, De falsis deis, and related sermons)

sources: Dictionary of Old English: A to I online

authors.name: Wulfstan the Cantor
authors.biography: Monk and precentor of the Old Minster, Winchester, active in the 990s; a leading figure of the literary culture of the Benedictine Reform.
authors.profile: Author of the Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno (c. 996), a verse life of St Swithun with an important prose preface describing the rebuilding of the Old Minster; also credited with the Life of St Æthelwold.
authors.style: Accomplished Latin hexameters in the classical revival manner of the tenth-century reform; encomiastic tone.
authors.concerns: The cult of the saints as the glory of the reformed church; the commemoration of Winchester's patrons and builders.
authors.significance: The principal Latin poet of the late Old English period; his Narratio is a major source for the architecture and liturgy of the Old Minster.
authors.uncertainty: Little biographical detail known; attributions of the Æthelwold life debated.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Medieval English Literature 1100–1500

authors.name: Ælfric Bata
authors.biography: A pupil of Ælfric of Eynsham who identifies himself by the nickname 'Bata' and addresses his master with affectionate humour in the colloquies. He probably taught at a monastic school in the first quarter of the eleventh century (fl. c. 1005-1025). His life is otherwise unknown.
authors.profile: Author of the Colloquia and the Colloquia difficiliora, Latin conversation manuals modelled on Ælfric's Colloquy but far more expansive and boisterous: they dramatize daily life in the monastic school with dialogue about food, drink, beatings, and petty theft.
authors.style: Colloquial, hyperbolic Latin with a taste for comic exaggeration and insult; the texts deliberately enlarge the vocabulary of daily life beyond the classroom classics.
authors.concerns: The teaching of spoken Latin; the discipline and everyday realities of the monastic school; the relationship between master and pupil.
authors.significance: His colloquies preserve a uniquely vivid picture of eleventh-century English school life and document the vitality of the vernacular-Latin classroom tradition founded by Ælfric.
authors.uncertainty: Known only from his texts; floruit approximate (c. 1005-1025); birth and death dates unknown.
sources: The Cambridge History of Early Modern English Literature

authors.name: Ælfric of Eynsham
authors.biography: Educated at Winchester under Bishop Æthelwold, the leading figure of the Benedictine Reform; monk and mass-priest at Cerne Abbas (c. 987–1005); first abbot of Eynsham (1005–c. 1010). The greatest and most prolific writer of Old English prose.
authors.profile: Author of the two series of Catholic Homilies (c. 989–995), the Lives of Saints (c. 993–998), the Grammar and Glossary (the first Latin grammar in a European vernacular), the Colloquy, translations of Genesis and other Old Testament books (the Old English Hexateuch), De temporibus anni, pastoral letters, and numerous shorter homilies and treatises.
authors.style: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of extraordinary clarity and control — a deliberately plain style designed to be read aloud and understood; careful avoidance of apocryphal excess.
authors.concerns: Orthodox teaching for clergy and laity; the dignity and capacity of the English language; the education of the young; resistance to superstition and error.
authors.significance: The culmination of the Old English prose tradition; his works circulated more widely than any other vernacular prose of the period and influenced English religious writing for centuries.
authors.uncertainty: Birth and death dates approximate; several works are attributed to him on stylistic grounds.
sources: Beowulf: A Verse Translation

authors.name: Æthelweard
authors.biography: Ealdorman of the western provinces and descendant of King Æthelred I; patron of Ælfric of Eynsham; died c. 998.
authors.profile: Author of the Chronicon (c. 980), a Latin version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle down to 973, written for his kinswoman Matilda, abbess of Essen, with a famous prologue praising King Alfred.
authors.style: Dense, hermeneutic Latin of the sort parodied by his contemporary William of Malmesbury's sources; learned vocabulary and Grecisms.
authors.concerns: The antiquity and dignity of the West Saxon royal line; the cultivation of Latin learning among the secular aristocracy.
authors.significance: An important witness to the text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and to lay Latin literacy in late Anglo-Saxon England.
authors.uncertainty: Dates approximate; identification with the ealdorman Æthelweard of the charters is standard but rests on prosopography.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

authors.name: Æthelwold of Winchester
authors.identity: monastic reformer; Latin and Old English prose writer; translator
authors.biography: Born into a noble Winchester family c. 904-909, brought up at the court of King Æthelstan, and ordained with Dunstan. He became a monk at Glastonbury under Dunstan, was made abbot of the derelict monastery of Abingdon (c. 954), and in 963 was appointed bishop of Winchester, where he expelled the secular clerics of the Old and New Minsters and installed monks. He was the most radical and effective leader of the Benedictine Reform, a teacher of Ælfric, and a patron of manuscript production and the arts. He died on 1 August 984.
authors.profile: Author of the Regularis Concordia (c. 970), the customary that unified English monastic observance under royal patronage; traditionally credited with the Old English translation of the Rule of St Benedict (c. 960s) and associated with the Old English New Minster Charter (966) and possibly the Benedictine Office. His school at Winchester created the standardized literary language ('Winchester words') used by Ælfric.
authors.style: In the Regularis Concordia, clear expository Latin organized for practical liturgical use, with vivid prescriptions for ceremony (the Visitatio Sepulchri, the 'tropes'); in the vernacular Rule, plain idiomatic Old English translating Benedict's Latin closely.
authors.concerns: Uniformity of observance; the king as protector of reformed monasticism; the education of monks in Latin and the vernacular; the liturgy as the centre of the religious life.
authors.significance: The architect of the English Benedictine Reform and of the alliance between the crown and the reformed monasteries; his Winchester school and standardized Old English shaped the literary language of the late tenth century and of Ælfric's and Wulfstan's prose.
authors.uncertainty: Birth year approximate (c. 904-909). The attribution of the Old English Benedictine Rule and Benedictine Office to him is traditional and widely but not universally accepted.
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice

works.title: The Old English Rule of St Benedict

sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: 'Tis Pity She's a Whore
works.description: John Ford's notorious tragedy of incestuous love between the siblings Giovanni and Annabella in Parma, and of Giovanni's murder of his sister and his entrance bearing her heart on his dagger.
works.plot: Governing himself by passion rather than religion, Giovanni declares his love to his sister Annabella; she yields, marries the noble Soranzo to conceal her pregnancy, is discovered, and is killed by Giovanni, who then dies fighting Soranzo's followers.
works.significance: The most powerful and most discussed Caroline tragedy; it pushed the theatre's moral limits further than any contemporary play and remains a central text in the study of early modern incest and tragic passion.
works.meter: Blank verse of sustained lyric intensity, with Ford's characteristic repetition and lament.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix in Drury Lane, probably c. 1629-33, and published in 1633 with a remarkable author's dedication defending the play's seriousness.
works.characters: Giovanni; Annabella; Soranzo; the Friar Bonaventura; Vasques; Grimaldi; Bergetto; Philotis; Richardetto; Hippolita
works.structure: Five acts of a single, tightly driven tragic action with subordinate comic plots, ending in the public catastrophe at the cardinal's feast.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Book of Airs
works.description: The songbook of 1601 by Thomas Campion (words and music) and Philip Rosseter (music): twenty-one lute songs and one masque song, including 'My sweetest Lesbia', 'Follow thy fair sun', 'When to her lute Corinna sings', and 'I care not for these ladies' — the volume that made Campion the supreme English lyricist of the lute-song golden age.
works.plot: No plot: the airs set the commonplaces of love — carpe diem, the lady's beauty, the lover's complaint, the joys of country over court — each song a perfected miniature in the courtly lyric tradition.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan lute-song tradition — poetry and music fused as nowhere else in the language, and a touchstone for every later English lyricist.
works.meter: Short-line lyric stanzas of exquisite finish — trochees, iambs, and the quantitative experiments of Campion's 'observations' — composed for music and printed with tablature.
works.context: Published 1601 in the first great decade of the English ayre, alongside Dowland's and Jones's books; Campion's preface defends the new union of English verse and music against the metrical pedants.
works.characters: the singer-lover; Lesbia; Corinna; the beloved ladies
works.structure: A printed songbook of twenty-one airs plus the masque song, arranged for voice and lute (some also for viol consort), in the standard format of the English ayre books.
works.attributionNotes: Words by Campion throughout, with one masque song; music by Campion for half the airs and by Rosseter for the rest.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Campion

works.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside
works.description: Middleton's comedy of London's sexual economy: the goldsmith Yellowhammer's daughter Moll, betrothed by her parents to the decadent knight Sir Walter Whorehound, loves the poor Touchwood Junior; the city's trades in food, sex, and legitimacy — the Allwits' household, the promoters, the puritans feasting at a christening — fill the play, until Sir Walter's ruin and Moll's mock-death restore the lovers.
works.plot: Sir Walter finances the Allwits and fathers their 'children' while courting Moll; Touchwood Senior's fertility and his brother's love-plot run through the middle acts; the christening feast and the arrest of the gallants expose the city's corruptions; and the final scene, with Moll's pretended death and revival, joins the lovers and topples the knight.
works.significance: The sharpest of the Jacobean city comedies — a play that makes money, sex, and religion a single system of exchange.
works.meter: Prose and verse of Middleton's quickest, cruellest wit, with the christening scene's hypocritical feasting as its summit.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men at the Swan in 1613 and printed in 1630; its satire of the Jacobean marriage market and puritan hypocrisy is the most scathing of the age.
works.characters: Moll Yellowhammer; Touchwood Junior; Touchwood Senior; Sir Walter Whorehound; Yellowhammer; Maudlin Yellowhammer; the Allwits; the Kixes; the promoters; the wench; the puritans
works.structure: A five-act cross-section of Cheapside — multiple households joined by Sir Walter's purse — in Middleton's most populous and corrosive comic design.

editions.title: A Chaste Maid in Cheapside (New Mermaids)

works.title: A Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine of the Sacrament
altTitles: The Defence of the True and Catholike Doctrine of the Sacrament of the Body and Bloud of Our Saviour Christ
works.description: Cranmer's principal theological work, published in 1550, defining the eucharist against both transubstantiation and mere memorialism; the fullest statement of the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament in English.
works.plot: The book argues from scripture and the fathers that Christ is truly but spiritually present in the eucharist, received by faith; it refutes the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (against Stephen Gardiner) and the Zwinglian reduction of the sacrament to a bare sign, distinguishing 'sacramentally' from 'corporally', and it defends the vernacular liturgy and communion in both kinds.
works.significance: The classic English statement of the Reformed eucharist and Cranmer's most sustained piece of theological prose; it fixed the middle course of Anglican sacramental doctrine for centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1550 during Cranmer's ascendancy under Edward VI, in the controversy with Bishop Stephen Gardiner (imprisoned for his opposition); the doctrine of the Defence shaped the communion rite of the 1552 Prayer Book, and Cranmer recanted it under Mary before renouncing his recantations at the stake in 1556.
works.structure: Five books of doctrinal argument with patristic citation, cast as a reply to Gardiner's defence of the corporal presence.

works.title: A Dialogue Concerning Heresies
altTitles: A Dialogue of Sir Thomas More, Knight
works.description: More's first and longest English polemical work against the Lutheran heresy, cast as a four-book dialogue between More and a young 'messenger' sent by a friend who is tempted by the reformers.
works.plot: In Book I More defends the veneration of images, pilgrimages, and miracles; Book II discusses the authority of the Church and the corruption of Tyndale's New Testament translation; Book III refutes Luther's and Tyndale's views on faith and works; Book IV defends the clergy and the burning of heretics, arguing that Luther's doctrine leads to sedition and the destruction of the sacraments.
works.significance: The major English Catholic response to the early Reformation, documenting the doctrinal battle over scripture and tradition, and one of the fullest exhibits of More's prose — combative, witty, and colloquial — outside the Latin works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written 1528–29 after More had read Tyndale's New Testament and his Obedience of a Christian Man; part of the print war between More (with Bishop John Fisher) and the English reformers conducted under Bishop Tunstall's licence to read heretical books.
works.characters: Thomas More (as speaker); The Messenger
works.structure: Four books of continuous dialogue; the anonymous messenger relays objections while More answers at length with authorities, anecdotes, and comic deflation of the reformers.

works.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation
works.description: More's last and greatest English work, written in the Tower of London while awaiting execution, a dialogue in which an elderly Hungarian uncle instructs his nephew on bearing tribulation, especially the fear of death under persecution.
works.plot: Set in Hungary on the eve of a Turkish invasion, the dialogue moves from the general consolation of tribulation, through the temptations of fear, scruple, and despair, to the specific comfort of martyrdom, culminating in the uncle's meditation on the passion of Christ as the pattern of all suffering.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English devotional prose of its age, and one of the great prison writings in the language; its controlled serenity under sentence of death has made it the most widely read of More's English works.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the Tower between More's arrest (April 1534) and execution (6 July 1535), after his refusal of the Oath of Succession; the manuscript was smuggled abroad and first printed in London by Richard Tottel in 1553, under Mary I.
works.characters: Anthony (the uncle); Vincent (the nephew)
works.structure: Three books of dialogue between the aged Anthony and his nephew Vincent, with inset parables and a famous treatment of the temptation to suicide; the fictional frame thinly veils More's own imprisonment.

editions.title: A Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 12)
editions.editor: Louis L. Martz and Frank Manley

works.title: A Jovial Crew
altTitles: A Jovial Crew; or, The Merry Beggars
works.description: Brome's most admired comedy, in which three gentlewomen run away to join a band of strolling beggars, and their idyll of freedom is tested by hunger, lust, and the law before they return home.
works.plot: Rachel, Amy, and the widow Springlove's daughters abandon their comfortable homes for the beggars' life; the beggar community is ruled by the mysterious Patrico, and the experiment ends with marriage and the reintegration of the runaways.
works.significance: Brome's masterpiece and the most substantial dramatic treatment of English beggar life in the period; it is a key text for Caroline social history and for the development of comic realism.
works.meter: Prose dominant, with songs and verses.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1641, just before the theatres closed; the play was popular again after the Restoration and inspired several adaptations, including the ballad opera The Jovial Crew (1731).
works.characters: Rachel; Amy; Meriel; Oldrents; Hilliard; Springlove; Patrico; Randall; Vincent; Martin
works.structure: Five acts, alternating between the gentleman's houses and the beggars' barn, with an unusually detailed portrait of vagrant society.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Letter Concerning Toleration
works.description: Locke's argument for religious toleration, written in Latin in Holland in 1685 and published anonymously in 1689 in William Popple's English translation; it separates the ends of civil government from the care of souls.
works.plot: The magistrate's power extends only to civil interests — life, liberty, health, and property; the care of souls belongs to no one but God, and persecution cannot produce sincere belief; therefore the state must tolerate all religions that do not threaten civil peace.
works.significance: The classic statement of the case for religious toleration and a foundational text of liberal pluralism; three further letters followed in 1690, 1692, and 1704.
works.meter: Clear Latin prose, widely read in Popple's English translation.
works.context: Written in 1685 after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, in correspondence with Philip van Limborch; published in 1689 at Gouda in the same year as the Revolution settlement.
works.structure: A single continuous letter addressed to an unnamed friend.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as Epistola de Tolerantia; the English translation was by William Popple; Locke's authorship was suspected but not acknowledged.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Mad World, My Masters
works.description: Middleton's early city comedy of tricks: the rake Follywit, disguised as a lord and then as a player, gulls his rich grandfather Sir Bounteous Progress; the courtesan Frank Gullman is passed off as a virgin; and the bawdy plot of Penitent Brothel and the Harebrain household runs alongside — the whole a 'mad world' of disguises whose final scene dissolves into the play-within-the-play of The Slip.
works.plot: Follywit robs his grandfather three times over in three disguises; the gullings of the 'virgin' Gullman and the jealousy comedy of Harebrain interweave; the final robbery turns into the play performed before Sir Bounteous, who is robbed as he watches — the trick revealed only in the last lines, when Follywit marries Gullman with his grandfather's blessing.
works.significance: The wittiest of Middleton's early comedies — a laboratory of the trick-plot and the play-within-the-play he would perfect.
works.meter: Prose and verse in Middleton's swift, sardonic mix, with the mock-tragedy of the players as its final parody.
works.context: Performed by the Children of Paul's in 1605 and printed in 1608; its frank bawdry answered the fashion of the private-theatre comedies.
works.characters: Follywit; Sir Bounteous Progress; Frank Gullman; Penitent Brothel; Harebrain; Mistress Harebrain; the Succubus (appearing as Mistress Harebrain); the players
works.structure: A five-act intrigue of triple disguise built on the trick-play device, with the play-within-the-play as its climactic joke on the audience as well as the gull.

editions.title: A Mad World, My Masters (Regents Renaissance Drama)

works.title: A Midsummer Night's Dream
works.description: Shakespeare's fairy comedy of lovers, artisans, and the dream-wood: four Athenian lovers flee into the forest, the fairy king and queen quarrel over an Indian boy, Puck's love-juice scrambles every affection, and the 'rude mechanicals' rehearse the tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe — the whole resolved at dawn into Theseus's wedding feast and the play-within-the-play.
works.plot: Hermia must marry Demetrius or die; she flees with Lysander, pursued by Demetrius and Helena; Oberon's magic makes both men love Helena; Titania, enchanted, dotes on Bottom the weaver in his ass's head; all is set right by dawn, and the mechanicals' catastrophic performance of 'Pyramus and Thisbe' crowns the triple wedding.
works.significance: The most perfect English comedy of the supernatural, and the play through which most of the world first meets Shakespeare.
works.meter: Lyric blank verse for the lovers and fairies, prose for the mechanicals, with the songs and charms of the fairy scenes.
works.context: Probably written for an aristocratic wedding about 1595–96; its 'rude mechanicals' satirize the artisan theatre culture of Elizabethan London.
works.characters: Theseus; Hippolyta; Lysander; Demetrius; Hermia; Helena; Oberon; Titania; Puck (Robin Goodfellow); Nick Bottom; Peter Quince; Francis Flute; Egeus
works.structure: Four interwoven plots — court, lovers, fairies, artisans — braided through the night and united in the final act's play-within-the-play.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: A Mirror for Magistrates
works.description: The great Elizabethan collection of 'complaints', planned by Thomas Sackville and others as a continuation of Lydgate's Fall of Princes: the ghosts of England's fallen rulers and nobles — from Albanact and Cordila to Richard III and the Duke of Buckingham — rise before the poets and tell their tragedies, warning magistrates against ambition, flattery, and misrule; Sackville's own 'Induction' and 'Complaint of Buckingham' crown the 1563 edition.
works.plot: In Sackville's Induction, the poet descends with Sorrow into the underworld and meets the train of the fallen; each ghost then speaks his or her complaint — the causes of the fall anatomized in de casibus form — in poems by Sackville, Baldwin, Ferrers, Churchyard, and others across the successive editions.
works.significance: The great poetic quarry of Elizabethan tragedy — the book Shakespeare, Marlowe, and the chroniclers all mined for their falls of princes.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and varied stanzas, with Sackville's Induction in his stateliest blank verse and rhyme.
works.context: The first edition (1559) was suppressed for its treatment of living magnates; the fuller editions of 1563 and later became the storehouse of plots and moral themes for the Elizabethan history play.
works.characters: Sorrow; the poet; the ghosts of Richard III, the Duke of Buckingham, Jane Shore, Cardinal Wolsey, Lord Hastings, the Black Prince, and many others
works.structure: A frame (the poets meeting to continue Lydgate) enclosing a series of dramatic monologues by the ghosts of the great, in the medieval de casibus tradition revived for Tudor statecraft.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative, planned by Sackville and written chiefly by William Baldwin and George Ferrers, with Sackville's Induction and Buckingham; individual attributions follow the early editions.

editions.title: The Mirror for Magistrates

works.title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts
works.description: Massinger's comedy of the extortioner's fall: Sir Giles Overreach, who has swallowed the estates of his neighbours through mortgage and fraud, plots the marriage of his daughter Margaret to the young Lord Lovell; the conspiracy of the just — Welborne's recovery of his lands, Lady Allworth's pretended favour, and the servants' evidence — brings Overreach to the mad scene in which he is dragged off 'in a frenzy', his schemes destroyed and his daughter married to the man she loves.
works.plot: Welborne, ruined by Overreach, is raised by Lady Allworth's courtesy and wins his lands back through Overreach's own greed; Overreach forces Margaret toward Lovell, who instead promotes her marriage to Allworth; the double exposure — the deeds and the daughter's defiance — breaks the extortioner; and the final scene's madness ('The devil has left his shape') closes the comedy on the ruin of the usurer.
works.significance: The last great comedy of the pre-Civil War stage — and the vehicle of one of the English theatre's most durable villains.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose in Massinger's careful, moral style, with Overreach's mad scene as the great actor's moment it became.
works.context: Written about 1625 and printed in 1633; Overreach was modelled on the notorious extortioner Sir Giles Mompesson; the role became the property of the great actors from the Restoration to the twentieth century.
works.characters: Sir Giles Overreach; Frank Welborne; Margaret Overreach; Tom Allworth; Lady Allworth; Lord Lovell; Justice Greedy; Marrall; Will-do; the parson; the servants
works.structure: A five-act city comedy of the Jonsonian school, built on the double plot of Welborne's restoration and Margaret's marriage, with Overreach's fall as its moral engine.

editions.title: A New Way to Pay Old Debts (New Mermaids)

works.title: A Nocturnal Reverie
works.description: Anne Finch's celebrated night-piece, in which the poet describes the peace and beauty of the natural world by moonlight and the freedom of the imagination in solitude, until daylight and the world's cares return — a poem Wordsworth praised as the finest nature poem between Milton and himself.
works.plot: In a night of perfect calm the speaker contemplates the sleeping landscape, the freedom of the birds and her own fancy, and the liberty of the night, until 'a rude voice' and the approaching day break the spell and recall her to the world.
works.significance: A precursor of Romantic nature poetry, admired by Wordsworth, and one of the finest descriptive lyrics by a woman of the period.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of quiet, sensuous description with a contemplative, almost Romantic tone.
works.context: Composed in the 1680s–90s and circulated in manuscript among Finch's literary circle; published in her Poems on Several Occasions (1713).
works.characters: the poet; nature; Ardelia (her pastoral name)
works.structure: A single meditative blank-verse-couplet reflection on a night scene, framed by the return of day.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Play of Love
works.description: John Heywood's debate interlude on the pains and pleasures of love, printed by William Rastell in 1534; the first English play devoted wholly to the analysis of courtship.
works.plot: A man loved but not loving pleads his case against a man loving but not loved, each claiming the sharper pain; their debate is referred to a woman neither loving nor loved, who judges between them; the argument moves through the paradoxes of desire to a reconciliation in which the four parties pair off, demonstrating that love's pleasures and pains are inseparable.
works.significance: The first sustained dramatic treatment of love in English and the purest example of the debate-interlude form; it links medieval love-casuistry to the Renaissance comedy of courtship.
works.meter: Couplets with stanzaic lyric interludes
works.context: Printed in 1534, the year of the Act of Supremacy; the play belongs to the courtly debate tradition of the early Tudor household, drawing on the amatory casuistry of the medieval demande d'amour and anticipating the love-debates of Elizabethan drama.
works.characters: Lover Not Loved; Loved Not Loving; Neither Lover Nor Loved; Both Lover and Loved
works.structure: A formal disputation in two parts, with the Vice 'Neither-lover-nor-loved' as referee and a concluding judgement that resolves the debate into mutual pairing.

works.title: A Priest to the Temple
works.description: Herbert's prose manual of pastoral practice, written for the guidance of country clergy; in short chapters it describes the parson's character, duties, preaching, catechising, visiting, and conduct, presenting the ideal of the devoted, humble, and practical parish priest.
works.plot: Each chapter ('The Parson's Character', 'The Parson Preaching', 'The Parson in Circuits', etc.) offers practical and spiritual counsel, arguing that the parson must know and love his flock, teach plainly, and sanctify every part of life.
works.significance: A classic of Anglican pastoral literature, valued for its humane wisdom and its influence on Izaak Walton's Life of Herbert and on the ideal of the country parson in English letters.
works.meter: Plain, homely, wise prose with occasional proverbial turns and scriptural allusion.
works.context: Written c. 1632 at Bemerton and circulated in manuscript; published in 1652 as part of Herbert's Remains, it reflects the Laudian and practical devotional ideals of the Caroline church.
works.characters: the country parson; his parishioners
works.structure: A series of short prose chapters forming a complete guide to the pastoral office.

editions.title: The English Poems of George Herbert
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Satire Against Reason and Mankind
altTitles: A Satyr Against Reason and Mankind
works.description: Rochester's most substantial philosophical poem, a libertine dialogue between a satirist who would rather be a dog than a man and a clergyman who defends reason, in which 'right reason' is reduced to the guidance of appetite.
works.plot: The poet attacks the pride and falsity of human reason; the bishop replies in defence of reason as the light of God; the poet answers by distinguishing true reason, which serves the senses, from speculative reason, which is mere fear and fancy.
works.significance: The most intellectually serious poem of Restoration libertinism and a central text for understanding Rochester's rehabilitation in the late twentieth century.
works.meter: Irregular pentameter couplets, colloquial and argumentative.
works.context: Composed c. 1674-5 and circulated in manuscript in the court coterie; Rochester's Hobbesian scepticism answers the Cambridge Platonists and the new natural philosophy.
works.characters: the speaker; the bishop (Thomas Sprat, according to tradition)
works.structure: A dramatic dialogue in two unequal parts, closing with the poet's self-portrait of the man of sense and pleasure.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Rochester in contemporary manuscript witnesses; authorship accepted, though individual lines vary between witnesses.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies, for the Advancement of Their True and Greatest Interest
altTitles: A Serious Proposal to the Ladies
works.description: Mary Astell's feminist treatise proposing a Protestant monastery or religious retirement where women could pursue education and the life of the mind free from marriage and male authority.
works.plot: Part I (1694) argues that women's intellectual inferiority is the product of defective education and proposes a religious community for their instruction; part II (1697) supplies a method for the improvement of women's minds based on Cartesian clear and distinct ideas.
works.significance: The first systematic argument for women's education in English and a founding text of English feminism; its proposal for a female intellectual community anticipates later educational reform.
works.meter: Vigorous, ironic, and rhetorically accomplished prose.
works.context: Part I published anonymously in 1694, part II in 1697; the proposal attracted the attention of Princess Anne of Denmark and provoked the suspicion that Astell was a crypto-Catholic.
works.structure: Two parts, each a continuous argument with a prefatory dedication.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously as 'A Lover of Her Sex'; attribution to Astell is established.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Song for St. Cecilia's Day, 1687
works.description: Dryden's first Cecilia ode, a Neoplatonic hymn tracing the creation of the world through the music of the spheres to the final dissolution of all things by the last trumpet.
works.plot: From discordant atoms, tuned by the voice of God, a harmonious universe arises; the stanzas then praise successive instruments and their passions, ending with the dread trumpet of the Last Judgement.
works.significance: One of the great English odes on music and the predecessor of Alexander's Feast; it became a staple of the choral repertoire through Handel and Purcell settings.
works.meter: A regular stanzaic form in mixed line lengths, with the famous four-beat 'The trumpet's loud clangour' passage.
works.context: Written for the London celebrations of St Cecilia's Day on 22 November 1687 and set to music by Giovanni Battista Draghi.
works.structure: Six stanzas plus a grand chorus, each stanza devoted to a different instrument or affect of music.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: A Summons to Prayer
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
works.description: A short poem calling the faithful to prayer at the ringing of the church bell, celebrating the power of the Lord's Prayer to guard the soul and summoning all creation to join in worship.
works.plot: At the sound of the bell the poet summons the congregation to prayer: the Lord's Prayer is a shield against the devil, and prayer joins earth to heaven; the poem closes by calling on all beings to praise the Lord.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem tied to the actual practice of the daily office, and a small masterpiece of liturgical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line, brief and incantatory, suited to its liturgical occasion.
works.context: The poem belongs to the CCCC 201 group and reflects the Benedictine Reform's emphasis on the daily offices and the sanctification of time through prayer.
works.structure: A liturgical summons organized around the bell, the prayer, and the assembly of creation in praise.

works.title: A Survey of London
works.description: John Stow's loving survey of the capital: London and its liberties described ward by ward, street by street — the walls, gates, churches, schools, markets, conduits, and customs of the city, with its antiquities recovered against the Reformation's destruction and the growth of the Elizabethan metropolis; the foundation of London historiography, enlarged in the 1603 edition.
works.plot: The survey proceeds from the city's Roman origins through the wards of London, then to the suburbs and out-parishes: each church, monument, and custom is given its history, with the old ceremonies and benefactions recorded against oblivion, and the river and its bridges described at the close.
works.significance: The founding text of London historiography — the book every later historian of the city has built upon, and a classic of English antiquarian prose.
works.meter: Prose of plain, affectionate exactness — the walker's and rememberer's style.
works.context: First published 1598 and enlarged in 1603; its record of the pre-Fire city and the pre-Reformation churches is the irreplaceable document of Elizabethan London.
works.characters: the city of London itself; its founders, benefactors, and chroniclers
works.structure: A topographical description organized by ward and place, in the antiquarian manner of Leland and the chroniclers, with Stow's own memory and reading as its sources.

editions.title: A Survey of London, 2 vols.

works.title: A Treatise of Moral Philosophy
altTitles: A Treatise of Morall Phylosophie, Contaynyng the Sayinges of the Wyse
works.description: William Baldwin's popular compilation of moral sayings and exemplary lives of philosophers, first published by Edward Whitchurch in 1547 and enlarged by Thomas Palfreyman; one of the most frequently reprinted English books of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.
works.plot: The book arranges the sayings of the ancient philosophers under topical heads — of God, of wisdom, of justice, of friendship — and follows them with brief lives of the philosophers, ending each section with moral application for Christian readers.
works.significance: The most widely read English wisdom-book of the early modern period and a key channel by which classical moral philosophy reached vernacular readers; it established Baldwin's reputation before his editorship of A Mirror for Magistrates.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled in the 1540s by Baldwin, then a corrector in Edward Whitchurch's printing house, during the flood of popular moral and sententious literature under Edward VI; Palfreyman's enlarged version (1555 onwards) carried it through dozens of editions to 1651.
works.structure: A compendium in four books: sayings of the philosophers, their lives, answers and apophthegms, and parables, with a running apparatus of moralization.

works.title: A View of the Present State of Ireland
altTitles: A View of the Present State of Irelande
works.description: Spenser's prose dialogue on the conquest and reform of Ireland, written from his experience as a New English planter and administrator: two speakers, Irenius and Eudoxus, survey Irish history, customs, law, and religion, and prescribe a programme of military subjection and re-education — including the infamous defence of famine as an instrument of policy.
works.plot: Eudoxus questions Irenius on the causes of Ireland's disorder — the Irish customs of tanistry and gavelkind, the brehon law, the bardic culture, the Old English degeneracy, and the Catholic religion — and Irenius answers each with diagnosis and remedy, ending with the scheme for garrisoning and resettling the country.
works.significance: The most sophisticated Elizabethan statement of the colonial programme in Ireland and a document central to the history of English rule there; it has been read ever since as both policy blueprint and confession.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Written about 1596, at the height of the Nine Years' War, when Spenser held the post of sheriff of Cork; it circulated in manuscript and was not printed until 1633.
works.characters: Irenius; Eudoxus
works.structure: A Socratic dialogue in two parts, framed as a single day's conference, with set-piece historical surveys and prescriptive argument.

editions.title: A View of the State of Ireland

works.title: A Woman Killed with Kindness
works.description: Heywood's domestic tragedy: the Yorkshire gentleman Frankford discovers his wife Anne's adultery with his guest Wendoll; instead of blood, he punishes her by banishment to a distant manor — kindness as execution — where she starves herself to death and dies on the marriage bed in the play's final scene, while the sub-plot of Sir Charles Mountford's imprisonment and Susan's sacrifice runs its parallel course.
works.plot: Frankford's friendship with Wendoll becomes the adulterer's entry; the discovery through the cards, the quiet banishment, and Anne's self-starvation follow; the sub-plot of Sir Charles's debt, his sister's sacrifice to Sir Francis Acton, and the reversal of fortune ends in the double marriage of the close, with Anne's deathbed forgiveness as the tragedy's summit.
works.significance: The masterpiece of English domestic tragedy — the play that brought the marriage bed, not the court, to the centre of the tragic stage.
works.meter: Plain, unadorned blank verse and prose — deliberately domestic, without the Senecan heights of the revenge school.
works.context: Performed by Worcester's Men in 1603 and printed in 1607; it founded the genre of domestic tragedy that runs through Arden of Faversham's earlier example to Lillo, Ibsen, and the modern theatre.
works.characters: Frankford; Anne Frankford; Wendoll; Sir Charles Mountford; Susan Mountford; Sir Francis Acton; Shafton; Nicholas; the servants
works.structure: A two-plot domestic tragedy — the Frankford household and the Mountfords — in Heywood's plain middle style, the first English tragedy of the ordinary marriage.

editions.title: Three Elizabethan Domestic Tragedies

works.title: A Yorkshire Tragedy
works.description: The short anonymous (or Shakespeare-attributed) domestic tragedy of the real Walter Calverley murders of 1605: the gambling squire, his estate devoured by dice, stabs his wife and murders two of his children in their beds — the third wounded — and, taken by his servants, goes to his execution repentant, the play compressing the whole crime into its ten scenes.
works.plot: The Husband's ruin at dice and the Wife's pleas frame the catastrophe; the murders of the children and the wounding of the wife are staged with brutal directness; the servants' arrest and the Husband's repentance before the officers close the play, with the real crime's ballads and pamphlets as its documentary frame.
works.significance: The most compressed of the domestic tragedies — ten scenes of crime and repentance that test the limits of the genre's documentary power.
works.meter: Verse and prose of violent economy — the play's brevity is its instrument of shock.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men about 1608 and printed the same year as 'written by W. Shakespeare' — an attribution now generally rejected, though the question remains open; it was one of four plays in the 1608 quarto whose title page claimed Shakespeare's name.
works.characters: the Husband (Walter Calverley); the Wife; the Master of the College (the Husband's brother); the Knight; the servants; the officers
works.structure: A one-act domestic tragedy in ten scenes, built on the pamphlet accounts of the Calverley murders of 1605.
works.attributionNotes: The 1608 title page names Shakespeare, an attribution now generally rejected by scholarship; the author is unknown.

editions.title: Three Elizabethan Domestic Tragedies

works.title: Abdelazer; or, The Moor's Revenge
works.description: Behn's revenge tragedy of the Moorish prince Abdelazer, who seduces and destroys the Queen of Spain in a series of murders; it reworks Marston's Lust's Dominion and supplied Purcell with the theme of 'The Prince of Denmark's March'.
works.plot: Abdelazer, the Moorish heir deprived of his throne, seduces the Queen, murders the King, and finally falls; the play is a sustained study of ambition and revenge without remorse.
works.significance: The most successful of Behn's tragedies and an important rewriting of the early modern Moor-revenge tradition; it influenced later representations of the Moorish villain.
works.meter: Blank verse with some rhyme.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1677 and published in the same year; a 1695 revival used Purcell's incidental music.
works.characters: Abdelazer; the Queen; the King of Spain; Florella; Osmin; Cardinal; Antonio; Philip
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a rapid succession of murders.

works.title: Absalom and Achitophel
works.description: Dryden's masterpiece of political satire, mapping the Exclusion Crisis onto the biblical story of Absalom's rebellion against David: Monmouth as Absalom, Shaftesbury as Achitophel, Charles II as David, and the Duke of York as the lawful successor.
works.plot: Achitophel seduces the ambitious Absalom into rebellion against his indulgent father David; the poem culminates in David's assertion of divine-right authority and the rout of the Whig opposition.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the greatest political poem in English; it created the model of the allegorical verse satire that Pope would inherit, and its character portraits remain a landmark of satirical psychology.
works.meter: Heroic couplets; the most supple and rhetorically varied use of the closed couplet in seventeenth-century English.
works.context: Published in November 1681 at the height of the Exclusion Crisis, apparently at the king's suggestion, and immediately answered by Settle and Shadwell.
works.characters: David (Charles II); Absalom (James, Duke of Monmouth); Achitophel (Anthony Ashley Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury); Zimri (George Villiers, Duke of Buckingham); Corah (Titus Oates); Israel (the English people)
works.structure: A two-part argumentative narrative: the diagnosis of national faction, then a series of extended character portraits, closing with the king's speech and the restoration of order.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; authorship undisputed, though Dryden claimed the plan was the king's.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Absalom and Achitophel, Part II
works.description: The continuation of Dryden's satire, largely written by Nahum Tate with Dryden supplying the portraits of Achitophel and the closing sections; it attacks Settle and Shadwell as Doeg and Og.
works.plot: The sequel extends the biblical allegory into the trials of the Whig leaders and the vindication of David's government, adding a second book that completes Tate's unfinished first part.
works.significance: Important chiefly for Dryden's contribution, which contains the famous second portrait of Achitophel and the Doeg-Og passage; the whole is far less read than Part I.
works.meter: Heroic couplets.
works.context: Published in November 1682, in the wake of Shaftesbury's flight and the Tory reaction; it answers Shadwell's The Medal of John Bayes.
works.characters: Doeg (Thomas Shadwell); Og (Elkanah Settle); Achitophel (Earl of Shaftesbury); Corah (Titus Oates)
works.structure: Two parts: Tate's first book of about 550 lines and Dryden's second book of about 450 lines.
works.attributionNotes: The 1682 title page names Tate and Dryden; modern scholarship assigns the first book to Tate and the second to Dryden, with Dryden also revising Tate's text.
