works.title: Actes and Monuments
works.description: John Foxe's 'Book of Martyrs': the vast church history and martyrology, first published in English in 1563 and expanded in 1570, tracing the true church from the apostles through Wyclif and the Lollards to the Protestant martyrs of Mary's reign — Cranmer, Latimer, Ridley, and hundreds more — with their examinations and burnings recorded in documentary detail and vivid woodcuts.
works.plot: The work moves from the early church through the medieval persecutions to the Marian burnings; each martyrdom is given its examinations, letters, and death-scene; the 1570 edition's calendar of martyrs and its apparatus made the book a national monument as well as a history.
works.significance: The most influential book of the English Reformation after the Bible itself — the founding text of English Protestant memory.
works.meter: Prose of documentary accumulation, with the set-piece death scenes (Latimer's 'we shall this day light such a candle') as its rhetorical peaks.
works.context: First English edition 1563, expanded 1570; ordered by Convocation to be placed in every cathedral church; its account of the Marian burnings shaped English Protestant identity for three centuries.
works.characters: Thomas Cranmer; Hugh Latimer; Nicholas Ridley; John Wyclif; John Rogers; the Marian martyrs
works.structure: A documentary martyrology in the tradition of Eusebius, organized chronologically by reign, with the records of trials and letters embedded in the narrative.

editions.title: The Acts and Monuments of John Foxe, 8 vols.

works.title: Aeditio
works.description: The elementary Latin grammar composed for St Paul's School, traditionally attributed to John Colet with the collaboration of William Lily and Erasmus; the English 'Accidence' later incorporated into the authorized Lily's Grammar.
works.plot: A short accidence of the eight parts of speech with English rules and Latin examples, designed for beginners at St Paul's, prefaced by Colet's school statutes and the 'Carmen de Moribus'.
works.significance: The germ of the national school grammar and a document of the Erasmian educational reform at its English source, St Paul's School.
works.meter: Prose with Latin verse
works.context: Composed c. 1509–18 for the school Colet founded in 1509 and refounded in 1512 with Mercers' Company endowment; the English Accidence printed as Aeditio in 1527 became the basis of the royal grammar of 1540.
works.structure: Pedagogical manual with rules and paradigms.
works.attributionNotes: The grammar is a collaborative production of the St Paul's circle; the traditional ascription to Colet as founder reflects the school's origin rather than sole authorship, and Erasmus revised the text.

works.title: Aeneid, Books II and IV (Surrey's translation)
works.description: Surrey's translation of Virgil's Aeneid, Books II and IV — the fall of Troy and the tragedy of Dido — in unrhymed iambic pentameter, the first English blank verse. Book IV was printed by John Day in 1554 and both books in Tottel's 1557 edition; the translation fixed the metre that Marlowe and Shakespeare made the language of English drama.
works.plot: Book II: Aeneas recounts Troy's last night — the horse, the burning, Priam's death, the loss of Creusa. Book IV: Dido's passion for Aeneas, their union in the cave, his departure, and her suicide on the pyre.
works.significance: The invention of blank verse, the metre of English tragedy and epic from Marlowe to Milton; alongside Douglas's Scots Eneados, the founding translation of Virgil into English.
works.meter: Blank verse — unrhymed iambic pentameter — used for the first time in English; the line Surrey invented from the Italian versi sciolti and Virgil's hexameter.
works.context: Translated in Surrey's last years, when he stood near the throne; the fall of Troy and the ruin of Dido's court read as parables of Henrician politics.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Priam; Sinon; Anna; Mercury
works.structure: Two books of the epic, chosen for their pathos; the translation follows Virgil book by book without prologue apparatus.

editions.title: The Aeneid of Henry Howard Earl of Surrey

works.title: Aenigmata
works.description: Aldhelm's collection of one hundred Latin riddles in hexameters, enclosed as the final part of the Epistola ad Acircium (addressed to King Aldfrith of Northumbria). The first riddle collection of medieval England and the direct model for the vernacular Exeter Book riddles.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person, obliquely describing its subject — the elements, creatures, household objects, tools of learning — with the last line of each revealing or hinting the solution (water, the wind, the raven, the pen, the alembic, and so on).
works.significance: The model and quarry of the entire insular riddle tradition, Latin and vernacular.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters, technically virtuosic.
works.context: Written c. 686-700 as part of the Epistola ad Acircium, a treatise on Latin metre for King Aldfrith; imitated by Tatwine, Eusebius, and Boniface, and translated into Old English in the Exeter Book tradition.
works.characters: the speaking objects of the riddles
works.structure: A numbered sequence of one hundred enigmas, framed by the prefatory acrostic poem on Aldhelm's own name.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography

works.title: Aenigmata (Hwætberht's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Tatwine
works.description: Forty Latin riddles composed by Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow (c. 716-c. 747) and associate of Bede, in the tradition of Symphosius and Aldhelm. The riddles range over the natural world, the cosmos, and the tools of learning — the sun and moon, the winds, the sea, the alphabet, and the liberal arts.
works.plot: The riddles personify their subjects, from celestial bodies and elemental forces to letters and numbers, each speaking obliquely of its nature and powers; the collection moves from the macrocosm of heaven and earth to the microcosm of human learning.
works.significance: The Northumbrian counterpart to Aldhelm's and Tatwine's riddle cycles, completing the Anglo-Latin riddle corpus that inspired the vernacular riddles of the Exeter Book.
works.meter: Latin hexameters modelled closely on Aldhelm, with his alliteration and ornamental diction; the verse is learned and allusive, written for readers trained in the monastic school.
works.context: Composed at Wearmouth-Jarrow in the age of Bede, when the twin monastery was the richest centre of learning in western Europe; the riddles show Aldhelm's influence carried into Northumbria and the riddle form serving the encyclopedic ambitions of the Northumbrian Renaissance.
works.structure: Forty self-contained hexameter riddles in an encyclopedic sequence, deliberately continuing and answering the tradition of Aldhelm's century of riddles; the arrangement suggests a curriculum of knowledge from cosmology to grammar.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Hwætberht (Eusebius), abbot of Wearmouth-Jarrow, by manuscript tradition.

works.title: Aenigmata (Tatwine's Riddles)
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Royal 12.C.xxiii (tenth century), with the riddles of Hwætberht
works.description: Forty Latin riddles with a verse preface composed by Tatwine, monk of Breedon-on-the-Hill and archbishop of Canterbury (731-734). The riddles treat theological, philosophical, and grammatical subjects — faith, hope, charity, the five senses, the letters of the alphabet, the books of the Bible — in the manner of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.plot: Each riddle speaks in the first person about its own nature, requiring the reader to identify abstractions (the virtues, the liberal arts, grammatical categories) and objects (the pen, the sword, the book) from oblique descriptions built on learning rather than natural history.
works.significance: With Aldhelm's and Hwætberht's collections, Tatwine's riddles define the Anglo-Latin riddle tradition that stands behind the Exeter Book Riddles; they document the teaching of abstract theology through the schoolroom genre.
works.meter: Latin hexameters of schoolmasterly correctness, plainer than Aldhelm's hermeneutic verse; the riddles average six to eight lines and often begin with a paradoxical self-description.
works.context: Composed in the learned milieu of Breedon and Canterbury in the generation after Aldhelm, the riddles show the classroom union of grammar, theology, and verse composition that characterized early Anglo-Latin culture and fed the vernacular riddle tradition.
works.structure: A preface followed by forty self-contained riddles arranged in a deliberate sequence from theological virtues through philosophical abstractions to grammatical and physical subjects; the collection is the earliest complete Latin riddle cycle composed in England.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Tatwine by manuscript tradition and internal evidence; the riddles are contemporary with his Canterbury years or earlier.

works.title: Aglaura
works.description: Sir John Suckling's first and most famous play, a tragicomedy of courtly love and intrigue performed by the King's Men in 1638 and lavishly printed at the author's expense, reflecting the gallant, platonic-love ideals of the Caroline court.
works.plot: The King of Bithynia's court is troubled by the amorous conflicts surrounding the Princess Aglaura, involving love, jealousy, and a plot against the throne, resolved in the tragicomic mode.
works.significance: A characteristic Caroline courtly drama, notable for its production history, its expression of Caroline platonic-love ideals, and its author's social prestige.
works.meter: Blank verse and prose with a gallant, witty, courtly manner.
works.context: Performed and printed in 1638 at Suckling's own great expense, reflecting his wealth and his standing among the Caroline court wits.
works.characters: Aglaura; the King of Bithynia; Ardebert; Orbella
works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy in blank verse and prose, produced in two alternative endings (tragic and comic).

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alcuin's Letters
works.description: The surviving correspondence of Alcuin of York — over 280 letters to kings, bishops, and friends, from Charlemagne and his court to the monks of Lindisfarne and the school of York: the richest epistolary record of the Carolingian Renaissance and of the network that carried Anglo-Saxon learning to the Continent.
works.plot: The letters range from affairs of state and church (the condemnation of adoptionism, the imperial coronation, the Danish raids) to friendship, consolation, and literary patronage; the most famous is the letter of 793 to the community of Lindisfarne after the Viking sack, interpreting the disaster as divine correction and urging repentance.
works.significance: The principal documentary source for the intellectual life of the Carolingian age and its English foundations.
works.meter: Latin prose, with verse epistles among the corpus.
works.context: Written 780-804 from York and the Frankish court; edited by E. Dümmler in MGH Epistolae IV (1895).
works.characters: Charlemagne; Arno of Salzburg; the monks of Lindisfarne; Æthelhard of Canterbury; Eanbald of York
works.structure: A chronologically arranged correspondence of over 280 items.
themes: The public theatre and the players' world
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alexander's Feast; or, The Power of Music
works.description: Dryden's second Cecilia ode, a dramatic narrative of the Greek musician Timotheus singing at Alexander the Great's victory feast and rousing him through pity, love, and finally revenge.
works.plot: Timotheus's song moves Alexander from triumph to tears to drunken fury, so that he burns Persepolis; the poem concludes that a nobler master of harmony — St Cecilia — raised the sacred organ and the divine affections.
works.significance: The culminating English ode of the seventeenth century; Handel's 1736 setting made it internationally famous and it remained a touchstone for poetic theories of versification through the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Irregular Pindaric stanzas; Dryden claimed to have written it in a single night and considered it his best work.
works.context: Written for the Music Society's St Cecilia's Day celebration of 1697 and set by Jeremiah Clarke.
works.characters: Alexander the Great; Timotheus; Thaïs; St Cecilia
works.structure: A continuous dramatic narrative in irregular stanzas, ending with an abrupt change of key in the final chorus.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Alfred's Domboc
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's law book: an introduction translating the Ten Commandments and Mosaic law into English, followed by Alfred's own code and an appendix of Ine's laws. A founding document of the idea of English law as the law of a Christian people, consciously modelled on the Old Testament.
works.plot: The prologue renders Exodus 20-23 — the commandments, the laws of injury, slavery, and property — as the ancient foundation of law; Alfred's own clauses then regulate oaths, treachery against lords, sanctuary, the church, marriage, wounds, theft, and the ordeal, closing with the principle of compensation where no earlier provision exists.
works.significance: The classic statement of Anglo-Saxon kingship as Christian legislation; the foundation text of the later English common law tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued in the later years of Alfred's reign, c. 893; preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173 (with the Chronicle).
works.characters: Alfred (legislator); Moses (prologue)
works.structure: Tripartite: Mosaic introduction, Alfred's code, and the appended code of Ine.
works.attributionNotes: Alfred's authorship of the prologue and code is certain.
movements: Civil War Radicalism: The Levellers and the Diggers
sources: The Cambridge Companion to English Renaissance Drama, 2nd edition

works.title: All for Love; or, The World Well Lost
works.description: Dryden's rewriting of Antony and Cleopatra in blank verse, observing the unities of time, place, and action and confining itself to the last day in Alexandria; it is his own favourite among his plays.
works.plot: After Actium, Antony refuses to fight Octavius again, is drawn into suspicion by Ventidius and Alexas, and Cleopatra feigns death; the lovers die together, and the world is 'well lost' for love.
works.significance: The greatest heroic tragedy of the Restoration and the standard version of the Antony story on the English stage for more than a century; it remains Dryden's most frequently performed play.
works.meter: Blank verse, written, Dryden said, 'in imitation of Shakespeare's style'; the prologue declares it the first play he ever wrote without rhyme.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1677 and published in 1678 with a preface defending the choice of blank verse and the observance of the unities.
works.characters: Marc Antony; Cleopatra; Ventidius; Alexas; Octavia; Serapion; Dolabella; Myris
works.structure: Five acts within the classical unities, with a single place (the temple of Isis at Alexandria) and a single day.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: All Ovid's Elegies
works.description: Marlowe's translation of Ovid's Amores into English heroic couplets — the first complete English version of the Roman love elegies, in which the poet-lover's campaigns in the bedroom, his mistress Corinna, and the whole erotic repertoire of Augustan Rome are rendered with Marlowe's characteristic audacity; the book was condemned and burned by the bishops' ban of 1599.
works.plot: The three books of the Amores move through the lover's slavery to Corinna, the rivalries, quarrels, and reconciliations of the affair, the impotence elegy, and the final renunciation of love elegy for tragedy — each poem an erotic set piece in the Ovidian manner.
works.significance: The first full English Ovid of the Renaissance erotic tradition — the text that made Marlowe's name a byword for atheism and licence, and a model for Donne's elegies.
works.meter: Heroic couplets — Marlowe's chosen form for Ovid's elegiacs — of a frankness that scandalized the authorities.
works.context: Printed surreptitiously in the late 1590s and burned under the Bishops' Ban of 1599 along with the satires of Marston and Hall; all early editions survive only in fragments.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Corinna; the eunuch Bagoas; the bawd Dipsas; Aurora
works.structure: A sequence of some forty-eight elegies in three books, translated in order from the Amores, with Marlowe's ten elegies to a serving-wench translating Ovid with his usual freedom.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Poems and Translations

works.title: All's Well That Ends Well
works.description: Shakespeare's 'problem comedy' from Boccaccio: Helena, the physician's daughter, cures the King of France and claims as her reward the reluctant Bertram, who flees to the wars of Italy — forcing Helena to win him by the bed-trick: taking Diana's place in the dark to fulfil his impossible conditions (his ring and his child), and exposing him at the play's end.
works.plot: Helena heals the King, chooses Bertram, is rejected and abandoned; in Florence she substitutes herself for Diana in Bertram's bed and secures ring and child; the final scene unravels Bertram's lies until Helena appears with both proofs and his conversion is wrung from him.
works.significance: The most disquieting of the comedies — a study of merit against rank, and of a woman's will — that has found its audience only in the modern era.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the exposure of Parolles; the style is spare and riddling, matching the play's moral knot.
works.context: Dated about 1604–05, in the same phase as Measure for Measure; its tone reflects the Jacobean darkening of Shakespeare's comedy.
works.characters: Helena; Bertram; the Countess of Rousillon; the King of France; Parolles; Lafew; Diana; the Widow; the two French lords (the Dumaine brothers)
works.structure: A fairy-tale plot (the healing of the king, the impossible tasks) crossed with the bed-trick of Renaissance novella, framed by the choric commentaries of the Countess, Lafew, and Parolles.

works.title: Alliterative Morte Arthure
works.description: The great alliterative tragedy of King Arthur: some 4,300 lines recounting Arthur's continental conquests, his war against the emperor Lucius, and his fall through Mordred's treason and his own pride, culminating in his dream of Fortune's wheel and his death. A poem of imperial ambition and Christian judgement, preserved in the Thornton manuscript, and a principal source of Malory's Morte Darthur.
works.plot: Arthur, refusing tribute to Rome, leads his army across the Channel, defeats the giant of Mont St Michel, and conquers the emperor Lucius; at the height of his power the dream of Fortune's wheel warns him of the fall to come, and the news of Mordred's rebellion and Guinevere's adultery brings him home to the final battle, where Gawain dies and Arthur, mortally wounded, is buried at Glastonbury.
works.significance: The most powerful Arthurian poem of the alliterative tradition and the classic English statement of Arthur's tragedy; its influence on Malory and on the modern Arthurian revival (Tennyson read it in Malory's shadow) is profound.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line at its most heroic, with formulaic battle diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, blending chronicle history with romance matter and the tragedy of Fortune; preserved in the Thornton manuscript (Lincoln Cathedral MS 91, c. 1440) and used by Malory in his tale of Arthur and Lucius.
works.characters: Arthur; Gawain; Mordred; Guinevere; Lucius; the giant of Mont St Michel; Fortune
works.structure: A two-movement tragedy of rise and fall, with the dream of Fortune as its pivot and the battles as its set-pieces.

works.title: Alms-Giving
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A nine-line homiletic poem urging the giving of alms while one still lives, since after death no gift can avail the soul. It is the briefest complete poem in the Exeter Book.
works.plot: The poet exhorts his audience to clothe the naked and feed the hungry now, in life, because the opportunity ends at death, when the soul must face judgment with only what it has given away.
works.significance: A miniature of the Old English homiletic tradition in verse, showing the poets' capacity for lapidary moral statement.
works.meter: Nine alliterative long lines; compressed formulaic phrasing typical of the Exeter gnomic-homiletic manner.
works.context: Almsgiving was a central obligation of Anglo-Saxon Christianity, legislated in the law codes and urged in the homilies of Ælfric and Wulfstan; the poem distils that teaching into a single memorable exhortation.
works.structure: A single compact exhortation built on the antithesis between the living body's power to give and the corpse's helplessness.

works.title: Amis and Amiloun
works.description: A romance of sworn brotherhood and sacrifice, adapted from the widespread European legend of the two friends: Amis and Amiloun, identical in appearance, exchange places in trial by combat and marriage, and Amis slays his own children to cure his friend's leprosy — before a miraculous restoration rewards their loyalty. One of the most powerful of the Auchinleck romances.
works.plot: The sworn brothers part; Amiloun takes Amis's place in a judicial combat over a false accusation, and later, when Amiloun is struck with leprosy for the deception, Amis learns in a vision that his children's blood will cure him — and the sacrifice, made in secret, is rewarded by the children's resurrection.
works.significance: The classic English treatment of the friendship-and-sacrifice legend, and a favourite test case for the romance's religious and ethical codes.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the Auchinleck manner.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 from an Anglo-Norman source (Ami et Amile), in the East Midlands; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and three later copies.
works.characters: Amis; Amiloun; Belisaunt; the steward (villain); Amiloun's wife
works.structure: A double-plot of symmetrical substitution (combat; wedding-night; sacrifice), resolved by miracle and final reunion.

works.title: Amoretti and Epithalamion
works.description: Spenser's sonnet sequence of eighty-nine sonnets tracing his courtship of Elizabeth Boyle, followed by the great marriage ode Epithalamion, which celebrates their wedding on 11 June 1594 through the hours of the wedding day.
works.plot: The Amoretti move from the lover's unrequited suit and the lady's proud refusals through reconciliation to the secure mutual love of the final sonnets, which lead directly into the wedding song; the Epithalamion summons the muses, the hours, and the guests, and blesses bride and bridegroom through the day and night of the feast.
works.significance: One of the greatest sonnet sequences in the language and, in the Epithalamion, the supreme English wedding poem.
works.meter: The Spenserian sonnet form (abab bcbc cdcd ee) throughout, followed by the long-lined stanzas and refrain of the Epithalamion.
works.context: Written during Spenser's courtship of his second wife Elizabeth Boyle at Kilcolman, Ireland, and printed together in 1595, the year after the marriage.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Elizabeth Boyle (the beloved); the assembled wedding guests
works.structure: A Petrarchan sequence with a calendrical design (the sonnets allude to Lent and Easter of 1594) climaxing in the 24-stanza Epithalamion, which is built on the canonical hours and the refrain of the echoing woods.

works.title: An Account of the Growth of Popery and Arbitrary Government in England
altTitles: An Account of the Growth of Popery
works.description: Marvell's anonymous political tract (late 1677/early 1678) warning that a design was afoot to establish both popery and arbitrary monarchy in England by dissolving Parliament and using a standing army; a foundational text of Whig resistance theory on the eve of the Exclusion Crisis.
works.plot: Marvell argues that the prorogation of Parliament and the court's policies reveal a plan to subvert English liberties, religion, and law, and that the people must resist arbitrary power.
works.significance: An important document of Restoration political radicalism and Whig ideology, attributed to Marvell and central to understanding his later politics.
works.meter: Vigorous, urgent argumentative prose of political polemic.
works.context: Published just before the Popish Plot (1678) and during the Exclusion Crisis, it expressed the emerging Whig critique of the court of Charles II and the Catholic succession.
works.structure: A political pamphlet of sustained argument and warning, published anonymously.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; attribution to Marvell is long-established and accepted.

editions.title: The Poems of Andrew Marvell
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Answer unto Sir Thomas More's Dialogue
altTitles: An Answere unto Sir Thomas Mores Dialoge
works.description: Tyndale's reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies, published in 1531; the central exchange of the great English print war between the two men.
works.plot: The book answers More point by point: Tyndale defends his translation of the New Testament against More's charges of corruption, argues that the church is the congregation of believers known by scripture, not the pope's institution, denies that he teaches rebellion, and attacks More's church of ceremonies with the full battery of scriptural citation, closing with a devastating personal address to 'Master More'.
works.significance: One half of the greatest controversy in early English prose: the Tyndale–More exchange fixed the rhetorical terms of the Reformation debate, and the Answer remains the fullest statement of Tyndale's ecclesiology and translation theory.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1531 as the direct reply to More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies (1529); More answered with the Confutation of Tyndale's Answer (1532–33), completing the most sustained intellectual duel of the English Reformation, conducted from exile and the chancellorship respectively.
works.structure: A point-by-point refutation following the order of More's Dialogue, in Tyndale's plain and urgent prose; the first major English controversy conducted wholly in print.

works.title: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
works.description: Locke's founding work of modern empiricism, an enquiry into the origin, certainty, and extent of human knowledge, which rejects innate ideas and argues that all thought derives from sensation and reflection.
works.plot: Book I refutes innate ideas; book II sets out the theory of simple and complex ideas derived from sensation and reflection; book III treats the philosophy of language and the abuse of words; book IV defines knowledge and probability and examines the grounds of belief.
works.significance: The founding text of British empiricism and of the Enlightenment theory of mind; it shaped Berkeley, Hume, and Kant, and its influence on eighteenth-century literature, psychology, and educational theory was pervasive.
works.meter: A clear, deliberate, sometimes conversational prose; Locke's plain style was consciously opposed to scholastic Latinism.
works.context: Begun in 1671 in discussion with friends including James Tyrrell, completed during Locke's exile in Holland, and published in December 1689 (dated 1690) after the Revolution.
works.structure: Four books in a systematic argument of 71 chapters.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay of Dramatic Poesy
works.description: Dryden's foundational work of English dramatic criticism, a dialogue among four friends on a barge during the Second Dutch War in which the merits of the ancients and moderns, and of the French and English stages, are debated.
works.plot: Crites defends the ancients; Eugenius defends the moderns; Lisideius argues for French regularity; Neander (Dryden's spokesman) defends the English drama's variety and life, arguing that rhyme may be natural to serious plays.
works.significance: The first major work of English literary criticism and the text that established Dryden as the father of English criticism; its comparative method and generous assessment of Shakespeare were decisive for the later canon.
works.meter: Elegant argumentative prose, one of the earliest examples of a distinctively modern English critical prose style.
works.context: Composed during 1666-8 and dedicated to Charles Howard, Earl of Dorset; it responds to the neoclassical controversy ignited by Corneille and the Académie française.
works.characters: Crites; Eugenius; Lisideius; Neander
works.structure: A four-part dialogue with an opening narrative frame.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden; the speaker Neander is Dryden's anagrammatic self-portrait.

The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Essay towards a Real Character and a Philosophical Language
altTitles: An Essay towards a Real Character
works.description: Wilkins's ambitious scheme for a universal philosophical language in which the characters would correspond directly to the things and ideas they signify, with a full classification of knowledge as its foundation.
works.plot: Wilkins proposes a 'real character' — a written symbol system independent of any natural language — and a taxonomic arrangement of all ideas into genera and species, so that the language would itself be a philosophy.
works.significance: The most elaborate of the seventeenth-century universal-language projects and a landmark in the history of taxonomy, semiotics, and information science; it influenced Leibniz and later classification systems.
works.meter: Systematic technical prose with extensive tables.
works.context: Published in 1668 for the Royal Society, of which Wilkins was a founding fellow and first secretary; it belongs to the seventeenth-century quest for a universal language.
works.structure: Four parts: the design of the character, the philosophical tables, the grammar, and a vocabulary.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: An Exhortation to Christian Living
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (eleventh century)
works.description: A homiletic poem of ninety-two lines urging its audience to keep God's commandments, resist the devil, and live in readiness for death and judgment. The poem is direct, urgent, and practical in its moral teaching.
works.plot: The poet exhorts the faithful to love God, keep his commands, avoid sin and the devil's snares, and remember the brevity of life and the certainty of judgment; wealth and pleasure are fleeting, but the soul's fate is eternal.
works.significance: A representative of the reform movement's verse catechesis, showing the homiletic mode of late Old English poetry at its most direct.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic formulas of late Old English preaching; the verse is plain and expository rather than ornamental.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English group of CCCC 201 (with Judgement Day II, A Summons to Prayer, and the Menologium), texts associated with the Benedictine Reform's devotional and catechetical programme.
works.structure: A sequence of direct exhortations in the second person, each grounded in the antithesis between this world's brevity and the soul's eternity, closing with the promise of heavenly reward.

works.title: An Horatian Ode upon Cromwell's Return from Ireland
works.description: Marvell's famous and much-debated ode on Oliver Cromwell's return from the Irish campaign in 1650, balancing admiration for Cromwell's irresistible, almost elemental force with a poignant lament for the executed Charles I — a masterpiece of political ambiguity.
works.plot: The ode urges the poet to leave the Muses and sing of Cromwell's active power, describes his campaign and the regicide (with the memorable image of Charles at the scaffold 'as the Royal Actor born'), and looks to Cromwell's future conquests.
works.significance: One of the greatest political poems in English, admired for its balance, its compression, and its capacity to hold conflicting judgments about power and legitimacy.
works.meter: A regular Horatian quatrain (alternating four- and three-stress lines) of restrained, balanced power.
works.context: Written in 1650, in the crisis after Cromwell's Irish campaign and before Dunbar; circulated in manuscript and published only in the 1681 Miscellaneous Poems, its political sympathies have been argued ever since.
works.characters: Oliver Cromwell; Charles I; the poet
works.structure: A Horatian ode in quatrains moving from the call to celebrate to the account of Cromwell's rise, the king's death, and the prospect of further conquest.

works.title: Ancrene Wisse
works.form: rule and devotional treatise in prose
works.description: A rule of life for three anchoresses, written in the West Midlands 'AB language' c. 1225–40: eight parts treating the devotional routine, the custody of the senses, temptation, confession, penance, love, and the inner life. It is the greatest prose work of early Middle English, celebrated for its psychological acuity, its homely and exact imagery, and its humane severity.
works.plot: Addressing the anchoresses as a loving director, the author regulates their prayers and reading, anatomizes the temptations of the solitary life (with the famous allegory of the royal wooing of the soul), teaches the art of confession, and unfolds the degrees of love culminating in union with Christ.
works.significance: The masterpiece of early Middle English prose and the supreme English contribution to the literature of the solitary life; its influence reaches the Cloud-author and beyond.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose of great art; concrete domestic metaphor (the anchorhold as house, the heart as its lady).
works.context: Written in Herefordshire or the Welsh Marches for three sisters enclosed near a church, in the milieu that produced the Katherine Group; revised and translated into French and Latin, and copied into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: the three anchoresses (addressees); Christ as lover-king (allegorical)
works.structure: Eight books moving from outer rule (devotions, senses) to inner rule (heart, conscience) and love; interlaced with exemplary tales and allegories.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; authorship_status reflects scholarly consensus (the author is sometimes speculatively identified with a Dominican or Augustinian director).

editions.title: Ancrene Wisse: A Corrected Edition of the Text in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 402

works.title: Andreas
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 1,722 lines on the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Matthias: the apostle Andrew, sailing incognito with Christ himself as his helmsman, voyages to the cannibal city of Mermedonia to rescue his fellow apostle Matthew. The poem recasts the apostle as a heroic seafarer in the manner of Beowulf, with some of the corpus's most vivid voyage imagery.
works.plot: Christ, disguised as a ship's captain, ferries the reluctant Andrew over the stormy sea, hearing his preaching on the way; in Mermedonia, Andrew is seized, tortured, and imprisoned, but a flood released from a stone pillar drowns his tormentors and revives them, converting the city; Andrew establishes a church and departs, leaving the poem's didactic epilogue.
works.significance: The fullest Old English saint's life in verse and a celebrated example of the heroic adaptation of hagiography.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in the classical heroic manner.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 29v-52v); based on a Latin version of the apocryphal Acts, itself known in Old English prose from the Blickling manuscript.
works.characters: Andrew; Christ (the helmsman); Matthew; the Mermedonians
works.structure: A sea-voyage frame enclosing the martyrdom-and-conversion narrative, with speeches, miracles, and a flood scene modelled on Exodus; the poem borrows formulaic lines directly from Beowulf.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Beowulf borrowings are stylistic, not evidence of authorship.
themes: Female authorship and the woman writer

works.title: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis
altTitles: The Satire of the Three Estates
works.description: Lindsay's great morality drama of the Scottish Reformation: King Humanitie, seduced by Sensualitie and the vices, is recalled to virtue by Divine Correction, and summons a parliament of the three estates — Spirituality, Temporalitie, Merchant — where John the Common-Weill indicts the church's abuses and the vices are tried and hanged. Played at Linlithgow in 1540 and enlarged at Cupar in 1552.
works.plot: Rex Humanitas falls under the rule of Wantonness, Placebo, and Solace; Divine Correction reforms him; the estates meet in parliament, hear John the Common-Weill's complaint, and pass the acts of reform, the play closing with the sermon of Folly.
works.significance: The greatest Scottish play and the dramatic summa of the northern Reformation; its parliament scene made drama an instrument of national reform and remained a living text into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Scots couplets of great stage energy; songs, interludes, and the sermon of Folly closing the action.
works.context: First played before James V at Linlithgow in 1540; the enlarged Cupar performance (1552) addressed the eve of the Scottish Reformation, and the play remained in performance for a century.
works.characters: Rex Humanitas; Divine Correction; Sensualitie; Flatterie; Falset; Dissait; John the Common-Weill; Spirituality; Temporalitie; Merchant
works.structure: A two-part morality expanded to a national parliament: the king's moral fall and recovery (Part I) and the public trial and reformation of the estates (Part II).

editions.title: Sir David Lindsay: Ane Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis

works.title: Annus Mirabilis
altTitles: Annus Mirabilis: The Year of Wonders 1666
works.description: Dryden's long historical poem on the two disasters of 1666 — the Second Anglo-Dutch War and the Great Fire of London — written from Charlton in Wiltshire, offering the nation an optimistic, providential reading of catastrophe.
works.plot: The poem narrates the naval victories over the Dutch, then the Fire, and concludes with a prophecy of London's rebirth as a greater commercial empire under Charles II.
works.significance: The major English public poem of the 1660s; it demonstrates Dryden's ability to turn current events into national myth and anticipates the scientific imagery of his later verse.
works.meter: Quatrains (alternately rhymed iambic pentameter, ABAB), deliberately chosen over couplets to imitate the stateliness of history writing.
works.context: Composed while Dryden was absent from plague-stricken London; dedicated to the City of London in the year of the Great Fire, and closely engaged with the Royal Society's new empiricism.
works.structure: A two-part public narrative (war, fire) framed by dedication and prophetic conclusion, with episodic set-pieces for individual battles.

works.title: Antonius
authors: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
works.description: Mary Sidney Herbert's translation of Robert Garnier's Senecan tragedy Marc-Antoine (1578), the first English version of a French classical tragedy: a closet drama in which Mark Antony, after Actium, debates his ruin with his friends and Cleopatra, and falls on his sword.
works.plot: Antony, defeated and despairing, rejects the counsel of his followers, is reproached and forgiven by Cleopatra, and kills himself; the play closes with the chorus's meditation on Fortune and with Cleopatra's grief and resolve.
works.significance: The bridge by which French neoclassical tragedy entered English, and the first English tragedy of Cleopatra.
works.meter: Blank verse with rhyming choruses, matching Garnier's French alexandrines with English iambic pentameter.
works.context: Published in 1592, amid the English vogue for Senecan tragedy and the Pembroke circle's literary patronage; it anticipated the Antony plays of Shakespeare and Daniel.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Charmian; Philostratus; Lucilius; the Chorus of Egyptians
works.structure: Five acts of Senecan structure with choruses, designed for reading rather than performance.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by Mary Sidney Herbert from Robert Garnier's Marc-Antoine (1578); uncontested.

editions.title: The Collected Works of Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
editions.editor: Margaret P. Hannay, Michael G. Brennan, and Mary Ellen Lamb (eds.)

works.title: Antony and Cleopatra
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of empire and desire: the ageing Antony, caught between Rome and Egypt, duty and Cleopatra, loses the world at Actium and, hearing the false report of her death, falls on his sword; Cleopatra, refusing Octavius's triumph, dies by the asp, and the play ends with the lovers' deaths transfigured into myth.
works.plot: Antony's dalliance in Alexandria draws him back to Rome and the marriage to Octavia; the breach with Caesar sends him back to Cleopatra; the sea-fight at Actium is lost when she flies and he follows; his rage, her feigned death, his botched suicide, and her staged one complete the tragedy — 'I am fire and air' — with Caesar left to bury them side by side.
works.significance: The greatest English poem of erotic grandeur — the tragedy in which the lovers outgrow tragedy itself.
works.meter: A hyperbolic, sensuous verse of superlatives — Enobarbus's barge speech its summit — with the prose of Egypt's court as the foil to Roman plainness.
works.context: Written about 1606–07 from North's Plutarch, whose phrasing Shakespeare follows at the barge and the death scenes; the play's imperial themes shadow the Jacobean debate over empire and union.
works.characters: Mark Antony; Cleopatra; Octavius Caesar; Enobarbus; Octavia; Charmian; Iras; Lepidus; Pompey; Alexas; Eros; Dolabella; the Clown
works.structure: A tragedy of scenes, not acts — forty-two rapid movements between Rome and Alexandria — in which the lovers' deaths are deliberately drawn out across the final acts as ceremony and apotheosis.

editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

works.title: Apollonius of Tyre
works.form: prose romance in Old English prose
works.description: The Old English prose translation of the Historia Apollonii regis Tyri — the story of the shipwrecked prince Apollonius, his lost wife and daughter, and their final reunion: the first prose romance in English and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Pericles and of the Apollonius tradition that runs through Gower and the Middle Ages.
works.plot: Apollonius of Tyre, having solved the riddle of the incestuous king Antiochus, flees by sea; shipwrecked at Pentapolis, he wins the king's daughter in marriage; at sea their daughter is born and the queen, apparently dead, is cast overboard in a sealed coffin; the daughter, raised at Mytilene, is sold to a brothel-keeper but preserves her honour by her wisdom; the story ends in the great recognition scene, when the family is reunited at Ephesus and Mytilene.
works.significance: The first English prose romance; the bridge between the classical romance tradition and the Middle English romances and Shakespeare's Pericles.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated c. 1000-1050 from the Latin Historia Apollonii (a late antique romance); the unique manuscript is Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201, which also contains Wulfstan's homilies.
works.characters: Apollonius; Antiochus; Arcestrates of Pentapolis; the queen; the daughter (Thasia); Athenagoras of Mytilene
works.structure: A continuous romance narrative of adventure, loss, and recognition, in the incest-riddle frame of the Latin source.

editions.title: The Old English Apollonius of Tyre

sources: The Cambridge Companion to English Literature, 1650–1740

works.title: Arcadia
works.description: Sidney's prose romance written for his sister Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke: the 'Old Arcadia' (c. 1577–80, complete in five books or acts) is a tragicomic tale of two princes in disguise among the shepherds of Arcadia; the unfinished 'New Arcadia' (c. 1584–86) reworks the first books into a heroic romance of chivalric adventure; the composite edition of 1593 joined the revised books to the old ending.
works.plot: Princes Musidorus and Pyrocles, in love with the princesses Pamela and Philoclea, disguise themselves as a shepherd and an Amazon to gain access to the secluded royal household; their courtships, the rebellion of the commons, the trial of the princes for the supposed death of King Basilius, and the oracles that haunt the plot drive the action of the Old Arcadia, while the New Arcadia expands it with the wars of the rebel Amphialus and the captivity episodes.
works.significance: The most influential prose fiction of the English Renaissance — the model for a century of romances and the direct ancestor of Wroth's Urania and of Shakespeare's borrowed plots.
works.meter: Prose of elaborate periodic balance, with verse eclogues in many stanza forms at the act divisions.
works.context: Written in retirement at Wilton after Sidney's withdrawal from court (1579) and revised in the mid-1580s; printed after his death in 1590 and, with his sister's composite arrangement, in 1593.
works.characters: Pyrocles; Musidorus; Philoclea; Pamela; Basilius, King of Arcadia; Gynecia; Euarchus; Amphialus; the shepherds Dorus and Strephon
works.structure: An interlaced romance in prose with verse eclogues between the books, deliberately organized by Sidney into 'five acts' on the model of drama.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the 1593 composite text was assembled by Mary Sidney Herbert.

editions.title: The New Arcadia

works.title: Arden of Faversham
altTitles: The Lamentable and True Tragedy of Master Arden of Faversham
works.description: The anonymous domestic tragedy of the real murder of Thomas Arden of Faversham in 1551: his wife Alice and her lover Mosby hire a succession of bungling assassins — Black Will and Shakebag among them — whose attempts fail comically until the murder is done in Arden's own house; the killers are caught, and the play ends with the executions and Alice's burning, 'the sin of murder' its homiletic close.
works.plot: Alice's adultery and Arden's blindness to it set the plot; the hired murders fail through fog, chance, and cowardice; the final ambush in the parlour succeeds; the discovery of the body, the flight of the murderers, and the punishment of all — including Alice, who dies 'bewailed' only by her guilt — complete the tragedy's documentary arc.
works.significance: The founding text of English domestic tragedy — the first play to make an English household and an English murder the matter of tragedy.
works.meter: A plain, powerful verse (and prose) of the provincial scene — the play's very anonymity has invited attribution to Shakespeare, Kyd, and others.
works.context: Printed in 1592 and performed by the Admiral's Men; based on the notorious Faversham murder of 1551 as told in Holinshed; it is the first English play of a real, recent, and domestic crime.
works.characters: Thomas Arden; Alice Arden; Mosby; Black Will; Shakebag; Greene; Michael; Franklin; the Mayor of Faversham; Susan; Clarke the painter
works.structure: A five-act tragedy built directly on Holinshed's account of the real 1551 murder, with the comic failures of the assassins as its counterpoint to the horror.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributions to Kyd, Shakespeare, and others have been proposed but none is proven.

editions.title: Arden of Faversham (Revels Plays)

works.title: Areopagitica
altTitles: Areopagitica: A Speech of Mr. John Milton for the Liberty of Unlicenc'd Printing
works.description: Milton's prose speech to Parliament (24 November 1644) against the Licensing Order of 1643, arguing that prior censorship of books destroys learning, virtue, and truth, and that a free people must be trusted to choose good over evil — the classic English defence of freedom of the press.
works.plot: Milton traces the history of licensing from the Inquisition, argues that books contain the 'life-blood of a master spirit', distinguishes the testing of virtue from its seclusion, and contends that truth will prevail in a free and open encounter.
works.significance: One of the foundational texts of the argument for free speech and a free press, still quoted in constitutional and press-freedom debates, and a masterpiece of English prose.
works.meter: Eloquent, Latinate prose with a powerful oratorical rhythm and dense classical allusion.
works.context: Published during the Civil War against Parliament's 1643 licensing order; it drew on Milton's own experience of unlicensed publication and the collapse of censorship.
works.structure: A classical oration in prose, modeled on Isocrates's Areopagiticus, moving through historical example, argument, and eloquent peroration.

works.title: As You Like It
works.description: Shakespeare's pastoral comedy, adapted from Thomas Lodge's Rosalynde: Duke Senior, exiled to the Forest of Arden, is joined by his daughter Rosalind (disguised as the boy Ganymede), her cousin Celia, the clown Touchstone, and eventually the melancholy Jaques and the reformed usurper — while Orlando's love-verses to Rosalind hang on every tree.
works.plot: Orlando, robbed of his birthright, flees to Arden; Rosalind, banished, tutors him in love while disguised as Ganymede; the usurping Duke is converted on the forest's edge; and the play ends with four weddings and the god Hymen's masque, followed by Rosalind's epilogue.
works.significance: The definitive English pastoral comedy and the vehicle of Shakespeare's greatest comic heroine.
works.meter: Alternating prose and blank verse — Rosalind's prose wit against Orlando's verses — with the songs 'Under the greenwood tree' and 'It was a lover and his lass'.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of the Globe's opening, from Lodge's Rosalynde (1590); the forest reimagines the Ardennes through Warwickshire memory.
works.characters: Rosalind; Orlando; Celia; Touchstone; Jaques; Duke Senior; Duke Frederick; Oliver; Adam; Silvius; Phebe; Audrey; William; Corin; Charles the wrestler
works.structure: A movement from court to forest and back, built on the contrast of the two worlds and on the play's chain of love-dialogues, with the 'Seven Ages of Man' speech and the songs of Amiens as set pieces.

works.title: Astraea Redux
altTitles: Astraea Redux: A Poem on the Happy Restoration & Return of His Sacred Majesty Charles the Second
works.description: Dryden's first public poem, celebrating the Restoration of Charles II in May 1660 and announcing the young poet's allegiance to the returning monarchy; it recasts the civil wars as a national illness now cured by the king's return.
works.plot: The poem traces the disorder of the Interregnum, praises General Monck's role, and celebrates Charles II as the providential healer of the nation, drawing on biblical and classical typology.
works.significance: Established Dryden's public reputation and set the tone for the political panegyric of the Restoration; a benchmark for his later development.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in closed iambic pentameter, with occasional alexandrines; one of the earliest displays of Dryden's mature couplet.
works.context: Written within weeks of Charles II's landing at Dover on 25 May 1660 and published in the same year.
works.structure: A panegyric in three movements: the diagnosis of national disorder, the mechanism of restoration, and the prophetic blessing on the new reign.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dryden on the title page of the 1660 quarto; authorship undisputed.

works.title: Astrophel and Stella
works.description: The first great English sonnet sequence: 108 sonnets and eleven songs tracing the love of Astrophel (the star-lover) for Stella (the star) — widely read as Sidney's love for Penelope Devereux, Lady Rich — from first sight through desire, frustration, and the lady's marriage to another, to the renunciation of the last sonnets.
works.plot: Astrophel falls in love with Stella at first sight; he pleads, she rebuffs; she marries Lord Rich; the poems anatomize every phase of the love — reason versus desire, sleep and dreams, the stolen kiss, jealousy, absence — until the final sonnets turn from the vain suit.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue: Spenser, Daniel, Drayton, and Shakespeare all wrote in its wake.
works.meter: The English (Shakespearean-type) sonnet form of Sidney's own stamp — abab abab cdcd ee — with hexameter final lines in several sonnets.
works.context: Composed about 1581–82 in the circle of the Earl of Oxford's and Sidney's London; printed posthumously in 1591 by Thomas Newman in an unauthorized edition, which launched the vogue of the sonnet sequence.
works.characters: Astrophel; Stella; Lord Rich (alluded to); Cupid; Reason; Virtue
works.structure: A sequence with a genuine plot — courtship, crisis, renunciation — varied by the eleven songs inserted at points of dramatic action.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the biographical reading as Sidney and Penelope Devereux is a later interpretation, not a fact in the text.

works.title: Athelston
works.description: A dark romance of kingship and treason, unique in the canon: the king Athelston, swayed by the traitor Wymond, puts his sworn brother and his family to the ordeal of fire, and is saved from tyranny only by the intervention of the archbishop and the test of the fire itself. Its grim political realism makes it unlike any other English romance.
works.plot: Four messengers become sworn brothers; Athelston becomes king, and the envious Wymond persuades him that Earl Egeland plots treason; Athelston's violence against the earl's pregnant wife and children is halted when the archbishop curses him and the ordeal of fire acquits the innocent, exposing Wymond and restoring the fellowship.
works.significance: The most politically serious of the English romances — a study of tyranny, sanctuary, and the ordeal — and a favourite text for the romance's engagement with law and kingship.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas, often grimly emphatic.
works.context: Composed c. 1355–80 in the East Midlands, drawing on the legend of St Edmund and on baronial and ecclesiastical politics; preserved uniquely in Cambridge, Gonville and Caius College, MS 175.
works.characters: Athelston; Wymond; Egeland; Edyff; the archbishop
works.structure: A compact tragedy of misrule in three movements (oath, slander, ordeal), with the archbishop's excommunication as its pivot.

works.title: Aureng-zebe; or, The Great Mogul
works.description: Dryden's heroic play on the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb's succession struggle, notable for its more restrained hero and for Dryden's prefatory doubt about the value of rhyme.
works.plot: The aged emperor Shah Abbas is suspected of loving his son Aureng-zebe's mistress Indamora; the prince's constancy and filial duty survive a rebellion by his brother Morat, and order is restored.
works.significance: The last of Dryden's heroic plays and the point at which he turned away from rhyme toward blank verse in All for Love; it marks the end of the heroic drama's ascendancy.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets, with a looser and more conversational movement than in The Conquest of Granada.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676, dedicated to the Earl of Mulgrave; the prologue's complaint about 'the dull duties of a poet's trade' reflects Dryden's growing disenchantment with rhyme.
works.characters: Aureng-zebe; Indamora; Shah Abbas; Morat; Nourmahal; Arban; Benducar
works.structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single main action and a rival brother subplot.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
