works.title: Croxton Play of the Sacrament
works.description: An East Anglian miracle play of c. 1461 on the host: the Jewish merchant Jonathas and his fellows buy the consecrated wafer from the Christian merchant Aristorius, subject it to their tests — and when they stab it, it bleeds, and the image of Christ appears, converting them all. Its staging directions (the cauldron, the severed hand, the miraculous oven) make it the most spectacular of the English miracle plays.
works.plot: Aristorius, tempted by gold, sells the host to Jonathas, who with his companions proves it in their own body of tests: boiling, oven, and dagger; the host bleeds, sticks to Jonathas's hand, and the image of Christ as a child reproves them; their conversion follows, the church is reconciled, and the play ends with the doctor's epilogue and the procession.
works.significance: The fullest English miracle play and the most spectacular document of the late medieval eucharistic cult; its staging is central to the history of English theatre.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, with stage directions prescribing spectacular effects.
works.context: Composed c. 1461 at Croxton, Norfolk (the banns name the village), when the cult of the host and the Corpus Christi confraternities flourished; its treatment of Jews reflects the period's anti-Judaism, and its conversion plot the theology of eucharistic miracle; preserved in Trinity College, Dublin, MS F.4.20.
works.characters: Jonathas; Aristorius the merchant; the priest Isoder; the Jews Jason, Jasdon, Masphat, Malchus; the Bishop; the Image of Christ
works.structure: A two-part miracle (the bargain and the testing; the miracle and conversion), framed by the banns and the closing sermon.

editions.title: Non-Cycle Plays and Fragments

works.title: Cursor Mundi
works.description: A vast northern verse history of the world, some 24,000 lines, 'running' (cursor) through sacred history from Creation to Doomsday: Old Testament narrative, the life of Christ, the Virgin, the apostles, and the finding of the cross. The most comprehensive biblical paraphrase in Middle English, designed to rival secular romance in the affections of its audience.
works.plot: The poem retells the Old and New Testament story in chronological sequence — Creation, the patriarchs, Christ's life and Passion, the early church — with moralizations and legends (including the harrowing of hell) woven into the biblical narrative.
works.significance: The largest Middle English biblical poem and the principal popular scriptural compendium before the Wycliffite Bible; a major witness to lay biblical culture.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets (with some septenary sections) in the northern dialect.
works.context: Composed c. 1300 in the north of England (Durham or Yorkshire), in the tradition of the Historia Scholastica and vernacular biblical paraphrase; preserved in nine manuscripts, with a southern version made c. 1400.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the patriarchs, apostles, and saints
works.structure: A seven-part chronicle following the ages of the world, with prologue and epilogue framing the narrative as a book for 'lewed' men.

works.title: Cygnea Cantio
works.description: Leland's Latin poem in praise of the Thames, in which a swan sings as it glides down the river from Oxford to London, celebrating the towns, palaces, and worthies along its banks; published with a long commentary by the author in 1545.
works.plot: The swan's song follows the Thames from its source past Oxford, Windsor, and Hampton Court to Westminster and London, praising each place and the Tudor dynasty; the commentary supplies the antiquarian and topographical learning that the verse compresses.
works.significance: The earliest sustained literary celebration of the Thames and the model for the river-poems of Spenser (the Thames–Medway marriage) and Denham's Cooper's Hill; a key monument of Tudor antiquarian humanism.
works.meter: Latin hexameters
works.context: Published 1545 during Leland's final productive years, as part of his programme of celebrating the antiquities of Britain in Latin verse (the unpublished Genethliacon and the unfinished De uiris illustribus).
works.characters: The Swan (speaker)
works.structure: A single long Latin poem with Leland's own prose commentary, a form modelled on the Renaissance edition of a classical text.

works.title: Cymbeline
works.description: Shakespeare's romance of ancient Britain: Imogen, married secretly to the low-born Posthumus, is slandered by the villain Iachimo's wager; banished and betrayed, she flees in disguise as the boy Fidele to Wales, where her lost brothers live in the cave of Belarius; the Roman war, the dream of Jupiter, and the final scene's cascade of recognitions restore the family and the kingdom.
works.plot: Iachimo hides in Imogen's trunk to 'prove' her infidelity; Posthumus orders her death; Pisanio spares her and she flees; the potion's mock-death, the cave, and Cloten's pursuit lead to the war with Rome; Posthumus fights for Britain in disguise; and the last scene unravels every knot — brothers, husband, father, and the tribute of peace.
works.significance: The most experimental of the romances — a laboratory of plot whose final scene outdoes all its rivals in the theatre of recognition.
works.meter: A late style of extreme compression and ellipsis, with the dirge 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' and the vision of Jupiter as its lyric heights.
works.context: Written about 1609–10 from Holinshed's British matter and Boccaccio; its peace with Rome mirrors James I's pacific foreign policy.
works.characters: Imogen (Fidele); Posthumus Leonatus; Cymbeline; the Queen; Cloten; Iachimo; Pisanio; Belarius; Guiderius; Arviragus; Caius Lucius; Jupiter (in the apparition)
works.structure: A romance of three worlds — court, Wales, Rome — braided into the single great recognition scene of Act 5, with the wager-plot from Boccaccio at its centre.

works.title: Cædmon's Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: margins of eighth-century manuscripts of Bede
works.description: A nine-line praise poem to God the Creator, composed, according to Bede's Historia ecclesiastica (IV.24), by the illiterate cowherd Cædmon after a dream in which he was commanded to sing of the beginning of created things. It is the earliest datable poem in Old English.
works.plot: The poem praises the heavenly Father, the measurer of fate, who established the beginning of every wonder: first he created heaven as a roof for the children of men, then the middle-earth, the guardian of mankind made the earth for men. (This is the traditional five-line paraphrase; the text runs to nine lines with epithets varying by version.)
works.significance: The earliest surviving English poem and the foundation of the English religious poetic tradition.
works.meter: Nine lines of alliterative accentual metre, with formulaic epithets ('heofonrices weard', 'moncynnes weard').
works.context: Composed c. 657–680 at Whitby under Abbess Hild; Bede gives a Latin paraphrase and says the vernacular text was preserved; it survives in Old English in the margins and endleaves of some twenty-one manuscripts of the Historia, the earliest (the 'Moore Bede') datable to 737.
works.characters: God the Creator
works.structure: A single doxological period: address, epithets of God, and the two works of creation (heaven, earth).
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Cædmon on Bede's authority; the extant Old English texts are translations back from oral memory of the original, which Bede knew only in paraphrase.

editions.title: The Anglo-Saxon Minor Poems (Anglo-Saxon Poetic Records, vol. VI)

sources: A Book of Middle English, 4th edition

works.title: Dame Sirith
altTitles: The Interlude of the Clerk and the Girl
works.description: The earliest English fabliau: a comic tale of 450 lines in which the clerk Wilekin, failing to seduce Margery, buys the services of the old bawd Dame Sirith, whose trick with a weeping dog convinces Margery to yield. The poem may have been designed for performance by one or two speakers.
works.plot: The lovesick clerk Wilekin woos Margery without success; Dame Sirith, hired for a fee, persuades Margery that her weeping bitch is a transformed woman punished for refusing a clerk — and Margery consents rather than share that fate.
works.significance: The first English fabliau and a landmark in the history of English comedy and secular drama; the bawd-and-trickster plot anticipates Chaucer's fabliaux.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets with dialogue assignable to speakers (semi-dramatic form).
works.context: Composed c. 1275 in the East Midlands; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 86 (c. 1300).
works.characters: Wilekin the clerk; Margery; Dame Sirith
works.structure: A short fabliau of courtship, trickery, and capitulation, largely in dialogue, with explicit staging cues.

works.title: Daniel
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 764 lines on the book of Daniel, from the Junius manuscript: the three youths in Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace, the king's dream of the tree and his madness, and the fall of Babylon to the Medes and Persians under the writing on the wall — with the liturgical Canticles of the three youths (the 'Azarias' material) expanded into songs of praise.
works.plot: The poem follows Daniel and his companions at the Babylonian court; Nebuchadnezzar's idol and the furnace; the king's dream of the great tree, interpreted by Daniel as his own pride and coming fall; his seven years of bestial madness and restoration; Belshazzar's feast, the writing on the wall, and the city's fall to Cyrus. The youths' prayers and songs in the furnace (the Canticum trium puerorum) are rendered as extended lyric passages.
works.significance: A sustained meditation on pride and the fall of kings, central to the Junius manuscript's providential scheme.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the canticle passages show a more ornate, lyrical style.
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11); related to the Exeter Book poem Azarias, which preserves a version of the first canticle.
works.characters: Daniel; Nebuchadnezzar; Belshazzar; Azarias, Ananias, and Misael (the three youths); Cyrus
works.structure: Episodic biblical narrative punctuated by lyric set-pieces (the canticles), with an admonitory frame on pride and the fall of kings.
themes: The New Science and experimental philosophy

works.title: Davideis
altTitles: Davideis: A Sacred Poem of the Troubles of David
works.description: Abraham Cowley's unfinished biblical epic in four books (in Poems, 1656), retelling the persecution of David by Saul in heroic couplets, with a preface defending the modern epic and arguing for a Christian verse built on rhyme rather than Milton's blank verse.
works.plot: The poem narrates David's flight and troubles under Saul's jealous pursuit, drawing on the books of Samuel, with digressions and a prefatory argument on epic theory and the state of English poetry.
works.significance: An influential, if unfinished, attempt at a modern Christian epic, important for its couplet form and its theory of epic, and as a foil to Milton's practice.
works.meter: Closed heroic couplets, which Cowley advocated against rhymeless verse in his preface.
works.context: Published in 1656 during the Interregnum; its preface engages the debate about epic form and the future of English poetry that Milton would answer with Paradise Lost's blank verse.
works.characters: David; Saul; Jonathan
works.structure: A heroic epic in rhymed couplets (four books of a planned twelve), with a critical preface on epic conventions.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: De Cive
altTitles: Philosophical Rudiments Concerning Government and Society
works.description: Hobbes's first published statement of his political theory, the third part of his philosophical system, which argues from the state of nature to the necessity of an absolute sovereign and was published in Latin in Paris in 1642.
works.plot: In three parts — Libertas (the state of nature), Imperium (the establishment of government), and Religio (the kingdom of God) — Hobbes derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the natural right of self-preservation.
works.significance: The prototype of Leviathan and the first full modern statement of social contract theory; its influence on seventeenth-century political thought was immediate and enormous.
works.meter: Latin philosophical prose; translated into English as Philosophical Rudiments in 1651.
works.context: Published at Paris in April 1642, on the eve of the English civil wars, which Hobbes said determined his subject; expanded edition 1647.
works.structure: Eighteen chapters in three sections.

editions.title: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts
editions.publisher: Clarendon Press (Clarendon Edition of the Works of Thomas Hobbes)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: De Civili Dominio
works.description: John Wyclif's most explosive treatise (1375–76), expounding his doctrine of dominion: lordship is founded on grace, so that the sinful clergy — the pope included — forfeit their right to temporal possessions, and kings may and must strip the church of its wealth. The book that made Wyclif the theorist of disendowment and the target of papal condemnation.
works.plot: Wyclif argues that all dominion derives from God and is held only by the righteous; the reprobate hold possessions unjustly; the clergy's endowment was conditional on their holiness and may be revoked by lay lords; and the English king, as God's vicar in his realm, is bound to reform and disendow the delinquent church.
works.significance: The theoretical charter of Lollardy's attack on ecclesiastical wealth and the most consequential political theology written in medieval England.
works.meter: Latin prose in the Oxford scholastic manner, relentlessly syllogistic.
works.context: Composed at Oxford and Lutterworth in 1375–76, when the papal-imperial politics of the Great Schism's prelude and the English crown's anti-papal statutes (Provisors, Praemunire) gave Wyclif's theories immediate political force; nineteen propositions from it were condemned by Gregory XI in 1377.
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Three books of scholastic argument, from the metaphysics of dominion through its application to the church to the duties of the king.

works.title: De Emendata Structura Latini Sermonis
altTitles: On the Correct Structure of Latin Prose
works.description: Thomas Linacre's treatise on Latin syntax, published in London by Richard Pynson in 1524; the first systematic Latin grammar composed by an Englishman and a landmark of the humanist reform of grammar.
works.plot: The work analyses Latin construction in six books, replacing the medieval speculative grammars with a descriptive account of syntax based on the usage of Cicero and the best classical authors, illustrated with abundant quotations.
works.significance: A founding document of English classical scholarship; its descriptive method influenced the whole European tradition of Latin grammar, and it secured Linacre's European reputation among humanists.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Linacre, physician to Henry VIII and the foremost English Greek scholar of his generation, composed the work over 1512–24 after his return from Italy; it was printed by Pynson and used in the schools alongside the authorized grammar.
works.structure: Six books of systematic grammatical exposition with a preface to Prince Arthur's tutor and a dedication to the grammar-school masters.

works.title: De excidio et conquestu Britanniae
altTitles: On the Ruin and Conquest of Britain
works.description: Gildas's jeremiad against the sins of the British kings and clergy, opening with the only near-contemporary narrative of the Saxon settlement of Britain, including the battle of Mount Badon. The principal source for post-Roman Britain and the foundation of the providential reading of British history that Bede adopted.
works.plot: Part I narrates the Roman occupation, the coming of the proud Saxons as mercenaries, their revolt, and the British resistance culminating in Ambrosius Aurelianus and the victory at Mount Badon. Parts II and III denounce the five tyrant kings (Constantine, Aurelius Caninus, Vortipor, Cuneglas, and Maglocunus) and the corrupt British clergy in the manner of the Old Testament prophets.
works.significance: The indispensable (if tendentious) source for the adventus Saxonum and for the moral theology of national disaster.
works.meter: Rhetorical Latin prose saturated with biblical allusion.
works.context: Composed in Britain, traditionally c. 540s, a generation after Mount Badon; the earliest surviving extended insular text after the Roman period.
works.characters: Ambrosius Aurelianus; the five tyrant kings; the Saxon mercenaries
works.structure: A tripartite sermon-polemic: historical prologue, royal denunciations, clerical denunciations — history entirely subordinated to moral exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Gildas's authorship is traditional and generally accepted; the dating rests on inference.
sources: English Literature in the Sixteenth Century, Excluding Drama

works.title: De Nugis Curialium
works.description: Walter Map's miscellany of court gossip, satire, Welsh legend, ghost story, and moral anecdote, assembled piecemeal during his service at the court of Henry II; 'a jest book and a jest at the same time', as one editor put it, and the only certain work by one of the wittiest Latin writers of the age.
works.summary: Five distinctiones gather tales of the court of Henry II, satirical portraits of monks and courtiers, the legend of Sadius and Galo, the story of the Welsh king Herla and the fairy bride, and the earliest surviving connected account of the birth of Lancelot; Map's dissuasio to his friend Ruffinus against marriage closes the work.
works.significance: A unique window onto the oral culture and court life of Henry II's England, an early witness to Arthurian material, and a masterpiece of twelfth-century Latin satire and narrative.

works.title: De temporum ratione
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin
works.description: Bede's treatise on time and its reckoning, the standard medieval textbook of computus: the calculation of Easter, the solar and lunar cycles, the ages of the world, and — decisively — the practice of dating years from the Incarnation of Christ (annus Domini), which the work made universal in western Europe.
works.plot: The treatise proceeds from the smallest units of time (moments, hours, days) through the calendar, the lunar cycles, and the Easter tables to the great divisions of world history — the six ages of the world and the seventh age of rest — closing with a chronicle of the world's six ages down to 725.
works.significance: The most influential computistical work of the Middle Ages; the origin of the BC/AD dating convention in general use.
works.meter: Latin prose.
works.context: Composed at Jarrow in 725 for the monks' instruction; a revision and expansion of Bede's earlier De temporibus (703).
works.characters: none
works.structure: A systematic didactic treatise in 71 chapters, concluding with the world chronicle (chapter 66) as the practical demonstration of its chronology.
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume II: 1042–1189

works.title: De virginitate (prose and verse)
works.form: didactic treatise in Latin prose and hexameter verse
works.description: Aldhelm's double treatise in praise of virginity, composed in both prose and verse: a celebration of chastity sustained by a vast catalogue of exemplars — biblical heroes, virgin martyrs, and ascetics — in the ornate 'hermeneutic' Latin that made Aldhelm the model of insular style.
works.plot: The prose treatise (addressed to the nuns of Barking, headed by Hildelith) argues the superiority of virginity over marriage and the other states of life, adducing the patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, and virgins as witnesses; the accompanying Carmen de virginitate recasts the argument in hexameters with a culminating allegorical battle of the vices and virtues.
works.significance: The founding text of the Anglo-Latin literary tradition and of its characteristic learned style.
works.meter: Ornate hermeneutic Latin prose; the Carmen is in dactylic hexameters.
works.context: Composed for the double monastery of Barking, probably c. 675-705; the prose was praised by Bede and widely imitated.
works.characters: Hildelith and the nuns of Barking (addressees); the exemplars: Elijah, Daniel, the Maccabees, Agnes, Cecilia, and others
works.structure: A thematic treatise built from scriptural and hagiographical exempla, concluded by the allegorical psychomachia of the verse version.
themes: Women's experience and the feminine voice
movements: English Petrarchism and the Sonnet Vogue
sources: TEAMS Middle English Texts Series

works.title: Defensio Pro Populo Anglicano
works.description: Milton's Latin defence of the English Commonwealth and the regicide, answering the Defensio Regia of Claudius Salmasius; written for a European audience in his capacity as Latin Secretary, it vindicates popular sovereignty and the English people against royalist propaganda abroad.
works.plot: Milton refutes Salmasius's defence of monarchy and attack on the regicide point by point, arguing that kings are accountable to the people, that tyrants may be judged, and that the English republic is lawful and honourable.
works.significance: The most important Latin political work of the English Revolution, defending republicanism to the continent and establishing Milton's international reputation as a political thinker.
works.meter: Eloquent, erudite Latin prose with powerful oratorical and satirical force.
works.context: Commissioned by the Council of State in 1650 and published in 1651; Milton's exertion on it (while already losing his sight) is said to have hastened his total blindness, and it earned him European fame.
works.structure: A learned Latin polemic of sustained argument, structured as a rebuttal of Salmasius's treatise.

editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Delia
works.description: Samuel Daniel's sonnet sequence of fifty sonnets to Delia, with the appended complaint 'The Complaint of Rosamond' (1592): a polished, plaintive sequence in which the lover vows constancy against time and the lady's coldness, and finds his best weapon in the immortalizing power of verse.
works.plot: The lover serves Delia through her disdain, argues with time and death, warns her that her beauty will fade unless his verse preserves it, and closes with the complaint of Rosamond — Henry II's mistress telling her ghost-story of seduction and murder by poison.
works.significance: The purest Elizabethan expression of the sonnet convention; Shakespeare borrowed from its phrasing, and its complaint of Rosamond founded the female-voiced 'mirror' complaints of the 1590s.
works.meter: The English sonnet form, handled with Daniel's characteristic smoothness and grave music.
works.context: Printed in 1592, in the first flush of the sonnet vogue after Astrophel and Stella; Delia's name glances at Sidney's Stella and at the 'Delia' of Tibullus.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Delia; Rosamond (in the Complaint); Henry II (in the Complaint)
works.structure: A sequence of fifty sonnets framed as a lover's diary, followed by the narrative complaint of Rosamond in rhyme royal.

editions.title: Samuel Daniel: Poems and A Defence of Ryme

works.title: Deor
works.description: A poem of 42 lines spoken by a displaced court poet, Deor, who consoles himself with a catalogue of legendary woes — Weland's captivity, Beadohild's pregnancy, Mæðhild's grief, Theodoric's exile, Eormanric's tyranny — each closed by the refrain 'Þæs ofereode, þisses swa mæg' ('That passed over, so may this').
works.plot: Deor, supplanted in his lord's favour by a rival scop named Heorrenda, lists the legendary sorrows that came to an end and applies the refrain to his own case, ending with a brief, ambiguous self-identification as the once-favoured poet of the Heodenings.
works.significance: A rare glimpse of the court poet's self-consciousness and of the consolation-structure that underlies the Old English elegies.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre with a six-part strophic structure marked by the refrain.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book; its allusions are the earliest English witnesses to the legends of Weland the smith and Eormanric the Goth.
works.characters: Deor (speaker); Weland; Beadohild; Mæðhild; Theodoric; Eormanric; Heorrenda
works.structure: Five legendary exempla framed by the refrain, followed by the poet's personal application; the refrain is the earliest in English poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the speaker's name is part of the fiction.
sources: Anglo-Saxon Poetry

works.title: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions
works.description: Donne's prose-and-prayer record of the near-fatal 'spotted fever' he suffered in December 1623, while Dean of St Paul's: twenty-three 'devotions', each in three parts — a Meditation on his sickness and the soul's, an Expostulation with God, and a Prayer — including the seventeenth, whose Meditation contains the most famous passage of his prose: 'No man is an island... for whom the bell tolls'.
works.plot: The book follows the stages of the illness — its first seizure, the physicians' consultations, the crisis, the convalescence — each stage becoming an emblem of the soul's disease and God's physic, from the opening meditation on man's miserable condition to the closing prayer of thankfulness.
works.significance: The classic of English devotional prose, whose 'No man is an island' meditation and 'for whom the bell tolls' have passed into the common language of mortality.
works.meter: Prose of the pulpit raised to art — the long periodic sentences, antitheses, and paradoxes of Donne's sermons compressed into the private page.
works.context: Written after the illness of late 1623 and published early in 1624; its great theme — sickness as the soul's education — belongs to Donne's last decade as Dean of St Paul's and the great plague years of Jacobean London.
works.characters: the sick man (Donne); God; the Physicians; the bell
works.structure: Twenty-three numbered devotions in strict tripartite form (Meditation, Expostulation, Prayer), each anchored to a moment of the illness — the tolling bell of the seventeenth marking the imagined death and burial.

editions.title: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions

works.title: Dido, Queen of Carthage
works.description: Marlowe's earliest surviving play, written with Thomas Nashe, from Virgil's Aeneid: Aeneas, shipwrecked at Carthage, tells Dido the tale of Troy's fall; she loves him, he is commanded away by Jove, and her suicide on the pyre ends the play — a tragedy of love's rhetoric and the gods' indifference, performed by the Children of the Chapel.
works.plot: Venus disguises herself to guide Aeneas ashore; the courtship in the cave, the rivalry with Iarbas, and the recital of Priam's fall fill the middle acts; the false Ascanius (Cupid) kindles Dido's passion; the gods recall Aeneas; and Dido, abandoned, mounts the pyre with his gifts and dies cursing him.
works.significance: The seed of English classical tragedy — Marlowe's and Nashe's schoolroom Virgil become a stage poem of love and abandonment.
works.meter: Blank verse of a chamber-music delicacy suited to the children's company, with the speeches of Dido's grief as its lyric summit.
works.context: Probably written at Cambridge in the mid-1580s and revised for the Children of the Chapel; printed in 1594 with both names on the title page.
works.characters: Dido; Aeneas; Anna; Iarbas; Achates; Venus; Juno; Jupiter; Cupid (as Ascanius); the Nurse
works.structure: A five-act tragedy for boy players, structured on the Virgilian books I–IV, with the great set piece of Aeneas's narration of Troy at its centre.
works.attributionNotes: Title page assigns the play to Marlowe and Nashe jointly; the division of scenes is uncertain.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: Digby Mary Magdalene
altTitles: The Digby Play of Mary Magdalene
works.description: The most ambitious of the English saints' plays (c. 1480–1500, 2,139 lines): the life of Mary Magdalene from her worldly grandeur and conversion through her apostolate in Marseilles to her thirty years as a desert hermit fed by angels. Its multiple locations, ship voyages, and spectacular effects make it the fullest surviving English drama of a female saint.
works.plot: Mary, the proud lady of Magdalene castle, falls into lechery; Christ's grace converts her, and after the Passion she sails to Marseilles, converts the king and queen, raises the queen from death, and converts the pagan priest; retiring to the wilderness, she is fed by angels, receives the last rites, and her soul is borne to heaven.
works.significance: The fullest English female saint's play and the most elaborately staged of the East Anglian dramas; its conversion and travel plot is a summit of the miracle play tradition.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, with macaronic Latin in the liturgical scenes.
works.context: Composed c. 1480–1500 in East Anglia, in the flourishing of the Mary Magdalene cult; preserved in Bodleian Library, Digby MS 133 (c. 1512), with The Conversion of St Paul and the morality Wisdom.
works.characters: Mary Magdalene; Christ; the King and Queen of Marseilles; the pagan priest; the angels; the devils
works.structure: A multi-location saint's play in the continental manner, moving between Jerusalem, Marseilles, and the wilderness, with ships, temple, and heaven's scaffolds.

editions.title: The Late Medieval Religious Plays of Bodleian MSS Digby 133 and E Museo 160
editions.editor: Donald C. Baker, John L. Murphy, and Louis B. Hall Jr (eds.)

works.title: Dives and Pauper
works.description: An anonymous prose treatise of c. 1405–10 in dialogue form on the Ten Commandments, in which the rich man Dives asks and the poor man Pauper answers — a vast compendium of moral theology, canon law, and social commentary, notable for its defence of poverty, its discussion of images and tithes, and its sympathy with reformist positions short of heresy. The great popular summa of fifteenth-century English orthodoxy.
works.plot: Dives, the wealthy layman, poses the hard questions of Christian practice — the worship of images, oaths, tithes, usury, the duties of the rich to the poor — and Pauper, the poor and learned clerk, answers each with doctrine, law, and exemplum, through all ten commandments.
works.significance: The most comprehensive vernacular treatment of the Decalogue in medieval England and a central witness to the social teaching of the late medieval church on wealth, poverty, and images.
works.meter: Plain, copious prose with Latin quotations translated for the lay reader.
works.context: Composed c. 1405–10, in the aftermath of Arundel's Constitutions (1409), by a learned clerk conversant with both orthodox and reformist positions; printed by Pynson (1493) and read into the Reformation.
works.characters: Dives; Pauper
works.structure: A sustained catechetical dialogue in ten commandments, with the social argument between rich and poor as its dramatic engine.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; a Franciscan authorship has been conjectured.

works.title: Doctor Faustus
altTitles: The Tragical History of the Life and Death of Doctor Faustus
works.description: Marlowe's tragedy of the scholar who sells his soul: Wittenberg's Faustus, sated with all knowledge, signs away his soul to Lucifer for twenty-four years of Mephistopheles' service — and spends them on empty marvels, pageants of the seven deadly sins, and the phantom Helen, whose kiss is the play's summit ('the face that launched a thousand ships') — until the last hour's soliloquy and the devils' claim.
works.plot: Faustus conjures Mephistopheles, signs the bond in blood, and debates theology with the demon; the good and evil angels contend for him through the middle acts of farce and magic; his repentance is always deferred — 'I'll burn my books' never said in time — and the midnight soliloquy ends with the Scholars finding his 'mangled limbs'.
works.significance: The founding myth of modern damnation drama — the play that gave Goethe, and the world, the figure of Faust.
works.meter: The mighty line at its most lyrical — the apostrophe to Helen and the final soliloquy are the touchstones of Elizabethan blank verse.
works.context: Based on the German Faustbuch in its English translation (c. 1592); the play exists in two texts (the A-text of 1604 and the expanded B-text of 1616), and its conjuring scenes were blamed for real devils in the audience.
works.characters: Doctor Faustus; Mephistopheles; Wagner; Lucifer; the Good Angel; the Evil Angel; the Old Man; Valdes; Cornelius; the Horse-Courser; Robin; Rafe; Helen of Troy; the Scholars
works.structure: A morality play inverted: the psychomachy of the angels, the pageant of sins, and the Old Man's pleas all fail against the irreversible bond, in a structure whose comic middle scenes are partly the work of collaborators.
works.attributionNotes: Marlowe's authorship of the core is uncontested; the comic scenes include the hand of collaborators (probably Samuel Rowley and William Bird).

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: Don Sebastian, King of Portugal
works.description: Dryden's last great tragedy, written after the Revolution of 1688, on the Portuguese king captured at Alcazarquivir, his enslavement in Morocco, and the discovery that the woman he loves is his own daughter.
works.plot: Don Sebastian, presumed dead, is enslaved to the Mufti Moluch; he loves Almeyda, who is revealed as his sister's daughter and thus his own child; both renounce the world and retire to a monastery and a convent.
works.significance: Dryden's most complex late tragedy and a veiled meditation on fallen kingship and the legitimacy of allegiance; the character Dorax, a Portuguese renegade, is his finest creation after Almanzor.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in December 1689 and published in 1690, after James II's flight and Dryden's loss of the laureateship for refusing the oaths to William and Mary.
works.characters: Don Sebastian; Almeyda; Muley Moluch; Dorax; Benducar; the Mufti; Johayma; Antonio
works.structure: Five acts combining a love tragedy with a political intrigue, ending in the tragic recognition of incest.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Du Bartas His Divine Weeks and Works
works.description: Joshua Sylvester's translation of Guillaume de Saluste du Bartas's biblical epic La Sepmaine: the creation of the world in the 'Divine Weeks', with the vast encyclopedic digressions on natural history, astronomy, and the wonders of the creation — published piecemeal from 1592 and complete in 1608, the most widely read religious poem of its generation after the Bible.
works.plot: The first Week narrates the seven days of creation with their cosmic and natural digressions; the second Week (incomplete in du Bartas) follows the history of the world from Eden toward the redemption; Sylvester's translation renders the whole with a copiousness and inventiveness that made the poem a schoolbook.
works.significance: The sacred epic of the English Renaissance — a formative book of the young Milton and the chief English poem of creation before Paradise Lost.
works.meter: Rhymed verse of extraordinary lexical invention — Sylvester's coinages and compounds feeding the word-hoard of the next generation.
works.context: Published in parts from 1592, complete in 1608; du Bartas's poem answered the Huguenot wars with cosmic piety, and Sylvester's version made it the English Protestants' epic, read by the young Milton.
works.characters: God the Creator; Adam; Eve; the patriarchs; the personified Creation
works.structure: The 'Weeks' of the hexameral tradition — creation and history in epic form, with the translator's dedications and apparatus.

editions.title: The Complete Works of Joshuah Sylvester, 2 vols.

works.title: Eastward Ho
works.description: The city comedy of 1605 by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston: the goldsmith's virtuous apprentice Golding prospers while the prodigal Quicksilver and the usurer Security speculate their way toward Virginia; Quicksilver's voyage ends in shipwreck on the Isle of Dogs and the counter, and the play ends with the prodigal's repentance — though not before its satire of the Scots landed the authors in prison.
works.plot: Touchstone the goldsmith divides his world between the good apprentice and the bad; Quicksilver drinks, cheats, and embarks for Virginia; the storms, the shipwreck, and the counter follow; Golding marries Touchstone's daughter and prospers; and the final scene distributes justice, mercy, and the play's famous verdicts on London's vices.
works.significance: The great satire of Jacobean London's money-madness and colonial fever — a collaboration of the age's three sharpest pens.
works.meter: Prose and blank verse in the collaborative mix, with Quicksilver's repentant ballad in the counter as its remembered set piece.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels in 1605; its gibes at the new Scots courtiers offended James I, and Chapman and Jonson were imprisoned for it — Marston escaping arrest — the most famous censorship case of the Jacobean stage.
works.characters: Touchstone; Golding; Quicksilver; Security; Mistress Touchstone; Gertrude; Mildred; Sir Petronel Flash; Winifred; Sindefy; the Captain; the Scrivener
works.structure: A five-act city comedy on the Jonsonian model, with the Virginia voyage as its satirical engine and the last act's trial-and-pardon as its resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly by Chapman, Jonson, and Marston, as stated in the stationers' records; the division of scenes is partly conjectural.

editions.title: Eastward Ho (New Mermaids)

works.title: Edward II
altTitles: The Troublesome Reign and Lamentable Death of Edward the Second
works.description: Marlowe's history play of a king undone by favouritism: Edward's dotage on Gaveston and then on the Spensers alienates his queen Isabella and the barons; rebellion, deposition, and the murder at Berkeley Castle follow — the famous stage direction of Lightborn's red-hot spit — in the first great English tragedy of state and private passion.
works.plot: Edward recalls Gaveston from exile; the barons capture and kill him; the king's grief turns to the Spensers and to revenge on Lancaster and Warwick; Isabella and Mortimer invade, the favourites fall, and Edward is deposed, imprisoned, and murdered by Lightborn, while the play ends with young Edward III's execution of Mortimer and the lament over his father's bier.
works.significance: The first fully achieved English history tragedy of psychology and state, and the direct model for Shakespeare's second tetralogy.
works.meter: A blank verse newly capable of the political and the intimate — the abdication scene and the prison soliloquy are its heights — which taught Shakespeare the form of Richard II.
works.context: Written about 1592 from Holinshed; printed 1594; its deposition scenes and its treatment of favouritism and sodomy made it the riskiest of the chronicle plays.
works.characters: King Edward II; Gaveston; Queen Isabella; Mortimer the younger; the Earl of Lancaster; the Earl of Warwick; the Spensers (father and son); Edmund of Woodstock, Earl of Kent; Lightborn; Prince Edward (Edward III)
works.structure: A chronicle tragedy of rise, fall, and retribution in the de casibus pattern, notable for the equal weight given to the king's grief and the barons' politics.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: Ego Dormio
altTitles: Ego Dormio et Cor Meum Vigilat
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle on the three degrees of love, written c. 1340 for a nun of Yedingham (or a recluse of his circle): a lyrical meditation, interspersed with the lyric 'My king that water grette', on the ascent from the love of God's creatures through the love of Christ's humanity to the highest love, which he describes as 'wonderful' — the experience he had felt at Hampole.
works.plot: Taking its text from the Song of Songs ('I sleep and my heart wakes'), the epistle teaches the recipient the three degrees of love — insuperable, inseparable, singular — describes Rolle's own experience of heavenly song, and closes with the Passion meditation and the lyric of Christ's weeping for man's sin.
works.significance: The classic statement of Rolle's three degrees of love and a key text of the early English mystical epistles.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose with the lyric 'My king' in rhymed stanzas.
works.context: Composed c. 1340 in Yorkshire, among Rolle's earliest English writings, for the guidance of a woman religious; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the other English epistles.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); the nun of Yedingham (addressee)
works.structure: A single epistle in three movements, with the inset lyric as its devotional climax.

works.title: Eikonoklastes
altTitles: Eikonoklastes: In Answer to a Book Intitl'd Eikon Basilike
works.description: Milton's point-by-point rebuttal of the Eikon Basilike, the hugely popular devotional memoir attributed to the martyred Charles I; as 'the image-breaker' (eikonoklastes), Milton dismantles the royalist cult of the king's suffering and exposes the book's political purposes.
works.plot: Following the chapters of the Eikon Basilike, Milton answers each pious self-portrait of the king with argument, scriptural counter-example, and political critique, denying Charles the status of martyr and the book its authority.
works.significance: A central text of the Eikon Basilike controversy and of Civil War print propaganda, important for understanding the battle over Charles I's image and the culture of polemic.
works.meter: Sustained, ironic, and forceful argumentative prose.
works.context: Commissioned by the Commonwealth in 1649 to counter the immense popularity of the Eikon Basilike; it forms part of Milton's official defence of the regicide alongside The Tenure.
works.structure: A chapter-by-chapter refutation in prose, mirroring and dismantling the structure of the royalist book it answers.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under Milton's name by order of the Council of State.

editions.title: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Elegies
works.description: Donne's love elegies, modelled on Ovid's Amores: some twenty poems in which the speaker moves through the bedrooms, streets, and jealous households of an erotic London — 'The Perfume', 'The Anagram', 'To His Mistress Going to Bed', 'The Change' — with a frankness and irony that scandalized and defined the genre in English.
works.plot: The elegies dramatize an erotic career: seduction, jealousy, constancy debated, the farewell, the anatomy of love's changes — each poem an argumentative scene in the Ovidian manner, from the perfumed lover detected to the mistress commanded 'License my roving hands'.
works.significance: The most powerful English answer to Ovid's Amores and the seedbed of the Restoration's libertine couplet.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of colloquial force — Ovid's couplet crossed with the speech of the Inns of Court — with enjambment and parenthesis as the instruments of wit.
works.context: Written in the 1590s, the decade of the English Ovidian vogue and of the 1599 ban that burned Marlowe's and Marston's elegiac verse; Donne's elegies circulated in manuscript and were printed in 1633.
works.characters: the poet-lover; the mistresses; the rival; the husband; the father (in 'The Perfume')
works.structure: A group of poems in the classical elegy form, not a sequence, gathered posthumously; individual poems circulated widely in manuscript from the mid-1590s.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the canon and order of the elegies vary among the early manuscripts.

editions.title: John Donne: The Complete English Poems
The Complete Poems of John Donne

works.title: Elene
altTitles: The Finding of the True Cross
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's longest signed poem (1,321 lines), on the legend of the Finding of the True Cross: the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, journeys to Jerusalem, compels the Jews to reveal the site of the Crucifixion, and recovers the cross. The poem is a masterpiece of typological narrative, casting Helena as a heroic queen and the cross as the sign of victory.
works.plot: Constantine, granted a vision of the cross before battle, sends his mother Helena to Jerusalem; her search, the interrogation of the Jew Judas (who resists, is imprisoned, converted by a sign, and baptized as Cyriacus), the miraculous finding of the three crosses, the proof by resurrection of a dead youth, the conversion of the Jews, and Helena's building of churches; the epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature and his meditation on judgment and poetry.
works.significance: The richest treatment in early English poetry of the cross as sign of victory; the locus classicus of Cynewulf's typological art.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the signature passage is among the most ornate in the corpus.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 121v-133v); based on the Latin Acta Cyriaci tradition of the Inventio crucis legend.
works.characters: Elene (Helena); Constantine; Judas/Cyriacus; Satan (in the debate with Judas)
works.structure: A conversion narrative in the heroic manner, organized around three debates (Constantine's vision, Helena's interrogations, Judas's conversion) and closing on the runic signature.
themes: Faith, grace, and the pilgrim's journey

works.title: Eleonora: A Panegyrical Dedication
works.description: Dryden's commissioned character-poem on an unnamed lady, written for the Earl of Abingdon in memory of his wife, whom the poem calls only Eleonora.
works.plot: The poem sets out to describe Eleonora's virtues in an ordered portrait of her soul, mind, and conduct, and concedes the impossibility of doing her justice in verse.
works.significance: An important experiment in the 'character' as a poetic form and a revealing document of Dryden's professional circumstances in the 1690s.
works.meter: Heroic couplets.
works.context: Composed in 1691-2 for a fee of £100 from the Earl of Abingdon; Dryden complained that he could not write a character-poem on commission.
works.characters: Eleonora (the Countess of Abingdon)
works.structure: A panegyrical character study in a continuous argument, deliberately refusing narrative.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Emaré
works.description: A Breton lay on the Constance legend: the princess Emaré, cast out by her incestuous father, drifts across the sea in a boat with her child, and through the marvellous cloth she weaves and the recognitions it brings, is restored to her husband and kingdom. The legend Chaucer used for the Man of Law's Tale, told as a fairy-tale of patient suffering.
works.plot: Emaré, given a magic cloth by the emperor, refuses her father's marriage proposal and is set adrift; she marries the king of Galys, is slandered by her wicked mother-in-law and cast out again with her son Segramour; after years in Rome, her husband finds her and all are reconciled.
works.significance: The most artful English version of the Constance story and a central text for the romance's treatment of incest, exile, and female patience.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas.
works.context: Composed c. 1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, from the Constance legend (ultimately Trivet's chronicle, as in Chaucer); preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Emaré; her father the emperor; the king of Galys; the wicked mother-in-law; Segramour
works.structure: A double exile-and-return plot organized by the magic cloth and the repeated sea voyages, in the Constance tradition.

works.title: Emblems
works.description: Francis Quarles's emblem book (1635), the most popular work of verse in seventeenth-century England, in which each of five books pairs an engraved emblem with a biblical motto, epigram, and moral verse, making religious meditation vivid and accessible to a mass readership.
works.plot: Each emblem presents a picture and motto drawn from scripture (largely the Song of Songs, Job, and Hosea) followed by meditative verse that moralises the image for the reader's devotion.
works.significance: Emblems shaped the popular religious imagination of the period and influenced Bunyan's allegory; it is the classic English emblem book and a key text of devotional culture.
works.meter: Varied verse forms (quatrains, couplets) accompanying engraved emblems, in a plain, proverbial, sometimes homely style.
works.context: Published in 1635 and reprinted constantly through the century and beyond; it was read by the devout and by Bunyan, and was both hugely popular and later critically scorned.
works.characters: the soul; Christ; biblical figures
works.structure: Five books of emblem-and-verse units, adapted from the Jesuit emblem books of Hugo Pia and others.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Enchiridion
works.form: didactic and scientific prose (computus) in Latin and Old English
works.description: Byrhtferth of Ramsey's bilingual manual of computus and the related sciences (c. 1011), written in alternating Latin and English: the fullest surviving treatise on the Anglo-Saxon science of time — the calendar, the lunar cycles, number symbolism, and the harmony of the cosmos — composed for the instruction of the young monks of Ramsey.
works.plot: The manual explains the computation of Easter, the course of the sun and moon through the zodiac, the elements, the ages of the world and of man, the symbolic meanings of numbers, and the figures of grammar and rhetoric, all ordered to the liturgical year and the contemplation of the world's design.
works.significance: The richest surviving witness to the scientific culture of the Benedictine Reform.
works.meter: Bilingual prose with verse passages.
works.context: Composed 1011 at Ramsey Abbey by Byrhtferth, pupil of Abbo of Fleury; unique manuscript: Oxford, Bodleian Library, Ashmole 328.
works.characters: the young monks of Ramsey (addressees)
works.structure: Four books of didactic exposition, alternating between Latin and English, with diagrams and tables.
works.attributionNotes: Byrhtferth's authorship is certain (he names himself).
themes: Petrarchan desire and the sonnet mistress
sources: The Works of Aphra Behn

works.title: Endymion
altTitles: Endymion, the Man in the Moon
works.description: Lyly's allegorical court comedy: Endymion's hopeless love for the moon-goddess Cynthia casts him into a forty-year sleep from which only her kiss can wake him; the intrigues of the sorceress Dipsas and the braggart Sir Tophas complicate the court, and the play ends with Endymion's awakening and the famous reading of Cynthia as the Queen whose 'virtue' the play mirrors.
works.plot: Endymion renounces Tellus for Cynthia; Tellus's jealousy and Dipsas's enchantment cast him asleep; his friend Eumenides quests for the cure, and the riddle of the fountain directs him to the kiss; the sub-plot of Sir Tophas's mock-chivalry and the pages' comedy runs alongside; Cynthia's kiss wakes the sleeper, and the play closes on the praises of her constancy.
works.significance: The most influential of the Elizabethan court allegories — the model of the dream-play of royal favour and disfavour.
works.meter: Prose for the court scenes, verse for the enchantments and the finale, with the songs of the fairies.
works.context: Performed at court in 1588 and printed in 1591; the play's veiled allusions to Leicester's fall and the Queen's favour have kept its allegory a critical puzzle for four centuries.
works.characters: Endymion; Cynthia; Tellus; Eumenides; Semele; Dipsas; Sir Tophas; Geron; Corsites; the Fairies; the pages (Epiton, Samias, Dares)
works.structure: A five-act court allegory with a fairy-tale centre (the sleep, the quest, the cure) and a burlesque chivalric sub-plot.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Eneados
works.description: Douglas's complete translation of Virgil's Aeneid into Scots couplets, completed on 22 July 1513 — the first full translation of the poem in any British language — with a thirteenth book from Mapheus Vegius, and a prologue to each book in which the translator speaks of the Scottish seasons, his art, and his critics. Printed at London in 1553.
works.plot: Virgil's epic entire: Aeneas's flight from Troy, the wanderings, the tragedy of Dido, the descent to the underworld, and the wars in Italy — with Vegius's supplement completing the hero's apotheosis.
works.significance: The first complete British Aeneid and the summit of Scots humanist translation; its prologues are the finest nature poetry in Scots, and the translation passed Virgil to the northern Renaissance.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in vigorous Scots; the prologues alternate aureate and plain registers with seasonal description.
works.context: Completed in the year of Flodden (1513), when the Scottish court and much of its nobility were destroyed; Douglas's translation of the epic of exile and foundation speaks to a nation in crisis.
works.characters: Aeneas; Dido; Turnus; Anchises; Venus; Juno
works.structure: Twelve books of the Aeneid plus the thirteenth book of Vegius; each book preceded by a prologue, of which the seasonal prologues (VII, XII, XIII) are the most celebrated.

editions.title: Virgil's Aeneid Translated into Scottish Verse by Gavin Douglas

works.title: England's Birth-Right Justified
altTitles: England's Birth-Right Justified Against All Arbitrary Usurpation
works.description: John Lilburne's principal Leveller pamphlet, in which he claims that the free-born people of England possess an inalienable birth-right of liberty that no parliament or king may take away.
works.plot: Lilburne argues that arbitrary imprisonment, taxation without consent, the monopoly of the law, and the power of the great are all violations of the birth-right of every free-born Englishman, and that the people's representatives must be accountable.
works.significance: A foundational text of English radicalism and of the doctrine of popular sovereignty; its language of birth-right influenced the Leveller Agreements and, through them, later democratic theory.
works.meter: Fierce, urgent, colloquial prose of the pamphlet wars.
works.context: Published in October 1645 during the civil wars, while Lilburne was serving in the parliamentary army; it laid the intellectual foundations of the Leveller movement.
works.structure: A single polemical tract with a dedicatory epistle.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Enthusiasmus Triumphatus; or, A Brief Account of the Nature, Causes, Kinds, and Cure of Enthusiasm
works.description: Henry More's influential analysis of religious enthusiasm as a disease of the imagination, published in his Collection of Several Philosophical Writings and directed against the sectarian excesses of the Commonwealth.
works.plot: More identifies enthusiasm with the disturbance of the animal spirits, with melancholy, with ignorance, and with the pride of private revelation, and proposes reason, self-examination, and the discipline of the church as its cure.
works.significance: The standard seventeenth-century treatment of enthusiasm and a key text in the history of the psychology of religion; it influenced Shaftesbury, Swift's Tale of a Tub, and the eighteenth-century debate on fanaticism.
works.meter: Learned, argumentative prose.
works.context: Published in 1656 during the Commonwealth, when the sects proliferated; More was a Cambridge Platonist concerned to defend a rational Christianity against both enthusiasm and materialism.
works.structure: A single treatise in sections.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Henry More; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Epicene
works.description: Jonson's comedy of noise and silence: Morose, who cannot bear sound, marries the 'silent woman' Epicene to disinherit his nephew Dauphine — only to find his bride a torrent of talk, his house invaded by the collegiate ladies and the barber Cutbeard, and the play's last trick the revelation that Epicene is a boy, Dauphine's instrument, and the marriage void.
works.plot: Dauphine plots to break his uncle's will: the silent bride, the mock divorce consultation, and the siege of Morose's house by the Otiers' collegiates drive the old man to any terms; the contract signed, Dauphine strips the boy of his disguise and the play ends on the audience's own exposure to satire.
works.significance: The most audacious of Jonson's comedies of sex and gender — the play Restoration comedy learned its tricks from.
works.meter: Predominantly prose — Jonson's most assured comic prose — with the wit-duels of Truewit as its set pieces.
works.context: First performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels at Whitefriars, 1609; its boy-bride was played by a boy, doubling the play's game with gender; printed in the 1616 Folio.
works.characters: Morose; Dauphine; Epicene; Truewit; Clerimont; Sir John Daw; Sir Amorous La Foole; Captain Otter; Mistress Otter; Cutbeard; Mavis; the collegiates
works.structure: A five-act farce of escalating noise and counter-plot, with the collegiate ladies' scenes as a satire of female learning and the divorce farce as its centrepiece.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Epigrammata
altTitles: Epigrammata clarissimi disertissimique viri Thomae Mori
works.description: More's collected Latin epigrams, printed together with his Utopia in 1518, including translations from the Greek Anthology, satirical and courtly verse, and the poems on his own fortune and on kingship.
works.plot: The collection has no single argument; it ranges from verse translations of Greek epigrams made with William Lily, through witty satires on astrologers and courtiers, to the programmatic 'Progymnasmata' and poems celebrating the accession of Henry VIII.
works.significance: The finest Latin verse written by an Englishman of the early Renaissance and a showcase of the Erasmian revival of classical epigram; the coronation poems mark the beginnings of English Renaissance panegyric.
works.meter: Elegiac couplets, hendecasyllables, and other classical metres
works.context: Composed across More's humanist career from the late 1490s; the Progymnasmata with Lily (an exercise translating Greek epigrams) dates from c. 1503–04; the collection was printed by Froben at Basel in 1518 together with the third edition of Utopia.
works.structure: A printed miscellany grouped by type: translations from the Greek Anthology, original epigrams, and the coronation poems of 1509.

works.title: Epigrams
works.description: Jonson's collection of 133 epigrams, printed in the 1616 Folio of his Works: poems of praise to the great and good of his acquaintance (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; the Sidneys; Donne; Shakespeare), and poems of satiric castigation to the vicious — 'On Court-Worm', 'On Gut', 'On My First Son', and the epitaphs on his children among them — the classical epigram remade as a moral instrument.
works.plot: No plot: the collection alternates poems of praise and blame, with the commendatory poems to patrons and fellow poets balancing the satires of fools and knaves, and the personal elegies (on his son, on his first daughter) at the collection's heart.
works.significance: The foundation of the English epigram tradition and the seedbed of the Augustan moral couplet.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of lapidary finish — the model for the Augustan couplet of the next century.
works.context: Written across Jonson's career and collected for the 1616 Works, the first folio of an English playwright's own canon; 'To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author, Mr. William Shakespeare' appeared separately in the 1623 Folio.
works.characters: the poet; the named patrons and poets (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; Donne; Shakespeare; the Sidneys); the satirized types (Court-Worm, Gut, Poet-Ape)
works.structure: A book of 133 short poems in the Martial tradition, arranged as a gallery of virtues and vices, prefaced by Jonson's defence of the genre.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Epistle on the Mixed Life
works.description: Walter Hilton's epistle addressed to a wealthy layman, probably a lord, teaching the 'mixed life' — the life that joins the active works of mercy and the duties of estate with the inner practice of contemplation. It is the classic English statement that contemplation is not the preserve of monks: lay people in the world may and should live the contemplative life in their degree.
works.plot: Hilton distinguishes three lives — active, contemplative, and mixed — and argues that the mixed life, combining works of charity and governance with prayer and meditation, is the life of prelates and devout lay lords; he then teaches his addressee the practice of this life in his daily affairs.
works.significance: The founding text of the 'mixed life' tradition that legitimized lay contemplation and shaped the spirituality of the fifteenth-century gentry.
works.meter: Plain, authoritative prose of the Hilton school.
works.context: Composed c. 1385, when the growth of lay piety and the demand for vernacular guidance was transforming English religious life; preserved in numerous manuscripts, often with the Scale of Perfection.
works.characters: Hilton (writer); the devout layman (addressee)
works.structure: A single epistle in two movements: the doctrine of the three lives, and its application to the recipient's estate.

works.title: Epsom Wells
works.description: Thomas Shadwell's most popular comedy, set at the Epsom mineral wells, in which the fashionable world of gallants, cits, and country justices is exposed in a series of comic intrigues.
works.plot: The rake Bellamour pursues Lucia while the city couple Woodly and Mrs Woodly play at adultery; the country justice Clodpate and his wife are gulled, and all is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: Shadwell's finest comedy and a principal example of his Jonsonian 'humours' method; it held the stage into the eighteenth century through adaptation.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden in 1672 and published in 1673, dedicated to the Duke of Newcastle; Shadwell claimed to have drawn the characters from life at the wells.
works.characters: Bellamour; Woodly; Lucia; Carolina; Mrs Woodly; Justice Clodpate; Mrs Clodpate; Bumpkin; Lucy
works.structure: Five acts of humours comedy with a strong Jonsonian comic portrait in Clodpate.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Essays in Verse and Prose
works.description: Cowley's posthumous essays (1668) — 'Of Myself', 'Of Solitude', 'Of Gardens', 'Of Liberty', 'Of the Late Civil War', and 'Of Plants' — which champion retirement, the country life, and the new experimental philosophy, and helped establish the familiar, conversational English essay.
works.plot: The essays reflect on retirement and the value of solitude, the love of gardening and the countryside, liberty, the recent Civil Wars, and the Royal Society's programme, in a personal, digressive, hortatory manner.
works.significance: Cowley's essays shaped the Restoration familiar essay and the ideal of cultivated retirement, influencing Steele, Addison, and Johnson, and linked literature to the Royal Society's ideals.
works.meter: Graceful, conversational prose with occasional verse; a cultivated, reflective tone.
works.context: Written after Cowley's retirement to Chertsey following the Restoration and published posthumously in 1668; 'Of Plants' is an Englishing of his Latin De Plantis and engages the new science.
works.structure: A collection of familiar essays, some with verse interspersed, on moral and philosophical subjects.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Euphues and His England
works.description: Lyly's sequel: Euphues and his friend Philautus sail for England, where the courtship of the ladies — Camilla, Surius's sister, and the rest — and the praises of Elizabeth I, the English court, and English women fill the book, in the second and final installment of the Euphuistic diptych.
works.plot: The voyage, the arrival in Dover, and the tour of England's marvels frame the main action: Philautus courts the ladies, Euphues plays the counsellor, and the long debate on love, beauty, and constancy ends with the famous 'glass for Europe' — the encomium of Queen Elizabeth that closes the book.
works.significance: The completion of the Euphuistic diptych and a founding text of English literary nationalism.
works.meter: The Euphuistic prose at its ripest, with the encomium of Elizabeth as its set piece.
works.context: Published in 1580, the year of Drake's circumnavigation and the Jesuit mission's arrival; its celebration of England answered the national mood and fixed Euphues as the English style's patron.
works.characters: Euphues; Philautus; Camilla; Lady Flavia; Surius; Fidus; Psellus; Queen Elizabeth (praised in the encomium)
works.structure: A travel frame enclosing the courtship debates, letters, and the concluding praise of England, mirroring the first book's structure.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit
works.description: Lyly's first Euphues book and the fountain of Euphuism: the young Athenian Euphues comes to Naples, where the friendship with Philautus, the love of Lucilla, and her inconstancy teach him the anatomy of wit — the whole told in the balanced, antithetical, simile-laden prose that took England by storm and gave the decade its style.
works.plot: Euphues wins Philautus's friendship and then Lucilla's love, betraying his friend; Lucilla's fickleness (she turns to Curio) punishes the traitor; the debate on love, the letters of counsel, and Euphues's departure close the book with the moral anatomy — 'wit' dissected into its deceits and remedies.
works.significance: The most influential prose style of the English Renaissance — the book that taught a generation to write, and to think in balances.
works.meter: Prose of elaborate Euphuistic balance — antithesis, isocolon, and the zoological similes of Pliny's natural history.
works.context: Published in 1578 and reprinted a dozen times by 1600; the style it founded was imitated by Greene, Lodge, and the court, and parodied by Shakespeare and Nashe within the decade.
works.characters: Euphues; Philautus; Lucilla; Curio; the old gentleman of Naples; the ladies of Naples
works.structure: A moral romance in the manner of the Italian questioni d'amore: narrative framed by debate, letters, and the concluding 'Cooling Card' against love.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Every Man in His Humour
works.description: Jonson's first great comedy of humours, performed by the Lord Chamberlain's Men with Shakespeare in the cast: the jealous merchant Kitely, the braggart Captain Bobadill, the town gull Matthew, and the poetaster's crew are all 'humorous' — each ruled by an obsession — until the exposure of the final act lets the sane (Clement, Wellbred) judge the fools, in a London whose names Jonson later anglicized from the Italian setting.
works.plot: Old Knowell worries over his son's London dissipations; Kitely suspects his wife; Bobadill boasts and fights by words only; the gulls and their plots collide at Cob's house, and Justice Clement's court of the final scene administers the comic verdicts — including the purging of the humours by the 'vent' of exposure.
works.significance: The foundation of Jonson's comic method and of the English comedy of character — the template for Restoration and eighteenth-century comedy alike.
works.meter: Mostly prose in the 1616 Folio revision, with the verse of the earlier Italian version smoothed away — the first great prose comedy of the English stage.
works.context: Performed 1598 at the Curtain by the Chamberlain's Men (Shakespeare played Old Knowell); Jonson revised the play, resetting it in London, for the 1616 Folio of his Works.
works.characters: Kitely; Dame Kitely; Captain Bobadill; Edward Knowell; Brainworm; Wellbred; Stephen; Matthew; Justice Clement; Downright; Bridget; Cob; Tib
works.structure: A unified-plot comedy on the classical model — one city, one day, one action — built on the humours theory announced in the Induction and resolved in the judgment scene.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Everyman
works.description: The most famous of the English moralities, translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) around 1500: Everyman, summoned by Death to render his account, finds that Fellowship, Kindred, Goods, and even his own Strength and Beauty desert him, and that only Good Deeds — and Knowledge, Confession, and the priesthood — go with him into the grave. Its stark allegory of death has kept it on the stage for five centuries.
works.plot: God, seeing mankind sunk in worldly love, sends Death to Everyman with the summons to his reckoning; one by one his companions refuse the journey — Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin, Goods — until Good Deeds, weakened by his neglect, sends him to Knowledge, who leads him through Confession and penance to the sacraments; at the grave, Strength, Discretion, Beauty, and the Five Wits desert him in turn, and only Good Deeds descends with him, as the angels receive his soul.
works.significance: The classic English play of death and the reckoning: its allegory has made it the most performed medieval English drama in the modern world.
works.meter: Couplets and stanza forms, plain and weighty, with the Dutch original's structure faithfully kept.
works.context: Translated from the Dutch Elckerlijc (c. 1495) c. 1500 and printed by Richard Pynson and John Skot c. 1510–1535; continuously performed since, including modern productions (Hofmannsthal's Jedermann at Salzburg descends from it).
works.characters: Everyman; Death; God; Fellowship; Kindred; Cousin; Goods; Good Deeds; Knowledge; Confession; Strength; Discretion; Beauty; the Five Wits; the Angel; the Doctor
works.structure: A single-movement morality of the final journey, with the successive desertions of the companions as its pitiless rhythm and the doctrine of the reckoning as its frame.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; translated from the Dutch, whose authorship is likewise disputed.

editions.title: Everyman and Mankind

works.title: Exodus
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 590 lines on the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea, from the Junius manuscript: a bravura reworking of Exodus 13-14 in which Moses becomes a heroic leader and the crossing a nautical epic, prefiguring the Christian's passage through the waters of baptism and the harrowing of hell.
works.plot: After a prologue on Moses and the law, the poem narrates the pursuit of the Israelites by Pharaoh's host, the pillar of cloud and fire, the parting of the waters, the drowning of the Egyptians, and the Israelites' division of spoils on the far shore; it closes with an allegorical exegesis of the crossing (the 'keys of the deep', the 'spiritual meanings') and allusions to Noah, Abraham, Solomon's temple, and the end of the world.
works.significance: The most stylistically daring of the Old Testament poems; its sea imagery is a high point of Old English diction.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of unusual density; famous kennings for the sea ('the whale's road', 'the swan's riding-place').
works.context: Preserved in the Junius manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Junius 11, pp. 143-171); the poem is often linked with the Cædmonian school of biblical paraphrase mentioned by Bede.
works.characters: Moses; Pharaoh; the Israelites; Abraham; Noah
works.structure: Narrative epic with an extended typological epilogue; the abrupt shifts of scene (Noah, Abraham, the temple) have prompted theories of textual disruption.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the Cædmonian attribution is traditional only.
themes: Country retirement and the estate poem

works.title: Expugnatio Hibernica
works.description: Gerald of Wales's history of the Anglo-Norman invasion and conquest of Ireland (1169–85), framed as a panegyric of Henry II and of Gerald's own relatives among the conquerors, the Geraldines; composed from 1188 and read publicly at Oxford in 1188 or 1189.
works.summary: Gerald recounts the coming of the Normans under Strongbow and the campaigns that established English lordship in Ireland, devoting special attention to the deeds of the FitzGeralds, to the character of the Irish, and to the prophecies and prodigies attending the conquest.
works.significance: The foundational narrative of the English presence in Ireland, shaped by family partisanship but indispensable as the earliest extended account of the conquest; a model of twelfth-century historical rhetoric.

works.title: Fables Ancient and Modern
works.description: Dryden's last volume, a collection of verse translations and adaptations from Homer, Ovid, Boccaccio, and Chaucer, dedicated to the Duke of Ormond and prefaced by his famous account of translation.
works.plot: The volume contains, among others, Palamon and Arcite (from Boccaccio's Teseida), The Cock and the Fox (from Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale), The Wife of Bath Her Tale, Theodore and Honoria, Cymon and Iphigenia, and the twelfth book of Ovid's Metamorphoses.
works.significance: The greatest achievement of Dryden's late career and a founding document of English translation theory; Palamon and Arcite and the preface are canonical texts in the history of Chaucer reception.
works.meter: Heroic couplets throughout, including the celebrated octosyllabic-free Chaucerian adaptations rendered in five-beat lines.
works.context: Published in March 1700, two months before Dryden's death, by subscription after he had been stripped of the laureateship in 1689.
works.characters: Palamon; Arcite; Emily; Chaunticlere; Pertelote; Reynard; Theodore; Honoria; Cymon; Iphigenia; the Wife of Bath
works.structure: A miscellany of narrative poems unified by the preface's theory of translation as the art of conveying a dead author's spirit in the living language.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Fall of Princes
works.description: John Lydgate's monumental translation (over 36,000 lines) of Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium, commissioned by Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and completed in 1438: a procession of the falls of princes from Adam to King John of France, moralized by the ghostly narrator Boccaccio himself. The encyclopedic English 'tragedy' of fortune, and the ancestor of the Mirror for Magistrates.
works.plot: The poet, in a Boethian frame, receives the sorrowing Boccaccio, who recounts example after example of greatness overthrown — Nimrod, Saul, Priam, Alexander, Caesar, Nero, Arthur, and the modern princes — each tale closing with the moral of fortune's wheel; the work ends with the falls of the French and English kings and a defense of poetry itself.
works.significance: The great English poem of the falls of princes and the conduit by which Boccaccio's tragic vision became the Tudor theory of tragedy; its influence on the Elizabethan stage is direct.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas with prose links, aureate and copious.
works.context: Commissioned by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, in 1431 and completed in 1438, during the wars in France and the king's minority; printed by Pynson (1494) and continuously read; the Mirror for Magistrates (1559) descends directly from it.
works.characters: Lydgate (dreamer); Boccaccio (narrator); the fallen princes of history
works.structure: Nine books of exemplary falls within the dream-vision frame, with the envoy to Duke Humphrey as its patronage climax.

editions.title: Lydgate's Fall of Princes

works.title: Festial
works.description: John Mirk's cycle of English sermons for the feasts of the church year, composed c. 1380s at Lilleshall Abbey: lively, exemplum-rich homilies designed for parish priests to read to their congregations, from Advent through the temporale and sanctorale to the dedication of the church. The most popular sermon collection of late medieval England.
works.plot: Each sermon expounds the day's feast — its history, its scripture, and its moral — with the miracle stories and exempla that made the Festial famous: the monk and the birds, the usurer's bees, the proud lady's punishment — and closes with practical instruction for the parish.
works.significance: The classic of the English late medieval sermon and the principal record of orthodox parish preaching in the age of Lollardy; its exempla are a treasury of popular piety.
works.meter: Plain, animated prose with verse tags and exemplary narrative.
