works.title: Hero and Leander
works.description: Marlowe's unfinished Ovidian epyllion, left at the lovers' first night and completed by George Chapman in 1598: the priestess Hero of Sestos and the youth Leander of Abydos meet at Venus's festival and fall in love; Leander swims the Hellespont nightly, and the poem breaks off with the consummation — 'Love is not full of pity, as men say' — before Hero's death in the familiar myth.
works.plot: Leander, 'amorous Leander, beautiful and young', woos Hero at the feast of Adonis; her vows to Venus yield to his eloquence; the first swim, the first embrace, and the lovers' debate with the dawn occupy the completed portion, with Neptune's dalliance with the swimming Leander as its most celebrated episode.
works.significance: The masterpiece of the Elizabethan epyllion and the direct ancestor of the Restoration erotic couplet — the poem Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis answered and vied with.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of extraordinary wit and sensuousness — the poem that defined the English erotic couplet for the next two centuries.
works.context: Written in 1593, the year of Marlowe's death; printed first by Edward Blount in 1598 and again the same year with Chapman's continuation ('Hero and Leander: Begun by Christopher Marloe; and finished by George Chapman').
works.characters: Hero; Leander; Neptune; Venus; Cupid; the Nurse (Chapman's continuation)
works.structure: Two completed sestiads (Marlowe's) followed by Chapman's four, the whole framed as a narrative of seduction and delay in the epyllion manner.
works.attributionNotes: Marlowe's two sestiads are uncontested; the continuation is Chapman's.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Poems and Translations

works.title: Hesperides
altTitles: Hesperides; or, The Works Both Humane and Divine of Robert Herrick
works.description: Robert Herrick's vast collection of some 1,400 poems (1648), divided into the pagan 'Hesperides' and the Christian 'Noble Numbers', which celebrates the seasonal rites, courtships, and superstitions of rural Devon and the pleasures of the present, shadowed by mutability and Anglican faith — including 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' ('Gather ye rosebuds while ye may').
works.plot: The poems range over love, wine, flowers, country customs, kings and loyalty, and devotion, urging carpe diem while acknowledging death, and pairing classical festivity with Christian piety.
works.significance: Hesperides is the most varied and charming of Cavalier collections, a treasury of English rural folklore and lyric, and 'Gather ye rosebuds' the most famous carpe diem poem in English.
works.meter: Short, musical, epigrammatic lyrics in a great variety of meters with a light, mellifluous touch.
works.context: Written largely during Herrick's years as vicar of Dean Prior (1629–47) and published in 1647/48 after his ejection by Parliament as a royalist; it preserves the ceremonial culture of the English countryside.
works.characters: the poet; Julia and other mistresses; the rural folk
works.structure: A large collection of short lyrics, epigrams, and songs in two parts, loosely grouped by theme.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Hickscorner
works.description: An anonymous early morality interlude of the conversion of three rogues — Freewill, Imagination, and the Vice Hickscorner — printed by Wynkyn de Worde c. 1513–15.
works.plot: Freewill and Imagination, fallen into idleness and vice, meet the hardened rogue Hickscorner, who boasts of his crimes and rails at virtue; Pity and Contemplation reprove them, and the three rogues are brought to repentance, confess their sins, and set out on pilgrimage, with the play ending in a vision of the joys of heaven.
works.significance: One of the earliest printed English moralities and the first to centre on the conversion of rogues; its Vice, Hickscorner, is a landmark in the development of the stage devil's comic heir, and its tavern realism anticipates the rogue literature of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Printed c. 1513–15 by Wynkyn de Worde, in the generation after Everyman; the play's tavern scenes and rogue-cant document the underworld of early Tudor London, and its popularity carried it through editions to the 1560s.
works.characters: Freewill; Imagination; Hickscorner; Pity; Contemplation; Perseverance
works.structure: A continuous morality play in two movements — the rogues' boasting fellowship and their conversion — with the Vice Hickscorner as the play's comic engine.

works.title: Historia Anglorum
works.description: Henry of Huntingdon's history of England from the earliest times to the accession of Henry II in 1154, notable for its vivid battle narratives, its interest in the English past as national history, and the substantial body of original verse — including the political poems addressed to Henry I — embedded in the prose.
works.summary: Ten books (the latest recension) move from Roman and Anglo-Saxon Britain through the Norman kings to the anarchy of Stephen's reign; the work incorporates earlier sources (Bede, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) while supplying independent contemporary witness for the twelfth century, including the famous account of the Battle of Lincoln.
works.significance: A principal narrative source for the reign of Stephen, and a central text of twelfth-century English national historiography; its verse makes it a bridge between Anglo-Latin and vernacular literary traditions.

editions.title: Historia Anglorum: The History of the English People

works.title: Historia Brittonum
works.form: history and chronicle (composite) in Latin prose
works.description: A composite history of the Britons compiled in Wales in 829/30 and traditionally attributed to Nennius: genealogies, origin legends (the Trojan descent of the Britons), the lives of St Patrick and St Germanus, and the earliest datable Arthur material — the list of Arthur's twelve battles culminating at Mount Badon.
works.plot: The work assembles disparate materials on the age of the world, the Trojan origins of the Britons, the Roman occupation, Vortigern and the coming of the Saxons, the boy-prophet Ambrosius, the wars of Arthur ('dux bellorum'), the genealogies of the Saxon and Welsh kings, and the 'wonders of Britain' — an anthology of British historical memory rather than a continuous history.
works.significance: The earliest extended Arthurian text in insular literature; the principal quarry of later Welsh and English Arthurian history (Geoffrey of Monmouth).
works.meter: Latin prose of varying registers.
works.context: Compiled in Gwynedd c. 829/30 during the Mercian ascendancy in Wales; preserved in some forty manuscripts in Welsh, English, and continental recensions.
works.characters: Vortigern; Ambrosius; Arthur; Patrick; Germanus; Hengist and Horsa
works.structure: Compilatory: a sequence of heterogeneous sections of varying provenance, several marked as the work of 'Nennius the disciple of Elvodugus'.
works.attributionNotes: The prologue attributes the compilation to Nennius, but not all manuscripts carry it; the work is demonstrably composite.
sources: The Oxford Handbook of Tudor Literature, 1485–1603

works.title: Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum
altTitles: Ecclesiastical History of the English People
works.form: history and chronicle (ecclesiastical history) in Latin prose
works.description: Bede's masterpiece, completed in 731: the history of the English church and people from Caesar's invasions to 731, in five books. It is the primary narrative source for early Anglo-Saxon history, the origin of the AD dating system's general use, and the conduit through which Cædmon's Hymn and much else survives.
works.plot: The five books trace the conversion of the English kingdoms — the mission of Augustine to Kent (597), the Northumbrian mission of Paulinus and Aidan, the Synod of Whitby (664) — interspersed with saints' lives (Cuthbert, Æthelthryth), miracles, letters, and the famous account of the poet Cædmon; the work closes with a summary of Britain's ecclesiastical state and Bede's autobiographical colophon.
works.significance: 'The father of English history'; the indispensable source for the first three centuries of English Christianity and for the early vernacular poetic record.
works.meter: Latin prose of classical clarity; contains the earliest recorded English verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in paraphrase.
works.context: Composed at the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow from earlier annals, lives, and documents; dedicated to King Ceolwulf of Northumbria.
works.characters: Augustine of Canterbury; Æthelberht; Edwin; Oswald; Aidan; Hild; Cuthbert; Cædmon; Theodore; Wilfrid
works.structure: Annalistic-chronological within each book, organized by kingdom and diocese; documentary (letters, synods) and hagiographical materials are woven into the narrative.
works.attributionNotes: Bede's authorship is certain (his own colophon).

editions.title: Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People
editions.editor: Bertram Colgrave and R. A. B. Mynors (eds.)

sources: The Riverside Chaucer, 3rd edition

works.title: Historia Regum Britanniae
altTitles: The History of the Kings of Britain
works.description: Pseudohistorical chronicle tracing the kings of Britain from the legendary Brutus of Troy to the Saxon conquest, the principal source of the Arthurian legend in England. Geoffrey claims to translate 'a certain very ancient book in the British tongue' given him by Walter, archdeacon of Oxford; its authority was attacked by William of Newburgh and Gerald of Wales but it decisively shaped medieval British historiography.
works.summary: Geoffrey of Monmouth narrates the foundation of Britain by Brutus, a descendant of Aeneas, and proceeds through the reigns of the legendary kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests extend over much of Europe — to the Saxon domination and the prophecies of Merlin (the Prophetiae Merlini, later incorporated as Book VII). The work made Arthur a pan-European figure and provided the framework for Wace, Layamon, and the later chronicle tradition.
works.significance: The single most influential piece of British historical writing of the Middle Ages: over 200 manuscripts survive, and it furnished the matter of Britain for romance, chronicle, and national myth from Wace's Roman de Brut to Malory and beyond.

editions.title: The History of the Kings of Britain

works.title: Holy Sonnets
works.description: Donne's nineteen divine sonnets — 'Batter my heart, three-personed God', 'Death be not proud', 'At the round earth's imagined corners', 'Since she whom I loved hath paid her last debt' — in which the erotic and argumentative energies of the love poems are turned on God, sin, death, and the soul's terror of damnation.
works.plot: The sonnets dramatize the soul's wrestling with God: pleas for violent grace, meditations on death and judgment, griefs of bereavement, and the final sonnets' fear and love of a God who must be wooed with the poet's whole art.
works.significance: The supreme English devotional sonnets — the bridge from the Elizabethan love sonnet to the sacred poetry of Herbert, Crashaw, and Hopkins.
works.meter: The Italian and English sonnet forms strained to the breaking point — spondaic openings, abrupt turns, and the metaphysical conceit turned to devotion.
works.context: Composed chiefly between 1609 and 1619, the years of Donne's ordination (1615) and of his wife's death (1617); the poems circulated in manuscript and were printed posthumously in 1633.
works.characters: the speaker; God (as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit); Death; the soul; the angels
works.structure: A cycle of nineteen sonnets (in the standard canon; twelve in the earliest manuscript group, with the later 'Westmoreland' sequence adding the rest), not a plotted sequence but a linked series of meditations.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the canon of nineteen and the ordering are the work of later editors, from the manuscript groups.

editions.title: John Donne: The Complete English Poems
The Complete Poems of John Donne

works.title: Homiletic Fragment I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII), late tenth century
works.description: Two homiletic poems in the Vercelli Book. Homiletic Fragment I (47 lines) is a meditation on deceitful friendship, comparing the false friend to the bee whose honey is sweet but whose sting is deadly. Homiletic Fragment II (20 lines) laments man's hardness of heart amid the world's sorrows.
works.plot: Fragment I warns against the friend who speaks fair but plots evil, elaborating the image of the bee through biblical and proverbial wisdom. Fragment II meditates on grief and the human failure to heed the truth, in a fragmentary surviving text.
works.significance: Witnesses to the close relationship between Old English homiletic prose and verse, and to the moral psychology of the late Anglo-Saxon church.
works.meter: Alliterative long line in the homiletic manner of the Vercelli Book's prose sermons; both texts are imperfectly preserved.
works.context: The Vercelli Book pairs these poems with its collection of doomsday homilies and with The Dream of the Rood, Elene, and Andreas; the fragments belong to the same culture of vernacular preaching and moral verse.
works.structure: Fragment I develops a single governing simile (the treacherous friend as bee) with proverbial expansions; Fragment II is a broken meditation on sorrow and heedlessness.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two fragments are distinct poems.

works.title: Hudibras
works.description: Samuel Butler's mock-heroic satire in three parts on Presbyterian and Independent hypocrisy, following the knight-errant Hudibras and his squire Ralpho through a series of absurd adventures in the wake of the Restoration.
works.plot: Hudibras, a Puritan knight of absurd learning and courage, sets out with his squire Ralpho to suppress bear-baiting, is beaten by the widow's champion Trulla, is rescued by the astrologer Sidrophel, and courts the wealthy widow; each part satirises a different aspect of sectary enthusiasm.
works.significance: The most popular poem of the Restoration — Charles II carried a copy in his pocket — and the principal English model of low mock-heroic, influencing Swift, Pope's Dunciad, and the whole tradition of comic verse satire.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with grotesque double and triple rhymes, deliberately anti-heroic; the 'Hudibrastic' verse.
works.context: Part I published 1663, Part II 1664, Part III 1678; written from Butler's experience as secretary to the Presbyterian Sir Samuel Luke during the civil wars.
works.characters: Sir Hudibras; Ralpho; Trulla; Magnano; Cerdon; Sidrophel; Whachum; the Widow; Talgol; Orsin
works.structure: Three parts in eight cantos each, a picaresque sequence of digressive episodes with extensive marginal notes and a prose epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Part I published anonymously but immediately ascribed to Butler; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Hyde Park
works.description: Shirley's comedy of fashionable London society, set on the day of the horse races in Hyde Park, in which the wooing contests of the gentry, the tricks of a returned 'dead' husband, and the rivalry of suitors are resolved in a multiple marriage.
works.plot: Three gentlemen compete for the hands of three ladies while a fourth, presumed dead, returns; the Park scene provides the public arena in which the rivalries are settled.
works.significance: A key document of Caroline court society and one of the earliest plays to make fashionable London topography its subject.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose in the comic low scenes.
works.context: First performed at the Cockpit in 1632 and dedicated to Queen Henrietta Maria; Hyde Park had been opened to the public by Charles I in 1637.
works.characters: Bonavent; Trier; Rider; Carol; Mistress Bonavent; Mistress Bonny; Juliet; Anne; the Hostess
works.structure: Five acts, moving from the London lodgings to the Park and back.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Hydriotaphia; or, Urn-Burial
works.description: Browne's treatise on the burial of the dead, occasioned by the discovery of Roman urns in Norfolk, which moves from antiquarian description to the great meditation on mortality and oblivion that is its famous second half.
works.plot: Chapters I-III survey the burial customs of the ancient world; chapter IV reflects on the vanity of funerary monuments; chapter V, the peroration, meditates on the certainty of oblivion and the Christian hope of resurrection.
works.significance: The supreme English meditation on death and oblivion; it has influenced writers from Johnson and De Quincey to W. G. Sebald, and its phrases ('that vulgar arithmetic of antiquity', 'to be ignorant of evil') are part of the language.
works.meter: The most magnificent prose of the seventeenth century; the closing paragraphs of chapter V are among the most quoted passages in English.
works.context: Published in 1658, in the same year as The Garden of Cyrus and the death of Cromwell; it was written during the Commonwealth when Browne was living quietly at Norwich.
works.structure: Five chapters of increasing rhetorical intensity, ending in the celebrated chapter V.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Idea
works.description: Michael Drayton's sonnet sequence, first published as Ideas Mirrour (1594) and revised across five editions into its final 63-sonnet form as Idea (1619): a sequence of farewells — to the lady, to the sonnet form itself, and to love — crowned by the great sonnet 'Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part'.
works.plot: The lover's suit to the lady moves through adoration and complaint to the sequence's famous gesture of renunciation — a farewell to love that is also a virtuoso leave-taking of the sonnet convention.
works.significance: Home of the most famous valedictory sonnet in the language and a case study in the Elizabethan sequence as revisable form.
works.meter: The English sonnet, in Drayton's plain-spoken, muscular style.
works.context: Drayton revised the sequence continuously from 1594 to 1619, mirroring the rise and self-conscious decline of the sonnet vogue he had helped create.
works.characters: the poet-lover; Idea (the beloved)
works.structure: A sequence revised over twenty-five years, ending in the 1619 form with its valedictory design.

editions.title: The Works of Michael Drayton, 5 vols.

works.title: Incendium Amoris
works.description: Richard Rolle's principal Latin treatise (c. 1340–43), an autobiographical and doctrinal account of the contemplative life as he himself had experienced it: the warmth of divine love (calor), its sweetness (dulcor), and its song (canor), with instruction on prayer, meditation, and the discernment of spirits. The founding text of the English mystical tradition.
works.plot: Rolle recounts his own conversion and his experience of the three degrees of love — fire, sweetness, and heavenly song — defends the contemplative life against its critics, and teaches the reader to progress from reading through prayer to the 'fire of love' that unites the soul to God.
works.significance: The first major work of the English mystical tradition and the fountainhead of its characteristic language of warmth, sweetness, and song.
works.meter: Latin prose, rhetorical and warm, with the psalm commentary woven in.
works.context: Composed c. 1340–43 in the north of England, early in Rolle's hermit career, and later translated into Middle English (the Fire of Love); among the most widely read Latin spiritual works of the English fourteenth century.
works.characters: Rolle (as witness and teacher)
works.structure: A prologue and forty-two chapters mixing autobiography, doctrine, and scriptural commentary, with the author's own experience as the organizing proof.

works.title: Institutes of Polity
altTitles: Institutes of Polity, Civil and Ecclesiastical
works.form: didactic treatise (political theology) in Old English prose
works.description: Wulfstan's treatise on the orders of Christian society: the duties of the king, the bishops, the clergy, the nobles, and the people in a rightly ordered realm — 'eight columns that support the kingdom'. The clearest statement of Anglo-Saxon political theology and the seedbed of Wulfstan's law codes.
works.plot: The treatise defines each estate's office: the king shall protect the church and rule justly; bishops shall teach and judge; the clergy shall keep chastity and learning; ealdormen shall give righteous judgments; the people shall labour and obey — all bound by the law of God, whose breach brings ruin on the land.
works.significance: The fullest Anglo-Saxon statement of the theory of the Christian commonwealth.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical two-stress prose.
works.context: Composed c. 1008-1020 in the crisis of Æthelred's reign and revised under Cnut; preserved in later eleventh-century manuscripts, chiefly Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201.
works.characters: the Christian king; the bishops; the estates of the realm
works.structure: A systematic treatise in chapters on the estates of the realm, from the heavenly king down through the earthly orders.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.
sources: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: Interlude of Youth
works.description: An anonymous morality interlude of the fall and repentance of Youth, composed c. 1513–14 and printed c. 1530–35; a compact dramatization of the prodigal's return.
works.plot: Youth, flattered by Riot, Pride, and Lechery, abandons Charity and Humility for the tavern and the stews; Charity and Humility lament and warn him, and Youth, brought low, repents and returns to virtue, ending with a prayer for the king and the audience's amendment.
works.significance: A compact and influential example of the early Tudor morality, dramatizing the prodigal theme that would run through the century to the Elizabethan stage; it survives as a witness to the interlude's household origins.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Composed c. 1513–14, probably for a noble household (the prayer for the king suggests courtly performance), and printed c. 1530–35; it belongs to the same early Tudor wave as Hickscorner and Magnificence, in which the morality play becomes a vehicle for aristocratic moral counsel.
works.characters: Youth; Charity; Humility; Riot; Pride; Lechery
works.structure: A short two-part morality play of temptation and return, with the Vices' songs and taunts alternating with Charity's warnings.

works.title: Itinerarium Cambriae
works.description: Gerald of Wales's account of the preaching tour of Wales undertaken in 1188 with Archbishop Baldwin of Canterbury to recruit for the Third Crusade, combining topographical description, ethnography of the Welsh, anecdote, and vigorous self-promotion; the companion work to the Descriptio Cambriae (1194).
works.summary: Gerald narrates the itinerary of Baldwin's mission through south and north Wales, recording the sermons, the reception of the party, local marvels and legends, the character and customs of the Welsh, and his own prominent role in the enterprise; the two books culminate in the preaching of the cross.
works.significance: One of the finest works of twelfth-century travel and ethnographic writing, a primary source for medieval Wales, and a major witness to the Latin literary culture of the Welsh marches.

works.title: Jack of Newbury
altTitles: The Pleasant History of John Winchcomb
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the clothier's golden age: John Winchcomb of Newbury rises from apprentice to the greatest clothier in England, his hundred looms employing hundreds, his wealth commanding kings, and his virtue (he feeds the poor, arms his men for Flodden, refuses a knighthood) making him the hero of England's craftsmen — the first English novel of the working world.
works.plot: Jack's rise, his marriage to his late master's widow, the great household of the looms, the visit of Queen Katherine, the expedition to Flodden, and the pranks of the courtiers against the honest clothier fill the episodic narrative, which closes on his death and the praise of his charity.
works.significance: The first great novel of English working life — the book that gave the artisan class its own literature, and the ancestor of the industrial novel.
works.meter: Plain, vigorous prose with interpolated songs and ballads, in the speech of shop and street.
works.context: Published 1597, in the decade of the cloth trade's crisis and the apprentices' unrest; its celebration of the clothier's charity answered the dearth and the poor laws with fiction.
works.characters: Jack (John Winchcomb); his wife (the widow); Queen Katherine; King Henry VIII; the courtiers; the clothiers of England
works.structure: An episodic biography in the jest-book and chronicle manner, built of set pieces — the banquet, the expedition, the courtiers' gulling — in the popular prose Deloney perfected.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Deloney

works.title: Jacob and Esau
altTitles: A New Mery and Wittie Comedie or Enterlude, Newely Imprinted, Treating upon the Historie of Jacob and Esau
works.description: An anonymous Protestant biblical interlude on the story of Jacob and Esau from Genesis, printed in 1568; one of the liveliest mid-century dramatizations of the doctrine of election.
works.plot: The play follows Genesis 25–27: the differing natures of the twins Jacob and Esau, the sale of the birthright for a pottage, Isaac's blessing of Jacob obtained through Rebecca's counsel, and Esau's rage and reconciliation; the serious matter of election is framed by the comic servants of the household (Ragan, Mido, and the boy Abra) whose tricks and misadventures mirror the plot.
works.significance: The most accomplished of the mid-century biblical interludes and an important document of Protestant dramatic theory; its comic subplot anticipates the structure of Elizabethan biblical and history plays.
works.meter: Couplets and 'rhyming fourteeners'
works.context: Composed c. 1550–58 in the Edwardian and Marian years, when the doctrine of predestination was at the centre of English religious debate; the play's prologue makes the case for the godly theatre, and it was printed in 1568 for the Elizabethan market.
works.characters: Isaac; Rebecca; Jacob; Esau; Ragan; Mido; Abra; Deborah; Hanan
works.structure: Five acts with act and scene divisions, alternating the biblical action with a fully developed comic subplot, and a prologue arguing that election is the play's theme.

works.title: James IV
altTitles: The Scottish History of James the Fourth
works.description: Greene's Scottish romance-play: King James IV of Scotland, married to Dorothea, falls in love with the English lady Ida and plots his queen's murder; Dorothea escapes in disguise, is saved by the English knight Sir Eustace and nursed back to health, and the play ends with the king's repentance, the recognition scene, and the reunion — a history play turned romance, framed by the chorus of Oberon and the fairies.
works.plot: James, corrupted by the flatterer Ateukin, orders Dorothea's death; the honest lords refuse and the queen flees in disguise; wounded, she is healed by Lady Anderson; the wars with England and the king's remorse lead to the final scene, where the disguised queen reveals herself and all is forgiven in the play's comedy of errors and recognitions.
works.significance: The bridge between the chronicle play and Shakespearean romance — the play in which Greene's pastoral art and the history vogue met.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the comic scenes, and the fairies' songs in the induction.
works.context: Printed in 1598 and performed about 1590; its Scottish matter predates James VI's accession to the English throne, and its 'history' is romance from the first.
works.characters: King James IV of Scotland; Queen Dorothea; Ida; Sir Eustace; Ateukin; Lady Anderson; Sir Cuthbert Anderson; the Bishop of St Andrews; Oberon; the fairies
works.structure: A five-act romance on a chronicle frame, with the fairy induction and interludes of Oberon, and the Anderson sub-plot as the comic engine of the recognition.

editions.title: James IV (Revels Plays)

works.title: Johan Johan
altTitles: A Mery Play between Johan Johan the Husbande, Tyb his Wyfe, and Syr Jhan the Preest
works.description: John Heywood's one-act farce of a cuckolded husband sent on errands by his wife and her lover the priest; printed by William Rastell in 1533.
works.plot: Johan Johan, suspecting his wife Tyb of entertaining Sir John the priest, is dispatched by her on a series of errands — to mend a pail, to fetch wax — while she dines with the priest; returning to find them feasting on a pie he was sent away from, Johan at last drives the priest out with blows, and the play ends with the husband's triumphant threat to beat Tyb too.
works.significance: The first English farce on the theme of the cuckolded husband and the anticlerical triangle that would recur through the century; its rapid domestic action makes it the most theatrically economical of Heywood's plays.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Printed in 1533 by Rastell, the year that saw the first parliamentary attacks on clerical marriage jurisdiction and mortuary fees; the play's satire of the lecherous parish priest draws on the fabliau tradition of Chaucer's Miller's Tale and the popular anticlerical jest.
works.characters: Johan Johan; Tyb (his wife); Sir John (the priest)
works.structure: A single-scene farce of errands and discovery, ending in a cudgel-fight; the play is a dramatization of the anti-clerical fabliau of the priest, the wife, and the credulous husband.

works.title: Judith
works.form: religious narrative (biblical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 349 lines (the opening is lost) retelling the apocryphal Book of Judith: the Hebrew heroine beheads the Assyrian general Holofernes in his tent and rouses her people to victory. The poem recasts the biblical heroine as a figure of the heroic tradition — a maiden of God wielding the sword against the enemies of her people.
works.plot: Judith, beautiful and wise, is brought to the drunken Holofernes's tent; praying for aid, she seizes his sword and strikes off his head in two blows, then carries the head back to Bethulia in a food-bag. At dawn she shows the head to her people and delivers a speech of triumph; the Hebrews attack the leaderless Assyrians, who flee; Judith receives the spoils of Holofernes as her reward, and the poem ends with praise of God.
works.significance: The finest Old English poem on a female biblical hero; a masterly fusion of heroic style and devotional purpose.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, with vigorous battle diction.
works.context: Preserved in the Nowell Codex (British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv) immediately after Beowulf; the biblical book of Judith was known to the Anglo-Saxons through the Vulgate and Ælfric's later prose homily on the same subject.
works.characters: Judith; Holofernes; the Bethulians
works.structure: Dramatic narrative in the heroic manner: the tent scene, the return, the battle, and the distribution of spoils; the heroine's speeches drive the action.
themes: Liberty of conscience and religious toleration

works.title: Juliana
works.form: religious narrative (hagiographical epic) in alliterative verse
works.description: Cynewulf's signed poem of 731 lines on the passion of St Juliana of Nicomedia: the virgin martyr who withstands her pagan suitor, defeats a demon sent to tempt her, and endures torture and death. The poem contains the most extended debate between saint and demon in Old English.
works.plot: Juliana refuses to marry the prefect Eleusius unless he converts; denounced by her father, she is beaten, hung by the hair, and thrown in prison, where a demon disguised as an angel urges her to yield; she seizes him and forces him to confess his works, then is subjected to fire and a boiling cauldron, and finally beheaded — her soul received into heaven, her persecutors drowned at sea. The epilogue carries Cynewulf's runic signature.
works.significance: The classic Old English virgin-martyr poem and the fullest statement of the saint-demon debate.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 65b-76v); based on a Latin passio of Juliana.
works.characters: Juliana; Eleusius; Africanus (her father); the demon; the angel
works.structure: A debate-driven passio: successive confrontations (suitor, father, demon, judge) leading to martyrdom, framed by the demon's confession of the history of evil and the poet's runic prayer.

works.title: Julius Caesar
works.description: Shakespeare's Roman tragedy of the republic's death: Brutus, honour's fool, joins the conspiracy against Caesar for Rome's sake; Caesar falls at the Capitol; Antony's funeral oration turns the crowd; and the play moves through the proscriptions and the quarrel of the conspirators to Philippi, where Brutus and Cassius die on their own swords.
works.plot: Cassius seduces Brutus into the conspiracy; Caesar, warned by the soothsayer and Calpurnia's dream, goes to the Senate and is murdered; Antony's 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' speech swings the mob to vengeance; the triumvirate proscribes its enemies; and the battles of Philippi complete the tragedy of Brutus, the noblest Roman of them all.
works.significance: The schoolroom tragedy of the English-speaking world — the standard by which political drama, and political oratory, have been measured ever since.
works.meter: A restrained, 'Roman' verse — no rhyme — with the prose of the plebeians and the two great orations as the peaks of its rhetoric.
works.context: Written 1599, the year of Essex's fall, from North's Plutarch; its anatomy of mob, coup, and civil war spoke to a court obsessed with succession and rebellion.
works.characters: Julius Caesar; Brutus; Cassius; Mark Antony; Portia; Calpurnia; Casca; Octavius Caesar; Cicero; Decius Brutus; the Soothsayer; Cinna the poet
works.structure: A two-part structure of conspiracy and war hinged on the assassination, with the funeral orations as the pivot of the play's rhetoric and the ghost of Caesar as its revenant.

works.title: King Arthur; or, The British Worthy
works.description: The Dryden-Purcell dramatic opera in five acts, celebrating Arthur's wars against the Saxons and his love for the blind Emmeline; it was originally conceived as a political allegory for the Exclusion Crisis and revived in the 1690s.
works.plot: Arthur pursues the Saxon Oswald, who has stolen Emmeline; through enchantment, battles, and the restoration of Emmeline's sight, Arthur defeats the Saxons and unites Britain.
works.significance: The greatest of the English semi-operas and the finest collaboration between a poet and a composer in the period; Purcell's score (including 'Fairest Isle' and the Frost Scene) is a landmark of English music.
works.meter: Mixed blank verse, rhyme, and song.
works.context: Drafted in the 1680s as a Whig allegory of the Exclusion Crisis and rewritten for performance by the United Company at the Queen's Theatre, Dorset Garden, in June 1691 with music by Henry Purcell.
works.characters: King Arthur; Emmeline; Oswald; Merlin; Osmond; Philidel; Grimbald; Conon; Aurelius
works.structure: Five acts with extensive music, masque episodes, and spectacular machinery; the spoken roles are limited to the principal characters.
works.attributionNotes: The text is by Dryden, the music by Purcell; the 1691 quarto names Dryden.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: King Hart
works.description: Douglas's allegory of the life of man: King Hart rules his castle of the body with the five senses as his servants until Dame Pleasance and her court — Youthheid, Fresche Delyte, Wantonness — enter and corrupt him; age, sickness, and death storm the castle, and the soul departs. The great Scots allegory of the body politic and the body natural.
works.plot: King Hart, counselled by Ressoun, admits Dame Pleasance and her court; the castle falls into riot; Conscience, Ressoun, and Wisdome are driven out; Age besieges and takes the castle, and Hart dies, leaving his soul to God's judgement.
works.significance: The finest Scots allegory of the body's rule and a bridge between the moralities and the Renaissance anatomy of the self; admired by the later Scots poets.
works.meter: Stanzaic verse in the Chaucerian tradition; vigorous personification allegory.
works.context: Written in Douglas's maturity, perhaps after the death of James IV at Flodden (1513); the castle's fall shadows the fall of the king's court.
works.characters: King Hart; Dame Pleasance; Youthheid; Fresche Delyte; Ressoun; Conscience; Age; Decrepitness
works.structure: A sustained allegory of the besieged castle in the morality tradition, moving from the entrance of pleasure through riot to death and judgement.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Douglas on manuscript authority; the attribution is generally accepted.

works.title: King Horn
works.description: The earliest surviving Middle English romance, some 1,500 short couplet lines telling the exile, adventures, and restoration of Horn, son of the murdered king of Suddene, who wins the love of Rymenhild, defeats the Saracen invaders, and regains his kingdom. Its spare, ballad-like narrative makes it the classic of the 'ancestral romance' of exile and return.
works.plot: Horn, cast adrift by the invaders who killed his father, grows up at the court of King Aylmar, where Rymenhild loves him; exiled through the envy of Fikenhild, he proves himself in Ireland, rescues Rymenhild from a forced marriage in disguise as a beggar, and returns to avenge his father and reclaim Suddene.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the English romance tradition and the earliest witness to the exile-and-return plot that governs the genre.
works.meter: Short rhyming couplets, often of three stresses, with formulaic diction.
works.context: Composed c. 1225 in the south of England from an Anglo-Norman source (the Romance of Horn of Thomas); preserved in Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27 (c. 1300) and two later manuscripts.
works.characters: Horn; Rymenhild; Fikenhild; King Aylmar; Athulf; the Saracen invaders
works.structure: A tripartite exile-and-return plot with disguise, recognition, and wedding scenes; narrated in terse couplets with abrupt transitions.

editions.title: King Horn: An Edition Based on Cambridge University Library MS Gg.4.27(2)

works.title: King Johan
works.description: John Bale's historical morality play of King John, composed c. 1538 and surviving in a single manuscript revised in the 1550s; regarded as the first English history play.
works.plot: King John, the champion of England's ancient liberties against the papal usurpation, is beset by the allegorical forces of Rome — Sedition, Dissimulation, Usurped Power, Private Wealth — and the clergy, who stir rebellion and bring about his poisoning by Dissimulation disguised as a monk; Widow England and her allies Verity and Imperial Majesty restore the true succession, and the play ends with John vindicated as a proto-Protestant martyr and the papal power expelled.
works.significance: The first English history play: its fusion of the morality tradition with national history and its anti-papal reading of King John set the pattern for the Elizabethan history play, directly anticipating Shakespeare's King John.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed c. 1538 during Bale's Protestant exile/activity under Cromwell's patronage, at the moment when Henry VIII's break with Rome made King John a usable hero; Bale revised the play for Elizabeth (the manuscript addresses her), aligning it with the Elizabethan settlement's anti-papal politics.
works.characters: King John; Widow England; Sedition; Dissimulation; Usurped Power; Private Wealth; Verity; Imperial Majesty; Nobility; Clergy; Civil Order; Stephen Langton; Pope Innocent III
works.structure: A two-part play mixing historical persons (John, Stephen Langton, the Pope) with morality personifications, revised by Bale to address Elizabeth I; the structure alternates the king's historical action with the Vices' comic plotting.

editions.title: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 1

works.title: King John
altTitles: The Life and Death of King John
works.description: Shakespeare's stand-alone history play of the Angevin crisis: King John's disputed title, the Bastard Faulconbridge's satirical commentary, the struggle with the papal legate Pandulph, and the play's terrible centre — the blinding of the boy Arthur and the grief of his mother Constance — ending in John's poisoning at Swinstead and the Bastard's closing appeal to England's unity.
works.plot: John defies Rome, battles France, captures Arthur, and orders his death; Hubert cannot blind the boy, but Arthur dies in his leap from the walls; the French invasion, the defection of the nobles, and John's poisoning follow, until the Bastard's loyalty and the Dauphin's withdrawal restore the kingdom.
works.significance: Shakespeare's boldest experiment in the history genre — a play without heroes, held together by the Bastard's irony and England's idea of itself.
works.meter: Blank verse of strong rhetorical sweep, with Constance's grief and the Bastard's 'commodity' soliloquy as the peaks.
works.context: Probably written 1595–96 in the anxious interval over the succession; its resistance to papal and foreign power spoke to Reformation England.
works.characters: King John; the Bastard (Philip Faulconbridge); Queen Elinor; Constance; Prince Arthur; Hubert; Cardinal Pandulph; King Philip of France; Lewis the Dauphin; Salisbury; Pembroke
works.structure: An episodic chronicle held together by the Bastard's choric commentary and by the Arthur tragedy at its centre.

works.title: King Lear
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of divided kingdom and broken nature: Lear abdicates, dividing Britain between the daughters who flatter him and disinheriting the one who loves him; cast out by Goneril and Regan, he goes mad on the heath in the storm with his Fool and the disguised Edgar, while the parallel plot of Gloucester and his sons runs to the blinding at Cornwall's hands — and the end brings Cordelia's death and Lear's over her body.
works.plot: Lear's love-test sets the tragedy in motion; Goneril and Regan strip him of his hundred knights; he rages into the storm, meets 'poor Tom' (Edgar), and is saved by Cordelia's French army; Gloucester, betrayed by Edmund and blinded, is led by Edgar to Dover; the battle is lost, Cordelia is hanged, and Lear dies of grief, leaving Edgar and Albany to close the play with its bleakest lines.
works.significance: By common consent the greatest tragedy in the language — the play that tests the limits of what tragedy can say about nature, justice, and the gods.
works.meter: A verse pushed to the edge of its resources — the storm scenes, Lear's curses, Edgar's mad speech, and the spare final lines — with prose for madness and the Fool's riddles.
works.context: Performed at court, 26 December 1606; the play draws on the old Leir play, Holinshed, and Sidney's Arcadia, and its two early texts (Quarto 1608 and Folio 1623) differ substantially.
works.characters: King Lear; Goneril; Regan; Cordelia; the Fool; the Earl of Gloucester; Edgar (Poor Tom); Edmund; the Duke of Albany; the Duke of Cornwall; Kent (Caius); Oswald; the King of France
works.structure: A double plot of Lear and Gloucester mirroring each other, built on the medieval morality pattern inverted — the trial of the daughters, the hovel, the cliff — and ending in the catastrophe that refuses consolation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the Quarto/Folio textual divergence is the play's standing editorial problem.

works.title: L'Allegro and Il Penseroso
works.description: A pair of companion poems contrasting two temperaments and ways of life: L'Allegro celebrates the active, social, cheerful mirth of the day and the countryside, while Il Penseroso praises the contemplative, melancholic, studious and religious delights of night and solitude.
works.plot: L'Allegro banishes melancholy and summons Mirth, tracing a day of rustic and urban pleasures culminating in music and masque; Il Penseroso banishes vain deluding joys and invokes 'pensive Nun', tracing a life of study, woodland meditation, church music, and a hoped-for prophetic vision.
works.significance: Among the most admired of Milton's shorter poems, they established his command of the English lyric and became models for eighteenth-century descriptive and meditative verse.
works.meter: Mixed tetrameter and pentameter couplets with varied lyric effects; the two poems mirror each other in structure.
works.context: Written during Milton's years of private study at Horton (c. 1632), published in the 1645 Poems; they reflect the Renaissance contrast of the active and contemplative lives.
works.characters: the poet; Mirth (Euphrosyne); Melancholy; the pensive Nun (Contemplation)
works.structure: Two matched lyrics in alternating tetrameter and pentameter couplets, structured as a balanced debate between the active and contemplative lives.

works.title: Lacnunga
works.form: medical manual and charm collection (Old English prose and verse)
works.description: A less orderly but more eclectic collection of remedies, charms, and prayers than Bald's Leechbook, compiled in the early eleventh century. It is best known for preserving the pagan-tinged metrical charms — above all the Nine Herbs Charm — alongside Christian prayers and learned Latin-derived recipes.
works.plot: The collection gathers remedies for wounds, fevers, eye and ear complaints, and childbirth, mixing herbal preparations with spoken charms and ritual instructions; its metrical charms invoke Woden and the herbs' powers while concluding with Christian formulas, in a characteristic fusion of traditions.
works.significance: The richest source of Old English charms, including the great Nine Herbs Charm, and a unique window onto the interface of learned medicine, popular healing, and pagan survival in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: The embedded charms are in alliterative verse (the Nine Herbs Charm, the Journey Charm); the surrounding recipes are plain instructional prose.
works.context: The manuscript belongs to the late Old English period's flourishing of vernacular medicine, when remedies circulated in monastic and lay households; the charms preserve elements of Germanic pre-Christian ritual under a Christian surface, a central document of the 'Christian-pagan synthesis'.
works.structure: A compilation in no strict order, grouping remedies by source rather than ailment; the metrical charms stand out from the surrounding prose as the collection's literary high points.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous compilation; the name 'Lacnunga' ('Remedies') is editorial, from the first remedy's heading.

editions.title: Anglo-Saxon Remedies, Charms, and Prayers from British Library MS Harley 585: The Lacnunga

works.title: Lament for the Makaris
works.description: William Dunbar's elegy on the poets ('makaris') of Scotland and the world (c. 1505, 100 lines): a procession of the dead — Chaucer, Lydgate, Gower, Henryson, and the court poets of the Stewart kings — each stanza closed by the refrain 'Timor mortis conturbat me' (the fear of death troubles me). The greatest short elegy of the Scottish tradition, and the poem that gave the makars their name.
works.plot: The poet, reflecting that all things must die, calls the roll of the dead poets: first the great English trio of Chaucer, Gower, and Lydgate, then the Scottish makers — Barbour, Hary, Holland, and above all 'the noble rhetor' Henryson — and finally the court poets of his own youth, closing with the fear of death and the petition that God provide for the poet before he joins them.
works.significance: One of the great elegies in the language: its roll-call fixed the canon of the makars and its refrain became the proverbial voice of late medieval mortality.
works.meter: Four-line stanzas with the Latin refrain, austere and musical.
works.context: Composed c. 1505 at the court of James IV, when Dunbar's generation was passing and the print era beginning; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508); it names the Scottish tradition 'makaris' for all later criticism.
works.characters: Dunbar (speaker); the dead poets (Chaucer, Gower, Lydgate, Barbour, Hary, Henryson, and others)
works.structure: Twenty-five stanzas of single-movement elegy, the refrain tolling each catalogue entry, in the ubi sunt tradition.

editions.title: The Poems of William Dunbar

works.title: Lancelot of the Laik
works.description: A Scottish romance of some 3,500 lines adapting the French prose Lancelot: Arthur's war with Galiot, Lancelot's secret love for Guinevere, and the dream-vision in which the lover's conscience anatomizes his state. The only Scottish Arthurian romance, composed in the age of the makars for a court that read both Chaucer and the French cycles.
works.plot: Arthur, weakened by tyranny and war with the rebel Galiot, is saved by Lancelot, who fights incognito and compels Galiot's submission; the second half turns inward, as a dream allegory of love's joys and pains lays bare Lancelot's adulterous devotion to the queen.
works.significance: The sole Scottish Arthurian romance and a significant witness to the reception of French Arthurian prose in the Stewart court.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in Older Scots, with aureate ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1460–79 in Scotland, adapting the French prose Lancelot and the amatory allegory tradition; preserved uniquely in Cambridge University Library MS Kk.1.5 (c. 1500).
works.characters: Lancelot; Arthur; Guinevere; Galiot
works.structure: A two-part structure — chivalric war, then amatory dream vision — that joins the French romance of arms to the Chaucerian allegory of love.

works.title: Laterculus Malalianus
altTitles: The Laterculus Malalianus of Theodore of Tarsus
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 139 (twelfth century)
works.description: A Latin exegetical and chronographical treatise on the life of Christ, attributed to Theodore of Tarsus, archbishop of Canterbury, and written at Canterbury in the 670s. Based on the Greek chronography of John Malalas, it expounds the gospel account of Christ's life in the light of eastern exegesis and computes the ages of the world; it is the principal surviving witness to the school of Theodore.
works.plot: The treatise moves through the life of Christ from the Incarnation to the Passion, glossing each episode with eastern exegetical traditions (on the Virgin, the baptism, the temptations, the crucifixion) and interweaving chronographical calculations of the world's ages drawn from Malalas's chronicle, concluding with eschatological reflection on the last things.
works.significance: The earliest theological work composed in England, and the founding document of the Canterbury school that made England a centre of Greek-influenced Latin learning; a unique witness to the eastern roots of Anglo-Saxon exegesis.
works.context: Written when Theodore and Hadrian were building the school of Canterbury, the treatise shows the direct importation of Greek and Syriac learning into England; the same exegetical traditions appear in the Canterbury biblical commentaries preserved in Milan, and Theodore's pupils carried them into the Northumbrian Renaissance of Bede.
works.structure: A continuous exegetical treatise organized by the gospel narrative, with digressions into chronology and typology; the style is dense and allusive, marked by the Greek learning of its source.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Theodore of Tarsus on the basis of its Greek sources, its Canterbury origin, and its consistent transmission with Theodore's school texts; the attribution is widely accepted but rests on inference rather than explicit ascription.

works.title: Layamon's Brut
works.description: Layamon's verse chronicle of Britain, some 16,000 lines adapting Wace's Roman de Brut with additions from Welsh and English tradition, from the Trojan Brutus to the Saxon conquest, including the fullest early English account of King Arthur. It is the first major treatment of the Arthurian legend in English.
works.plot: Following the Trojan Brutus's settlement of Britain, the poem recounts the line of British kings — Lear, Cymbeline, and above all Arthur, whose conquests, Round Table, and death it narrates at length — down to the Saxon victory and Arthur's prophesied return.
works.significance: The first Arthurian epic in English and the bridge from the alliterative tradition to Middle English romance; its Arthur material influenced the entire subsequent Arthurian tradition in England.
works.meter: A hybrid line blending the native alliterative half-line with loose rhyme and French-derived couplets; formulaic and archaic diction.
works.context: Composed by the priest Layamon of Areley Kings, Worcestershire, c. 1190–1215, in the generation after the loss of Normandy, when English was re-emerging as a literary language; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ix (earlier, longer) and Cotton MS Otho C.xiii (later, shortened, fire-damaged).
works.characters: Brutus; King Lear; Arthur; Guinevere; Merlin; Vortigern; Hengest; Cadwalader
works.structure: A continuous regnal chronicle organized by successive kings, with Arthur as its structural and emotional centre.
works.attributionNotes: Authorship secured by the prologue's self-naming of Layamon, priest of Ernleye (Areley Kings).

editions.title: Layamon's Brut, or Hystoria Brutonum
editions.editor: W. R. J. Barron and S. C. Weinberg (eds.)

works.title: Le Morte Darthur
altTitles: The Whole Book of King Arthur and of His Noble Knights of the Round Table
works.description: Sir Thomas Malory's great prose compilation of the Arthurian legend, completed in prison in 1469–70 and printed by Caxton in 1485: from the sword in the stone and the winning of Guinevere, through the adventures of Lancelot, Tristram, and the Grail quest, to the breaking of the Round Table, the last battle, and Arthur's passing to Avalon. The definitive English Arthurian book.
works.plot: Malory weaves the French prose cycles and English alliterative poems into a single tragic narrative: Arthur's accession and marriage, the founding of the Round Table, the quests and loves of its knights, the Grail quest that divides the fellowship, the adultery of Lancelot and Guinevere, and the final war against Mordred in which Arthur falls — his body borne to Avalon, his epitaph 'Rex quondam Rexque futurus'.
works.significance: The summit of English Arthurian literature and the conduit of the Arthurian story to Spenser, Tennyson, and the modern novel; its vision of chivalry — at once idealized and doomed — is the period's most enduring legacy.
works.meter: Prose: paratactic, ritual, and rhythmic, with the famous Malorian cadence of balanced clauses and repeated key words.
works.context: Completed by the 'knight prisoner' Thomas Malory in the ninth year of Edward IV (1469–70), during the Wars of the Roses; Caxton's 1485 print fixed the text for three centuries until the discovery of the Winchester manuscript (1934) revealed the pre-print version.
works.characters: Arthur; Lancelot; Guinevere; Gawain; Tristram; Isolde; Galahad; Merlin; Morgan le Fay; Mordred
works.structure: Eight books (Caxton's twenty-one divisions) of interlaced adventure compressed into linear narrative, with the Grail and the Lancelot-Guinevere tragedy as the arcs that break the fellowship.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sir Thomas Malory of Newbold Revel (d. 1471) on the evidence of the colophons; the identification is widely though not universally accepted.

editions.title: The Works of Sir Thomas Malory
editions.editor: Eugène Vinaver (ed.); rev. P. J. C. Field

works.title: Legends of Holy Women
works.description: Osbern Bokenham's collection of thirteen verse lives of female saints, written 1443–47 at the request of a circle of East Anglian patrons, several of them women: Margaret, Anne, Christine, the Eleven Thousand Virgins, Faith, Agnes, Dorothy, Mary Magdalene, Katherine, Cecilia, Agatha, Lucy, and Elizabeth of Hungary. The major fifteenth-century English legendary of women's sanctity.
works.plot: Each life narrates the saint's birth, conversion, and martyrdom (or holy death), with the debates, torments, and miracles of the genre; the framing prologues record the patrons who commissioned each legend, making the work a document of literary patronage as much as of hagiography.
works.significance: The principal fifteenth-century English collection of female saints' lives and a uniquely documented instance of women's literary patronage in the period.
works.meter: Couplets and rhyme royal in the Lydgatean style, aureate but warm.
works.context: Composed 1443–47 by the Augustinian friar Osbern Bokenham of Stoke by Clare, Suffolk, for Lady Katherine Denston, Isabel Hunt, and other East Anglian gentry women; preserved in BL Arundel MS 327 (the author's own manuscript).
works.characters: St Margaret; St Anne; St Katherine; St Mary Magdalene; St Cecilia; and the other saints; Bokenham (narrator)
works.structure: A sequence of independent verse legends, each with its own prologue naming the patron, in the Chaucerian-Lydgatean manner.
works.attributionNotes: Bokenham's authorship secure; he names himself and his patrons throughout.

works.title: Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple
works.description: The seventy-seven surviving letters written by Dorothy Osborne to William Temple during their long courtship in 1652-4, in which she discusses her family's opposition to the match, the books she is reading, and the state of the country under the Commonwealth.
works.plot: The letters trace the progress of the courtship against Osborne's brother's opposition and her own reluctance; they range freely over literature, gossip, politics, and the difficulty of a woman's position.
works.significance: The finest English letters of the seventeenth century and a crucial document of women's writing; their spontaneous style was admired by Virginia Woolf and they are the standard by which later familiar letters are judged.
works.meter: An easy, natural, unselfconscious prose that is the earliest great example of familiar English letter-writing.
works.context: Written 1652-4, during the Commonwealth, when Osborne was confined at Chicksands and Temple was travelling; they married in 1654.
works.characters: Dorothy Osborne; Sir William Temple; Sir Peter Osborne; Osborne's brother Henry
works.structure: A sequence of letters over about two years, with gaps.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Osborne; the manuscripts were printed in 1847 from the family papers (first partly published in 1713).

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Leviathan; or, The Matter, Forme, and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
works.description: Hobbes's masterwork of political philosophy, in which the commonwealth is conceived as an artificial man whose soul is sovereignty, founded on a covenant by which individuals transfer their right of self-government to an absolute sovereign.
works.plot: Part I ('Of Man') sets out Hobbes's materialist psychology and his state of nature, in which life is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; part II ('Of Common-Wealth') derives the sovereign's absolute authority from the social contract; part III ('Of a Christian Common-Wealth') subordinates the church to the state; part IV ('Of the Kingdom of Darkness') attacks scholastic and papal claims.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern political philosophy and of social contract theory; it transformed the vocabulary of politics, founded the modern theory of sovereignty, and provoked responses from Locke, Rousseau, and every subsequent theorist of the state.
works.meter: A powerful, lucid English prose deliberately free of rhetorical ornament; Hobbes's style became a model of the plain philosophical sentence.
works.context: Composed in Paris during Hobbes's exile and published in London in 1651, two years after the execution of Charles I; it was condemned by royalists and by Presbyterians alike and was later attacked in Parliament as an encouragement to atheism.
works.structure: Four parts in 47 numbered chapters, with the famous engraved frontispiece of the giant sovereign composed of his subjects.

editions.title: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts
editions.publisher: Clarendon Press (Clarendon Edition of the Works of Thomas Hobbes)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Life of King Alfred
works.description: Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893 by the Welsh bishop of Sherborne: the principal contemporary portrait of the king — his childhood, illnesses, wars against the Vikings, piety, and program of learning — and the main source for the Alfredian Renaissance.
works.plot: The life follows Alfred from birth (849) through his education and accession (871), the Viking wars culminating in Edington (878) and the treaty with Guthrum, the rebuilding of London and the kingdom's defences, and the gathering of scholars — Werferth, Plegmund, Æthelstan, Grimbald, John the Old Saxon — for the translation program; an annalistic section covers the years to 887, and the work ends with Alfred's daily round of prayer, judgment, and study.
works.significance: The primary source for Alfred's reign and the only near-contemporary biography of an Anglo-Saxon king.
works.meter: Latin prose of the ninth-century insular school.
works.context: Composed 893 at the West Saxon court; the unique manuscript (British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.xii) was largely destroyed in 1731, and the text rests on the 1574 edition and sixteenth-century transcripts.
works.characters: Alfred; Asser (narrator); Guthrum; Werferth; Plegmund; Ealhswith
works.structure: Biography modelled on Einhard's Charlemagne, with an embedded chronicle of the years 849-887 and anecdotal set-pieces (the story of the cakes is a later interpolation).
works.attributionNotes: Asser's authorship is stated in the text and generally accepted after long debate.
sources: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume B: The Sixteenth Century and the Early Seventeenth Century

works.title: Lily's Grammar
works.description: The authorized Latin grammar of the English schools, compiled from the grammars of William Lily and John Colet, edited and revised by Erasmus, and imposed by royal proclamation of Henry VIII in 1540 as the single grammar to be used in all schools.
works.plot: A textbook in two parts: the English 'Introduction of the Eight Parts of Speech' (the Accidence) and the Latin 'Brevissima Institutio' (syntax and prosody), with the famous prefatory poem 'Carmen de Moribus' on schoolboy manners.
works.significance: The most influential textbook in the history of English education: in use (as the 'Eton Grammar') for three centuries, it shaped the Latinity of every educated English writer from Shakespeare to Johnson, and its jingling rules became proverbial.
works.meter: Prose with Latin verse paradigms
works.context: The grammar grew out of Colet's statutes for St Paul's School (c. 1509), Lily's part in its composition, and Erasmus's revisions; after Lily's death (1522) it was printed in various forms until the royal proclamation of 1540 and the authorized edition of 1549 standardized it, making it the one book every grammar-school boy knew.
works.structure: Two-part pedagogical manual, with rules, paradigms, and examples arranged for memorization.
works.attributionNotes: A collaborative compilation traditionally credited to William Lily as first high master of St Paul's; Colet and Erasmus contributed substantially, and the standard attribution to Lily is conventional rather than strictly authorial.

works.title: Linacre's Galen translations
altTitles: The Galen Translations of Thomas Linacre
works.description: Thomas Linacre's Latin translations of six treatises of Galen, printed by Richard Pynson between 1521 and 1523, which restored the Greek Galen to European medicine and established Linacre as the founder of the English school of medical humanism.
works.plot: The translations cover Galen's De sanitate tuenda, Methodus medendi, De temperamentis, De naturalibus facultatibus, De pulsuum usu, and De symptomatum differentiis, rendered into a purified humanist Latin from the Greek texts Linacre collated.
works.significance: The founding texts of English medical humanism: by purging the medieval Latin Galen of Arabist corruption, Linacre transformed European medical education and helped found the Royal College of Physicians (1518), of which he was first president.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Translated c. 1517–23 after Linacre's Greek studies under Chalcondyles and Politian in Italy; Pynson printed the treatises in 1521–23, and they were reprinted on the continent, remaining the standard Latin Galen for over a century.
works.structure: Six separate treatises translated and printed with prefaces to Henry VIII and to Linacre's medical colleagues.

works.title: Lives (Walton)
altTitles: The Lives of Doctor John Donne, Sir Henry Wotton, Mr Richard Hooker, Doctor George Herbert, and Doctor Robert Sanderson
works.description: Walton's five biographies of Donne (1640), Wotton (1651), Hooker (1665), Herbert (1670), and Sanderson (1678), collected in 1670 and revised until his death in 1683; they created the modern English literary biography and the hagiographic ideal of the Anglican divine.
works.plot: Each life presents its subject as a model of Christian virtue: Donne the penitent preacher, Wotton the courtier-diplomat, Hooker the learned divine, Herbert the country parson, Sanderson the casuist.
works.significance: The Lives established Walton as the founder of English biographical prose and shaped the Anglican devotional ideal of the holy life; modern scholarship has shown their factual liberties, but their literary influence is immense.
works.meter: A deceptively simple, warm prose of anecdote and character.
works.context: Written across the civil wars, Commonwealth, and Restoration; the Life of Donne was based on Walton's personal knowledge and on Donne's own papers.
works.characters: John Donne; Sir Henry Wotton; Richard Hooker; George Herbert; Robert Sanderson
works.structure: Five separate lives, each with a portrait, letters, and verses.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Walton; the Life of Donne has been shown to borrow heavily from Donne's own writings and from earlier sources.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Lives of Saints
works.form: hagiography (saints' lives) in Old English prose
works.description: Ælfric's collection of saints' lives, passions, and legends (c. 993-998), composed for his patron Æthelweard: the largest vernacular hagiographical collection of the Anglo-Saxon period — virgins, martyrs, kings, and hermits of the universal church, told in Ælfric's rhythmical prose with his characteristic doctrinal care.
works.plot: The lives recount the passions of the early martyrs (Agnes, Alban, Lucy, the Forty Soldiers), the deeds of the virgin saints (Æthelthryth, Agatha, Cecilia), the kings and missionaries of England (Edmund, Oswald, Swithun, Cuthbert), and the great ascetics (Antony, Basil, Martin, Benedict) — each life framed by Ælfric's homiletic introductions and conclusions drawing out the moral for his audience.
works.significance: The fullest vernacular hagiography of the period; the principal vehicle of the saints' cults in late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Rhythmical, alliterative prose.
works.context: Composed at Cerne Abbas c. 993-998; the principal manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Julius E.vii.
works.characters: the saints of the collection; Æthelweard and Æthelmær (patrons)
works.structure: A collection of over thirty independent lives, each a self-contained narrative homily.
sources: The Poems of Andrew Marvell

works.title: Love and a Bottle
works.description: Farquhar's first comedy, a lively if derivative play of intrigue in which the Irish adventurer Roebuck arrives in London with nothing but love and a bottle and sets about marrying an heiress.
works.plot: Roebuck, newly arrived from Ireland, pursues the heiress Lucinda while his servant and the town's rogues complicate the plot; the intrigue is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: The debut of the last important Restoration dramatist and the beginning of the transition from the comedy of manners to the sentimental comedy of the eighteenth century.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1698 and published in 1699; Farquhar was a young Irish actor turned playwright after a stage accident.
works.characters: Roebuck; Lucinda; Leanwell; Clear; Sabina; Mrs Gainall; Lyrick
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love and Honour
works.description: Davenant's tragi-comedy of love tested by honour, in which a noble lady disguises herself as a poor servant to try the constancy of her lover before the war separates them.
works.plot: Evadne, beloved of the noble Prothall, disguises herself to test his faith; a series of misunderstandings, a supposed death, and a battlefield reunion resolve the conflict between love and honour.
works.significance: Davenant's first major success and a key example of Caroline tragicomedy; it also shows the beginnings of his interest in music and spectacle that would produce The Siege of Rhodes.
works.meter: Blank verse with songs.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men at the Blackfriars in 1634 and published in Davenant's collected Plays of 1639.
works.characters: Evadne; Prothall; Alphonso; Melora; the Duke; Aurelio
works.structure: Five acts with a disguise-testing plot and a final recognition.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love for Love
works.description: Congreve's most popular comedy, in which the improvident Valentine, disinherited by his father and pressed by his creditors, feigns madness to escape a forced marriage and finally wins Angelica.
works.plot: Valentine signs away his inheritance to Trapland and Forester; his father Sir Sampson Legend tries to marry him to Miss Prue; the scheming Angelica and the mad prophet Tattle are entangled until the plot resolves in Valentine's recovery and marriage.
works.significance: The most frequently revived of Congreve's comedies in his own lifetime and a principal model for eighteenth-century comedy; its treatment of debt and disinheritance is unusually sharp social commentary.
works.meter: Prose of great variety, from high wit to coarse farce.
works.context: First performed at the new Lincoln's Inn Fields Theatre on 30 April 1695, the opening of the breakaway actors' company under Betterton, and published the same year.
works.characters: Valentine; Angelica; Sir Sampson Legend; Ben Legend; Tattle; Mrs Frail; Miss Prue; Foresight; Jeremy; Trapland; Buckram; Scandal
works.structure: Five acts with a rich comic subplot of the nurse, the astrologer Foresight, and the country Miss Prue.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love in a Wood; or, St. James's Park
works.description: Wycherley's first comedy, a sprawling intrigue play set in St James's Park, in which masked gallants and ladies pursue one another through a series of night adventures.
works.plot: Several couples are entangled in the fashionable world of the Park and the Exchange; disguises, duels, and betrayals are resolved in a set of marriages, with the virtuous Dapperwit exposed as a wit.
works.significance: An early and uneven but energetic comedy that anticipates Wycherley's later severity; its portrait of the Park is a valuable document of Restoration London.
works.meter: Prose dominant with some verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1671 and published in 1672, dedicated to the Duchess of Cleveland.
works.characters: Ranger; Vincent; Lydia; Martha; Dapperwit; Mrs Crossbite; Alderman Gripe; Simon
works.structure: Five acts with multiple plots and a low comic subplot of the city.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love's Labour's Lost
works.description: Shakespeare's most verbally extravagant comedy: the King of Navarre and his three lords swear a three-year vow of study, fasting, and no women — a vow broken at once by the arrival of the Princess of France and her ladies, whose wit outmatches the men's until the play's astonishing turn: news of the Princess's father's death converts the comedy into a year of penance and a set of unfinished songs.
works.plot: The lords woo the ladies in disguise and are exposed; the pedants Holofernes and Nathaniel stage the pageant of the Nine Worthies and are mocked; and just as the marriages are to be concluded, Marcade enters with the news of the French king's death, and the ladies impose their year-long conditions on the suitors.
works.significance: The summit of Elizabethan verbal comedy and the play in which Shakespeare's lyric genius first runs free.
works.meter: The highest proportion of rhyme in Shakespeare, with sonnets, songs, and the prose of the pedants' Latinity.
works.context: Written about 1594–95 amid the French succession crisis and the Euphuistic wordplay fashion it both satirizes and surpasses; first printed in quarto, 1598.
works.characters: Ferdinand, King of Navarre; Berowne; Longaville; Dumaine; the Princess of France; Rosaline; Maria; Katherine; Boyet; Don Armado; Holofernes; Nathaniel; Costard; Jaquenetta; Moth
works.structure: A plotless, tournament-like comedy of wit built on symmetrical scenes of courtship, masque, and pageant, ending in the deliberately anti-comic 'dialogue' of Spring and Winter songs.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Love's Last Shift; or, The Fool in Fashion
works.description: Colley Cibber's first comedy, in which the rake Loveless is reformed by his long-suffering wife Amanda; the play's famous double structure — libertine comedy in the first half, moral reform in the second — provoked Vanbrugh's answer in The Relapse.
works.plot: Loveless, believing Amanda a stranger, seduces her in disguise; she reveals herself and he is reformed; the comic subplot of Sir Novelty Fashion satirises the fashionable fop.
works.significance: Usually cited as the first sentimental comedy in English and the pivot between Restoration libertinism and eighteenth-century moral reform; Cibber's career as actor-manager of Drury Lane shaped the Georgian stage.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in January 1696 with Cibber himself as Sir Novelty Fashion; the role made him famous and the play was a great success.
works.characters: Loveless; Amanda; Sir Novelty Fashion; Young Worthy; Snap; Narcissa; Flareit
works.structure: Five acts with a sharp generic shift at the centre that critics have called the origin of sentimental comedy.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love's Sacrifice
works.description: Ford's tragedy of unwarranted jealousy, in which the Duke of Pavy, persuaded by his secretary Nibrassa, believes his duchess Bianca unfaithful to him with his friend Fernando, and kills her before learning the truth.
works.plot: The Duke marries Bianca but loves his friend Fernando more; Fernando and Bianca love each other chastely; the malicious secretary sows suspicion; the Duke murders Bianca and Fernando, then kills himself in remorse.
works.significance: A notable Caroline reworking of the Othello situation, and an important example of Ford's preoccupation with honour and the destruction of innocence.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Published 1633, performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Phoenix.
works.characters: the Duke of Pavy; Bianca; Fernando; Nibrassa; Fiormonda; Colona; Petruchio
works.structure: Five acts following the Othello pattern of jealousy induced by a villain and resolved in catastrophe.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
works.description: Behn's epistolary novel in three parts, based on the real scandal of Lord Grey of Warke's elopement with his wife's sister, in which Philander seduces Silvia and she descends through a series of lovers into prostitution and political intrigue.
works.plot: Philander writes to Silvia, his sister-in-law; they elope; he tires of her and takes another mistress; Silvia responds by seducing and abandoning a series of men, becoming a courtesan and finally a political agent of Monmouth's rebellion.
works.significance: The first major English epistolary novel and a decisive step toward the eighteenth-century novel of Richardson and Laclos; its portrayal of a woman's sexual and political agency was unprecedented.
works.meter: Prose with interpolated verse.
works.context: Published in three parts between 1684 and 1687, at the time of the Monmouth Rebellion; it is a roman à clef on the Grey-Sisters scandal.
works.characters: Philander; Silvia; Calista; Octavio; Don Alonzo; Cesario; the Countess
works.structure: Three parts (1684, 1685, 1687) of letters with narrative interludes, the first substantial English epistolary fiction.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in parts; attribution to Behn is long-established and undisputed.

editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)
