works.title: Lucasta
works.description: Richard Lovelace's collection of Cavalier verse (1649), named for his mistress Lucy Sacheverell ('Lucasta'), containing his most famous lyrics — 'To Althea, from Prison', 'To Lucasta, Going to the Wars', and 'The Grasshopper' — which made the code of love and honour the motto of the royalist gentleman.
works.plot: The poems celebrate love, friendship, loyalty, and liberty of spirit even in prison and defeat, arguing that honour and constancy survive political ruin ('Stone walls do not a prison make, / Nor iron bars a cage').
works.significance: Lucasta is the classic Cavalier collection; 'To Althea' and 'To Lucasta' are among the most quoted poems of the seventeenth century and define royalist gallantry.
works.meter: Musical, dignified lyrics in varied meters with argumentative conceits of love and honour.
works.context: Lovelace prepared the collection during his imprisonment in the Gatehouse (1648–49) for his royalist loyalty; it was published in 1649, the year of the regicide.
works.characters: the poet; Lucasta; Althea; fellow Cavaliers
works.structure: A collection of songs, odes, elegies, and occasional verse unified by the Cavalier ethos and the figure of Lucasta.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; a posthumous second part appeared in 1659/60.

works.title: Lucius Junius Brutus, Father of His Country
works.description: Lee's republican tragedy on the expulsion of the Tarquins and the founding of the Roman republic, banned by the Lord Chamberlain in 1680 for its allegedly republican politics.
works.plot: Brutus feigns idiocy under the tyrant Tarquin; after the rape of Lucretia he leads the revolt, and sacrifices his own sons for treason rather than betray the new republic.
works.significance: An important document of Whig political sentiment in the drama and a forerunner of the eighteenth-century republican tragedies of Addison and Thomson; its suppression is a classic case of Restoration censorship.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Prohibited from performance in 1680 by the Lord Chamberlain on the ground that it contained 'very scandalous expressions and reflections upon monarchical government'; printed in 1681 during the Exclusion Crisis.
works.characters: Lucius Junius Brutus; Tarquin; Lucretia; Teraminta; Titus; Tiberius; Collatinus; Herminius
works.structure: Five acts of political tragedy culminating in the hero's filial sacrifice.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Lusty Juventus
works.description: A Protestant morality interlude of the youth Juventus, tempted by Hypocrisy and the devil but restored by Good Counsel and God's Merciful Promises; printed c. 1550 with the author's name given as R. Wever.
works.plot: Juventus (Youth), fresh from his conversion, is tempted by the devil's instruments — Hypocrisy, Fellowship, and Abominable Living — who draw him into sin and despair; Good Counsel and Knowledge recall him, God's Merciful Promises assures him of forgiveness through Christ, and the play ends with Juventus's restoration and a call to the audience to follow his example.
works.significance: The most explicitly doctrinal of the Edwardian moralities and a prime example of the interlude as Reformation propaganda; its title character became the proverbial type of the reformed youth.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages
works.context: Composed in the early years of the Edwardian Reformation (c. 1547–53) and printed c. 1550; its polemic against hypocrisy and works-righteousness and its emphasis on justification by faith make it a direct dramatic expression of Protestant doctrine for a young audience.
works.characters: Juventus; Good Counsel; Knowledge; God's Merciful Promises; The Devil; Hypocrisy; Fellowship; Abominable Living
works.structure: A continuous morality play of temptation, fall, and restoration, with the devil and Hypocrisy as the comic Vices and a concluding address to the young.
works.attributionNotes: The title page names 'R. Wever' as author; nothing further is known of him, and the ascription cannot be independently confirmed.

works.title: Lycidas
works.description: Milton's pastoral elegy for Edward King, a Cambridge contemporary drowned off the Irish coast in 1637, written for the memorial volume Justa Edouardo King; it mourns the young poet's death, indicts the corrupt clergy, and consoles with the promise of resurrection and fame in heaven.
works.plot: The shepherd-poet mourns Lycidas, questions divine justice, invokes the Muse and St Peter (who denounces the 'blind mouths' of the corrupt church), hears the tale of Lycidas's drowning and apotheosis, and finds consolation in the belief that he is 'sunk low, but mounted high' as the genius of the shore.
works.significance: Widely regarded as the greatest pastoral elegy in English, Lycidas combines personal grief, political and religious satire, and visionary consolation in a uniquely wrought form.
works.meter: A varied and intricately rhymed pastoral stanza of irregular line lengths, with carefully placed short lines and refrains.
works.context: Written in 1637 for the collection Justa Edouardo King Naufrago (1638); it draws on the pastoral elegiac tradition from Theocritus and Virgil to Spenser, transfigured by Milton's Puritan faith and anticlerical anger.
works.characters: the uncouth swain (Milton); Lycidas (Edward King); St Peter; the Muse; Jove
works.structure: A pastoral elegy in irregular verse, moving from grief and doubt through the prophetic denunciation by St Peter to Christian consolation and the poet's turn to 'pastures new'.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; signed 'J.M.' in the 1638 volume and included in the 1645 Poems.

The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

works.title: Mac Flecknoe
altTitles: Mac Flecknoe: A Satire upon the True-blew-Protestant Poet, T. S.
works.description: Dryden's short mock-heroic satire on Thomas Shadwell, imagining the dull poet Richard Flecknoe abdicating his empire of nonsense and choosing Shadwell as his heir.
works.plot: Flecknoe, monarch of the realm of dullness, delivers a coronation speech naming Shadwell as his successor; Shadwell is crowned amid burlesque pomp and vanishes through a trapdoor.
works.significance: The first sustained mock-heroic in English and the direct model for Pope's The Dunciad; it established the 'empire of dullness' conceit that dominated Augustan satire.
works.meter: Heroic couplets used to comic effect by sustaining an epic register throughout.
works.context: Written between about 1678 and 1682, circulated in manuscript, and printed without Dryden's name in 1682; it arises from the quarrel over dramatic criticism that began with The Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
works.characters: Richard Flecknoe; Thomas Shadwell (Sh—-); Henry VIII's ghost; Arion
works.structure: A single continuous mock-coronation scene in elevated epic diction, ending with the sudden comic collapse of the hero.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously in 1682 and ascribed to Dryden by contemporaries; attribution undisputed.

The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: Macbeth
works.description: Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, of ambition and the supernatural: the Scottish general Macbeth, told by the Weird Sisters that he shall be king, murders Duncan in his sleep and enters a reign of blood — Banquo's murder, the apparitions' riddling prophecies, the slaughter of Macduff's family — until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane and the tyrant falls to the man 'not of woman born'.
works.plot: The prophecies kindle Macbeth's ambition and Lady Macbeth steels him to the murder; the crown brings only sleeplessness and escalating violence; Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking confession and death precede the final battle, where the equivocations of the witches are fulfilled and Macduff beheads the tyrant.
works.significance: The supreme English tragedy of evil's self-entrapment — the shortest road to the heart of darkness the stage has ever built.
works.meter: The densest verse in Shakespeare — image packed and accelerated — with the witches' tetrameter charms and the Porter's prose as deliberate descents.
works.context: Written 1606 for the new king, James I, the patron of the company and the author of Daemonologie; the play's Scottish matter, witchcraft, and Banquo's royal line all court the Stuart interest.
works.characters: Macbeth; Lady Macbeth; Banquo; the Weird Sisters; Duncan; Macduff; Lady Macduff; Malcolm; Donalbain; Ross; Lennox; the Porter; Fleance
works.structure: A single-line tragedy of mounting speed, structured by the three prophecies and their ironic fulfilments, with the banquet scene as its turning point and the sleepwalking scene as its moral climax.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the Hecate scenes may be later interpolations (possibly by Middleton).

works.title: Magnificence
works.description: Skelton's morality play: Prince Magnificence, a figure of the good ruler (and transparently of Henry VIII), is seduced by the courtly vices — Fansy, Counterfeit Countenance, Cloaked Collusion, Courtly Abusion — into riot and misrule, stripped of his wealth and driven to despair, and finally restored by Good Hope, Perseverance, and Measure.
works.plot: Liberty and Measure advise the Prince against Fansy; Magnificence follows the vices, is robbed and reduced to suicidal despair by Adversity, and is rescued by Good Hope, Redress, and Perseverance, who restore him to the rule of Measure.
works.significance: The first English morality play with a political programme and the bridge between the medieval moralities and the Tudor interludes; it established the genre of the king-as-everyman that Bale and the Elizabethans inherited.
works.meter: Couplets and short stanzas of functional verse, with Skeltonic flourishes in the Vice speeches.
works.context: Written in the years of Wolsey's ascendancy, when Skelton watched the young king's government with alarm; the play reads as a warning to Henry VIII against misrule and extravagance.
works.characters: Magnificence; Fansy; Counterfeit Countenance; Cloaked Collusion; Courtly Abusion; Adversity; Good Hope; Perseverance; Measure
works.structure: A full-scale morality in the tradition of Everyman, with a political allegory of the prince's fall and amendment; the Vice roles carry the comic weight.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: Mandeville's Travels
altTitles: The Voyage and Travels of Sir John Mandeville
works.description: The Book of Sir John Mandeville, the most popular travel book of the Middle Ages: a compilation, originally in French (c. 1357), of pilgrimage routes to Jerusalem, the marvels of Asia, the lands of Prester John, and the wonders of the East, framed by the persona of an English knight of St Albans whose travels are largely fictive. Its Middle English versions (from c. 1375) circulated more widely than any other travel narrative.
works.plot: The narrator describes the way to Jerusalem and the holy places, then the farther East — Egypt, India, Cathay, the isles of the East — collecting marvels (the vegetable lamb, the phoenix, the fountain of youth), the palace of Prester John, and the customs of strange peoples, in a geography poised between pilgrimage, wonder, and imperial fantasy.
works.significance: The great medieval bestseller of travel and wonder, and a foundational text of the European imagination of the East — read by explorers into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose: plain, fluent, and endlessly translatable; the English versions descend from the French via Latin.
works.context: Composed in French c. 1357, probably by a clerk in Liège or northern France using genuine itineraries and encyclopedias; translated into English from c. 1375 in several versions (the 'Defective' version foremost); printed by Wynkyn de Worde (1496); Columbus and Raleigh read it.
works.characters: Sir John Mandeville (persona); Prester John; the Great Khan
works.structure: An itinerary organized by regions and routes, with the pilgrimage to Jerusalem as its centre and the marvels of the East as its circumference.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the 'Sir John Mandeville' persona is generally regarded as fictional.

editions.title: Mandeville's Travels

works.title: Mankind
works.description: The liveliest of the English moralities (c. 1465–70): the comedy of Mankind, the East Anglian farmer, tempted from his spade and his beads by Mischief, New Guise, Nowadays, and Nought, and the devil Titivillus, whose whispered discouragements drive him to despair — until Mercy reclaims him. Famous for its scatological comedy and its collection of money from the audience, it shows the morality in its most theatrical form.
works.plot: Mercy instructs Mankind in labour and prayer; the vice-companions tempt him to idleness and lechery; the devil Titivillus, appearing under the stage, whispers despair and steals his devotion; Mankind falls, is saved from suicide by Mercy's return, and repents, beating off the vices with his spade.
works.significance: The most theatrical of the moralities and a key witness to professional playing in the fifteenth century; its Titivillus and audience games bridge medieval and Tudor comedy.
works.meter: Couplets, stanza forms, and the macaronic dog-Latin of the vices, with remarkable metrical variety.
works.context: Composed c. 1465–70 in East Anglia (Cambridgeshire/Norfolk), for performance by a travelling company; preserved in the Macro manuscript (Folger MS V.a.354).
works.characters: Mankind; Mercy; Mischief; New Guise; Nowadays; Nought; Titivillus
works.structure: A compact morality of temptation, fall, and mercy, in the alternating mode of sermon and farce, with direct address and the audience collection ('Now gostly to our purpose') as its signature.

editions.title: The Macro Plays

works.title: Marriage à la Mode
works.description: Dryden's tragicomedy, dedicated to the Earl of Rochester, which joins a high heroic plot of usurpation and concealed royalty with a low prose comedy of cuckoldry and gallantry.
works.plot: In Sicily, the usurped king's true son Polydamas is discovered and restored, while in the comic plot Rhodophil and Palamede pursue each other's wives and are undone by their own devices.
works.significance: The finest Restoration tragicomedy and Dryden's best comedy; Melantha is one of the great comic portraits of the period and the play remained a repertory favourite.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets in the high plot and prose in the low plot.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1672 and published in 1673; Melantha's affectation of French fashions satirises the court's Francophilia.
works.characters: Polydamas; Leonidas; Amalthea; Palmyra; Rhodophil; Palamede; Doralice; Melantha; Selin
works.structure: Five acts with a double plot: heroic verse tragedy above and prose comedy below, ending in both a recognition and a set of marriages.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden

works.title: Maxims I and II
works.form: wisdom poetry (gnomic verse) in alliterative verse
works.description: Two collections of gnomic verse — Maxims I in the Exeter Book (204 lines, in three sections) and Maxims II in British Library Cotton Tiberius B.i (66 lines) — assembling traditional wisdom about the order of the world: what befits a king, a warrior, a woman, a tree, frost, the sea, and the road; 'wyrd goes as it shall'.
works.plot: The maxims proceed by association through the natural and social orders: the king belongs in the hall, the sword in battle, the hawk on the glove, the frost to the earth, the mind to wisdom; each thing is 'in its place' — a poetic articulation of the period's sense of a world arranged by custom and providence.
works.significance: The fullest repository of Old English gnomic wisdom and of the period's sense of natural and social order.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre in short, proverb-like units.
works.context: Maxims I: Exeter Book (fols. 88b-92b); Maxims II: London, British Library, Cotton MS Tiberius B.i (with the Menologium, c. 1050).
works.characters: none
works.structure: Catalogue structure: strings of 'X shall be / belongs to' gnomes, organized by loose association rather than narrative.

works.title: Measure for Measure
works.description: Shakespeare's great comedy of justice and mercy: the Duke of Vienna, disguised as a friar, leaves the puritanical Angelo to enforce the city's neglected laws; Angelo condemns Claudio to death for fornication, then offers to spare him if his sister Isabella will yield her virginity — a bargain exposed in the final judgment scene, where the Duke returns to measure all by their own measure.
works.plot: Angelo revives the death penalty for lechery; Claudio's sister Isabella pleads for him; Angelo's blackmail and the bed-trick with the jilted Mariana preserve Isabella and expose Angelo; the Duke's staged return conducts the play's long trial-and-pardon finale, ending with his abrupt proposal to Isabella.
works.significance: Shakespeare's deepest study of law, sex, and power — a play that has grown darker and more central with every century.
works.meter: A grave, economical blank verse, with the prose of the Vienna underworld (Pompey, Lucio) as corrosive chorus.
works.context: Performed at court, 26 December 1604; the play's Vienna shadows Jacobean London's anxieties over plague, puritanism, and the royal exercise of mercy.
works.characters: Duke Vincentio; Angelo; Isabella; Claudio; Mariana; Lucio; Escalus; Pompey; Mistress Overdone; Elbow; the Provost; Barnardine
works.structure: A legal fable on the title's biblical text, built on the Duke's disguised supervision and resolved in the massed judgment scene of Act 5.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; minor passages possibly revised by Middleton.

works.title: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson
altTitles: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel John Hutchinson
works.description: Lucy Hutchinson's biography of her husband, the regicide Colonel John Hutchinson, written in the 1670s as a vindication of his honour and of the parliamentary cause, and the most important work of prose by a woman of the seventeenth century.
works.plot: The memoir narrates Hutchinson's life from his education at Nottingham through his service for Parliament in the civil wars, his governance of Nottingham Castle, his refusal to vote at the king's trial, his imprisonment after the Restoration, and his death at Sandown Castle in 1664.
works.significance: A canonical work of women's writing and of Restoration literary history; it is the most important prose life of a parliamentarian and a central text in the study of seventeenth-century women's authorship.
works.meter: A clear, vigorous, and emotionally restrained prose, with moments of great eloquence.
works.context: Written in the 1670s for her children and not published until 1806; it is a rare first-hand account of the parliamentary side by a woman of the gentry.
works.characters: Colonel John Hutchinson; Lucy Hutchinson; Sir Allen Apsley; Colonel Thomas Hutchinson; Oliver Cromwell; Charles I
works.structure: A continuous biographical narrative with digressions on Lucy's own life and on the politics of the period.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand.

works.title: Menaphon
works.description: Greene's pastoral romance: the shepherd Menaphon, the disguised princess Sephestia and her son, and the rival suitors of Arcadia play out the loves, riddles, and recognitions of the pastoral world, with the inserted eclogues and the story of the treacherous Samela — the whole prefaced by Thomas Nashe's address 'To the Gentlemen Students', with its famous survey of the English poets.
works.plot: Sephestia, shipwrecked and disguised as Samela, is wooed by the shepherd Menaphon, the courtier Melicertus (her own husband in disguise), and the tyrant Democles; the oracles, the riddles of parentage, and the final recognitions restore the royal family, with the eclogues and debates of the shepherds as interludes.
works.significance: The best of Greene's Arcadian romances and the vehicle of Nashe's manifesto — the first public statement of the new Elizabethan literary generation.
works.meter: Prose of the pastoral mode with interpolated verse, in Greene's most polished Arcadian style.
works.context: Published 1589, in the wake of Sidney's Arcadia's manuscript fame; Nashe's preface praises Sidney, Spenser, and the new poetry and dismisses the 'deep read grammarians' — a manifesto of the 1590s avant-garde.
works.characters: Menaphon; Sephestia (Samela); Melicertus (Maximius); Democles; the child Pleusidippus; Doron; Carmela
works.structure: A prose romance with verse eclogues in the Sidneyan manner, prefaced by Nashe's critical epistle — one of the key documents of Elizabethan literary self-consciousness.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; Nashe's preface is his own.

editions.title: The Life and Complete Works in Prose and Verse of Robert Greene, 15 vols.

works.title: Micrographia: or, Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses
works.form: scientific treatise; natural history; illustrated book
works.description: Robert Hooke's account of his observations through the compound microscope, published by the Royal Society in 1665 with fifty-seven magnificent engraved plates, in which he first used the word 'cell' for the units of plant tissue.
works.plot: Hooke describes and illustrates the point of a needle, the edge of a razor, silk, cork, charcoal, moss, nettles, insects including the fly's eye and the flea, the moon, and the stars, arguing that microscopy reveals a hidden order in nature.
works.significance: The founding work of microscopy and of cell biology; the word 'cell' originates here, and its plates created the visual language of modern science.
works.meter: Precise descriptive prose; the plates by Hooke himself are among the finest scientific illustrations ever made.
works.context: Published in September 1665 by the Royal Society; it was the first major publication of the Society and a sensation at court, where Pepys recorded it as 'the most ingenious book that ever I read in my life'.
works.structure: A series of numbered observations, each with an engraved plate and a commentary.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Middle English Religious Lyrics
works.description: The devotional strand of the Middle English lyric corpus: meditations on the Passion ('I syng of a myden', 'Lullay, myn lykyng'), laments of the Virgin at the cross (the planctus Mariae), prayers to Christ and the saints, and poems on death and judgement. These lyrics carry the affective piety of the period into verse of great formal variety and emotional power.
works.plot: The poems stage the central scenes of late medieval devotion — the Annunciation, the Nativity, the Crucifixion as witnessed by Mary, the soul's dialogue with the crucified Christ, the memento mori — in first-person, lyric form.
works.significance: The most intimate record of late medieval English piety; together with the mystery plays, the religious lyrics are the principal vernacular vehicle of Passion and Marian devotion.
works.meter: Carol form, tail-rhyme, rhyme royal, and macaronic verse, often with musical settings implied by burdens and refrains.
works.context: The lyrics were copied into preaching and devotional manuscripts (the Vernon manuscript, Digby 102, Sloane 2593) and printed in early sixteenth-century carol collections; many served Franciscan and parochial devotion.
works.characters: Christ; the Virgin Mary; the soul (speaker)
works.structure: A corpus of independent lyrics; the characteristic movements are invocation, meditation, and petition.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous as a corpus; a few poems are attributed to known devotional writers.

works.title: Milton's Sonnets
works.description: Milton's twenty-four English and five Italian sonnets, written over some thirty years: a sequence of public and private meditations including 'How soon hath Time', 'On His Blindness' ('When I consider how my light is spent'), the political sonnets 'On the Late Massacre at Piemont' and 'To the Lord General Cromwell', and the dream-elegy 'Methought I saw my late espoused saint'.
works.plot: Rather than a love sequence, the sonnets treat vocation, blindness, public service, religious persecution, friendship, and loss, each an argument or meditation resolved in the closing lines.
works.significance: Milton restored the sonnet to serious public and moral use, breaking from the Elizabethan love sequence and influencing Wordsworth and the modern sonnet ('Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour').
works.meter: The Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet with Miltonic enjambment and a grand, sonorous syntax that overflows the traditional divisions.
works.context: Composed from about 1630 to the 1650s–60s; most were published in the 1673 Poems, and they record Milton's engagement with the Civil Wars, the Commonwealth, his blindness, and personal bereavement.
works.characters: the poet; Patience (in 'On His Blindness'); various dedicatees (Cromwell, Vane, Fairfax)
works.structure: A non-sequential collection of occasional and meditative sonnets, unified by Milton's concern with duty, faith, and his poetic calling.

works.title: Miscellaneous Thoughts and Posthumous Works of Samuel Butler
altTitles: The Genuine Remains in Verse and Prose of Mr. Samuel Butler
works.description: Butler's posthumous collection of notebook verses, characters, letters, and prose satires, including 'The Elephant in the Moon', printed from his manuscripts long after his death in 1680.
works.plot: The volume gathers Butler's satirical characters (a set of prose portraits in the tradition of Theophrastus), his philosophical squibs against the Royal Society, and longer poems such as the lunar fable.
works.significance: 'The Elephant in the Moon' is a notable early satire on the new experimental philosophy, and the characters are an important link between Earle's Microcosmographie and Addison's Spectator papers.
works.meter: Mixed: prose characters and octosyllabic verse satires.
works.context: Butler's notebooks passed to William Longueville and were printed as The Genuine Remains in 1759 by John Thyer; some pieces are of doubtful authenticity.
works.structure: A miscellany of prose characters, notes, letters, and verse satires.
works.attributionNotes: Printed from manuscripts attributed to Butler; a small number of pieces are of doubtful authenticity.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler

works.title: Mucedorus
altTitles: A Most Pleasant Comedy of Mucedorus, the King's Son of Valentia
works.description: The anonymous romance-comedy that became the best-selling play of the age: Mucedorus, prince of Valentia, disguises himself as a shepherd to woo the princess Amadine of Aragon; the wild man Bremo, the bear, and the clown Mouse fill the forest adventures; and the play ends with the lovers' marriage, Bremo's defeat, and — in the 1610 revision — the added scenes of the bear's death and the king's feast.
works.plot: Mucedorus leaves court in disguise; Amadine, fleeing the wild man Bremo, meets the shepherd; the courtship, the clown Mouse's cowardice, and the fight with Bremo follow; the play moves to the recognition and the wedding, with the 1610 additions (attributed to Shakespeare in the printed text) supplying the bear scene and the final entertainment.
works.significance: The most popular play of the early Stuart stage — the romance-comedy that travelled England with the strolling players.
works.meter: Loose blank verse and prose, with the clown's jests and the Induction's debate of Envy and Comedy.
works.context: Probably written about 1590, printed in 1598, and revised in 1610 with additions 'newly set forth'; it went through more editions before 1642 than any other play, its Shakespearian ascription a bookseller's later device.
works.characters: Mucedorus; Amadine; Bremo the wild man; Mouse the clown; the King of Aragon; Segasto; Envy, Comedy (the Induction); the bear; the King of Valentia
works.structure: A five-act romance-comedy in the old-fashioned mode — disguised prince, wild man, clown — that its very simplicity made immortal in the provinces.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the 1610 additions were claimed for Shakespeare by the publisher, an ascription now generally rejected.

works.title: Much Ado About Nothing
works.description: Shakespeare's comedy of wit and slander: the 'merry war' of Beatrice and Benedick is tricked into love by their friends, while the villain Don John's plot makes Claudio believe his bride Hero unfaithful — a lie that kills her (apparently) at the altar, until the watch's comic detective work exposes the plot and Hero returns from the dead.
works.plot: Don Pedro's court at Messina: Claudio and Hero are betrothed; Beatrice and Benedick are gulled into confessing love by overheard conversations; Don John stages the scene of Hero's infidelity with Margaret; Hero is denounced and shammed dead; Dogberry and the Watch stumble on the truth, and the double wedding concludes the play.
works.significance: The model of the comedy of wit, whose sparring lovers founded a tradition running through Restoration comedy to the screwball film.
works.meter: Prose for the wit-combats, blank verse for the romantic crises, with the songs of Balthasar.
works.context: Written about 1598–99 from Bandello via Ariosto; printed in quarto, 1600; among the first plays staged after the reopening of the theatres under James I.
works.characters: Beatrice; Benedick; Claudio; Hero; Don Pedro; Don John; Leonato; Dogberry; Verges; Margaret; Borachio; Conrade; Friar Francis
works.structure: Twin plots of courtship — the gulling of Beatrice and Benedick, and the destruction and restoration of Hero — joined by the watch's comic inquest.

works.title: N-Town Plays
works.description: A cycle of forty-two plays compiled in East Anglia in the second half of the fifteenth century, so called because its banns announce performance 'in N-town' — the name to be supplied by whatever town staged it. Its distinctive compilation includes a Passion play of great elaboration (the Mary Play tradition), the Parliament of Heaven, and the trial of Joseph and Mary, with a strong Marian and doctrinal emphasis.
works.plot: From the Parliament of Heaven and the fall of Lucifer, the cycle moves through the Old Testament, the life of the Virgin (her conception, presentation, and betrothal, the trial of Joseph and Mary), the Nativity, the ministry and Passion — with its long two-part Passion sequence — to the Resurrection, the Assumption, and the Last Judgement.
works.significance: The most learned and Mariological of the cycles, and the principal witness to the East Anglian Passion play tradition; its compilation shows the cycle form in the making.
works.meter: Thirteen-line and eight-line stanza forms, with the rime couée of the incorporated plays.
works.context: Compiled c. 1468–1500 in East Anglia (perhaps at Bury St Edmunds or Thetford), in the devotional culture that produced Bokenham and Capgrave; preserved in BL Cotton MS Vespasian D.viii.
works.characters: God; the Virgin Mary; Joseph; Christ; Pilate; Satan; the Prolocutor
works.structure: A compilation cycle: some pageants written for the cycle, others (the Mary Play, the Passion Play) incorporated from self-standing East Anglian dramas, under a general prologue claiming the N-town staging.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (compilational); authorship_status reflects the cycle's collective making.

editions.title: The N-Town Play

works.title: Narratio metrica de Sancto Swithuno
altTitles: The Metrical Life of St Swithun
works.form: hagiography (saint's life) in Latin hexameter verse
works.description: Wulfstan the Cantor's verse life of St Swithun, bishop of Winchester (d. 862), composed c. 996 for the translation of the saint's relics into the rebuilt Old Minster: a Latin epic in the classical revival manner of the Benedictine Reform, with a prose preface (a letter to Bishop Ælfheah) describing the rebuilding of the cathedral and its monuments.
works.plot: The poem narrates Swithun's life and episcopate, his humility, his miracles (the broken eggs restored, the bridge-mending saint), and the translation of 971, when the reluctant saint consented at last to be moved indoors; the preface details the new tower, crypt, organ, and bells of Æthelwold's Old Minster — a unique architectural record.
works.significance: The principal Latin poem of the late Old English period and a major source for Winchester's architecture and liturgy.
works.meter: Dactylic hexameters in the tenth-century classical manner.
works.context: Composed c. 996 at the Old Minster, Winchester, following the translation of Swithun's relics (971) and Æthelwold's building campaign; unique manuscript: British Library, Royal MS 15 C.vii.
works.characters: Swithun; Æthelwold; Ælfheah (dedicatee); Edgar
works.structure: A verse vita in two books framed by the prose dedicatory epistle.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan the Cantor's authorship is certain (he names himself in the prose preface).
sources: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse

works.title: Nature
altTitles: Nature, a goodly interlude of Nature
works.description: Henry Medwall's morality play of the fall and reformation of Man, the earliest surviving full-scale English morality written for a noble household; printed c. 1530–34 by William Rastell.
works.plot: Nature creates Man and sets Reason and Sensuality over him; Man follows Sensuality into the tavern and the arms of Pride, and the seven deadly sins strip him of his goods; Age and Shamefacedness bring him to repentance, and Reason restores him to grace. The play dramatizes the cycle of innocence, sin, and penitential return.
works.significance: The earliest surviving English morality play composed for a secular household audience and the first full example of the genre after Everyman; it documents the adaptation of the morality tradition to Renaissance taste and anticipates the moral interludes of the 1560s.
works.meter: Rhyme royal and couplets
works.context: Written in the late 1490s, probably for Morton's household like Fulgens and Lucrece; it draws on the tradition of The Castle of Perseverance and Everyman while giving new prominence to worldly temptation, and William Rastell's printing (c. 1530–34) secured its influence on the mid-century interludes.
works.characters: Nature; Man; Reason; Sensuality; Pride; World; Age; Shamefacedness; Innocence
works.structure: Two-part morality play with allegorical personifications, alternating processional scenes of the sins with debate between Reason and Sensuality.

editions.title: The Plays of Henry Medwall

works.title: New Atlantis
works.description: Bacon's unfinished utopian fable, published posthumously with Sylva Sylvarum: a ship lost in the Pacific reaches the unknown island of Bensalem, where the narrator is received into a society organized around Salomon's House — the college of the 'Merchants of Light' whose institutes of experiment and invention anticipate the modern research laboratory.
works.plot: The sailors' arrival, the quarantine, and the Feast of the Family occupy the early pages; the governor's account of Bensalem's Christian origins and its concealment from the world follows; and the narrative climaxes in the Father of Salomon's House describing the college's 'preparations and instruments' — the prolongation of life, the making of new species, the knowledge of causes and secret motions of things.
works.significance: The great English utopia of science — the blueprint of the modern research institution and the ancestor of the scientific romance.
works.meter: Prose of ceremonial dignity, with the Father's discourse as the work's set piece.
works.context: Written about 1624, in Bacon's last years at Gorhambury, and published by William Rawley in 1627; its Bensalem answered More's Utopia and anticipated the Royal Society, which took Salomon's House as its inspiration.
works.characters: the narrator; the Governor of the Strangers' House; the Father of Salomon's House; Joabin; the sailors
works.structure: A utopian narrative in the Platonic and Morean tradition, unfinished, ending on the Father's promise that the narrator shall receive 'a relation of the true state of Salomon's House'.

editions.title: Francis Bacon: The Major Works

works.title: New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air
works.description: Boyle's report of his experiments with the air-pump built for him by Robert Hooke, in which he demonstrated the elastic 'spring' of air, its necessity for respiration and sound, and stated the inverse relation between pressure and volume now known as Boyle's Law.
works.plot: Forty-three experiments establish the properties of the air and answer the objections of Hobbes and the Peripatetics; the famous Experiment 41 shows that a sound cannot be heard in an evacuated vessel.
works.significance: The foundational text of modern experimental physics and chemistry; it established the experimental report as a literary form and Boyle's Law as the first quantitative gas law.
works.meter: Detailed experimental prose; Boyle's practice of reporting full particulars became the model for the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions.
works.context: Published in 1660 at Oxford, where Boyle worked with Hooke; the second edition of 1662 added the Defence of the Doctrine Touching the Spring and Weight of the Air, containing the pressure-volume relation.
works.structure: A series of numbered experiments with descriptions of apparatus, results, and objections answered.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Boyle; Hooke built the apparatus and is credited in the text.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Nice Wanton
altTitles: A Preaty Interlude Called Nice Wanton
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality interlude of the divergent fates of three children, printed in 1560; a dramatization of godly education and its neglect.
works.plot: Xantippe's three children grow up under her indulgence: Ishmael and Dalila fall into idleness, gambling, and prostitution, and come to the gallows; the godly Barnabas, who studies scripture, is spared and comforts his repentant mother and sister; the Vice Iniquity frames the action, and the epilogue draws the moral of education and the rod.
works.significance: A representative Protestant morality whose twin plots of the saved and the damned child dramatize the educational programme of the Reformation; it marks the absorption of humanist pedagogy into the morality tradition.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1547–53, in the years of the Edwardian Reformation, when the godly education of children became a central Protestant theme; printed in 1560 for the Elizabethan market, with a title-page woodcut of the flogging schoolmaster.
works.characters: Xantippe; Barnabas; Ishmael; Dalila; Iniquity; Eulalia; The Worldly Shame
works.structure: A continuous morality play of two contrasted life-paths, with Iniquity as the linking Vice, songs, and a concluding moral address.

works.title: Nosce Teipsum
works.description: Sir John Davies's philosophical poem on the immortality of the soul: 'Know thyself' — the soul's nature, its faculties, its independence from the body, and the proofs of its immortality — argued in some 2,000 lines of didactic couplets, the poem that made Davies famous overnight and earned him the favour of James I.
works.plot: The poem proceeds from the Delphic command through the soul's definition, its powers of sense, fancy, and reason, the distinction of soul and body, the refutation of the soul's mortality, and the closing proof of its divine origin and destiny — a scholastic summa rendered in verse.
works.significance: The most accomplished English philosophical poem of its generation and a direct ancestor of the Augustan poetry of statement.
works.meter: Iambic pentameter couplets of a clear, dry, argumentative elegance — the manner that would become the Augustan couplet's parent.
works.context: Published 1599, in the same years as Donne's satires and the philosophical poems of the Inns of Court; Davies, a lawyer who became Attorney General for Ireland, dedicated it to Elizabeth I, and its success made his reputation at both courts.
works.characters: the poet as philosopher; the Soul; Reason; the Body
works.structure: Two books of sustained didactic argument, each section a step in the proof, with the famous passage on the soul's 'infinity of desire' as its centre.

editions.title: The Poems of Sir John Davies

works.title: Novum Organum
works.description: Bacon's second part of the Instauratio Magna, published in Latin: the 'New Instrument' of science, in which the old logic of Aristotle is replaced by the new method of induction — the doctrine of the idols (of the tribe, cave, marketplace, and theatre), the tables of presence and absence, and the 'prerogative instances' that guide the interpretation of nature.
works.plot: Book I clears the ground: the idols that beset the mind, the signs of philosophy's failure, and the hope of a new beginning; Book II lays out the method — the tables of instances, the first vintage, and the ascending ladder of axioms that ends in the knowledge of forms and the power over nature ('knowledge and human power are synonymous').
works.significance: The founding document of the scientific method — the text that named the idols and invented induction as the modern world understands it.
works.meter: Latin aphorisms of epigrammatic force, with the prefatory matter framing the work as the 'second part' of the Instauratio.
works.context: Published in 1620, the year of the Mayflower, as the manifesto of the new experimental science; Bacon's idols doctrine became the common vocabulary of seventeenth-century epistemology.
works.structure: Two books of aphorisms, deliberately fragmentary, in the oracular style Bacon devised for his philosophical testament.

editions.title: The New Organon

works.title: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy
altTitles: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, to Which is Added The Description of a New Blazing World
works.description: Cavendish's philosophical critique of the new experimental philosophy, attacking the Royal Society's microscopy, Hooke's Micrographia, and the corpuscular theories of Hobbes, Descartes, and Boyle, and proposing her own vitalist materialism.
works.plot: Cavendish argues that matter is self-moving, sentient, and rational; she rejects the mechanical philosophy's reliance on instruments, which she thought distorted nature, and asserts a holistic, animistic view of the natural world.
works.significance: The most substantial philosophical work by an English woman of the seventeenth century and an important early critique of instrumental science; it has been revalued as a serious contribution to natural philosophy.
works.meter: Argumentative prose of remarkable originality and density.
works.context: Published in 1666; Cavendish was one of the few women to engage directly with the Royal Society, and her critique of Hooke's microscopy was a direct response to Micrographia (1665).
works.structure: A systematic critique in chapters, followed by the appendix The Blazing World.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Observations upon the United Provinces of the Netherlands
works.description: Temple's political and social analysis of the Dutch Republic, written after his years as English ambassador at The Hague, and one of the most influential English works of political observation of the period.
works.plot: Temple describes the constitution, government, religion, military strength, trade, and character of the United Provinces, and analyses why a small republic could rival the great monarchies of Europe.
works.significance: A classic of early modern political analysis and a model of plain prose; it influenced Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws and the English debate on republicanism.
works.meter: Clear, urbane prose in the new plain style.
works.context: Written in 1672-3 during the Franco-Dutch War and published in 1673; Temple was a leading Whig diplomat and a patron of Swift.
works.structure: A series of short chapters on the several aspects of Dutch government and society.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Of Ancient and Modern Learning
altTitles: Essay upon the Original and Nature of Poetry (included)
works.description: Temple's essay defending the ancients against the moderns, written in reply to Fontenelle and the French Académie, and containing the famous praise of the Epistles of Phalaris; it opened the English Quarrel of the Books.
works.plot: Temple argues that the ancients surpassed the moderns in poetry, oratory, and philosophy, cites the Epistles of Phalaris as the oldest and best of the ancient letters, and dismisses modern learning as pedantic.
works.significance: The opening salvo of the English Battle of the Books, which Swift satirised in The Battle of the Books (1704); it is a key text in the history of the quarrel between the ancients and the moderns.
works.meter: Plain, urbane prose.
works.context: Published in 1692 in Temple's Miscellanea; it provoked Wotton's Reflections upon Ancient and Modern Learning (1694) and Bentley's demonstration that the Epistles of Phalaris were a later forgery, in which the young Swift served as Temple's amanuensis.
works.structure: A single continuous essay.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Of Education
works.description: A letter to the educational reformer Samuel Hartlib proposing a complete humanist and practical curriculum for young gentlemen, combining classical languages, science, physical training, and moral and religious formation to fit them for public and private service.
works.plot: Milton sets out the ends of education ('to repair the ruins of our first parents by regaining to know God aright'), then details a graded curriculum from languages through literature, science, ethics, and rhetoric, with exercises, travel, and music.
works.significance: A key document of seventeenth-century educational reform, combining Renaissance humanism with the new practical and scientific emphasis, and influential in the history of pedagogy.
works.meter: Clear, argumentative prose with an idealistic and practical tone.
works.context: Written in 1644 for Samuel Hartlib's circle of educational reformers, reflecting Comenian and humanist ideals and Milton's own experience as a schoolmaster and private tutor.
works.structure: A short prose tract addressed as a letter, moving from first principles to a detailed syllabus.

editions.title: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity
works.description: Hooker's great defence of the Elizabethan church: Books I–IV (1593) and Book V (1597) of the eight-book treatise answer the Puritan platform by grounding church order in the law of reason and nature — the famous account of law's hierarchy from God through angels and man to the laws ecclesiastical — in the prose that founded Anglican theology.
works.plot: Book I derives the kinds of law (eternal, celestial, natural, human, divine) and the necessity of law for the good life; Books II–IV refute the Puritan claim of scriptural exclusivity; Book V, the longest, defends the Prayer Book's liturgy, sacraments, and discipline against the Admonition controversies; the posthumous Books VI–VIII treat jurisdiction, episcopacy, and royal supremacy.
works.significance: The intellectual foundation of Anglicanism and of the English theory of law and consent — a book Locke and the constitutional tradition built upon.
works.meter: Prose of unrivalled dignity and clarity — the 'judicious' style that Izaak Walton celebrated and that set the standard for English theological writing.
works.context: Written through the 1590s against the Admonition controversy and the Presbyterian challenge; the completed books were printed in 1593 and 1597, with the later books posthumous and textually vexed.
works.structure: Eight books of systematic theological argument, each built on the scholastic method of position, objection, and answer, in the majestic periodic prose Hooker perfected.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the posthumous books VI–VIII survive in imperfect texts.

editions.title: Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (Folger Library Edition)

works.title: Old English Bede
works.form: translation (ecclesiastical history) in Old English prose
works.description: The anonymous Old English translation of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica, produced in the Alfredian circle: the earliest vernacular rendering of a major historical work in England and a primary witness to the text of Bede. It preserves the Old English text of Cædmon's Hymn in the West Saxon dialect.
works.plot: The translation follows Bede's five books closely, rendering the history of the conversion and the saints of the early English church into fluent West Saxon prose, with the Hymn of Cædmon given in a West Saxon verse translation rather than in the original Northumbrian form.
works.significance: The standard vernacular text of Bede in late Anglo-Saxon England and a monument of the Alfredian translation program.
works.meter: Old English prose; contains alliterative verse (Cædmon's Hymn) in translation.
works.context: Translated c. 890-930, probably in Mercia within the Alfredian orbit; principal manuscripts: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 41, and Oxford, Bodleian Library, Tanner 10.
works.characters: Bede (author); the saints and kings of the Historia
works.structure: Five books of translated ecclesiastical history.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; no evidence for the older attribution to Alfred himself.
sources: Poetry and Politics in the English Renaissance, revised edition

works.title: Old English Boethius (with the Meters of Boethius)
altTitles: The Old English Consolation of Philosophy
works.form: translation (philosophical dialogue) in Old English prose and verse
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the most important philosophical work of the period in English: Boethius's dialogue with Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, and providence, transformed by the translator into the idiom of the Germanic heroic world (Wyrd becomes a goddess of fate under God's governance). An alliterative verse rendering of the work's songs, the Meters of Boethius, accompanies the prose.
works.plot: The imprisoned Boethius, lamenting his fall, is visited by Philosophy (Wisdom), who teaches him that true happiness lies not in wealth, power, or fame but in God; the dialogue moves through the problem of evil to the reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with human freedom — the translator's expansions turning Philosophy's arguments into vivid vernacular images (the wheel of fate, the tyrant's empty power, the 'tool' of kingship).
works.significance: The first English philosophical classic; the Meters are the largest surviving corpus of Alfredian verse.
works.meter: Old English prose; the Meters of Boethius are in alliterative verse.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899 from the Latin of Boethius with the help of a commentary tradition; preserved in Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Bodley 180 (prose, mid-tenth century) and British Library, Cotton MS Otho A.vi (meters, burned 1731, transcript).
works.characters: Boethius (the Mind); Wisdom (Philosophy); Wyrd (Fate)
works.structure: Five books of alternating prose and verse (the metra), the prose translated freely, the verse rendered both in prose and, in a separate version, in alliterative verse.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Alfred himself; modern scholarship sees his close direction with the possibility of personal composition.
themes: The Virgin Mary and Marian devotion
sources: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

works.title: Old English Dialogues of Gregory
works.form: translation (hagiographical dialogue) in Old English prose
works.description: Bishop Werferth of Worcester's translation of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, the collection of Italian saints' lives and miracle stories that was among the most popular books of the Middle Ages, including the life of St Benedict. Commissioned by King Alfred, it is the only Alfredian translation securely assigned to a named scholar other than the king.
works.plot: Gregory, in dialogue with his deacon Peter, recounts the lives and miracles of the holy men of Italy in four books: Benedict and his monks, the visionary saints, the raising of the dead, and the fate of souls after death — the work that fixed Benedict's cult in the west and fed the homiletic imagination of Anglo-Saxon England (its 'Vision of Fursey' and soul-journey stories echo through the Blickling and Vercelli homilies).
works.significance: The earliest extensive Old English translation of a major patristic work and the conduit of Gregory's hagiography into the vernacular.
works.meter: Old English prose, close and literal in style.
works.context: Translated by Werferth, bishop of Worcester (c. 872-915), at Alfred's request c. 890s; principal manuscripts: British Library, Cotton MS Otho C.i (fragmentary) and Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 322.
works.characters: Gregory the Great; Peter the deacon; Benedict of Nursia; the Italian saints
works.structure: Four books of dialogue, each a collection of miracle narratives framed by Gregory's conversation with Peter.
works.attributionNotes: Werferth's authorship rests on Asser's Life of Alfred and Alfred's own Preface.
sources: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition

works.title: Old English Hexateuch
works.description: The Old English translation of the first six books of the Bible (Genesis through Joshua), composed principally by Ælfric (who translated Genesis with his own preface) and completed by an anonymous translator: the earliest substantial rendering of the Bible into English and the most lavishly illustrated vernacular manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon period.
works.plot: The Hexateuch renders Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua into English — the patriarchal narratives, the exodus and the law, the conquest of Canaan — in Ælfric's lucid prose for the first portion and a more literal style thereafter; the preface explains Ælfric's reluctance to translate scripture, lest the unlearned mistake its plain sense.
works.significance: The first English Bible translation of scale and a monument of late Anglo-Saxon book art.
works.meter: Old English prose; rhythmical in the Ælfrician portions.
works.context: Ælfric's Genesis and preface c. 1000; the whole compiled with the remaining books by the mid-eleventh century; principal manuscript: British Library, Cotton MS Claudius B.iv, with over 390 illustrations.
works.characters: Adam, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, and the biblical patriarchs
works.structure: Six biblical books in translation, prefaced by Ælfric's preface to Genesis.
works.attributionNotes: Ælfric's authorship of Genesis (and the preface) is certain; the other books are by an anonymous contemporary.
sources: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts

works.title: Old English Martyrology
works.description: An anonymous ninth-century calendar of saints, the earliest substantial martyrology in any European vernacular: entries for each day of the year recording the feasts, passions, and wonders of the saints, compiled from Latin sources and full of exotic geographical and zoological lore.
works.plot: The martyrology proceeds day by day through the calendar year, each entry briefly narrating the saint's life or passion — apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins of east and west — with digressions on the places and creatures mentioned (the phoenix, the whale, the peoples of India).
works.significance: The earliest vernacular martyrology of Europe and a major source for Anglo-Saxon hagiography and geography.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Compiled in Mercia in the ninth century, probably before the Viking wars; survives in six fragmentary manuscripts, none complete.
works.characters: the saints of the universal church
works.structure: A calendar-ordered compendium of short hagiographical notices.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Ben Jonson

works.title: Old English Orosius
altTitles: The Old English History of the World
works.form: translation (universal history) in Old English prose
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Orosius's Seven Books of History against the Pagans, the standard ancient universal history, expanded with original accounts of the geography of northern Europe and the voyages of the Norwegian Ohthere and the Dane Wulfstan — the first travel literature in English.
works.plot: Orosius's history narrates the calamities of the world from creation to his own day (c. 417) to prove that the pagan past was more wretched than the Christian present; the translator condenses and adapts the narrative, and prefaces it with a geographical survey of the world that includes the famous reports of Ohthere's voyage around the North Cape into the White Sea and Wulfstan's voyage into the Baltic, told to King Alfred by the travellers themselves.
works.significance: The first universal history in English and the earliest English travel narrative (the Ohthere and Wulfstan passages).
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899; the principal manuscript is British Library, Additional MS 47967 (the Lauderdale or Tollemache Orosius, early tenth century).
works.characters: Ohthere; Wulfstan; Alfred (as recipient of the voyage accounts); the rulers of world history
works.structure: Seven books of world history, preceded by the translator's original geographical preface.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation of the Alfredian circle.
sources: The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church

works.title: Old English Pastoral Care (with Alfred's Preface)
altTitles: Gregory's Pastoral Care in Old English
works.form: translation (didactic treatise) in Old English prose
works.description: King Alfred's translation of Gregory the Great's Regula pastoralis, the handbook of episcopal duties, prefaced by Alfred's own letter on the decay of learning and his program of translation — the founding document of English prose. Copies were sent to every bishopric, and the surviving manuscripts are the earliest extensive works of Old English prose.
works.plot: Gregory's treatise instructs the pastor in the office of the soul's physician — how the teacher must adapt his speech to each condition of his flock, the virtues required of rulers of souls, and the discipline of preaching; Alfred's Preface recounts how learning had decayed in England ('so clean fallen away'), and how he therefore resolved to translate into English the books most needful for all men to know.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the Alfredian program and of the entire Old English prose tradition.
works.meter: Old English prose of the early Alfredian style.
works.context: Translated c. 890-899 with the help of Plegmund, Asser, Grimbald, and John; the earliest manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library, Hatton 20, c. 890-897) was sent to Bishop Werferth of Worcester.
works.characters: Alfred (preface); Gregory the Great (text)
works.structure: Preface (prose letter) followed by the four books of the translation, with Alfred's characteristic expansions of Gregory's images.
works.attributionNotes: The Preface is Alfred's own; the translation was executed by his circle under his direction.
sources: Sir Thomas Wyatt: The Complete Poems

works.title: Old English Soliloquies
altTitles: The Old English Soliloquies of Augustine
works.form: translation (philosophical dialogue) in Old English prose
works.description: The Alfredian translation of Augustine's Soliloquies — a dialogue between Augustine and his Reason on God and the immortality of the soul — with additions from Augustine's other works and the translator's own reflections, including the famous image of gathering timber in the forest to build a fair dwelling (the book as a house of wisdom).
works.plot: Reason leads Augustine (the translator's 'Mind') through the argument for the soul's immortality: from the desire for knowledge to the certainty of one's own existence ('I know that I am'), the nature of truth, and the vision of God after death; the work closes with the image of the king's woodcutters gathering timber for the house of the mind, where each man may rest and live.
works.significance: The first English rendering of Augustine and a central text of the Alfredian philosophic program.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Translated in Alfred's circle c. 890-899; the unique manuscript is British Library, Cotton MS Vitellius A.xv, fols. 4-59 (mid-twelfth century), copied with the same manuscript tradition as Beowulf.
works.characters: the Mind (Augustine/Alfred); Reason
works.structure: A question-and-answer dialogue in the Boethian manner, with the translator's expansions (the ship and anchor, the lord's favourite, the timber image) added to Augustine's text.
works.attributionNotes: Traditionally attributed to Alfred; the attribution rests on the Preface of the work and the conventions of the Alfredian canon.
sources: Tudor Drama before Shakespeare, 1485–1590: New Directions for Research, Criticism, and Pedagogy

works.title: Olor Iscanus
altTitles: Olor Iscanus: The Swan of Usk
works.description: A collection of Vaughan's earlier secular and occasional verse, published by his brother William in 1651 against the poet's wish, including love poems, elegies, satires, epigrams, and translations of Boethius, The Distichs of Cato, and Casimire Sarbiewski.
works.plot: The volume gathers Vaughan's pre-conversion and secular work — amatory and elegiac poems, versions of Ovid and Ausonius, the satirical 'Time' poems, and pious translations — representing the literary range before his mystical turn.
works.significance: Important for understanding Vaughan's development and his classical and secular range, and as a document of royalist literary culture during the Interregnum.
works.meter: Varied lyric meters; translation in verse; a more worldly, sometimes uneven, manner than Silex Scintillans.
works.context: Composed largely in the 1640s; Vaughan suppressed it, but his twin brother Thomas's death and William's initiative led to its publication in 1651, dedicated with the 'swan of Usk' emblem of the river on which Vaughan lived.
works.structure: A miscellaneous collection of secular lyrics, translations, and epigrams without a unifying sequence.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published by Vaughan's brother against his expressed preference.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: On Monsieur's Departure
works.description: Queen Elizabeth I's lyric on the departure of François, Duke of Anjou, her last serious suitor, about 1582: the queen's grief at parting, her public duty's compulsion to conceal it, and the paradox of a heart that cannot show what it feels — 'I grieve and dare not show my discontent' — the most personal of her surviving poems.
works.plot: The poem moves through the queen's private grief to the public impossibility of expressing it: love, duty, and statecraft in the single voice of the sovereign, with the refrain of the divided self as its burden.
works.significance: The queen's most intimate poem — the lyric in which the sovereign's two bodies, private and public, speak in one voice.
works.meter: Short-lined lyric stanzas with refrain, in the manner of the court's song-poetry.
works.context: Written about 1582, at the collapse of the French marriage negotiations that had divided the court for a decade; the poem survives only in manuscript, its attribution resting on the queen's circle's testimony.
works.characters: Elizabeth (as speaker); the departing Monsieur (François, Duke of Anjou)
works.structure: A single lyric of three movements — grief, concealment, resignation — in the courtly complaint mode.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Elizabeth I by manuscript tradition; the attribution is generally accepted.

editions.title: Elizabeth I: Collected Works
editions.editor: Leah S. Marcus, Janel Mueller, and Mary Beth Rose (eds.)

works.title: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity
works.description: Milton's first major poem, written at twenty-one: a hymn celebrating the Incarnation, in which the birth of Christ brings universal peace and harmony, silencing the oracles and the pagan gods and summoning a heavenly music that the poet longs to join.
works.plot: A prologue in four stanzas asks whether the poet's verse may be laid in the manger before the Magi; the Hymn then describes the peaceful night, the music of the spheres, and the flight of the pagan deities (Apollo, Osiris, Typhon) before the true God.
works.significance: A precocious masterpiece of the early English baroque, it announces Milton's ambition to Christian epic and his fusion of classical and biblical learning.
works.meter: Prologue in rhyme royal; the Hymn in a complex varied stanza (aabbcccddedeeff) that Milton devised for the occasion.
works.context: Composed in December 1629, the year Milton took his MA at Cambridge; published in his Poems of Mr. John Milton (1645), where it leads the collection as his claim to a great poetic vocation.
works.characters: the poet; the infant Christ; Nature; Peace; the pagan gods (Apollo, Osiris, Typhon)
works.structure: A four-stanza prologue followed by an irregular Pindaric-style Hymn in varied stanza form, moving from celebration to the rout of the old gods.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; dated by Milton himself in the 1645 volume.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: On the Properties of Things
works.description: John Trevisa's English translation of Bartholomaeus Anglicus's De proprietatibus rerum (On the Properties of Things), the great medieval encyclopedia of nature, man, and the cosmos, completed c. 1398–99: nineteen books from God and the angels through the elements, animals, and plants to the human body and soul. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1495, it was the standard English encyclopedia for two centuries.
works.plot: The work proceeds systematically through the orders of creation — God, angels, the soul, the elements, the heavens, birds, beasts, herbs, and the arts and sciences — describing each thing's properties and their moral and medical meanings, in a summa of medieval natural knowledge.
works.significance: The great English encyclopedia of the Middle Ages and the principal channel by which medieval natural science entered English prose.
works.meter: Prose: Trevisa's learned yet idiomatic English, rich in technical vocabulary.
works.context: Completed in 1398–99 at Berkeley, dedicated to Thomas, Lord Berkeley; printed by Wynkyn de Worde (c. 1495), when it served the medical and scientific reading of the Tudor period; Shakespeare drew on it.
works.characters: none (encyclopedia)
works.structure: Nineteen books of encyclopedic description, each subdivided by topic, in the tradition of Isidore and the thirteenth-century encyclopedists.
works.attributionNotes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the text).

works.title: Opus Maius
works.description: Roger Bacon's encyclopedic proposal for the reform of learning, written c. 1267 at the request of Pope Clement IV and sent to him with the Opus Minus and Opus Tertium; its seventh part on moral philosophy and its treatment of optics, experimental science, and the applications of mathematics to theology make it a landmark of thirteenth-century thought.
works.summary: Bacon surveys the causes of error, the relation of philosophy to scripture, the utility of grammar and of the learned languages (Hebrew, Greek, Arabic), mathematics and its uses (including calendar reform and geography), the science of perspective, experimental science, and moral philosophy — arguing throughout that the sciences are necessary instruments for the understanding and defence of the faith.
works.significance: The fullest medieval statement of an experimental and mathematically grounded program of learning; a foundation text for the later reputation of Bacon and a principal witness to thirteenth-century optics and natural philosophy.

editions.title: The 'Opus Majus' of Roger Bacon

works.title: Order and Disorder; or, The World Made and Undone
works.description: Lucy Hutchinson's biblical epic on Genesis, of which only canto V was published in her lifetime and the complete text survives in manuscript; it is the first epic poem in English by a woman and a direct answer to Milton's Paradise Lost.
works.plot: The poem retells the story of creation, the fall, and the expulsion, interpreting Genesis through a Calvinist theology and a republican politics that laments the Restoration of monarchy.
works.significance: The first English epic by a woman and an important early response to Paradise Lost; its republicanism and its female epic voice have made it a canonical text of seventeenth-century women's writing.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter.
works.context: Written after the Restoration, when Hutchinson, a widow and a Puritan, was reflecting on the failure of the republican cause; it engages directly with Milton's epic.
works.characters: Adam; Eve; God; Satan; the angels
works.structure: Twenty cantos in heroic couplets, of which only canto V was printed in 1679.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand and was first published complete in 2001.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Ordinatio
works.description: Duns Scotus's great revision of his Oxford lectures on the Sentences of Peter Lombard, left unfinished at his death; the Ordinatio sets out the subtle doctor's metaphysics of univocity, his formal distinction, his defence of the Immaculate Conception, and his voluntarist ethics, and became the authoritative alternative to Thomism in late medieval theology.
works.summary: In four books following the structure of the Sentences, Scotus develops a systematic theology distinguished by its precise use of logic: the univocal concept of being, the formal distinction, the primacy of the will, the demonstration of God's existence through the concept of infinite being, and the case for Mary's immaculate conception — arguments that set the agenda for fourteenth-century scholasticism.
works.significance: One of the most demanding and influential works of medieval philosophy and theology; the foundation of the Scotist school, taught in the universities into the seventeenth century and beyond.

works.title: Oroonoko (Southerne's adaptation)
works.description: Southerne's stage version of Behn's novella, which added a comic subplot of two London ladies and made Oroonoko the standard tragic role of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: Oroonoko, sold into slavery in Surinam, is reunited with Imoinda; he leads a failed revolt; the lieutenant-governor betrays him; Imoinda kills herself and Oroonoko is executed.
works.significance: The adaptation that made Oroonoko a canonical stage figure and that spread Behn's story, and the issue of slavery, to eighteenth-century audiences across Britain and America.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose in the comic plot.
works.context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in 1695 and published in 1696; it was the most frequently performed tragedy of the eighteenth century after Shakespeare and Otway.
works.characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; Aboan; Charlotte; the Lieutenant-Governor; Widow Lackitt; Welldon; Blandford
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a substantial comic subplot and a large sentimental role for the hero.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Southerne; his prologue acknowledges Behn as the source.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave (Behn)
works.description: Behn's short novel, narrated by a female traveller in the English colony of Surinam, on the African prince Oroonoko, who is sold into slavery, leads a failed revolt, and is barbarously executed; it is the founding text of English anti-slavery fiction.
works.plot: Oroonoko, grandson of the king of Coramantien, loves Imoinda; both are sold into slavery and reunited in Surinam; he leads an unsuccessful rebellion, is captured, promises peace, is whipped and dismembered, and kills his pregnant wife before his own execution.
works.significance: The most influential prose fiction of the Restoration; it established the 'noble savage' trope, initiated the English anti-slavery literary tradition, and has become a canonical text of early modern women's writing and of postcolonial criticism. Thomas Southerne's 1695 stage adaptation held the stage for over a century.
works.meter: Elegant Restoration prose combining travel description with tragic narrative.
works.context: Published in 1688, the year of the Revolution and of Behn's death; it draws on her claimed residence in Surinam in 1663-4.
works.characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; the narrator; Caesar; Trefry; Byam; Banister; the Indian lovers
works.structure: A first-person frame narrative with the narrator's eyewitness account, digressions on Surinam's flora, fauna, and indigenous people, and a sustained portrait of Oroonoko as a European-style hero.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Behn; the narrator's identity is a literary persona, though the Surinam material is generally accepted as drawing on her experience.

works.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
works.description: Robert Henryson's retelling of the Orpheus myth (c. 1480, 633 lines): the harper-king's descent to the underworld to reclaim Eurydice, his fatal backward look, and — in Henryson's distinctive addition — a long moralitas allegorizing Orpheus as the intellect, Eurydice as the appetite, and the harrowing journey as the soul's quest for its lost harmony. The most learned of the makars' classical poems.
works.plot: Orpheus, whose harping masters the beasts and the spheres, loses Eurydice to the serpent's bite and follows her to the underworld, where his music wins her release on the one condition; his backward look loses her forever, and the poet's moralitas expounds the fable as the story of reason seeking the soul's lost good.
works.significance: The classic Scottish treatment of the Orpheus myth and a landmark in the allegorical reading of classical poetry that runs from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the moralitas in Henryson's plainest expository verse.
works.context: Composed c. 1480, drawing on Boethius's Consolation (the standard medieval source for the myth) and the commentary tradition; printed by Chepman and Myllar (1508), the first printed Scots poem.
works.characters: Orpheus; Eurydice; Pluto; Proserpina; the Furies; the narrator
works.structure: A bipartite poem: the classical narrative (with its celebrated catalogue of the underworld's inhabitants) followed by the allegorical moralitas.

works.title: Othello
altTitles: The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice
works.description: Shakespeare's tragedy of jealousy: the Moorish general Othello, married secretly to Desdemona, is undone by his ensign Iago — 'honest Iago' — whose insinuations about Cassio and the handkerchief persuade him of his wife's infidelity, until the murder in the marriage bed and the discovery of Iago's villainy leave Othello to execute judgment on himself.
works.plot: Iago, denied promotion, plots against Othello: he makes Cassio drunk and cashiered, then uses the dropped handkerchief to 'prove' Desdemona's adultery; Othello's jealousy mounts through the eavesdropping scene to the murder of Desdemona; Emilia exposes Iago, who kills her and is taken for torture; Othello, recognizing what he has destroyed, stabs himself on the bed.
works.significance: The definitive study of jealousy and of the will to destroy — the most painful, because the most intimate, of the great tragedies.
works.meter: Othello's 'Othello music' — the great periodic verse of the senate speech and the farewell to the 'Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war' — against Iago's prose of reduction.
works.context: Performed at court, 1 November 1604; its sources are Cinthio's novella of the Moor and the Venetian setting of the Cyprus wars; its treatment of race has made it the most urgently debated of the tragedies.
works.characters: Othello; Desdemona; Iago; Emilia; Cassio; Roderigo; Brabantio; Bianca; the Duke of Venice; Lodovico; Montano
works.structure: The most tightly constructed of the tragedies — a single plot of insinuation compressed into some thirty-six hours, with Iago's soliloquies as its engine.
