works.title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
altTitles: The XV Books of P. Ovidius Naso, Entitled Metamorphosis
works.description: Arthur Golding's complete translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses (the first four books in 1565, all fifteen in 1567): the myths of transformation — Daphne, Actaeon, Narcissus, Pyramus and Thisbe, Medea, and the rest — rendered in rollicking rhymed fourteeners with a Puritan's moralizing commentary, the version that was 'Shakespeare's Ovid' and the Renaissance Englishman's classic.
works.plot: The fifteen books run from the Creation through the myths of gods and mortals, metamorphosis by metamorphosis, to the apotheosis of Caesar; Golding's translation adds the epistle and preface that turn the pagan fables into allegories of divine and moral truth.
works.significance: The English Ovid — the book through which the Renaissance knew its mythology, and the source of a thousand plots, images, and lines.
works.meter: Rhymed fourteeners (seven-stress couplets) of tremendous gusto — the metre the Elizabethans read aloud and imitated.
works.context: The four-book version of 1565 was completed in 1567, in the decade of the Ovidian revival; Shakespeare's allusions to the Metamorphoses — in Midsummer Night's Dream, Titus, and The Tempest — run through this translation.
works.characters: Jupiter; Apollo; Daphne; Actaeon; Narcissus; Echo; Pyramus; Thisbe; Medea; Orpheus; and the hundreds of Ovid's figures
works.structure: The fifteen books of Ovid in order, with Golding's prefatory apparatus (the epistle to Leicester and the preface to the reader) framing the whole.

editions.title: Shakespeare's Ovid: Arthur Golding's Translation of the Metamorphoses

works.title: Pandosto
works.description: Greene's romance of jealousy and recognition, subtitled 'The Triumph of Time': King Pandosto of Bohemia, seized by groundless jealousy of his queen Bellaria and his friend King Egistus, destroys his family; the lost daughter Fawnia grows up a shepherd's daughter, is wooed by Egistus's son Dorastus, and the final recognitions restore her — though Pandosto's own suicide shadows the happy ending; the direct source of Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
works.plot: Pandosto's jealousy kills Bellaria and exposes the infant Fawnia; the shepherds raise her; Dorastus loves her despite his father's opposition; the lovers flee to Bohemia, where the recognition scene discloses Fawnia's birth; the marriages are made — and Pandosto, overcome, kills himself, the 'triumph of time' his epitaph.
works.significance: The romance that became The Winter's Tale — the most consequential of the Elizabethan prose fictions by its afterlife.
works.meter: Prose of Greene's pastoral sweetness, with the euphuistic balance softened into narrative flow.
works.context: Published 1588; it went through many editions as 'Pandosto' and 'Dorastus and Fawnia', and supplied Shakespeare with the plot, names, and even phrases of The Winter's Tale.
works.characters: Pandosto; Bellaria; Egistus; Fawnia; Dorastus; the shepherd Porrus; Capnio
works.structure: A prose romance in the Greek manner — jealousy, exposure, pastoral, recognition — with the oracles and storms as its machinery.

editions.title: The Life and Complete Works in Prose and Verse of Robert Greene, 15 vols.

works.title: Paradise Lost
works.description: Milton's epic of the Fall of Man in blank verse: Satan's rebellion and expulsion from heaven, his voyage to the new world to corrupt God's creatures, the temptation of Adam and Eve, and their expulsion from Eden — 'to justify the ways of God to men'. Published in ten books (1667) and reissued in twelve (1674).
works.plot: Satan, cast into hell, rallies the fallen angels, volunteers to explore the new world, seduces Eve through the serpent, and Adam falls with her through love; the Son pronounces judgment, Michael shows Adam the future of mankind, and the pair leave Paradise 'hand in hand' with providence their guide.
works.significance: The greatest epic in the English language and a central work of world literature; it shaped English poetry, theology, and political imagination for centuries and inspired responses from Blake and Shelley to modern criticism.
works.meter: Unrhymed iambic pentameter (blank verse), with Milton's 'sense variously drawn out from one verse into another' and a Latinate grandeur of diction and syntax.
works.context: Composed chiefly after the Restoration (c. 1658–65), when Milton was blind, politically defeated, and in danger; dictated to amanuenses and published in 1667, it transposes the failed republican cause into a theodicy of obedience, liberty, and inner paradise.
works.characters: Satan; Adam; Eve; God the Father; the Son; Raphael; Michael; Beelzebub; Sin and Death
works.structure: An epic in twelve books with invocations, in medias res opening, councils in heaven and hell, extended similes, and a vast temporal and cosmic scope, drawing on classical epic and biblical narrative.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton

works.title: Paradise Regained
works.description: Milton's 'brief epic' in four books, retelling the temptation of Christ in the wilderness (Luke 4): Jesus resists Satan's offers of bread, wealth, empire, and classical learning through patient faith and reasoned constancy, thereby regaining Paradise lost through Adam.
works.plot: Satan, disguised, tempts the fasting Christ first with hunger, then with the kingdoms of the world and the glory of Athens; Christ refuses each, exposing Satan's false values, and stands unshaken on the pinnacle of the temple, whereupon Satan is confounded and angels minister to him.
works.significance: A deliberately quiet, intellectual counterpart to Paradise Lost that redefines the epic hero as the patient, obedient Christ; long undervalued, it is now admired for its severity and argumentative power.
works.meter: Blank verse, more austere and restrained than Paradise Lost, suited to the patient heroism of 'the better fortitude / Of patience and heroic martyrdom'.
works.context: Composed after Paradise Lost and published with Samson Agonistes in 1671; it reflects Milton's post-Restoration meditation on true heroism as inner, spiritual constancy rather than martial glory.
works.characters: Jesus (the Son); Satan; the disciples; Mary
works.structure: A dialogue-driven brief epic in blank verse, structured as a series of debates and temptations rather than action, with an austere, argumentative style.

works.title: Passio Sancti Eadmundi
altTitles: Life of St Edmund, King and Martyr
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius B.ii; also transmitted through Ælfric's Old English adaptation
works.description: The earliest Latin life of Edmund, king of East Anglia, killed by the Viking Great Army in 869 and venerated as a martyr at Bury St Edmunds. Abbo of Fleury wrote it at Ramsey Abbey (985-987) from the eyewitness testimony of the aged Dunstan, who had heard the story from Edmund's own sword-bearer, and dedicated the work to Dunstan.
works.plot: The Danish army of Ingwar and Ubba invades East Anglia and demands Edmund's submission; the king, a model Christian ruler, refuses to deny Christ or rule as a viking's vassal, and is beaten, shot with arrows, and beheaded. A wolf guards the severed head until the faithful find it; the head rejoins the body, and Edmund is buried and venerated as a martyr whose body remains incorrupt.
works.significance: The founding text of the cult of St Edmund, England's royal patron saint, and the direct source of Ælfric's Old English life; an important link between continental hagiography and the English Benedictine Reform.
works.context: Written in the 980s when England again faced Danish attacks and when the cults of royal martyrs were being cultivated by the reformers; Abbo's Ramsey sojourn made the text a channel of continental learning into the English reform, and its story became the foundation of Bury St Edmunds' great cult.
works.characters: Edmund of East Anglia, Ingwar, Ubba, Bishop Theodred, Dunstan (as source)
works.structure: A classic passio in three movements: the invasion and the tyrant's demands, the martyrdom itself with its arrow-martyrdom patterned on St Sebastian, and the discovery and incorruption of the body, framed by Abbo's prefatory letter to Dunstan.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Abbo of Fleury, who dedicates the work to Dunstan and describes its composition at Ramsey.

works.title: Paston Letters
works.description: The correspondence and papers of the Paston family of Norfolk, spanning 1422–1509: over a thousand letters, wills, and memoranda recording the family's rise from yeoman stock to gentry status, their lawsuits (above all the struggle for Caister Castle), their marriages, and the texture of fifteenth-century provincial life. The richest surviving archive of medieval English family letters.
works.plot: The letters move among the three generations of Pastons — the judge William, his sons John I and John II, their wives Margaret and Margery — and their circle: the siege of Caister, John II's life at court, Margery's secret marriage, the boys' schooling, and the daily business of land, law, and loyalty in East Anglia.
works.significance: The first great English family letter collection: a unique window on the language, law, and life of fifteenth-century England, and the ancestor of the English epistolary tradition.
works.meter: Prose: the varied, idiomatic English of a literate gentry family, from Margaret's dictated letters to John II's courtier prose.
works.context: Written 1422–1509 by the Norfolk Pastons, whose archive passed to the Earl of Yarmouth and was edited by John Fenn (1787); it documents the Wars of the Roses from the perspective of a gentry family and is a primary source for the period's social history.
works.characters: William Paston; Margaret Paston; John Paston I; John Paston II; Margery Paston; the family's servants and opponents
works.structure: An epistolary archive, not a composed work: its order is chronological and documentary, spanning the reigns of Henry VI, Edward IV, and Henry VII.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative (many family members and correspondents); authorship_status reflects the archive's collective character.

editions.title: Paston Letters and Papers of the Fifteenth Century

works.title: Patience
works.description: The Gawain-poet's homiletic poem of 531 lines on the prophet Jonah, expounding the beatitude 'blessed are the patient' through the comic drama of the reluctant prophet, the storm, the whale, and the withered woodbine. Patience, the poem argues, is the virtue God himself practises with sinners — and the one Jonah must learn.
works.plot: Jonah, fleeing God's command to preach at Nineveh, boards ship for Tarshish; the storm God raises forces the sailors to cast him overboard, and he is swallowed by the whale, in whose belly he prays his psalm of thanksgiving; delivered, he preaches at Nineveh, whose repentance God accepts — to Jonah's fury, which the parable of the woodbine answers: if Jonah pities a plant, shall not God pity a city of a hundred and twenty thousand?
works.significance: The liveliest biblical poem of the alliterative revival and the most sustained Middle English treatment of patience; its comic sympathy with the reluctant prophet is without parallel in the period.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, handled with colloquial vigour.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x. The Jonah story had a special medieval resonance through its typological link to the Resurrection.
works.characters: Jonah; God; the sailors; the Ninevites
works.structure: A homiletic prologue on the eight beatitudes, then a three-movement biblical narrative (flight and storm; whale and prayer; Nineveh and the woodbine), with the parable as the poem's doctrinal climax.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.

editions.title: Patience

works.title: Pearl
works.description: The great elegiac dream vision of the Gawain-poet: 1,212 lines in 101 twelve-line stanzas linked by concatenation, in which a grieving father, mourning a lost 'pearl' (his infant daughter), dreams of her transfigured among the blessed, debates with her the theology of grace, and glimpses the heavenly Jerusalem. The most perfectly wrought poem of the Alliterative Revival.
works.plot: In an arbour where his pearl slipped from his hand, the dreamer falls asleep and finds himself by a crystal stream; across it stands a maiden crowned with pearls, whom he recognizes as his lost child grown in heaven. Their dialogue unfolds the parable of the vineyard — the justice of the penny's wage, the grace that admits the innocent and the repentant alike — and culminates in his vision of the New Jerusalem and the Lamb, before his waking returns him to the earth where the pearl is buried.
works.significance: The greatest English religious elegy and the most technically brilliant poem of the Middle English period; its theology of grace and its jewelled art have made it the centre of a vast critical literature.
works.meter: Twelve-line alliterative stanzas rhyming ababababbcbc, with concatenatio linking stanza to stanza.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by the Gawain-poet in the north-west Midlands, in the Ricardian flowering of the dream vision; preserved uniquely in Cotton Nero A.x with Sir Gawain, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: the Dreamer (father); the Pearl-maiden; the Lamb; St John
works.structure: Twenty sections of five stanzas each, the last line of each stanza echoed by the first of the next, and the poem's final line repeating its first; the stream divides the poem into the two worlds of earth and heaven.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; assigned to the Gawain-poet on grounds of style and shared manuscript.

editions.title: Pearl

works.title: Pericles, Prince of Tyre
works.description: The first of the late romances, written with George Wilkins: the wanderings of Pericles, who flees Antiochus's riddle, wins Thaisa at Pentapolis, loses her in childbirth at sea, leaves their daughter Marina at Tarsus, and — after shipwreck, brothel, and the years of grief — is reunited with both in the recognition scenes at Mytilene and Diana's temple at Ephesus.
works.plot: Pericles solves the incest riddle and flees; he wins Thaisa in the tournament; Thaisa 'dies' at sea and is revived at Ephesus; Marina is raised at Tarsus and saved from murder by pirates; the brothel scenes test her virtue; and the double recognition — father and daughter, then husband and wife — restores the family under Diana's guidance.
works.significance: The gateway to the late romances — the play in which Shakespeare turned from tragedy to the art of restoration.
works.meter: Gower's tetrameter choruses frame a prose-and-verse play of variable texture, reflecting its joint authorship.
works.context: Based on the Apollonius of Tyre story via Gower's Confessio Amantis and Lawrence Twine's prose version; the play was a popular success, printed in 1609 and omitted from the First Folio.
works.characters: Pericles; Thaisa; Marina; Gower (the Chorus); Antiochus; Cleon; Dionyza; Simonides; Lysimachus; Cerimon; the Bawd; Boult; Diana
works.structure: An episodic sea-romance narrated and moralized by the poet Gower, who returns as chorus, in a deliberately archaic structure of storms, riddles, and reunions.
works.attributionNotes: Collaboration with George Wilkins for the first two acts is now generally accepted; the Folio omitted the play, which entered the canon in the Third Folio (1664).

works.title: Perkin Warbeck
altTitles: The Chronicle History of Perkin Warbeck
works.description: Ford's 'strange truth' chronicle play on the Yorkist pretender Perkin Warbeck, who claimed to be Richard Duke of York and was received by James IV of Scotland before his capture and execution by Henry VII.
works.plot: Warbeck, protected in Flanders and married in Scotland, asserts his claim to the English crown; Henry VII's cautious statecraft and the defection of Warbeck's supporters lead to his capture and execution at Tyburn.
works.significance: Ford's only history play and one of the last serious English chronicle dramas; it was praised by Weber and revived in the nineteenth century for its political seriousness.
works.meter: Blank verse of grave, stateliest register.
works.context: Performed at the Phoenix in 1634 and published the same year, dedicated to William Cavendish, Earl of Newcastle.
works.characters: Perkin Warbeck; Henry VII; James IV of Scotland; Katherine Gordon; the Earl of Huntley; Lord Bacon; Sir William Stanley; Frion
works.structure: A five-act chronicle history with a double plot of state politics and Warbeck's personal constancy to his wife Katherine.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1634 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Pharaoh
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative fragment in alliterative verse
works.description: An eight-line fragment on the drowning of Pharaoh's host in the Red Sea, dramatizing the moment when the returning waters destroy the pursuing Egyptians. Probably a fragment of a longer Exodus poem or a brief independent composition.
works.plot: Pharaoh's army, pursuing the Israelites across the sea-bed, is engulfed when the waters return; the poem emphasizes the totality of the destruction and the might of the God who saved his people.
works.significance: A witness to the popularity of the Exodus story in Old English verse beyond the Junius manuscript, and to the heroic idiom's capacity to render scriptural battle scenes.
works.meter: Eight alliterative long lines of heroic density; the diction of battle and the sea is that of the heroic tradition applied to scriptural warfare.
works.context: The Exodus was the type of baptism and of the Church's deliverance throughout Anglo-Saxon literature, most elaborately in the Junius manuscript Exodus.
works.characters: Pharaoh
works.structure: A single dramatic scene in eight lines, culminating in the overwhelming of the Egyptian host.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The fragment's relationship to the Junius Exodus is uncertain.

works.title: Philaster
works.description: Beaumont and Fletcher's tragicomedy of the rightful heir: Philaster, prince of Sicily displaced by the usurper, loves the usurper's daughter Arethusa; his page Bellario (really the girl Euphrasia in disguise) is accused of adultery with her; and the play moves through the forest scenes, the attempted murders, and the double wounding to the final scene, where the king's lust is exposed, the lovers reconciled, and the kingdom restored to its prince.
works.plot: Arethusa is betrothed to the boorish Pharamond but loves Philaster; the page Bellario's devotion and the court's slanders complicate the love; the hunting scene's wounds — Philaster stabbing Arethusa and himself — lead to the trial; the king's attempt on Bellario reveals Euphrasia's disguise; and the final act restores all, with the rebellious citizens of Sicily as the deus ex machina of justice.
works.significance: The play that founded the Beaumont–Fletcher tragicomedy — the mode that would rule the English stage for the next fifty years.
works.meter: The supple Beaumont–Fletcher blank verse — run-on, conversational, and swift — that set the style of the Caroline stage.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men about 1609–10 and printed in 1620; its popularity (it was the company's signature new play) made the partnership's name and the tragicomic genre's fortune.
works.characters: Philaster; Arethusa; Bellario (Euphrasia); the King of Sicily; Pharamond; Megra; Dion; Cleremont; Thrasiline; the citizens
works.structure: A five-act tragicomedy in the new Fletcherian mode — suffering, apparent death, and restoration — with the page's disguise and the citizens' rising as its hinges.
works.attributionNotes: Jointly by Beaumont and Fletcher; the division of scenes is broadly agreed though not certain.

editions.title: Philaster (Revels Plays)

works.title: Philip Sparrow
works.description: A mock-elegy of some 1,400 Skeltonic lines in which Jane Scrope, a young gentlewoman of the household at Carrow Abbey, laments her pet sparrow Philip, killed by the cat Gib — the lament swelling into a virtuoso parody of the Latin Office of the Dead, with a commendation of Jane and a digressive defense of women.
works.plot: Jane Scrope mourns her sparrow; the poem moves from tender elegy through liturgical parody (Placebo, Dirige) to the praise of Jane's beauty and virtue, ending with an envoy sending the book to her.
works.significance: The classic of the English mock-elegy and a touchstone of Skelton's art; its play with the liturgy and its defense of women made it one of the most read poems of the century.
works.meter: The Skeltonic at its most supple: short lines of two or three stresses, tumbling rhymes, and Latin tags woven into English.
works.context: Written for the household of Sir Philip Calthorpe's widow at Carrow; the text's allusions to Jane Scrope's family place it about 1505.
works.characters: Jane Scrope; Philip (the sparrow); Gib (the cat)
works.structure: A single-voiced lament that repeatedly breaks its frame: elegy, liturgical parody, blazon, and envoy succeed one another by association.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: Philobiblon
works.description: Richard de Bury's treatise in praise of books and of the love of learning, completed on his birthday, 24 January 1345 (i.e., 1344 by modern reckoning), while he was bishop of Durham; the work draws on his experience assembling one of the great private libraries of medieval England.
works.summary: In twenty chapters the Philobiblon celebrates the wisdom preserved in books, argues that they should be shared with scholars rather than hoarded, defends the clergy against the charge of neglecting their books, and prescribes the care, repair, and circulation of manuscripts; it closes with provisions for the dispersal of the author's own library to the scholars of Oxford.
works.significance: The most famous medieval book about books, a primary witness to the book culture of fourteenth-century England, and a key document for the history of libraries and of Oxford scholarship.

works.title: Pierce Penniless His Supplication to the Devil
works.description: Nashe's first great pamphlet: Pierce Penniless, a scholar out of money and patience, writes his supplication to the devil, anatomizing the seven deadly sins as the diseases of London — greed, drunkenness, pride, and the rest — with the famous digression on the 'upstart' playwrights and the defence of poetry, in the fastest prose of the decade.
works.plot: Pierce, penniless, petitions the devil through the knight of the post; his catalogue of sins prosecutes each vice with its London specimens — the usurer, the drunkard, the proud courtier — and the digressions on players and poets mount the first defence of the professional writer's trade.
works.significance: The great satirical pamphlet of the 1590s — the prose in which the Elizabethan town found its voice and its conscience.
works.meter: Prose of furious energy — colloquial, learned, and comic by turns — with the famous passage on the theatre's power.
works.context: Published 1592 in the plague year; its satire of the sins and its praise of the stage (the passage on Talbot in Henry VI) made it the talk of London and fixed Nashe's reputation.
works.characters: Pierce Penniless; the Devil; the Knight of the Post; the personified sins; the poet and the player (in the digression)
works.structure: A mock-oration in the complaint tradition — the supplication as satirical frame — with the sin-catalogue and the digressions as its bravura set pieces.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Nashe, 5 vols.
editions.editor: R. B. McKerrow (ed.), revised by F. P. Wilson

works.title: Piers Plowman
works.form: allegorical dream vision in alliterative verse
works.description: William Langland's visionary masterpiece, surviving in three authorial versions (the A-text c. 1367–70, B-text c. 1377–79, C-text c. 1386–88): a sequence of ten dream visions in which the dreamer Will searches for Truth, Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the estates of fourteenth-century England — the fair field full of folk, the pilgrimage of the seven deadly sins, the Tree of Charity, and the harrowing of hell. The greatest English poem of social and spiritual reform.
works.plot: Will falls asleep on the Malvern Hills and sees a field full of folk between the Tower of Truth and the Dungeon of Wrong; the quest for St Truth becomes the ploughing of the half-acre under Piers the Plowman; the later visions pursue Dowel, Dobet, and Dobest through the confession of the sins, the feast of Patience, the Tree of Charity, the Passion and harrowing of hell, and the founding of Holy Church, which the final vision shows besieged from within by Antichrist and the friars.
works.significance: With the Canterbury Tales and Sir Gawain, one of the three summits of Ricardian literature: its blend of estates satire, theological vision, and vernacular prophecy made it the rallying text of reform for two centuries, from the rebels of 1381 to the Tudor reformers who printed it.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, ranging from colloquial satire to liturgical sublimity.
works.context: Composed and revised c. 1367–88, probably in London, against the background of plague, labour legislation, the Peasants' Revolt (1381), and Wycliffite controversy — all refracted in the poem's satire; preserved in over fifty manuscripts, more than any English poem except the Prick of Conscience.
works.characters: Will (the dreamer); Piers the Plowman; Holy Church; Lady Meed; Conscience; Patience; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Samaritan; Christ; Antichrist
works.structure: A series of ten (or eight) dream visions within dreams, progressing from social satire through theological allegory to apocalyptic vision, with Will's own spiritual biography as the connective thread; the B-text adds the great inner dreams of the C-text's revisions.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to William Langland by manuscript evidence and internal acrostic signatures; the three texts represent the author's own revisions.

editions.title: Piers Plowman: The B Version
editions.editor: George Kane and E. Talbot Donaldson (eds.)

works.title: Piers the Plowman's Creed
works.description: A Lollard-leaning alliterative satire of some 850 lines in imitation of Piers Plowman: a simple man, seeking to learn his creed, questions the four orders of friars in turn and finds only greed, sophistry, and pride — until the ploughman Piers teaches him the creed in the plain words of charity and labour. The fiercest of the Piers Plowman imitations.
works.plot: The narrator, who cannot say his creed, applies to the friars; each order's answer is a satiric portrait — their fine houses, their begging, their hatred of the ploughman's tithes — until Piers and his family, labouring in poverty, recite the creed and denounce the friars with apocalyptic anger.
works.significance: The most important literary offspring of Piers Plowman and the principal verse monument of Lollard satire; its Tudor printing made 'Piers Plowman' a name for English reform.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line with rhyme incorporated in places.
works.context: Composed c. 1395 in the orbit of the Lollard movement, satirizing the friars' wealth in the spirit of FitzRalph and Wyclif; preserved in BL Royal MS 18 B.xvii and printed by the Tudor reformers (1553).
works.characters: the narrator; the four friars; Piers the Plowman; his wife and children
works.structure: A quest-satire in the Piers tradition: four failed consultations with the friars, resolved by the ploughman's plain teaching.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; formerly attributed to the author of the Plowman's Tale.

works.title: Pindarique Odes
works.description: The odes in Cowley's Poems (1656) that established the loose, irregular 'Pindaric' form in English — ambitious, varied-line odes on great subjects, including 'The Muse', 'To Mr Hobs' (Thomas Hobbes), and 'The Plagues of Egypt' — which became a major vehicle for Restoration and Augustan poetry.
works.plot: The odes treat poetry and its critics, philosophy, biblical and heroic subjects, and public occasions in an elevated, digressive manner, claiming the liberty of Pindaric inspiration.
works.significance: Cowley's odes created the English Pindaric, used by Dryden ('Alexander's Feast'), Congreve, and the eighteenth-century ode-writers, and important in the history of the ode.
works.meter: Irregular line lengths and stanzas, giving the effect of inspired freedom — the 'Pindaric' that Dryden and others adopted.
works.context: Published in Poems (1656); Cowley mistook Pindar's regular triadic form for inspired irregularity, but his 'Pindaric' became a fashionable English form for grand subjects.
works.structure: A group of irregular odes with varied line lengths and stanza forms, loosely modeled on (a mistaken idea of) Pindar's structure.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Plays, Never Before Printed (Cavendish)
works.description: Cavendish's collection of dramatic works, written in exile and never performed, including comedies, tragicomedies, and closet plays that experiment with genre and defend female authorship.
works.plot: The volume contains Loves Adventures, The Comical Hash, Youth's Glory and Death's Banquet, The Lady Contemplation, and others; The Convent of Pleasure, a separate 1668 publication, imagines a female community free of men.
works.significance: The largest body of drama by a seventeenth-century English woman and a pioneering experiment in the closet play; The Convent of Pleasure is a landmark of early feminist literature.
works.meter: Mixed prose and verse.
works.context: Published in 1662 while Cavendish was in exile with her husband William Cavendish, Duke of Newcastle; a second volume of plays appeared in 1668.
works.characters: Lady Happy (The Convent of Pleasure); Affectionata; Innocencia; various
works.structure: A collection of plays in mixed prose and verse, with prefaces defending the author's right to write.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
altTitles: The Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
works.description: Sir Thomas North's translation of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, made from Jacques Amyot's French (1559): the paired biographies of the Greek and Roman great — Theseus and Romulus, Alexander and Caesar, Coriolanus and Alcibiades, Antony and Demetrius, and the rest — in the full, energetic English prose that became Shakespeare's quarry for Julius Caesar, Coriolanus, Antony and Cleopatra, and Timon of Athens.
works.plot: Each pair of lives narrates its heroes' births, deeds, and deaths with the parallel moral comparisons; the collection as a whole is a gallery of virtue and vice in action — the school of statesmen and the storehouse of tragedy.
works.significance: The most consequential translation of the English Renaissance — the book through which Plutarch's heroes became Shakespeare's Romans.
works.meter: Prose of dramatic vividness and copiousness — Shakespeare followed its phrasing so closely that whole speeches of the Roman plays are North's sentences re-lined as verse.
works.context: Published 1579, in the decade of the English Plutarch vogue; it went through editions in 1595, 1603, and beyond, and was the most-read secular book of the Elizabethan age after the chronicles.
works.characters: Theseus; Romulus; Alexander; Julius Caesar; Coriolanus; Alcibiades; Mark Antony; Demetrius; the Greek and Roman worthies
works.structure: The paired lives in the Amyot order, with the comparisons of the pairs and North's dedication to Queen Elizabeth.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by North from Amyot's French; uncontested.

editions.title: Sir Thomas North's Plutarch: Selections from the Lives

works.title: Poema Morale
works.description: A sermon in verse of some 400 lines on the conduct of life and the last things, often called the earliest Middle English poem of any consequence: the aged speaker meditates on a misspent youth, the brevity of life, and the terrors and joys of judgement, urging repentance before death.
works.plot: The speaker reviews the stages of life, the certainty of death and judgement, the pains of hell and the bliss of heaven, and counsels amendment of life while time remains.
works.significance: A touchstone of early Middle English: its popularity (seven manuscripts) and its homiletic style anticipate the great penitential literature of the thirteenth century.
works.meter: The loose fourteener (septenarius) couplet of the earliest Middle English homiletic verse.
works.context: Composed in the south of England c. 1170, in the Kentish or south-western dialect; preserved in seven manuscripts, the earliest in the Lambeth and Trinity homily collections of c. 1200.
works.characters: the aged speaker
works.structure: A monologic homily moving from personal confession through doctrinal exposition (death, judgement, heaven, hell) to exhortation.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the speaker's self-description as old is a homiletic persona.

works.title: Poems by the Most Deservedly Admired Mrs Katherine Philips
works.description: The collected poems of Katherine Philips ('the Matchless Orinda'), published posthumously in 1667 (an unauthorized edition appeared in 1664), celebrating idealised female friendship, royalist loyalty, and retirement in polished couplets, and asserting a woman's place in the literary world.
works.plot: The poems address the members of her 'Society of Friendship' under pastoral names, praise virtuous female friendship and retirement, and express royalist politics, all with chaste, platonic idealism.
works.significance: Philips was the first Englishwoman to gain wide literary fame and to have her verse printed and celebrated by Dryden and others; her poems on female friendship are foundational to women's literary history.
works.meter: Polished heroic couplets and songs in a refined, chaste, and graceful manner.
works.context: Written in retirement at Owenia (Cardigan) and in London; the 1664 edition was pirated and disowned by Philips, who died of smallpox that year before the authorised 1667 edition appeared.
works.characters: Orinda (the poet); the friends of the Society (Poliarchus, Lucasia, etc.)
works.structure: A collection of lyrics, songs, and occasional poems, with a prefatory apparatus of commendations.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the 1667 edition is authoritative over the pirated 1664 text.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Poems on Several Occasions (Rochester)
works.description: The collected verse of John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester, issued in the year of his death, containing the satires, songs, and obscene verses that made him the most notorious poet of the Restoration court.
works.plot: The volume gathers Rochester's satires on the court and on Charles II ('I dreamt last night, though not designed to do so'), his songs including 'The Disabled Debauchee' and 'To a Lady in a Letter', his versified letters, and the bawdy lampoons.
works.significance: Rochester is now recognised as the most original English poet between Milton and Pope; his combination of Horatian ease with Hobbesian materialism anticipates the eighteenth century and the modern lyric of disillusion.
works.meter: Varied: heroic couplets in the satires, song stanzas and octosyllables in the lyrics.
works.context: Rochester's verse circulated mainly in manuscript within the court coterie; the 1680 edition was pirated and unauthorised, and the canon has been established only by modern editorial work on the manuscripts.
works.structure: A miscellany of satires, songs, epistles, and lampoons; the 1680 edition includes the prose speech on the death of Colonel Blood.
works.attributionNotes: The 1680 and 1716 printed collections contain pieces of doubtful authenticity; Vieth's 1968 edition establishes the canon from manuscript witnesses.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Poems upon Several Occasions with a Voyage to the Island of Love (Behn)
works.description: Behn's collected verse, including her celebrated lyric 'The Disappointment', the Pindaric odes to political occasions, and the translation of Fontenelle's Voyage to the Island of Love.
works.plot: The volume gathers court odes, love lyrics, songs, elegies, and political verse, including the Whig odes to Monmouth and the Tory poems of the 1680s.
works.significance: The most important collection of poetry by an English woman before the eighteenth century; 'The Disappointment' is a canonical treatment of female sexual experience and its failure.
works.meter: Varied: Pindaric odes, heroic couplets, song stanzas.
works.context: Published in 1684 by Tonson, establishing Behn as the first English woman to earn a living by her pen; a second volume appeared posthumously in 1701.
works.structure: A poetical miscellany with an appended translation of Fontenelle.

Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Works of Aphra Behn
editions.publisher: William Pickering / Ohio State University Press

works.title: Policraticus
altTitles: Policraticus: Of the Frivolities of Courtiers and the Footprints of Philosophers
works.description: John of Salisbury's treatise on politics, court life, and philosophy in eight books, completed in 1159 and dedicated to Thomas Becket; the first full work of medieval political theory, famous for its organic metaphor of the body politic and its defence of tyrannicide.
works.summary: The Policraticus satirizes the frivolities of courtiers, expounds the duties of prince and magistrate under the image of the body politic (the prince as head, the clergy as soul), argues that the tyrant is a public enemy whose killing may be lawful, and ends with a survey of ancient philosophy and the true happiness of the contemplative life.
works.significance: The most important political treatise written in twelfth-century Europe, a conduit of classical political thought into the Middle Ages, and a standard authority cited into the seventeenth century.

editions.title: Ioannis Saresberiensis Policraticus I–IV

works.title: Polychronicon (Trevisa's translation)
works.description: John Trevisa's English translation of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon, the universal history that dominated English historical reading: the world's geography, the history of Britain from the Britons to the fourteenth century, and the wonders of the world, in Trevisa's fluent, expansive prose, completed in 1387 for Thomas, Lord Berkeley. Printed by Caxton in 1482, it is the great English prose chronicle of the period.
works.plot: Following Higden's seven books, the work describes the world and Britain, then narrates English history from the Britons and Saxons through the Norman kings to the reign of Edward III, with its famous prefatory Dialogue on Translation in which Trevisa defends the rendering of Latin learning into English.
works.significance: The principal English universal history of the later Middle Ages and, with its Dialogue on Translation, a classic text of vernacular self-consciousness.
works.meter: Prose: fluent, idiomatic, and expansive — a landmark of fourteenth-century English prose style.
works.context: Completed in 1387 by Trevisa, chaplain of Thomas, Lord Berkeley, at Berkeley Castle; printed by Caxton (1482, with his continuation to 1460) and read into the sixteenth century.
works.characters: the kings and peoples of British history
works.structure: Seven books of world and British history, with Trevisa's Dialogue and the Berkeley continuations as its frame and sequel.
works.attributionNotes: Trevisa's authorship of the translation secure (named in the Berkeley manuscripts).

works.title: Pompey (a translation of Corneille)
works.description: Katherine Philips's translation of Pierre Corneille's La Mort de Pompée, performed in Dublin in 1663 and printed the same year — the first play by a woman to be performed on the English (here Irish) public stage — with a second Corneille translation, Horace, printed posthumously.
works.plot: The tragedy follows Corneille's neo-classical treatment of the death of Pompey and its aftermath in Egypt, rendered by Philips into English heroic verse.
works.significance: Philips's Pompey was the first play by an Englishwoman produced on the public stage, a landmark in women's literary history and in the reception of French neoclassical drama in England.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in a vigorous, dignified translation of French neoclassical drama.
works.context: Written during Philips's stay in Dublin (1662–63) and performed at the Theatre Royal, Smock Alley; it broke new ground for women in the professional theatre.
works.characters: Pompey; Cornelia; Caesar; Ptolemy
works.structure: A five-act neoclassical tragedy in heroic couplets, after Corneille.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Philips's translation of Corneille.

editions.title: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Prayers or Meditations
altTitles: Prayers Stirring the Mind unto Heavenly Meditations
works.description: Catherine Parr's book of devotional prayers and meditations, published in 1545; the first book published by an English queen under her own name, which ran through nineteen editions by 1600.
works.plot: The book adapts the third book of Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ into a sequence of prayers, meditations on the passion, and exhortations to penitence, faith, and the amendment of life, addressed to the reader in the queen's own voice as a fellow sinner seeking grace.
works.significance: The first printed book by an English queen and a landmark in the history of women's devotional writing; its combination of à Kempis's piety with Reformation emphasis on faith made it the century's most popular royal book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Published in 1545 by Thomas Berthelet with the queen's name on the title page, in the months when Parr's evangelical household (including Askew's associates) was under suspicion; the book's success established the royal devotional voice that Elizabeth I and others would imitate.
works.structure: A devotional manual of prayers and meditations arranged by spiritual states — contrition, faith, thanksgiving — with scriptural centos and personal application.

editions.title: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence

works.title: Precepts
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A wisdom poem of 94 lines in which a wise father addresses ten counsels to his son, one by one: to avoid anger and envy, choose wise companions, keep faith, practise generosity, and fear God. Each counsel is introduced by a repeated formula of address.
works.plot: The father, speaking 'many winters' of experience, delivers ten distinct precepts to his son on the conduct of a good life — on anger, friendship, wisdom, speech, generosity, and the fear of the Lord — closing with an exhortation to remember the counsels always.
works.significance: The most elaborate surviving Old English example of the father-to-son instruction genre, valuable for its picture of the ethical ideals taught to the young Anglo-Saxon elite.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the gnomic compression of the Exeter wisdom tradition; the anaphoric frame gives the poem its ceremonial regularity.
works.context: The father-son instruction poem has biblical and classical roots (Proverbs, the Disticha Catonis) and was a recognized genre in Anglo-Saxon England, as the Old English translation of the Distichs shows.
works.characters: the wise father, his son
works.structure: A decalogue structure: ten formally parallel counsels, each marked by the repeated address 'the wise father said to his son', framed by an introduction and a concluding admonition.

works.title: Prothalamion
works.description: A wedding song ('spousal verse') written for the double marriage of the daughters of the Earl of Worcester, Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset, celebrated at Essex House on the Thames in 1596; the poem follows the bridal procession along the river and closes with the refrain 'Sweet Thames, run softly, till I end my song'.
works.plot: The poet, walking the Thames bank in dejection, sees two swans (the brides) float down the river attended by nymphs; the vision becomes the wedding procession itself, and the poem blesses the marriages and the house of Essex.
works.significance: One of the two great English wedding odes, and the source of a refrain that became a byword of English poetry.
works.meter: The Spenserian stanza with a refrain line, lending the poem its processional music.
works.context: Written in 1596 in the orbit of the Earl of Essex, to whom the poem glances in its praise of Essex House; published the same year.
works.characters: the poet; Elizabeth and Katherine Somerset (the brides); the nymphs of Thames and Lee
works.structure: Ten stanzas with a refrain, moving from the poet's melancholy through the visionary river scene to the ceremonial blessing of the brides.

editions.title: The Yale Edition of the Shorter Poems of Edmund Spenser
editions.editor: William A. Oram, Einar Bjorvand, Ronald Bond, Thomas Cain, Alexander Dunlop, and Richard Schell (eds.)

works.title: Pseudodoxia Epidemica; or, Enquiries into Very Many Received Tenets
works.description: Browne's encyclopaedic survey of popular errors, in seven books examining and correcting the received beliefs of his time about natural history, medicine, geography, history, and Scripture.
works.plot: Book I analyses the causes of error; books II-IV treat errors concerning animals, plants, minerals, and man; books V-VII treat errors of history, chronology, and Scripture.
works.significance: The greatest English work of popular scepticism and one of the most important documents of seventeenth-century intellectual life; it influenced Baconian empiricism and the Royal Society's programme.
works.meter: Learned, allusive prose of great compression; the work went through five editions in Browne's lifetime.
works.context: Published in 1646, in the midst of the civil wars; it belongs to the new empirical spirit that would found the Royal Society, though Browne's method is as much scholarly as experimental.
works.structure: Seven books of learned enquiry organised by subject, each entry stating the received opinion and Browne's correction.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Ralph Roister Doister
works.description: Nicholas Udall's five-act comedy of the braggart Ralph Roister Doister, written c. 1552–54 and printed c. 1566–67; generally regarded as the first English comedy.
works.plot: Ralph Roister Doister, a vainglorious suitor encouraged by the parasite Merrygreek, woos Dame Christian Custance, who is betrothed to the merchant Gawin Goodluck; his letters and verses are read to her as insults, and his siege of her house ends in a comic battle with her maids, the braggart routed by a broom; the play closes with the lovers reunited and Roister Doister invited to dinner — folly corrected without malice.
works.significance: The first English comedy: it transplants the Roman braggart soldier and parasite into a London setting, joins classical form to native farce, and inaugurates the line that runs through Gammer Gurton's Needle to Shakespeare and Jonson.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets ('rhyming fourteeners'), with songs
works.context: Written c. 1552–54, probably for performance by the boys of Westminster School (Udall was headmaster there from 1555, earlier at Eton); drawing on Plautus's Miles Gloriosus and Terence's Eunuchus, it belongs to the academic revival of Roman comedy that would produce Gammer Gurton's Needle and the school drama of the 1560s.
works.characters: Ralph Roister Doister; Matthew Merrygreek; Dame Christian Custance; Gawin Goodluck; Tristram Trusty; Madge Mumblecrust; Tibet Talkapace; Annot Alyface
works.structure: Five acts modelled on the Roman comedy of Plautus and Terence, with a braggart soldier, a parasite, and a reunion plot; the action is domestic and the verse a rollicking doggerel.

editions.title: Three Sixteenth-Century Comedies

works.title: Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye
altTitles: The Recuyell of the Histories of Troy
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Raoul Lefèvre's French Recueil des histoires de Troyes, begun in Bruges in 1468 and completed in Cologne in 1471, and printed by Caxton at Bruges in 1473–74 as the first book printed in English. A courtly Troy compilation made for the Burgundian duchess Margaret of York, it inaugurated both Caxton's career and the English printed book.
works.plot: The compilation recounts the deeds of Hercules and the first destruction of Troy, then the rebuilding of the city under Priam and the second war — the rape of Helen, the battles before Troy, the deaths of Hector and Achilles, and the fall of the city through the wooden horse.
works.significance: The first book printed in English and the founding text of the English print tradition; its Troy matter carried the medieval romance of antiquity into the print era.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's early style, French-inflected and courtly, before his London plainness matured.
works.context: Begun in Bruges in 1468 for Margaret of York, sister of Edward IV, and printed at Bruges c. 1473–74 — the first English printed book; Caxton's famous prologue records his despair over the labour of translation and the duchess's command to finish.
works.characters: Hercules; Jason; Priam; Hector; Achilles; Paris; Helen; Ulysses
works.structure: Three books in Lefèvre's arrangement, translated in full, with Caxton's prologue and epilogue recording the circumstances of its making.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's authorship of the translation and printing is documented in his own prologue and epilogue.

editions.title: The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye

works.title: Regularis Concordia
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Tiberius A.iii (mid-eleventh century) and Cotton Faustina B.iii
works.description: The customary drawn up at the Council of Winchester (c. 970) under Æthelwold of Winchester to unify the observance of all English monasteries: a national supplement to the Rule of St Benedict, adapting continental customaries from Fleury and Ghent to English conditions and binding the reformed houses together under royal protection.
works.plot: The Concordia sets out the daily, weekly, and yearly round of the monastic life — the hours of prayer, the psalms and canticles, the ceremonies of the great feasts, the commemoration of the king and queen, and the dramatic rites of Holy Week, including the earliest recorded Visitatio Sepulchri (the 'Quem quaeritis' dialogue) in England.
works.significance: The founding document of the unified English monasticism of the late tenth century, and the source of the earliest English dramatic text (the Visitatio Sepulchri), making it a landmark in the history of English theatre as well as of monasticism.
works.context: Produced at the high point of the Benedictine Reform under King Edgar (959-975), the Concordia institutionalized the alliance of crown and monastery: the king and queen are commemorated in the daily office, and the text was issued with royal authority for all houses.
works.structure: A prologue addressed to King Edgar, followed by a systematic customary organized by the liturgical day and year; the prescriptions culminate in the elaborated rites of the Triduum, with the dialogue of the three Marys and the angel at the Easter sepulchre.
works.attributionNotes: Written by Æthelwold of Winchester, who names himself as the compiler; the text is securely attributed.

editions.title: Regularis Concordia Anglicae Nationis

works.title: Religio Laici
altTitles: Religio Laici: or, A Layman's Faith
works.description: Dryden's philosophical poem defending the Anglican via media against both Catholic tradition and Protestant private judgement, written while he was still a conforming member of the Church of England.
works.plot: The poem argues that Scripture is the sole rule of faith but is obscure in places, that private interpretation leads to chaos, and that the established church's tradition supplies the necessary authority.
works.significance: A key text in the history of English apologetics and the immediate predecessor of Pope's Essay on Man; it also marks the religious position Dryden abandoned when he converted to Catholicism in 1685-6.
works.meter: Heroic couplets, deliberately roughened, with frequent alexandrines and triplets.
works.context: Published in November 1682, after Dryden's translation of Simon's Criticial History; it responds to the Deist and Socinian challenge to revelation.
works.structure: A continuous argumentative poem with a prose preface defending its 'fugitive' method and rough verse.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Religio Medici
altTitles: Religio Medici: Its Author's Name is Thomas Browne
works.description: Sir Thomas Browne's meditative confession of faith, written privately in the 1630s and pirated in 1642 before Browne issued his own authorised text in 1643; it is the founding work of English introspective prose.
works.plot: In two parts Browne sets out his religious faith and his moral philosophy: the first defends his adherence to the Church of England against the charges of atheism and scepticism, the second explores charity and the duty to one's neighbour.
works.significance: The most influential work of English prose of the seventeenth century after the Authorised Bible; it created the genre of the personal religious meditation in prose and influenced Montaigne's English readers, Coleridge, Lamb, and Virginia Woolf.
works.meter: A richly Latinate, periodic prose with a strong personal cadence; Browne's style became the model of English 'character' writing.
works.context: Written while Browne was practising medicine, probably in the late 1630s; circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent in 1642, then authorised in 1643 with his own preface.
works.structure: Two parts of continuous meditative prose without formal division into chapters in the first edition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Browne; he authorised the 1643 edition after the pirated 1642 printing.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Resignation
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A first-person penitential prayer in which the speaker, an exile and outcast from his lord's favour, submits himself wholly to God's will and prays for guidance through the storms of life. The poem fuses the secular conventions of the exile's lament with Christian devotion.
works.plot: The speaker, alienated from his earthly lord and wandering in misery, turns to God as his true protector, acknowledging that he has suffered for his sins, and prays for wisdom, steadfastness, and a safe passage through life's sea of troubles to the heavenly home.
works.significance: A major example of the Old English religious lyric's absorption of elegiac conventions, and a witness to the penitential spirituality of late Anglo-Saxon England.
works.meter: Standard alliterative long line with the formulaic diction of the elegiac tradition; the poem is textually imperfect, with apparent lacunae.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English religious lyric, where the conventions of heroic exile poetry were appropriated for penitential devotion; comparable to The Wife's Lament in its fusion of personal loss and landscape imagery.
works.structure: A sustained first-person prayer in which the imagery of exile, sea-voyage, and homelessness is progressively reinterpreted as the soul's spiritual condition; some editors detect a break in the middle of the text suggesting an incomplete or composite poem.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The title 'Resignation' is an editorial convenience, not in the manuscript.

works.title: Respublica
works.description: An anonymous Protestant morality play of the commonwealth, written for performance at Christmas 1553 during the first months of Mary I's reign; a sophisticated political allegory of the misgovernment of the 1540s.
works.plot: Respublica, the widowed commonwealth, is robbed by Avarice and his crew — Oppression, Adulation, and Insolence (disguised as Policy, Honesty, and Authority) — who plunder her goods and divide them among themselves; the four sisters People, Verity, Peace, and Justice return, strip the thieves of their disguises, and restore the commonwealth, with Mercy pronouncing judgement and the audience promised amendment under the new queen.
works.significance: The most politically sophisticated of the sixteenth-century moralities: its allegory of the commonwealth, its disguised Vices, and its address to the monarch anticipate the political drama of the Elizabethan stage, and it documents the mid-Tudor crisis of counsel and plunder.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic speeches
works.context: Performed at Christmas 1553, evidently by a company of boys, in the first months of Mary's reign; the play's allegory of the plunder of the commonwealth under Edward VI's ministers (Somerset and Northumberland) and its restoration under the Catholic queen marks a rare moment when the morality tradition served immediate dynastic politics.
works.characters: Respublica; Avarice; Adulation; Oppression; Insolence; People; Verity; Peace; Justice; Mercy; Nemesis
works.structure: Five acts of morality allegory applied to contemporary politics, with the Vice Avarice doubling his disguises and a final scene of restoration and loyal address to Mary I.
works.attributionNotes: No author is named in the manuscript; Nicholas Udall has been proposed by some scholars, but the attribution remains unproven, and the work is treated as anonymous.

works.title: Revelations of Divine Love
works.description: Julian of Norwich's account of the sixteen revelations ('showings') she received during a grave illness on 8 May 1373, in two versions — the Short Text written soon after, and the Long Text, the fruit of some twenty years of meditation, completed c. 1393. Its theology of divine love — 'all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' — and of Jesus as mother makes it the greatest work of English mysticism and the first book in English known to be by a woman.
works.plot: At the point of death, the thirty-year-old Julian receives a series of visions of Christ's Passion, the Virgin, the world's littleness (the hazelnut), and the Lord's meaning: that love is his meaning; the Long Text unfolds these showings into a theology of sin, suffering, divine motherhood, and the 'great deed' by which all shall be made well.
works.significance: The summit of the English mystical tradition: the first major theological work by an English woman, and a text of the first importance for the history of women's writing and of Christian theology.
works.meter: Plain, meditative prose of extraordinary depth; homely images (the hazelnut) carrying speculative theology.
works.context: The showings occurred in Norwich on 8 May 1373; Julian became an anchoress at St Julian's church and wrote the Short Text shortly after and the Long Text c. 1393; Margery Kempe visited her c. 1413; the Long Text circulated in manuscript and in the printed editions of Serenus Cressy (1670).
works.characters: Julian (visionary); Christ; the Virgin Mary; the fiend
works.structure: Eighty-six (or more) chapters of vision, exposition, and prayer, organized by the order of the showings and the decades of their meditation.
works.attributionNotes: The author is known only as Julian of Norwich (from her church); her name in the world is unknown.

editions.title: The Writings of Julian of Norwich

works.title: Reynard the Fox
altTitles: The History of Reynard the Fox
The Historye of Reynart the Foxe
works.description: William Caxton's translation of the Dutch prose Reinaert de Vos, printed at Westminster in 1481: the beast epic of the fox Reynard, whose crimes are arraigned at the court of King Noble the lion, and whose cunning turns every accusation — and his own execution — into the ruin of his accusers. Caxton's print brought the European Reynard tradition to English readers and printers alike.
works.plot: Summoned to the lion's court to answer the complaints of the wolf Isengrim, the bear Bruin, and the other beasts, Reynard tricks each accuser in turn, confesses to save his neck, and is sent on pilgrimage only to murder his escort; his enemies' heads decorate his house, and the lion makes him his counsellor — the trickster triumphant.
works.significance: The classic English Reynard and the ancestor of the beast satire that runs through Spenser's Mother Hubberds Tale to the seventeenth-century Reynard reprints; a landmark of Caxton's publishing program.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's plain, lively narrative style at its best.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from the Dutch and printed in 1481, in the same year as his Godfrey of Boulogne; it fed a long English print tradition of Reynard editions and the beast satire of the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Reynard the Fox; King Noble the Lion; Isengrim the Wolf; Bruin the Bear; Tibert the Cat; Chanticleer the Cock
works.structure: A beast epic in episodic form: arraignment, defence, confession, and triumph, in the framework of the animals' court.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation documented in his own colophon.

editions.title: The History of Reynard the Fox

works.title: Richard II
altTitles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Second
works.description: Shakespeare's lyrical tragedy of deposition, opening the second tetralogy: Richard's misgovernment, the quarrel of Bolingbroke and Mowbray, and the king's fall from the throne of England — the first English history play written entirely in verse, culminating in Richard's murder at Pomfret and the new king's guilt.
works.plot: Richard banishes Bolingbroke and seizes his inheritance on Gaunt's death; Bolingbroke returns to claim his own, and the king's support melts away; in the deposition scene Richard unkings himself before Parliament; the plot of Aumerle is discovered, and Exton, reading Henry's wish, kills Richard in prison.
works.significance: The great English meditation on kingship, legitimacy, and the theatre of power — the seed of the Henriad that follows.
works.meter: Entirely in verse, much of it rhymed — Richard's elegiac lyricism is the play's signature music.
works.context: Written 1595 and printed 1597; the deposition scene was omitted from the early quartos for political reasons, and the play was notoriously performed on the eve of Essex's rising in 1601.
works.characters: King Richard II; Henry Bolingbroke; John of Gaunt; the Duke of York; the Duke of Aumerle; Thomas Mowbray; the Queen; Northumberland; the Bishop of Carlisle; Exton; the Gardener
works.structure: A five-act fall of princes, symmetrical in its structure of deposition, prophecy, and fulfilment, with the garden scene as the play's emblem of the commonwealth.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Richard III
altTitles: The Tragedy of King Richard the Third
works.description: Shakespeare's first great tragedy, completing the first tetralogy: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, murders his way to the crown through his brothers, his nephews (the Princes in the Tower), and his allies, seducing and discarding Lady Anne along the way, until the ghosts of his victims curse him at Bosworth and Richmond's victory ends the Wars of the Roses and plants the Tudor line.
works.plot: Richard announces his villainy in the opening soliloquy, eliminates Clarence, Hastings, Buckingham, Rivers, and the young princes, weds Anne and then plans her death; at Bosworth the procession of ghosts damns him and blesses Richmond, who slays him and marries Elizabeth of York.
works.significance: The first fully achieved Shakespearean tragedy of character, and the role that has defined the tragic actor from Burbage to Olivier.
works.meter: A verse of rhetorical virtuosity — Richard's soliloquies are among the most quoted in the canon — with the stichomythia of the wooing scene.
works.context: Written about 1592–93 from More's History of King Richard III via the chronicles of Hall and Holinshed; the Tudor myth of Richard's monstrosity serves the founding ideology of the Elizabethan state.
works.characters: Richard, Duke of Gloucester (Richard III); the Duke of Buckingham; Lady Anne; Queen Elizabeth; Queen Margaret; the Duke of Clarence; Lord Hastings; King Edward IV; the Duchess of York; Henry, Earl of Richmond; the two young Princes
works.structure: A Senecan revenge-cum-chronicle play driven by Richard's direct address — the audience as confidant — and crowned by the symmetrical dream of ghosts.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Robert Mannyng's Chronicle
works.description: Robert Mannyng of Brunne's verse history of England from Noah and the Trojan Brutus to the death of Edward I (1307), completed in 1338: the first part translates Wace's Roman de Brut, the second Peter Langtoft's French chronicle. It is the principal vernacular chronicle in English verse between Layamon and the fifteenth century.
works.plot: The poem narrates British and English history in sequence — Brutus, Arthur, the Saxon kings, the Norman Conquest, and the Plantagenet reigns — with particular fullness on the baronial wars of the thirteenth century.
works.significance: The chief English verse chronicle of the fourteenth century and a key witness to the national, vernacular historical consciousness of the period.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets in the first part, six-line tail-rhyme stanzas in the second.
works.context: Completed in 1338 by Mannyng, Gilbertine canon of Sempringham, at Sixhills, for the instruction of lay readers in English history; preserved in two manuscripts, BL Harley MS 1317 and Lambeth Palace MS 131.
works.characters: Arthur; the English kings from William I to Edward I; Simon de Montfort
works.structure: A two-part regnal chronicle (Brut section; Langtoft section) with patriotic and didactic digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Securely attributed to Mannyng in the poem's own colophon.

works.title: Roman Forgeries
altTitles: Roman Forgeries: Giving an Account of False Records
works.description: Traherne's only work published in his lifetime: an anti-Catholic polemic exposing spurious documents and legends in Roman tradition (the Donation of Constantine, fictitious councils and decrees), arguing for Protestantism on grounds of historical truth.
works.plot: Traherne catalogues and refutes alleged forgeries and false records in the Roman church's history, contending that the truth of a religion can be tested by the authenticity of its documents and tradition.
works.significance: Important as Traherne's only lifetime publication and as a document of seventeenth-century anti-Catholic polemic; it contrasts with his unpublished mystical writings.
works.meter: Argumentative, learned prose of controversial divinity.
works.context: Published in 1673 amid the anti-Catholic controversies that preceded the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis, reflecting Traherne's Anglican commitment.
works.structure: A polemical treatise of historical argument and refutation.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Romeo and Juliet
altTitles: The Most Excellent and Lamentable Tragedy of Romeo and Juliet
works.description: Shakespeare's lyric tragedy of young love: the star-crossed children of Verona's feuding houses meet at the Capulet feast, marry in secret, and are destroyed by chance and haste — the deaths of Mercutio and Tybalt, the exile, the sleeping potion, and the double suicide in the tomb that reconciles the houses too late.
works.plot: Romeo and Juliet fall in love across the family feud; Friar Laurence marries them; the street brawl kills Mercutio and Tybalt and exiles Romeo; the Capulets press Paris's suit; Juliet takes the friar's potion; the undelivered letter dooms the lovers; and the play ends with the discovery in the tomb and the prince's judgment on 'a glooming peace'.
works.significance: The archetype of the love tragedy in world literature — the play that fixed 'star-crossed lovers' in the language and on every subsequent stage and screen.
works.meter: The lovers' first dialogue is a shared sonnet; the play's verse runs from Mercutio's prose fantasia on Queen Mab to Juliet's aubade, with the final couplets of the tomb scene.
works.context: Written about 1595–96 from Arthur Brooke's poem Romeus and Juliet (1562) via continental novella; printed in quarto in 1597 and in a fuller text in 1599.
works.characters: Romeo; Juliet; Friar Laurence; Mercutio; Tybalt; the Nurse; Benvolio; Lord and Lady Capulet; Lord and Lady Montague; Paris; Prince Escalus
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of accelerating momentum — comedy in the first two acts, catastrophe in the last — built on the sonnet-form exchanges of the lovers and the antitheses of love and hate.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: Rosalynde
works.description: Lodge's pastoral romance, the direct source of Shakespeare's As You Like It: Rosader (Orlando), disinherited by his brother, flees to the forest of Arden, where the banished king, the disguised Rosalynde, and the shepherds' loves play out the courtships, disguises, and recognitions of the greenwood — the whole styled 'Euphues' golden legacy' and salted with eclogues.
works.plot: Saladyne's cruelty drives Rosader to the forest; Rosalynde, banished by the usurper Torismond, walks there disguised as Ganymede; the lovers' meetings in disguise, the lion's attack, the rescue of Saladyne, and the final scene's restorations — the true king, the brothers, and the three marriages — close the romance in Arden's court.
works.significance: The pastoral romance that became one of Shakespeare's greatest comedies — the greenwood's prose and the stage's poetry in one tradition.
works.meter: Euphuistic prose with pastoral verse, in Lodge's sweetest and most musical register.
works.context: Published 1590, at the height of the pastoral vogue; Shakespeare followed its plot closely in As You Like It (1599), keeping the forest, the disguises, and even the names of Phoebe and Adam.
works.characters: Rosader; Rosalynde (Ganymede); Saladyne; Alinda (Aliena); Torismond; Gerismond the exiled king; Phoebe; Montanus; Corydon; Adam Spencer
works.structure: A prose romance of exile and disguise in the pastoral mode, with verse eclogues and the euphuistic style of its subtitle.

editions.title: Rosalynde: Euphues Golden Legacie

works.title: Salmacida Spolia
works.description: The last masque performed at the court of Charles I, presented at Whitehall on 21 January 1640 with designs by Inigo Jones and with the young Prince Charles and his brothers among the masquers.
works.plot: Discord, in the person of a malicious spirit, has troubled the land; Wisdom and the genius of Britain, embodied in the king, restore concord, and the masquers descend to dance with the ladies.
works.significance: The final Caroline masque and a poignant document of a court culture on the eve of destruction; it also marks Davenant's official succession to Jonson as laureate.
works.meter: Verse and song with prose description; Inigo Jones's scenery and machinery.
works.context: Presented at Whitehall in January 1640, months before the calling of the Short Parliament and the collapse of Charles's personal rule; Davenant had been made Poet Laureate in 1638 on Jonson's death.
works.characters: Discord; Wisdom; the Genius of Britain; the masquers
works.structure: The standard court masque form: antimasque of discord, main masque of harmony, and the revels.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Davenant as laureate; Jones's designs are documented.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Salve Deus Rex Judaeorum
works.description: Aemilia Lanyer's volume of sacred poetry, one of the first books of poems published by an Englishwoman: the long title poem on Christ's Passion — with its celebrated 'Eve's Apology' defending women against the blame of the Fall — framed by the eleven dedicatory poems to the great ladies of the court and followed by 'The Description of Cooke-ham', the first country-house poem in English.
works.plot: The Passion poem narrates Christ's betrayal, trial, and crucifixion through the eyes of the women who followed him, with Pilate's wife's dream and the 'Eve's Apology' arguing women's innocence and worth; the dedications praise the Queen, the Countess of Pembroke, and the other patronesses; and Cooke-ham celebrates the estate of Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland, in the farewell of its trees and walks.
works.significance: A founding text of English women's poetry — the first sustained feminist argument in English verse, and the first country-house poem.
works.meter: Rhyme royal for the Passion poem, with the varied stanzas of the dedications and the elegiac couplets of Cooke-ham.
works.context: Published 1611, in the year of the King James Bible, by a woman of the court's margins; its argument for women's learning and worth answered the querelle des femmes with theology, and its Cooke-ham preceded Jonson's 'To Penshurst' in the country-house genre.
works.characters: Christ; Pilate's wife; Eve; the women of Jerusalem; Margaret Clifford, Countess of Cumberland; Anne Clifford; the dedicatees
works.structure: A tripartite volume — dedications, Passion poem, country-house poem — organized as a woman's address to women, the patrons and readers its intended audience.

editions.title: The Poems of Aemilia Lanyer

works.title: Samson Agonistes
works.description: A Greek tragedy in English on the blind Hebrew hero Samson, written to be read rather than performed: imprisoned and blinded by the Philistines, Samson moves from despair to renewed faith and, at the feast of Dagon, pulls down the temple, destroying himself and his enemies in an act of divine vengeance.
works.plot: Samson laments his blindness and capture; he is visited in turn by the Chorus of Danites, his father Manoah, his wife Dalila, and the giant Harapha; summoned to make sport before the Philistine lords at the temple of Dagon, he prays for strength, topples the pillars, and dies triumphantly with his enemies.
works.significance: The greatest English example of classical closet tragedy, it fuses Greek form with Hebrew subject and Milton's own condition, and has generated sustained debate about its violence, its politics, and its catharsis.
works.meter: Blank verse with choruses in varied lyric meters, using the Greek tragic forms of strophe and antistrophe.
works.context: Published with Paradise Regained in 1671; the blinded, politically defeated hero has long been read as a figure of Milton himself after the Restoration, and the play engages the problem of violent divine justice.
works.characters: Samson; the Chorus of Danites; Manoah; Dalila; Harapha; the Philistine Officer; the Messenger
works.structure: A classical drama observing the unities of time and place, with chorus, stichomythia, messenger, and catharsis, modeled on Sophocles and Aeschylus.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the title page notes it was 'never intended' for the stage.

The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)
