works.title: Sapho and Phao
works.description: Lyly's mythological court comedy: the ferryman Phao, made beautiful by Venus, is loved by the queen Sapho; Venus, jealous of the queen she meant to humble, afflicts Phao with love of herself; and the play resolves through Cupid's arrows and Sybilla's lore into Sapho's triumph over Venus and the renunciation of Phao's love.
works.plot: Venus, angered by Sapho's chastity, arms Cupid against her; the arrows misfire, Phao is loved and Sapho infatuated; the court's debates (between the scholars and the women) anatomize love; Sybilla's counsel and Venus's flight end the play with Sapho restored to rule and Phao banished from desire.
works.significance: The classic of the Elizabethan mythological court play — a genre in which the Queen's own image was negotiated on stage.
works.meter: Prose of Euphuistic balance, with songs and the debate set pieces.
works.context: Performed at court in 1584 and printed the same year; its Sapho is read as a mirror of Elizabeth I, and its love-psychology answers the Alençon courtship debates of the early 1580s.
works.characters: Sapho; Phao; Venus; Cupid; Sybilla; the court ladies; the scholars; the pages
works.structure: A five-act mythological debate-comedy of the Ovidian type, with the low comedy of the pages and servants as counterpoint.

editions.title: The Complete Works of John Lyly, 3 vols.

works.title: Satires
works.description: Donne's five formal verse satires of the 1590s — on the foppish courtier, the corrupt lawyer, religion and the quest for true church, the court, and the suitors and officers of the law — the poems that established the English formal satire and prompted the 1599 ban on satires, with their Juvenalian 'railing' and their portrait of Elizabethan London's vices.
works.plot: Each satire is a walk through a vice — the courtier's affectations, the lawyer's bribes, the sects' errors, the court's vanity, the law's extortion — with the poet as reluctant companion and ironist, and the third satire's 'On a huge hill, / Cragged and steep, Truth stands' as the sequence's moral summit.
works.significance: The foundation of English formal satire — the model for Pope's couplet and for every later poet of the town's vices.
works.meter: Rough, deliberately harsh heroic couplets — 'strong lines' — whose jagged enjambment and parenthesis imitated the speech of the town and the Roman satirists' abruptness.
works.context: Written 1593–98, in the decade that also produced the satires of Hall and Marston; the bishops' ban of 1599, which ordered the burning of satires, answered this vogue directly.
works.characters: the satirist; the fop; the lawyer; the courtier; the officers and suitors
works.structure: Five numbered satires in the formal Roman manner, each a single scene or progress through the city, in the couplet form Donne hardened into an instrument of speech.

editions.title: John Donne: The Complete English Poems
The Complete Poems of John Donne

works.title: Sawles Warde
works.description: An allegorical homily in AB-language prose on the custody of the soul: the house of the body is governed by Wit and Will, guarded by the five senses, threatened by the devil, and comforted by the virtues and the joys of heaven. It adapts Hugh of St Victor's De Anima and is the earliest extended allegory of the inner life in English prose.
works.plot: Wit (reason), with his wife Will, rules the soul's house; the messenger Fear of Death warns of the devil's assaults; the virtues — Prudence, Strength, Moderation, Righteousness — and the vision of the heavenly bliss fortify the household against temptation.
works.significance: A foundation stone of English allegory: its personified psychology anticipates the moralities (The Castle of Perseverance) and the dream allegories of the fourteenth century.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative AB-language prose.
works.context: Composed in the early thirteenth-century West Midlands, adapting Hugh of St Victor; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34, BL Cotton MS Titus D.xviii, and Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: Wit; Will; Fear of Death; the Virtues; the Devil
works.structure: A continuous allegorical narrative built on the house/castle metaphor, with set-piece descriptions of the pains of hell and the joys of heaven.

works.title: Seasons for Fasting
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Additional MS 43703 (a sixteenth-century transcript by Laurence Nowell of the lost Cotton Otho B.xi)
works.description: A poem of some 230 lines on the proper observance of the Ember fasts, defending the English custom of four seasonal fasts against the laxity of those who fast only once a year, and citing biblical and canonical authority for the practice. The text breaks off imperfectly.
works.plot: The poet rebukes priests who observe the Ember days wrongly, argues from scripture (Moses, Elijah, the Ninevites, Christ's forty days) that fasting is commanded, sets out the correct times of the four seasonal fasts, and attacks drunken priests; the poem ends incomplete amid a catalogue of fasts.
works.significance: A rare Old English poem on a live question of ecclesiastical discipline, valuable for its picture of eleventh-century religious controversy and its fusion of homiletic and satirical verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with the homiletic urgency of Wulfstan's prose; the text is incomplete, and some lines are metrically irregular.
works.context: The poem belongs to the late Old English period's debates over ecclesiastical discipline, contemporary with Wulfstan's legislation on fasting and the reform of the clergy; its strictures on drunken priests echo the reformers' campaigns.
works.structure: An argumentative structure: rebuke, biblical proof-texts, prescription of the fasts, and invective against clerical abuses, in the manner of Wulfstanian homiletic verse.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The poem's Wulfstanian manner has suggested to some scholars an origin in his circle, but no attribution is established.

works.title: Sejanus His Fall
works.description: Jonson's Roman tragedy of the favourite's fall: the ambitious Sejanus, minister of Tiberius, destroys the house of Germanicus piece by piece and rises toward the throne itself — until Tiberius's letter from Capri, read in the Senate, turns the city against him, and the mob tears him to pieces in the streets, his children executed, his statues melted down.
works.plot: Sejanus corrupts and removes Drusus, Agrippina, and their sons; the senators' servility and the informers' trade fill the middle acts; the emperor's withdrawal and the counter-plot of Macro prepare the fall; the Senate scene reverses Sejanus's fortunes in a single letter, and the final act follows the executioners through the city's vengeance.
works.significance: The first great English political tragedy of the Jacobean age and the founding text of the Roman play's documentary tradition.
works.meter: A grave, scholarly blank verse with extensive marginal annotation in the printed text — the play as documented history.
works.context: Performed at the Globe in 1603 (with Shakespeare in the cast), then revised for print in 1605, with Jonson's marginal notes citing his classical authorities; it landed him before the Privy Council on charges of 'popery and treason'.
works.characters: Sejanus; Tiberius; Macro; Silius; Arruntius; Agrippina; Drusus; Livia; the Senate; Cordus; Natta; Eudemus
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of state built on Tacitus, with the Senate scenes as its rhetorical engine and the messenger's report of the mob's savagery as its climax.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested, though the original Globe version contained a share by another hand, which Jonson replaced for the printed text.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos
altTitles: The Sermon of the Wolf to the English
works.description: Wulfstan's most famous sermon, preached in the crisis year 1014 as the Danish conquest of England was completed: an impassioned jeremiad interpreting the Viking devastation as God's punishment for the nation's sins, culminating in the vision of the enslaved nation — 'an Englishman is not worth more to a Dane than a dog'. The masterpiece of Old English pulpit rhetoric.
works.plot: The sermon catalogues the nation's sins — betrayal of lords, perjury, oppression of the poor, the violation of churches — and reads the tribulations of Æthelred's reign (the treachery of Eadric Streona, the burning, plundering, and enslavement of the people) as the biblical pattern of divine wrath; it calls the nation to repentance before the last things overtake it, in a crescendo of Wulfstan's two-stress rhythms.
works.significance: The greatest Old English sermon and the classic statement of the period's theology of national sin.
works.meter: Wulfstan's rhythmical prose: two-stress phrases, alliteration, anaphora, and word-pairs ('byman and bærnan' — burn and ravage).
works.context: Preached in 1014, after the expulsion of Æthelred and before Cnut's final conquest (1016); preserved in five manuscripts, including British Library, Cotton MS Nero A.i.
works.characters: Wulfstan (preacher, as 'Lupus'); the English nation
works.structure: A single continuous exhortation built on the antithesis of sin and punishment, with the historical crisis framed as the fulfilment of prophecy.
works.attributionNotes: Wulfstan's authorship is certain ('Lupus' is his Latin signature).

editions.title: The Homilies of Wulfstan

sources: The Pilgrim's Progress

works.title: Sermon of the Plough
works.description: Hugh Latimer's most famous sermon, preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548 and printed the same year; the classic Protestant sermon of social criticism, built on the text of the sower.
works.plot: Taking the gospel of the sower, Latimer expounds the 'plough' of preaching, the 'seed' of God's word, and the spiritual husbandry required of clergy and laity alike; he attacks the idleness of prelates ('unpreaching prelates'), the rack-renting of landlords, and the neglect of the poor, calling the realm to the work of the spiritual plough — a sustained sermon of estates satire turned to gospel ends.
works.significance: The most celebrated English sermon of the Reformation: its homely agricultural allegory and its fearless attack on clerical and landlord abuses made it the model of the Protestant pulpit's social criticism from the sixteenth century to the nineteenth.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Preached at Paul's Cross on 18 January 1548, in the first months of Edward VI's reign, as part of the reform campaign against images and non-residence; printed by John Day in 1548 and reprinted through the century, the sermon made Latimer the voice of the Edwardian Reformation's social conscience.
works.structure: A single sermon structured by the parable's allegory — the plough, the seed, the soil — with digressions into the abuses of church and commonwealth.

editions.title: Sermons by Hugh Latimer

works.title: Sermons upon Several Occasions (Tillotson)
altTitles: The Works of the Most Reverend Dr John Tillotson
works.description: The collected sermons of John Tillotson, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1691, published posthumously by his chaplain Ralph Barker; they are the model of latitudinarian preaching and were among the most widely read religious works of the eighteenth century.
works.plot: The sermons expound a rational, moral, and tolerant Christianity: the reasonableness of revelation, the duties of charity and justice, the evil of strife and persecution, and the practical character of true religion.
works.significance: Tillotson's sermons defined latitudinarian prose style and were a principal influence on Addison, Swift's models of plain preaching, and the moral temper of eighteenth-century Anglicanism.
works.meter: Clear, balanced, plain prose that became the standard of English pulpit eloquence.
works.context: Tillotson preached at St Lawrence Jewry and at court through the Restoration and after the Revolution; he was made Archbishop of Canterbury in 1691 and died in 1694; the folio of his Works appeared in 1696.
works.structure: A collection of occasional sermons arranged by subject and occasion.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Tillotson; the posthumous collection was edited by Ralph Barker.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Shakespeare's Sonnets
works.description: The 154 sonnets printed in 1609, with the long poem 'A Lover's Complaint' appended: a sequence to a beautiful young man urging him to marry and immortalizing him in verse, shadowed by a rival poet and by the 'dark lady' of the later sonnets — the greatest sonnet collection in the language, and the most argued-over book of poems in English literary history.
works.plot: The first seventeen sonnets press the youth to marry; the middle poems anatomize love, jealousy, absence, and the rival poet; the dark lady sequence (127–152) turns on lust and self-betrayal; and the final poems rework Cupid and the cures of love, closing with 'A Lover's Complaint' spoken by a forsaken maid.
works.significance: The summit of the English sonnet tradition; its identities, erotic shapes, and textual mysteries have made it a permanent site of scholarship and dispute.
works.meter: The Shakespearean sonnet (abab cdcd efef gg) brought to its definitive form, with 'A Lover's Complaint' in rhyme royal.
works.context: Composed across the 1590s and early 1600s, partly circulating in manuscript; printed by Thomas Thorpe in 1609 with the dedication 'To the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets, Mr. W.H.' — the most famous crux in English bibliography.
works.characters: the poet; the young man (Fair Youth); the dark lady; the rival poet; the maid (in the Complaint)
works.structure: A sequence of 154 sonnets with a detectable narrative arc — courtship, crisis, self-reproach — followed by the appended complaint.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested as Shakespeare's; the identities of the Fair Youth, the dark lady, and 'Mr. W.H.' remain unknown.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Sonnets (Arden Shakespeare, 3rd series)
The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: She Would if She Could
works.description: Etherege's second comedy, a brilliant but famously unsuccessful intrigue play in which two rakes, Courtall and Sir Joslin Jolly, pursue two masked beauties through a series of crossed appointments.
works.plot: Courtall and Sir Joslin arrange assignations with Ariana and Gatty; the women appear in disguise, the men are deceived, and a series of farcical failures leads to the marriages the title promises.
works.significance: Now recognised as one of the finest and most formally daring Restoration comedies, its plotless brilliance anticipating Congreve.
works.meter: Sparkling prose throughout.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields on 6 February 1668 and failed with the audience, though Pepys admired it; it was long undervalued before the twentieth-century revival.
works.characters: Courtall; Sir Joslin Jolly; Ariana; Gatty; Lady Cockwood; Rakehell; Mr Trim; Betty
works.structure: Five acts of almost pure intrigue with a single day's action and minimal plot.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Silex Scintillans
altTitles: Silex Scintillans; or, Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
works.description: Henry Vaughan's great collection of mystical religious verse (1650, expanded 1655), whose poems seek God through nature, childhood memory, and visionary longing — 'The Retreat', 'The World', 'Peace', and the 'Rules and Lessons' — earning him the title 'the Silurist' and a place among the metaphysical poets.
works.plot: The poems move between longing for a lost innocence and eternity glimpsed behind the world ('Eternity' in 'The World'), meditations on scripture and the sacraments, elegies, and practical rules for holy living.
works.significance: Once obscure, Silex Scintillans was recovered by the Romantics and Coleridge (whose 'intimation of immortality' echoes 'The Retreat') and is now recognised as major mystical poetry of the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Luminous, musical verse with emblematic structure and a visionary intensity drawn from Herbert but wilder and more personal.
works.context: Written in the aftermath of the Civil Wars and Vaughan's royalist seclusion in Breconshire, and deeply influenced by Herbert's Temple; the 1655 edition added secular and satirical pieces.
works.characters: the poet; God; the soul; natural and biblical figures
works.structure: A two-part collection (1650, then 1655 with 'Flamma sine Fumo') of devotional lyrics, translations, and epigrams loosely ordered around themes of nature, eternity, and faith.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published under the initials 'H.V.' and the title 'the Silurist'.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Sir Degaré
works.description: A Breton lay of the foundling knight: Degaré, son of a fairy knight who ravished his mother, is exposed at birth, raised by a hermit, and wins his spurs through combat with a dragon; his search for his father ends in recognition, reunion, and the marriage of his widowed mother to her long-lost lover. Preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Degaré, given his father's broken sword at birth, defeats the dragon, unhorses the knights of Arthur's court, and proves himself; seeking his father, he jousts with the fairy knight himself, and the two recognize each other; the poem ends with the father's return and the family's reunion.
works.significance: A representative minor lai valuable for the incest-anxieties and recognition patterns of the genre, and a staple of romance anthologies.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets, plain and rapid.
works.context: Composed c. 1325, probably in the south-east; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and later copies including the Percy Folio.
works.characters: Degaré; the fairy knight (his father); his mother; the hermit
works.structure: A foundling-quest in the lai manner, with the father-son combat as its climactic recognition scene.

works.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
works.description: The supreme masterpiece of the Alliterative Revival and one of the greatest poems of the English Middle Ages: 2,530 lines in alliterative stanzas with the 'bob and wheel' close, recounting Gawain's beheading-game with the Green Knight and his testing in the castle of Sir Bertilak. A romance of courtesy, chastity, and shame, in which the pentangle and the green girdle measure the hero against an ideal he cannot perfectly keep.
works.plot: At Arthur's Christmas court, the Green Knight offers his axe-blow for a return stroke a year hence; Gawain beheads him, and the knight rides off alive. The following winter Gawain journeys to the Green Chapel, is entertained for three days at Hautdesert — where his host's wife tests his chastity with escalating temptations while the host hunts deer, boar, and fox in parallel scenes — and, having accepted the protective green girdle and concealed it, receives at the Chapel a nick on the neck: the girdle's shame is revealed as the whole adventure was Bertilak's design, set on him by Morgan le Fay.
works.significance: The most admired English romance ever written: its fusion of alliterative craft, courtly ideals, and moral seriousness — and its unmatched winter landscapes and temptation scenes — have made it a touchstone of English literature (translated by Tolkien, Armitage, and many others).
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line in stanzas of varying length, each closed by the five-line rhymed 'bob and wheel'.
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400 by an unknown north-west Midlands poet (the 'Gawain-poet'), probably in the household circle of the Cheshire/Staffordshire gentry; preserved uniquely in BL Cotton MS Nero A.x, with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness.
works.characters: Gawain; the Green Knight (Sir Bertilak); Lady Bertilak; Arthur; Guinevere; Morgan le Fay; the guide
works.structure: A two-part structure (the beheading game at Camelot; the journey, temptations, and exchange of winnings at Hautdesert), interlaced by the three parallel hunts and the three bedroom temptations, and closed by Gawain's return and Arthur's court's adoption of the girdle.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed with Pearl, Patience, and Cleanness to the single 'Gawain-poet' on grounds of style, dialect, and shared manuscript.

editions.title: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
editions.editor: J. R. R. Tolkien and E. V. Gordon (eds.); rev. Norman Davis

works.title: Sir Launfal
works.description: Thomas Chestre's late fourteenth-century Breton lay of the fairy mistress: the knight Launfal, impoverished and slighted at Arthur's court, receives boundless wealth and the love of the fairy lady Tryamour on condition of secrecy, and is saved from death by her at his trial. The most accomplished English version of Marie de France's Lanval.
works.plot: Launfal, neglected by Arthur, rides out in despair and meets Tryamour, whose gifts restore his magnificence; his boast of her beauty at court — provoked by the queen's advances — brings trial for treason, but Tryamour appears at the judgement, vindicates him, and carries him to the fairy isle of Olyroun.
works.significance: The finest English fairy-mistress lay and the standard version of the Lanval story in English; a key text for the romance's treatment of women and power.
works.meter: Twelve-line tail-rhyme stanzas of the popular romance kind.
works.context: Composed c. 1390 by Thomas Chestre (who names himself in the poem), reworking the earlier Sir Landevale and Marie de France; preserved in BL Cotton MS Caligula A.ii.
works.characters: Launfal; Tryamour; Arthur; Guinevere (unnamed queen); the mayor of Caerleon
works.structure: The classic lai structure: courtly exclusion, otherworld encounter, transgression, trial, and translation to the otherworld.
works.attributionNotes: The author names himself 'Thomas Chestre' in the poem's opening lines.

editions.title: The Middle English Breton Lays

works.title: Sir Orfeo
works.description: The masterpiece of the English Breton lay: the classical myth of Orpheus and Eurydice retold as a Celtic fairy romance, in which King Orfeo, harper of Winchester, loses his queen Heurodis to the fairy king and wins her back through the power of his music. Some 600 lines of haunting narrative, preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript.
works.plot: Heurodis is taken by the fairy king from under the ympe-tree; Orfeo abandons his throne to live as a harper in the wilderness, sees his queen among the fairy riders, follows them into their castle, and recovers her by his harping; the poem ends with the steward's loyalty tested and the kingdom restored.
works.significance: Universally regarded as the finest of the Middle English Breton lays and one of the great short narratives of the period; the classical myth's medieval transformation is a touchstone of romance criticism.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lyrical set-pieces; economical and evocative.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in the London area, reworking the Orpheus myth through Celtic fairy-lore and the Breton lai tradition; preserved in the Auchinleck manuscript (c. 1330) and two fifteenth-century copies.
works.characters: Orfeo; Heurodis; the fairy king; the steward
works.structure: A lai of loss, wilderness exile, and recovery, framed by the steward episode; the Otherworld journey is its centre.

works.title: Solomon and Saturn I and II
altTitles: The Dialogue of Solomon and Saturn
works.description: Two wisdom dialogues in which Solomon, the biblical master of wisdom, contends with Saturn, the legendary Chaldean sage, over questions of fate, prayer, and the powers of the Pater Noster — its letters imagined as armed warriors assailing the devil. The poems are the most extravagant of the Old English wisdom tradition.
works.plot: In Solomon and Saturn II, the sages debate the powers of the Pater Noster: each letter becomes a warrior with a specific weapon against the fiend ('P has a golden rod and fights the devil...'); the poem surveys the poem's battles against evil in a fantasia of personified letters. Solomon and Saturn I concerns the praise of the Pater Noster and the books it governs, with a runic passage on the letter R.
works.significance: The wildest flights of the Old English wisdom tradition; central to the study of Anglo-Saxon learned imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense, sometimes eccentric diction.
works.context: Preserved in Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MSS 41 and 422; the dialogues draw on apocryphal Solomonic and computistical lore.
works.characters: Solomon; Saturn; the personified letters of the Pater Noster
works.structure: Question-and-answer dialogue in the wisdom-contest tradition, elaborated with the allegorical letter-warfare of the Pater Noster passages.

works.title: Some Reflections upon Marriage, Occasion'd by the Duke and Duchess of Mazarine's Case
works.description: Astell's second major feminist work, written in response to the scandalous separation of the Duke and Duchess of Mazarin, arguing that the legal subjection of wives is a form of arbitrary power inconsistent with the principles of the Glorious Revolution.
works.plot: Astell asks how it can be that all men are born free, yet every woman is born a slave; she argues that marriage as constituted gives husbands arbitrary power over wives, that women must cultivate their reason, and that a rational education would make better wives and mothers.
works.significance: One of the most powerful early feminist critiques of marriage and of the sexual double standard; its argument that arbitrary power over women is inconsistent with the principles of 1688 has made it a canonical text of political theory.
works.meter: Ironical, pointed prose with a sustained rhetorical question.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1700, with second and third editions in 1703 and 1706; the Mazarin case was a cause célèbre in Restoration and post-Revolution London.
works.characters: the Duchess of Mazarin; Hortense Mancini (alluded to)
works.structure: A continuous argument in three parts with a preface to the third edition of 1706.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; attribution to Astell is established.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Some Thoughts Concerning Education
works.description: Locke's influential treatise on the education of a young gentleman, which grew out of letters to his friend Edward Clarke and argued for physical hardiness, moral habituation, and a practical curriculum over rote learning.
works.plot: Locke advises on the health of the body, the formation of the mind through habit and example, the teaching of reading, writing, languages, history, geography, arithmetic, and a trade, and the importance of curiosity over coercion.
works.significance: The most influential English work on education of the eighteenth century; it shaped Rousseau's Emile, and its emphasis on habit and on the child's own interest transformed educational theory.
works.meter: Practical, conversational prose.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1693, expanded in the 1695 and 1705 editions; it derived from Locke's letters to Edward Clarke of Chipley concerning Clarke's son.
works.structure: A series of numbered sections following the natural order of education.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; authorship was publicly acknowledged only in the 1705 edition.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Songs and Poems of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
altTitles: The Works of Charles Sackville, Earl of Dorset
works.description: The small but influential body of verse by the Earl of Dorset — courtier, wit, and patron — including the famous sea-song 'To all you ladies now at land', written, according to tradition, the night before the battle of Solebay.
works.plot: The poems are light, graceful lyrics of love and parting, several written on public occasions and to particular women of the court; the sea-song consoles the ladies ashore while the men fight at sea.
works.significance: 'To all you ladies now at land' became one of the best-known songs of the period; Dorset's work is a touchstone for the ideal of effortless courtly wit.
works.meter: Short song stanzas in an easy, colloquial register.
works.context: Dorset's verse circulated in manuscript at the court of Charles II; he was a leading patron of Dryden and Prior and a central figure in Restoration literary society.
works.structure: A short miscellany of songs and occasional verse.
works.attributionNotes: The canon is small and some attributions are uncertain; the sea-song is traditionally ascribed to Dorset.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Songs and Sonnets
works.description: The collective title given in the 1633 posthumous Poems to Donne's lyrics of love — 'The Good-Morrow', 'The Sun Rising', 'The Canonization', 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning', 'The Ecstasy', 'The Flea', and some fifty more — in which the conventions of Petrarchan love are re-forged by argument, paradox, and the new 'metaphysical' wit.
works.plot: No single plot: the poems dramatize the phases of love — waking, parting, quarrelling, dying, transcending — each lyric a miniature drama of persuasion in which a lover argues a mistress, a rival, the sun, or himself into a truth about love.
works.significance: The founding book of metaphysical poetry — the lyric revolution that Jonson's classicism answered and that the twentieth century would re-canonize.
works.meter: Dramatic, speech-like rhythms within stanza forms of Donne's own devising — the 'strong lines' of the metaphysical manner, with conceits drawn from astronomy, alchemy, law, and cartography.
works.context: Written from the 1590s (the 'Jack Donne' of Lincoln's Inn and the Essex and Ralegh voyages) into his middle years, circulating in manuscript among the wits and Inns of Court; printed only after his death in the 1633 Poems.
works.characters: the poet-lover; the beloved (unnamed); the Sun; Death; God (in the religious lyrics)
works.structure: A group of some fifty-five lyrics gathered posthumously under a title Donne never gave them, arranged in the 1633 edition as a loose anthology of the love poems.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the group's composition dates span at least two decades, and individual datings are widely disputed.

editions.title: John Donne: The Complete English Poems
The Complete Poems of John Donne

works.title: Sophonisba; or, Hannibal's Overthrow
works.description: Lee's early heroic tragedy on the Carthaginian princess Sophonisba, who drinks poison rather than fall into Roman hands, and whose lines 'O happiness! O pleasure!' became proverbial for heroic bombast.
works.plot: Sophonisba, betrothed to Massinissa, is captured by the Romans; to save her from their triumph she takes poison given by Massinissa, and Hannibal's cause collapses.
works.significance: An important early heroic tragedy and the source of some of the most frequently quoted lines of Restoration bombast; it establishes Lee's reputation before The Rival Queens.
works.meter: Blank verse of high rhetorical strain.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1675 and published in 1676; it was one of the earliest plays in which the young actor Thomas Betterton shone in a heroic role.
works.characters: Sophonisba; Massinissa; Hannibal; Syphax; Scipio; Melbo; Narbal
works.structure: Five acts in the heroic manner with a single tragic action.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Soul and Body I and II
altTitles: The Soul's Address to the Body
works.form: religious debate poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A pair of related poems (Vercelli Book I, 166 lines; Exeter Book II, 121 lines) in which the soul, revisiting its decaying body once a week, reproaches it for the sins of the flesh and foretells the torments of judgment. The earliest English body-and-soul debate, ancestor of a long medieval tradition.
works.plot: The damned soul, forced to revisit its corpse, addresses the silent body: 'Where are the riches you gathered? The hall you feasted in?' — enumerating the body's pleasures and their price in hell, the worms and the fire; the Exeter version closes with a brief address to the blessed soul by contrast. The debate's later fortunes run through the Middle English 'Desputisoun bitwen the Bodi and the Soule' to the danse macabre.
works.significance: Inaugurates the body-and-soul debate tradition that runs through Middle English literature.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 101v-103v) and the Exeter Book (fols. 98a-100a); the genre derives from Latin and homiletic sources.
works.characters: the Soul; the Body; (in II) the blessed soul
works.structure: A monologue of reproach and warning, spoken by the soul to the body at the grave; the two versions differ in length and ending.

works.title: Speke Parrot
works.form: verse satire in Skeltonics with macaronic Latin
works.description: The first of Skelton's great anti-Wolsey satires: a parrot — polyglot, learned, and fearless — speaks the court's dangerous truths in a torrent of macaronic verse, attacking the Cardinal's pride, his monopoly of the king's ear, and the corruption of the church, all under the parrot's traditional licence of the fool.
works.plot: The Parrot complains of his cage and his mistress's neglect, then turns to the abuses of the age: Wolsey's supremacy, clerical greed, and the decay of learning; the poem closes with a prayer for amendment.
works.significance: The founding text of the English tradition of political satire under censorship; its speaking-bird device recurs through the century to Spenser and beyond.
works.meter: Skeltonic lines studded with Latin, Greek, and school tags; the parrot's 'speaking' is a display of learned polyglot wit.
works.context: Written in 1521 as Wolsey's power peaked; the parrot's cage is the poet's own position under surveillance, and the poem circulates the satirical truths the court could not speak.
works.characters: the Parrot; (implicitly) Cardinal Wolsey
works.structure: A monologue of the speaking bird in the complaint tradition, shifting between personal grievance and public satire without fixed argument.

works.title: St Erkenwald
works.description: An alliterative miracle-legend of 352 lines on the discovery, during the rebuilding of St Paul's, of a pagan judge's incorrupt tomb: the bishop Erkenwald's tearful prayer draws from the corpse the story of his just life and the baptism that, in the moment of his speech, admits the just pagan to heaven. The finest short alliterative poem of the period.
works.plot: Workmen excavating at St Paul's find a tomb whose body lies uncorrupted as in life; none can identify it, until Bishop Erkenwald, summoned to the mystery, speaks to the dead man, who reveals himself as a judge of heathen London, just in all his dealings; at the bishop's words of baptism, the corpse — denied heaven's sight so long — sighs, and crumbles to dust as its soul ascends.
works.significance: The classic Middle English treatment of the salvation of the just pagan (the problem Dante faced with Trajan and Virgil), and one of the most moving poems of the alliterative tradition.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line, restrained and solemn.
works.context: Composed c. 1386–1400 in the north-west Midlands, in the circle of the Gawain-poet (many scholars assign it to him), perhaps occasioned by work on St Paul's; preserved uniquely in BL Harley MS 2250 (dated 1477).
works.characters: Erkenwald; the pagan judge; the London crowd
works.structure: A single dramatic episode: discovery, wonder, dialogue, and resolution, in the manner of the alliterative miracle-legend.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; attributed by many scholars to the Gawain-poet.

works.title: Steps to the Temple
altTitles: Steps to the Temple: Sacred Poems with Other Delights of the Muses
works.description: Richard Crashaw's first English collection (1646), containing his religious epigrams, hymns, and translations, including the famous 'The Weeper' on Mary Magdalene, 'Musicks Duell', versions of Marino, and sacred epigrams — the baroque, sensuous devotional verse that distinguishes him among the metaphysicals.
works.plot: The poems celebrate the saints and sacraments and the mysteries of faith in ecstatic, image-laden verse, turning epigrammatic wit and continental baroque conceit to Catholic-inflected devotion.
works.significance: 'The Weeper' and the sacred epigrams are among the most striking religious lyrics of the century, admired by Cowley and later critics for their daring imagery and fervour.
works.meter: Elaborate, musical, sometimes extravagant conceits; epigrammatic compression; a lush, sensual baroque style.
works.context: Published in London in 1646 while Crashaw was an Anglican; he converted to Catholicism and went into exile, and a further collection, Carmen Deo Nostro, appeared in Paris in 1652.
works.characters: Mary Magdalene; the Virgin; Christ; the saints
works.structure: A collection of sacred epigrams, hymns, elegies, and translations, framed by a commendatory poem on Herbert's Temple.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: Summa Logicae
works.description: William of Ockham's systematic treatise on logic, written c. 1323 before his summons to Avignon; in three parts it expounds terms, propositions, and the theory of argument, developing the nominalist ontology — the rejection of universals as real entities — for which Ockham is chiefly remembered.
works.summary: Part I analyses terms and the problem of universals, arguing that only individuals exist and that universal concepts are signs in the mind; Part II treats propositions and the properties of terms; Part III examines syllogistic, demonstrative, and probable argument, including the analysis of fallacies. The work is the vehicle of Ockham's razor in its methodological form: entities are not to be multiplied without necessity.
works.significance: The most influential logic textbook of the later Middle Ages; its nominalism reshaped fourteenth-century philosophy and theology and remains a principal point of reference in the history of logic.

editions.title: Guillelmi de Ockham Summa Logicae

works.title: Summer's Last Will and Testament
works.description: Nashe's one surviving solo play, a summer show performed at Archbishop Whitgift's palace at Croydon: Summer, dying of the plague-year's sickness, makes his will and bequeaths the world to Autumn and Winter, while the seasons, the personified vices, and the jester Will Summer pass in review — the play's songs ('Adieu, farewell, earth's bliss') and its memento mori making it the great plague elegy of the Elizabethan stage.
works.plot: Summer, sick and dying, summons his officers — Ver (Spring), Solstitium, and the rest — to account for the year; the debate of the seasons, the entertainment of the Harvest lord, and the pageant of the vices fill the show; Summer makes his will, bequeathing the world to the colder seasons, and dies, with the songs and the jester's epilogue closing the play on mortality itself.
works.significance: The great plague poem of the English Renaissance and Nashe's masterpiece of the mixed mode — masque, satire, and elegy in one.
works.meter: Mixed verse and prose, with the famous lyric 'Adieu, farewell, earth's bliss' ('A Litany in Time of Plague') as its summit.
works.context: Performed at Croydon in the plague summer of 1592 (perhaps September), for the Archbishop of Canterbury's household; printed in 1600.
works.characters: Summer; Autumn; Winter; Ver (Spring); Solstitium; Bacchus; Harvest; Will Summer (the jester); the satyrs; the nymphs; Death (in the songs)
works.structure: A masque-like entertainment of pageants, debates, and songs, loose in structure but unified by the dying Summer's progress to his will and death.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Nashe, 5 vols.
editions.editor: R. B. McKerrow (ed.), revised by F. P. Wilson

works.title: Surrey's Poems
altTitles: Sonnets and Lyrics of Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
works.description: The collected shorter poems of the Earl of Surrey — sonnets in the new 'English' form he devised (three quatrains and a couplet), elegies, and lyrics such as 'The soote season', 'Alas, so all things now do hold their peace', and the elegy on Wyatt — printed posthumously in Tottel's Miscellany (1557).
works.plot: A courtier's lyric record: love's complaints, the seasons' changes, the deaths of friends, and the poet's imprisonment at Windsor, all in a grave, musical decasyllabic line.
works.significance: With Wyatt, the founder of the English sonnet; Surrey's smoother line and his rhyme scheme became the Elizabethan standard, and Tottel's printing of his verse made him the model of the English courtly poet.
works.meter: The regular iambic pentameter and the English sonnet rhyme scheme (abab cdcd efef gg) that Surrey perfected and Shakespeare inherited; smooth alternation of the accents.
works.context: Written in the last decade of Surrey's life, under the factional warfare that ended in his execution in 1547; the elegy on Wyatt makes the dead poet a mirror of his own fate.
works.characters: the speaker; the beloved ('Geraldine', Elizabeth Fitzgerald); the court
works.structure: Miscellany of sonnets and lyrics without narrative frame; Tottel's printed canon of forty poems is the principal witness.
works.attributionNotes: The Tottel canon of forty poems is accepted in the main; a few attributions are contested.

editions.title: Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey: Poems

works.title: Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees and the Propagation of Timber
works.description: Evelyn's treatise on trees and timber, written at the request of the Royal Society and the first book it published, which urged the planting of oaks and other timber for the navy and became a classic of forestry.
works.plot: Evelyn describes the principal forest trees of England, their uses, propagation, and management, and argues that the nation's naval strength depends on the systematic planting of timber.
works.significance: The founding text of English forestry and an important document of the new scientific culture; its practical influence on tree-planting was immediate and long-lasting.
works.meter: Learned but readable prose, with verse quotations and classical allusion.
works.context: Published in 1664 as the first book issued by the Royal Society; four editions appeared in Evelyn's lifetime.
works.structure: Four books, each treating a group of trees, with appended treatises on fruit trees and on the propagation of timber.

works.title: Tamburlaine the Great, Part 1
works.description: Marlowe's first play and the manifesto of Elizabethan blank verse drama: the Scythian shepherd Tamburlaine rises by conquest to overthrow kings, takes the Egyptian princess Zenocrate, defeats the Persian Cosroe, and tramples the Turkish emperor Bajazeth in his cage — the play closing with Tamburlaine's marriage and his vow of further conquests, 'still climbing after knowledge infinite'.
works.plot: Tamburlaine, armed with eloquence and terror, wins Zenocrate, deposes Mycetes, and crowns himself after Cosroe's fall; Bajazeth and Zabina are caged and mocked; Damascus is sacked for its defiance, Zenocrate's father pardoned for her sake; the play ends with the betrothal and the tyrant's speech of unappeasable aspiration.
works.significance: The first great English blank-verse tragedy and the fountainhead of Elizabethan heroic drama; its hero became the type of the Renaissance overreacher.
works.meter: The 'mighty line' — Marlowe's blank verse of sweeping hyperbole and classical allusion, which transformed the English stage.
works.context: Performed by the Admiral's Men in 1587, the Armada year; its prologue's defiance of 'jigging veins of rhyming mother-wits' announced the new poetics that Shakespeare's generation inherited.
works.characters: Tamburlaine; Zenocrate; Bajazeth; Zabina; Mycetes; Cosroe; Theridamas; Techelles; Usumcasane; Agydas; the Soldan of Egypt
works.structure: A two-part rise structured as a chain of conquests and debates, with the great set speeches — 'Is it not passing brave to be a king' — as its pillars.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: Tamburlaine the Great, Part 2
works.description: The sequel Marlowe was pressed to write after Part 1's success: Tamburlaine's further conquests — the slaughter of the virgins of Damascus, the bridling of the conquered kings who draw his chariot, his burning of the Koran at Babylon — until the death of Zenocrate breaks him, his own sickness follows, and the 'scourge of God' dies in his camp, his empire uncompleted.
works.plot: Tamburlaine defeats the Christian Sigismund's treachery, kills his coward son Calyphas, humbles the Turkish and Egyptian powers, and burns the Koran in defiance; Zenocrate's death opens the way to his own — the physician's verdict, the self-anatomy in the mirror, and the dying survey of the map of the world he could not finish conquering.
works.significance: The completion of the first great two-part epic of the English stage and the template for the overreacher's fall.
works.meter: The mighty line at its most sustained, with the dying speeches of Zenocrate and Tamburlaine as its elegiac close.
works.context: Written immediately after Part 1 and printed with it in 1590; its burnings and blasphemies made Marlowe's name feared as well as famous.
works.characters: Tamburlaine; Zenocrate; Calyphas; Amyras; Celebinus; Orcanes; Sigismund; Callapine; the Turkish Concubines; the Physician
works.structure: A series of conquests and defiances culminating in the two deaths, with the chariot scene and the burning of the books as the peaks of its provocation.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: Testament of Love
works.description: Thomas Usk's allegorical prose apologia, written in the Tower of London before his execution in 1388: the imprisoned author, in Boethian dialogue with Love and her company, defends his political career, expounds free will and grace, and seeks the 'Margaret' of his devotion. For three centuries it was printed and read as Chaucer's.
works.plot: The narrator, cast down by fortune and imprisoned, laments until the lady Love appears with her sisters; in three books she teaches him the nature of love and virtue, vindicates his service and his betrayals, and leads him through the doctrine of predestination and free will to the vision of the pearl of perfect bliss.
works.significance: The first major prose work in the Chaucerian line and a unique document of the political prisoner's consolation; its false attribution shaped the early reception of Chaucer himself.
works.meter: Prose, richly Chaucerian in vocabulary and cadence.
works.context: Composed 1384–88 in prison, in the factional struggles of Richard II's London (Usk had betrayed John of Northampton to Nicholas Brembre); the author's identity was recovered from the acrostic, overturning the Chaucerian attribution, only in the nineteenth century.
works.characters: the Narrator (Usk); Love; Margaret (the pearl); Fortune; the Virtues
works.structure: Three books of Boethian consolation, with the acrostic of the opening chapters spelling the author's name and his lady's — 'MARGARETE OF VIRTW HAVE MERCI ON THIN USK'.
works.attributionNotes: Attribution to Usk secure from the acrostic and the records of his trial; previously attributed to Chaucer.

editions.title: Thomas Usk: Testament of Love

works.title: The Advancement of Learning
altTitles: The Two Books of Francis Bacon of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning, Divine and Human
works.description: Bacon's great survey and defence of knowledge, addressed to James I: the first book vindicates learning against its 'distempers' and detractors; the second maps the whole territory of human knowledge — history, poesy, and philosophy, with their divisions and gaps — in the programme that the Latin De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623) would expand.
works.plot: Book I argues the dignity and utility of learning against the objections of divines, politicians, and the learned themselves; Book II proceeds through the three faculties of memory, imagination, and reason, charting each science, noting its deficiencies, and closing with the practical counsel for the advancement of knowledge in Bacon's own time.
works.significance: The founding charter of English scientific and philosophical prose — the map of knowledge that organized the intellectual world until the Encyclopedists.
works.meter: Prose of sustained periodic power, with the famous catalogue of the impediments to learning.
works.context: Published in 1605, in the first years of James I's reign, as Bacon's bid for the role of philosophical counsellor; it is the seed of the Instauratio Magna and the later Latin works.
works.structure: Two books of systematic argument — apology, then map — in the humanist tradition of the treatise addressed to a prince.

editions.title: The Advancement of Learning (Oxford Francis Bacon)

works.title: The Adventures of Master F.J.
altTitles: A Discourse of the Adventures Passed by Master F.J.
works.description: Gascoigne's prose fiction of seduction, printed in A Hundred Sundry Flowers (1573): the gallant F.J., a guest in a northern castle, conducts an affair with the lady Elinor — their letters, verses, and assignations documented in the narrative's self-conscious apparatus — until the affair sours into jealousy, betrayal, and the narrator's moralizing close; the first English novel of intrigue, revised and bowdlerized in The Posies (1575).
works.plot: F.J. arrives at the castle, courts Elinor by letter and verse; the affair progresses through the night meetings and the gift of the sword; the secretary's treachery and Elinor's inconstancy turn love to jealousy; and the narrator's apparatus — the editor's letters and comments — frames the tale as 'translated' from Italian and morally cautioned.
works.significance: The first original English novel of manners — the seed of the English tradition of prose fiction that runs through Deloney and Nashe to Defoe.
works.meter: Prose with interpolated verses, in the manner of the Italian novella and the French Heptameron tradition.
works.context: Printed in 1573 and revised in The Posies (1575) after the scandal of its supposed real-life originals; it anticipated the psychological fiction of the next century by a generation.
works.characters: Master F.J.; Elinor; the secretary; Dame Frances; the narrator-editor (G.T.)
works.structure: A framed novella with the editorial machinery of letters, verses, and marginal commentary — the first English fiction to flaunt its own making.

editions.title: The Complete Works of George Gascoigne, 2 vols.

works.title: The Alchemist
works.description: Jonson's comedy of alchemical confidence tricks: in Lovewit's vacated London house during the plague, Subtle the alchemist, Face the housekeeper, and Doll Common the prostitute run their roaring shop, fleecing the knight Sir Epicure Mammon, the tobacconist Abel Drugger, the Puritan brethren Ananias and Tribulation, and the quarrelling Kastril — until Lovewit's return and the final distribution of the spoils.
works.plot: Each gull arrives with a different dream — the philosopher's stone for Mammon, a lucky shop for Drugger, the widow Pliant for Kastril, the orphans' goods for the Puritans — and each is worked by the 'venture tripartite' of Subtle, Face, and Doll; the quarrels of the conspirators and the return of the master bring the whole house of cards down in the last act's cascade of exposures.
works.significance: Generally reckoned the greatest English comedy after Shakespeare — the most perfect machine of comic construction in the language.
works.meter: Verse for the gulls' fantastic speeches (Mammon's visions of the stone), prose for the roaring shop's business — Jonson's richest mix.
works.context: Performed by the King's Men in 1610 and printed in 1612; its plague setting mirrored the London closures of 1609–10, and its Puritans were recognized at once.
works.characters: Subtle; Face (Jeremy); Doll Common; Sir Epicure Mammon; Surly; Abel Drugger; Ananias; Tribulation Wholesome; Kastril; Dame Pliant; Lovewit; the Neighbours
works.structure: A single-day, single-house intrigue observing the classical unities to the letter, with each act a fresh round of gulling and the final act a tournament of unmaskings.

works.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
works.description: Robert Burton's encyclopedic treatise-masquerading-as-self-cure, written under the name 'Democritus Junior': the causes, symptoms, and cures of melancholy anatomized across three 'partitions' — its kinds, its cure, and the special melancholies of love and religion — in a prose of endless quotation, digression, and humane wit, expanded by Burton through five editions to 1651.
works.plot: The First Partition defines melancholy, its causes, and symptoms; the Second prescribes the cures — diet, medicine, mirth, and the consolation of philosophy; the Third anatomizes love-melancholy and religious melancholy, with the great final meditation on despair; the whole is a labyrinth of authorities, stories, and self-portraiture.
works.significance: The great English anatomy — the book that taught Sterne, Lamb, and every digressive prose writer since how to wander gloriously.
works.meter: Prose of magnificent copiousness — the style of the study, the pulpit, and the joke fused — with Latin tags and verse interludes.
works.context: Published 1621, with enlargements in 1624, 1628, 1632, 1638, and posthumously 1651; its melancholy was the century's master-disease, and its book the century's master-digression.
works.characters: Democritus Junior (the author's persona); the melancholic patient; the lover; the religious despairer; the quoted authorities
works.structure: Three partitions with their sections, members, and subsections in the scholastic manner, the apparatus of quotation and marginalia making the book a library in itself.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; published pseudonymously as Democritus Junior.

editions.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy, 6 vols.
editions.editor: Thomas C. Faulkner, Nicolas K. Kiessling, and Rhonda L. Blair (eds.)

works.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
works.form: history and chronicle (prose with verse insertions)
works.description: A set of interrelated vernacular annals recording English history from the arrival of Julius Caesar to 1154, begun c. 892 (the 'Common Stock') in the circle of King Alfred and continued in centres across England for over two and a half centuries. The earliest continuous vernacular history of any European people and the backbone of the period's historiography.
works.plot: The annals record year by year the wars of the kings of Wessex and England, the Viking invasions, ecclesiastical events, and natural portents; they incorporate poems (The Battle of Brunanburh, The Capture of the Five Boroughs, the deaths of Edgar and Edward), documents, and, in the Peterborough continuation (to 1154), the last original Old English prose composed in England.
works.significance: The foundation of English historical prose; a continuous vernacular record unmatched elsewhere in early medieval Europe.
works.meter: Prose, with alliterative verse poems incorporated at several annal years.
works.context: The Common Stock was compiled c. 892, probably under Alfred's direction, from earlier annals, Bede, and oral tradition; continuations were kept at Winchester, Abingdon, Worcester, Peterborough, and Canterbury.
works.characters: Alfred; Æthelstan; Edgar; Æthelred; Cnut; Edward the Confessor; William the Conqueror; Peterborough continuator
works.structure: Annalistic: brief yearly entries of varying fullness, from single sentences to extended narrative set-pieces; the seven manuscripts (A-G) diverge into regional continuations.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous, corporate authorship; traditionally associated with Alfred's court for the Common Stock.

editions.title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle: A Revised Translation

sources: Middle English Dictionary

works.title: The Anniversaries
altTitles: Of the Progress of the Soul
works.description: Donne's two commemorative poems for Elizabeth Drury, the fifteen-year-old daughter of his patron Sir Robert Drury, who died in 1610: 'An Anatomy of the World' (1611) and 'Of the Progress of the Soul' (1612) — cosmic elegies in which the girl's death becomes the death of the world's coherence, her virtue the measure of its decay, and her translation to heaven the poem's only consolation.
works.plot: The First Anniversary anatomizes the world's sickness — 'new philosophy calls all in doubt' — and finds in the dead girl the pattern of lost virtue; the Second follows her soul's progress beyond the corrupt world to the joys of heaven, ending with the praise of the 'she' whose worth the world could not hold.
works.significance: The great English poems of the scientific revolution's first shock — and the most extreme test of the elegy's power to make a private grief cosmic.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of extraordinary intellectual density, with the famous passage on the 'new philosophy' as its centre of gravity.
works.context: Written 1611–12 in the household of Sir Robert Drury, whose patronage they repaid with a hyperbole that scandalized Ben Jonson; the poems register the crisis of cosmology after Copernicus, Kepler, and Galileo.
works.characters: Elizabeth Drury (the subject); the poet as anatomist; the World; the Soul; Death
works.structure: Two linked poems of several hundred couplets each, built as formal 'anatomies' — the dissection of the world, then the itinerary of the soul — with the funerary apparatus of elegies and epitaphs.

works.title: The Antipodes
works.form: comedy; masque-comedy; play within a play
works.description: Shirley's fantastic dream comedy in which Peregrine, a man crazed by reading travel books, is carried to an imaginary antipodal world where everything is inverted, and is cured by the dream itself.
works.plot: Peregrine, obsessed with Mandeville's travels, is drugged and conveyed to the Antipodes, a world of reversed customs and reversed theatre; the experience restores him, and the play ends with marriages.
works.significance: Shirley's most formally daring play and an important document of the Caroline fascination with travel, utopia, and the theatre's own conventions.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at Salisbury Court in 1636 and dedicated to the Earl of Newcastle.
works.characters: Peregrine; Lord Letoy; Doctor Hughball; Diana; Martha; Joyce; the Antipodal king
works.structure: Five acts with a large embedded play-within-the-play occupying most of the second half.

works.title: The Arraignment of Paris
works.description: Peele's pastoral-mythological court play: the shepherd Paris, commanded by the gods, judges the beauty contest of Juno, Pallas, and Venus; he awards the golden apple to Venus, whose bribe is the love of the nymph Oenone, and the play ends — after the goddesses' appeal — with Diana's famous judgment awarding the apple to 'Eliza', the Queen herself, a 'nymph' above all the goddesses.
works.plot: At the wedding feast of Peleus and Thetis, Discord casts the golden apple; Paris, in his pastoral solitude with Oenone, receives the task of judgment; the three goddesses plead their cases in set speeches; Paris judges Venus; the goddesses appeal to the Olympian court; and Diana's final verdict transfers the prize to Eliza, flattering the Queen beyond the myth.
works.significance: The founding text of the Elizabethan court pastoral and of the genre of the Queen's mythological flattery.
works.meter: Mixed verse forms — blank verse, rhyme, and songs — with the pageantry of the goddesses' entries.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Chapel before the Queen about 1581–84 and printed in 1584; its compliment to Elizabeth made Peele's name at court.
works.characters: Paris; Oenone; Juno; Pallas; Venus; Diana; Eliza (Elizabeth I); Colin; Hobbinol; Thenot; the shepherds and nymphs
works.structure: A masque-like pastoral in five acts, built on the judgment set piece and the appeals, with the shepherd scenes of Colin and the nymphs as pastoral interludes.

editions.title: The Works of George Peele, 2 vols.

works.title: The Atheist's Tragedy
works.description: Tourneur's tragedy of providence: the atheist D'Amville murders his brother to advance his house, plots the ruin of his nephew Charlemont and the rape of his niece Castabella, and is finally killed by his own axe — striking his own brains out as he raises it against his son's head — in a play whose argument is the certainty of divine justice, staged against the atheist's every calculation.
works.plot: D'Amville kills Montferrers and blames bandits; Charlemont is sent to the wars and believed dead; the uncle's schemes against Castabella and his own sons proceed; the ghost of Montferrers appears, the counter-plots of the villains fail one by one; and the last act's trial and the accidental suicide of D'Amville ('the justice of God') complete the demonstration, with the lovers' marriage as the play's reward.
works.significance: The great counter-revenge tragedy of the Jacobean stage — the play that turned the genre's own machinery against the atheism it usually indulged.
works.meter: A harsh, emblematic blank verse with the sententious choruses of the play's moral argument.
works.context: Printed in 1611 with a dedication to Sir Walter Chute; it answered the decade's revenge vogue with an anti-revenge tragedy, and its atheist answered the Marlovian overreachers.
works.characters: D'Amville; Charlemont; Castabella; Montferrers (the Ghost); Levidulcia; Sebastian; Rousard; Borachio; Snuffe; the Puritan chaplain Languebeau Snuffe
works.structure: A five-act tragedy of providence built as a counter-argument to the revenge play — the wronged hero refuses revenge, and heaven's engines work without him.

editions.title: The Atheist's Tragedy (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Awntyrs off Arthure
altTitles: The Anturs of Arther at the Tarnewathelan
works.description: An alliterative Arthurian poem of some 700 lines in two adventures: the ghost of Guinevere's mother, risen from a lake in Tarn Wadling to warn of pride and the fall of the Round Table, and the duel in which Gawain and Galeron contest disputed lands before Arthur's judgement. Its spectral first episode is among the most powerful scenes in the alliterative corpus.
works.plot: While hunting at Tarn Wadling, Guinevere and Gawain meet a ghost who prophesies the ruin of Arthur's court and shows the torments of the dead; in the second adventure, Gawain fights the knight Galeron for the lands Arthur has granted him, and Arthur's equitable judgement restores them — with the ghost's warning shadowing the court's splendour.
works.significance: The finest of the northern Gawain romances after Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, and the classic statement of the ghost-warning topos in Arthurian verse.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel.
works.context: Composed c. 1400 in the north of England, perhaps for a northern gentry audience with an interest in its Cumberland setting; preserved in four manuscripts and printed in the sixteenth century.
works.characters: Gawain; Guinevere; the ghost of Guinevere's mother; Galeron; Arthur
works.structure: A two-part romance (ghostly warning; judicial combat) linked by the theme of land, justice, and mortality.

works.title: The Ayenbite of Inwyt
works.description: The Kentish translation, completed in 1340 by Dan Michel of Northgate, monk of St Augustine's, Canterbury, of the Somme le Roi of Frère Lorens: a comprehensive prose manual of the vices, virtues, commandments, and the art of holy dying. Its title — 'remorse of conscience' — gives the work its penitential keynote.
works.plot: The treatise anatomizes the deadly sins and their remedies, the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the preparation for death, in a systematic scheme of moral and catechetical instruction.
works.significance: The most extensive Kentish text in Middle English, invaluable to historical linguistics, and a principal document of lay catechesis in the age of the Somme le Roi tradition.
works.meter: Prose; a famously conservative Kentish dialect with heavy French-derived vocabulary.
works.context: Completed in 1340 at St Augustine's Abbey, Canterbury, on the eve of the Black Death; preserved in a single autograph manuscript, BL Arundel MS 57.
works.characters: none (doctrinal treatise)
works.structure: A systematic doctrinal handbook following the structure of the French Somme le Roi, with illustrative exempla.
works.attributionNotes: The translator names himself in the colophon: Dan Michel of Northgate.

works.title: The Babees Book
works.description: The classic late medieval courtesy book: a poem of instruction for young boys ('babees') entering noble households, teaching them how to stand, dress, serve at table, and speak to their betters, with the companion courtesy poems and John Russell's Boke of Nurture that accompany it in the manuscripts. The standard English manual of the civility that defined the late medieval and early modern gentleman.
works.plot: The poem addresses the boy entering service, prescribing his conduct from rising to bedtime — cleanliness, table manners, deference of speech and gesture — and moralizing the discipline of courtesy as the school of virtue, in the tradition of the medieval courtesy literature descended from the classical 'nurture' of the young.
works.significance: The classic English courtesy book and the ancestor of the early modern conduct tradition (Erasmus, Castiglione's English imitators); its rules of table and speech chart the history of English civility.
works.meter: Couplets and seven-line stanzas, plain and mnemonic.
works.context: Composed c. 1475, when the great households' demand for trained service and the school curriculum of manners converged; preserved in BL Harley MS 5086 and related manuscripts; edited by F. J. Furnivall (1868) in the volumes that founded the study of English manners literature.
works.characters: the 'babee' (addressee); the master
works.structure: A single didactic poem in the courtesy tradition, with the companion poems (Urbanitatis, Stans Puer ad Mensam, Russell's Boke of Nurture) forming a curriculum in the manuscripts.

works.title: The Battle of Brunanburh
works.form: battle poetry (chronicle poem) in alliterative verse
works.description: A panegyric of 73 lines, entered in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for the year 937, celebrating the crushing victory of King Æthelstan and his brother Edmund over a coalition of Scots, Strathclyde Britons, and Dublin Norsemen led by Constantine and Anlaf (Olaf) Guthfrithson. The greatest of the Chronicle's poems, composed in the full heroic manner.
works.plot: The poem exults in the day-long battle — 'never was greater slaughter in this island' — as the West Saxons and Mercians pursue the fleeing allies; Constantine, his son slain, and Anlaf flee to their ships, and the victors return to Wessex leaving the battlefield to the carrion beasts, the raven, eagle, and wolf.
works.significance: The masterpiece of late heroic panegyric; Tennyson's translation (1880) is a landmark of Victorian medievalism.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; dense use of kennings and the beasts-of-battle formula.
works.context: The battle of Brunanburh (937), the greatest English victory of the tenth century, secured Æthelstan's supremacy in Britain; the poem is preserved in four manuscripts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
works.characters: Æthelstan; Edmund; Constantine of Scotland; Anlaf Guthfrithson
works.structure: A compact celebration in the heroic mode: the boast of victory, the pursuit, the flight of the kings, and the 'beasts of battle' topos, with a closing return to the annalistic frame.
themes: Death, the soul, and the afterlife

editions.title: The Battle of Brunanburh: A Casebook

sources: British Library Digitised Manuscripts

works.title: The Battle of Maldon
works.description: A fragmentary poem of 325 lines commemorating the battle of Maldon (10 or 11 August 991), in which Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex and his retinue fought a Viking army at the causeway of the Blackwater and were destroyed; the poem is the last great expression of the heroic code, celebrating loyalty unto death.
works.plot: Byrhtnoth arrays his levies against the Vikings on the tidal causeway of the Pante; he refuses tribute, and when the Vikings ask passage he grants it 'for his ofermod' (overconfidence) — the poem's great crux — drawing up for battle on the shore. After Byrhtnoth falls, a series of retainers make speeches vowing to avenge him or die beside him, and the poem breaks off in the midst of the last stand.
works.significance: The fullest poetic statement of the comitatus ethic of loyalty unto death; Byrhtwold's speech is among the most quoted passages of Old English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of the classical kind, with sustained martial diction.
works.context: The battle is recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle s.a. 991 and in the Vita Oswaldi; the poem survives only in an early eighteenth-century transcript of Cotton MS Otho A.xii, destroyed in the Cotton fire of 1731. The tribute of 10,000 pounds paid after the battle began the Danegeld payments.
works.characters: Byrhtnoth; Wulfstan; Ælfhere; Maccus; Offa; Ælfwine; Leofsunu; Dunnere; Byrhtwold; Godric (the betrayer)
works.structure: A single continuous battle-narrative built from speeches: the Viking messenger's demand, Byrhtnoth's reply, the combat, and the laddered sequence of retainers' vows (Ælfwine, Offa, Leofsunu, Dunnere, Byrhtwold — 'will shall be the harder, heart the keener').
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the opening and closing of the poem are lost with the manuscript.

editions.title: The Battle of Maldon

sources: Dictionary of Old English: A to I online

works.title: The Beaux' Stratagem
works.description: Farquhar's last and greatest comedy, written on his deathbed, in which the fortune-hunters Archer and Aimwell arrive at Lichfield to repair their ruined estates and encounter the unhappily married Mrs Sullen.
works.plot: Archer and Aimwell take turns posing as lord and servant at Lichfield; Aimwell courts Dorinda, Archer is drawn into the unhappy marriage of Mrs Sullen and Sullen; a highway robbery, a French invasion scare, and the discovery that Aimwell is not the real lord resolve the plot in marriage and reconciliation.
works.significance: The finest comedy of the early eighteenth century and the culmination of the Restoration tradition; its treatment of divorce and of provincial English society was ahead of its time, and it has been continuously revived since.
works.meter: Prose of remarkable richness and speed.
works.context: Performed at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket on 8 March 1707 and published the same year; Farquhar died in March or April 1707, weeks after the first performance.
works.characters: Archer; Aimwell; Mrs Sullen; Sullen; Dorinda; Lady Bountiful; Cherry; Boniface; Gibbet; Count Bellairde; Foigard
works.structure: Five acts with the celebrated bedroom scene (III.iii) in which Archer and Mrs Sullen debate marriage and divorce.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Bestiary
works.description: A Middle English bestiary of 802 lines, probably of East Anglian origin, describing the nature of the lion, eagle, serpent, stag, whale, and other creatures and drawing from each a moral and allegorical lesson, in the tradition of the Physiologus. It is the earliest English bestiary to survive in the vernacular.
works.plot: Each animal's natural history — the lion's sleep with open eyes, the whale luring sailors, the phoenix's rebirth — is expounded as a figure of Christ, the devil, or the Christian soul.
works.significance: The link between the Old English Physiologus poems and the later English bestiary tradition, and a vivid example of medieval allegorical natural history in the vernacular.
works.meter: Irregular rhyming couplets of varying length, with some alliterative ornament.
works.context: Composed c. 1250, translated from the Latin Physiologus of Theobaldus; preserved uniquely in BL Arundel MS 292, with Norwich connections.
works.characters: the animals (lion, eagle, serpent, stag, fox, spider, whale, siren, elephant, turtle-dove, panther, dove)
works.structure: A sequence of discrete animal exempla, each divided between natural description (natura) and moralization (significacio).

works.title: The Boke Named the Governour
works.description: Elyot's treatise on the education and conduct of the English ruling class, the first major work of English political and educational theory written in the vernacular rather than Latin.
works.plot: The first book prescribes the upbringing of a future governor from infancy — nurses, tutors, the curriculum of classical authors, music, painting, and physical exercise. The second book treats the virtues proper to a ruler: justice, fortitude, temperance, wisdom, and the golden mean. The third discusses the cardinal virtues and their application in counsel and judgement.
works.significance: A founding text of English humanism in the vernacular: it established the ideal of the educated magistrate, coined or first recorded many English words ('education', 'encyclopaedia'), and remained an authority on gentlemanly conduct for two centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written c. 1530–31 while Elyot, a diplomat and clerk, was out of royal favour after Wolsey's fall; dedicated to Henry VIII, it drew on Castiglione's Il Cortegiano and Patrizi's De regno, and shaped the humanist programme of gentlemanly education institutionalized in the grammar schools.
works.structure: Three books of systematic exposition, dense with citation of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and Plutarch, and illustrated with exemplary stories of classical princes.

editions.title: The Book Named the Governor

works.title: The Book of Common Prayer (1549)
altTitles: The First Prayer Book of Edward VI
The Booke of the Common Prayer and Administracion of the Sacramentes
works.description: The first Book of Common Prayer, compiled chiefly by Thomas Cranmer and imposed by the Act of Uniformity of 1549 as the single liturgy of the English church; the foundational text of Anglican worship.
works.plot: The book replaces the medieval service books (missal, breviary, manual, pontifical) with one English liturgy: Morning and Evening Prayer, the collects, the order for Holy Communion, baptism, confirmation, matrimony, visitation of the sick, burial, and the ordination rites, with the psalter and lectionary — retaining much medieval devotion while recasting the eucharist as a communion of all the people in both kinds.
works.significance: The greatest single achievement of English liturgical prose: Cranmer's collects ('whose service is perfect freedom', 'read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest') entered the language itself, and the book's cadences shaped English prose from Hooker to the Authorized Version and beyond.
works.meter: Prose with psalmody
works.context: Drafted in 1548–49 by Cranmer with a committee of bishops and divines, authorized by the first Act of Uniformity (January 1549), and introduced at Whitsun 1549, provoking the Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall; the book was revised in 1552 (the Second Prayer Book), restored by Elizabeth in 1559, and its language survives in the 1662 book used for four centuries.
works.structure: A complete liturgical manual arranged by rite, with rubrics, calendar, and lectionary; the prose is Cranmer's — sonorous, cadenced, and scriptural.
works.attributionNotes: The book is the work of Cranmer and his committee; the title page names no author, and the record attributes the compilation to Cranmer as chief author, following universal scholarly usage.

editions.title: The Book of Common Prayer: The Texts of 1549, 1559, and 1662

works.title: The Book of Faith
works.description: Reginald Pecock's vernacular treatise of 1456 on the nature of faith and its relation to reason, written in the last years before his condemnation: faith, he argues, is a species of knowledge grounded in evidence and reason, not mere belief on authority — the doctrine that brought him to trial and abjuration. It survives in the author's own manuscript.
works.plot: Pecock analyzes faith as intellectual assent produced by the 'doom of reason' on credible testimony, distinguishes it from opinion and knowledge, answers the objections of the 'unbilevers', and defends the lay person's right and duty to understand what he believes.
works.significance: The boldest medieval English statement of the rationality of faith, and the terminus of vernacular theology before the Reformation.
works.meter: Argumentative English prose, technical and precise.
works.context: Completed in 1456, a year before Pecock's trial; its rationalism was among the charges against him, and the work survives only in the Trinity College, Cambridge, autograph manuscript (MS B.14.45).
works.characters: none (theological treatise)
works.structure: Two books of philosophical-theological analysis, in the scholastic quaestio manner adapted to English.

works.title: The Book of Homilies
altTitles: Certain Sermons or Homilies Appointed by the King's Majesty to Be Declared and Read
works.description: The first official book of sermons of the Church of England, issued in 1547 under the direction of Thomas Cranmer (who wrote several of the homilies himself) to be read in parish churches; a principal vehicle of Reformation doctrine for the laity.
works.plot: Twelve homilies expound the Protestant faith in plain English: on scripture, the misery of mankind, salvation by faith alone, good works, Christian love, against swearing and perjury, against strife, obedience to rulers, and against whoredom and adultery — each designed to be read from the pulpit by clergy who could not preach.
