works.significance: The official voice of the English Reformation for ordinary congregations: the homilies translated Protestant doctrine into a national plain style and remained binding on the church for three centuries, feeding directly into the religious language of the Elizabethans.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Issued in 1547, the first year of Edward VI, as part of the royal Injunctions requiring the homilies' use; the homily 'Of Good Works' and others are Cranmer's own, and the second book (with the famous homily 'Against Disobedience and Wilful Rebellion') followed in 1571, making the two books the official theology of the Elizabethan church.
works.structure: Twelve self-contained sermons, each with a scriptural text, exposition, and application, written for oral delivery by non-preaching clergy.
works.attributionNotes: The book is a collaborative production of Cranmer, Thomas Becon, and other reformers; the record attributes it to Cranmer as the supervising compiler, following standard scholarship, while noting the collaboration.

works.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
works.description: The dictated spiritual autobiography of Margery Kempe of King's Lynn (c. 1436–38), commonly called the first autobiography in English: her conversion after childbirth, her marriage and vow of chastity, her uncontrollable weeping at the thought of the Passion, her pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, and Santiago, and her examinations for heresy before the archbishops of Canterbury and York. A unique document of female lay piety and of fifteenth-century English life.
works.plot: Margery recounts her visionary conversations with Christ, her struggle with her husband for chastity, her travels through Europe and the Holy Land, her clashes with hostile clergy and her vindications, her visit to Julian of Norwich, and her old age caring for her ailing husband — the whole narrated in the third person through her scribes.
works.significance: The first autobiography in English and the earliest extended account of a laywoman's religious life; its frankness about body, marriage, and authority has made it a founding text of women's literary history.
works.meter: Direct, colloquial prose, vivid in dialogue and detail, mediated by her scribes.
works.context: Dictated c. 1436–38, with a second book of the 1430s–40s, in the East Anglian culture of orthodox lay devotion shadowed by the Lollard trials; the complete text was lost until the discovery of the manuscript in 1934 (BL Additional MS 61823), and first published in 1936.
works.characters: Margery Kempe; John Kempe (her husband); Julian of Norwich; Christ (in dialogue); the archbishops
works.structure: Two books of episodic autobiography, moving between mystical colloquy and the social world of East Anglian towns, courts, and pilgrim routes.
works.attributionNotes: Margery Kempe's authorship (by dictation to scribes) is recorded within the book itself.

editions.title: The Book of Margery Kempe
editions.editor: Sanford Brown Meech and Hope Emily Allen (eds.)

works.title: The Book of St Albans
altTitles: The Book of Hawking, Hunting, and Heraldry
works.form: courtesy book and household manual (verse and prose)
works.description: The gentleman's handbook printed at St Albans in 1486: treatises in verse and prose on hawking, hunting, and heraldry, together with the terms of venery and the 'companies of beasts', traditionally attributed to Dame Juliana Berners, prioress of Sopwell. It is the classic English manual of the gentleman's arts, reprinted and expanded into the seventeenth century.
works.plot: The book instructs the reader in the falconer's and hunter's crafts — the mews, the lure, the chase of the hart, the terms of the hunt — and in the blazoning of arms, closing with the famous catalogues of collective nouns ('a parliament of rooks', 'a murmuration of starlings') that fixed the English vocabulary of the field.
works.significance: The foundational English manual of the gentleman's arts: its venery terms entered the language and its heraldry shaped Tudor and Stuart practice.
works.meter: Mixed: the hawking and hunting treatises in rhyme royal and couplets, the heraldry in prose.
works.context: Printed at the schoolmaster press of St Albans in 1486 (a colophon names 'the schoolmaster of St Albans'), in the post-Caxton provincial print boom; the attribution to Juliana Berners appears in the 1496 de Worde reprint.
works.characters: none (manual)
works.structure: A compilation of distinct treatises (hawking; hunting; arms; blazoning) in the practical-manual tradition.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Dame Juliana Berners (prioress of Sopwell) in the 1496 reprint; the attribution is traditional and doubted. authorship_status reflects this traditional attribution.

works.title: The Book of the Duchess
altTitles: The Deth of Blaunche the Duchesse
works.description: Chaucer's earliest major poem (1,334 lines in octosyllabic couplets), a dream vision elegy for Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster, who died in 1368: the insomniac dreamer overhears a grieving knight in black, whose lament for his lost lady — 'White' — unfolds the ideal of courtly love into a meditation on death and consolation. The poem that founded the English dream-vision tradition.
works.plot: The dreamer, sleepless from an eight-year love-sickness, reads Ovid's tale of Ceyx and Alcyone and falls asleep; in his dream he meets the Man in Black, who tells of his long service to Fortune and of the peerless lady White whom he won and has now lost; only the dreamer's blunt question — 'she is dead?' — breaks the elegy's obliqueness, and the dream ends with the hunting of the hart and the poem's closure on the word 'king'.
works.significance: The first great English dream poem and the foundation of Chaucer's mature art; its fusion of consolation, allegory, and courtly elegy shaped the entire English dream-vision tradition.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of courtly grace, adapted from Machaut and the Roman de la Rose.
works.context: Composed c. 1368–72, commemorating Blanche of Lancaster (d. 12 September 1368), first wife of John of Gaunt, Chaucer's patron; the poem's courtly audience would have recognized the dead duchess in the knight's 'White'.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Man in Black; Lady White; Fortune
works.structure: A double frame (reading; dream) enclosing the knight's elegiac autobiography, in the French dit manner; the wordplay on 'White', 'hart/heart', and 'king' ties consolation to allegory.
works.attributionNotes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the occasional reference to Blanche is universally accepted.

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

works.title: The Bowge of Courte
works.description: Skelton's first major poem, a dream satire in rhyme royal: the dreamer Drede boards the ship Bowge of Courte, where the personified vices of the court — Flattery, Suspicion, Harvy Hafter, Disdain, Riot, Deceit — successively menace and betray him, until he leaps overboard. It is the founding text of the Tudor court-satire tradition.
works.plot: Drede, standing at the shore, is invited aboard the Bowge of Courte; each passenger woos him and then turns on him, and the poem breaks off as he prepares to leap from the ship to save his life.
works.significance: The first sustained court satire of the English Renaissance, combining the dream vision of Chaucer with the estates satire of the Middle Ages and setting the pattern for the complaint literature of the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Seven-line rhyme royal stanzas, handled with Chaucerian fluency but a distinctly satirical edge.
works.context: Written at the turn of the century, when Skelton was moving from court service to the country living at Diss; its portrait of court corruption anticipates his later anti-Wolsey satires.
works.characters: Drede (the dreamer); Flattery; Suspicion; Harvy Hafter; Disdain; Riot; Deceit
works.structure: Dream vision with prologue; an allegorical sea voyage in which successive encounters with the courtly vices build to a single climactic decision to abandon the court.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1499.

editions.title: John Skelton: The Complete English Poems

works.title: The Broken Heart
works.description: Ford's stately tragedy set in Sparta, in which the enforced marriage of Penthea to the aged Bassanes destroys her love for Orgilus, and the play ends in a chain of ritual deaths.
works.plot: Orgilus, cheated of his love Penthea by her brother Ithocles' ambition, returns in disguise; Ithocles loves the Spartan princess Calantha, whose father the king dies; Orgilus kills Ithocles, Penthea starves herself, and Calantha dies of a broken heart.
works.significance: Ford's most artistically controlled tragedy and the clearest Caroline example of a tragedy of honour, obligation, and emotional starvation.
works.meter: Blank verse with lyric interludes and songs, of unusually measured and elegiac cadence.
works.context: Published in 1633; probably written for a private playhouse or for court reading, given its restrained action and heavy lyricism.
works.characters: Orgilus; Penthea; Ithocles; Calantha; Bassanes; the King of Sparta; Tecnicus; Christalla
works.structure: Five acts of a slow, ceremonially patterned tragedy in which the final scene of deaths is framed by the wedding masque.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1633 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Brus
works.description: John Barbour's verse chronicle of Robert Bruce and the Scottish wars of independence, completed c. 1375 in some 14,000 octosyllabic lines: the murder of the Red Comyn, the crowning at Scone, the years of guerrilla warfare, and the great victory at Bannockburn (1314), with James Douglas as the poem's second hero. The first great work of Scottish literature and the fountainhead of the nation's heroic self-image.
works.plot: The poem follows Bruce from the killing of Comyn and his coronation through defeat, exile, and the legendary perseverance of the spider episode to the recovery of the kingdom castle by castle, the battle of Bannockburn, the raids of Douglas into England, and the king's death — all framed by the poem's great theme, that 'fredome is a noble thing'.
works.significance: The first great poem in Scots and the founding text of Scottish national literature; Burns's 'Scots Wha Hae' and the whole Bruce tradition descend from it.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of energy and speed, in Older Scots.
works.context: Completed in 1375 by the archdeacon of Aberdeen, in the court of Robert II (Bruce's grandson), when the Stewart dynasty needed a heroic past; preserved in two manuscripts (1487, 1489) and printed in 1571.
works.characters: Robert Bruce; James Douglas; Edward II; Edward Bruce; the Scottish and English armies
works.structure: Twenty books of continuous narrative in the romance-chronicle manner, with set-piece battles and speeches, closed by the king's death and the poet's envoy.
works.attributionNotes: Barbour's authorship secure (named in the text and the royal records).

editions.title: Barbour's Bruce
editions.editor: Matthew P. McDiarmid and James A. C. Stevenson (eds.)

works.title: The Brut Chronicle
works.description: The Middle English prose Brut, the most popular secular text in late medieval England: a chronicle of Britain from the Trojan Brutus through the Arthurian kings to the fourteenth century, with continuations carrying the story through the Wars of the Roses. Over 180 manuscripts survive in English — more than any other secular work — and Caxton's print (1480) made it the standard popular history of England.
works.plot: The chronicle narrates the legendary British history of the Brut tradition — Brutus, Lear, Arthur — then the Saxon, Norman, and Plantagenet reigns, with the continuations adding the Lancastrian and Yorkist wars; its plain, annalistic prose made it the layman's history of England.
works.significance: The bestselling secular book of the English Middle Ages: its diffusion defines the popular historical culture out of which Tudor history writing grew.
works.meter: Plain, formulaic prose of the chronicle tradition.
works.context: The earliest version was made in the later fourteenth century, probably in London, from French and Latin sources; it was expanded continuously through the fifteenth century (the 'common version' to 1419, continuations to 1461 and later) and printed by Caxton in 1480.
works.characters: Brutus; Arthur; the kings of England to Edward IV
works.structure: A regnal chronicle in the Brut tradition, open-ended and continuously continued by successive compilers.

works.title: The Buke of the Howlat
works.description: Richard Holland's Scottish alliterative beast-allegory of some 1,000 lines, composed c. 1448 for the Douglas family: the owl, ashamed of his ugliness, appeals through the assembly of birds to the pope and the emperor, each bird vying in flattery, until Dame Nature restores him to his proper worth. A satire of pride, courts, and flattery, and the last major alliterative poem of the tradition.
works.plot: The howlat, complaining of his feathers, is counselled by the peacock to seek redress; the birds assemble in parliament before the pope and emperor, but the debate degenerates into mutual slander and sycophancy, until Nature intervenes, clothes the owl in dignity, and the poem ends with the Douglas heraldry and the family's praise.
works.significance: The last major alliterative poem in the British tradition and a key document of Douglas politics, heraldry, and the Scottish reception of the Alliterative Revival.
works.meter: Thirteen-line alliterative stanzas with rhyme and wheel, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1448 by Richard Holland, secretary to Archibald Douglas, Earl of Moray, for the Douglas family at a moment of their power; preserved in the Asloan and Bannatyne manuscripts (c. 1515, 1568).
works.characters: the Howlat; the Peacock; the Pope; the Emperor; Dame Nature; the birds of the parliament
works.structure: A beast-parliament in the Chaucerian manner, framed by the owl's complaint and closed by the heraldic celebration of the Douglases.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Richard Holland on the evidence of the poem's colophon and Douglas records.

works.title: The Canterbury Tales
works.description: Chaucer's unfinished masterpiece and the supreme achievement of Middle English literature: a frame-tale collection in which some thirty pilgrims journeying from the Tabard Inn to Canterbury agree to a storytelling contest, the tales ranging from the Knight's romance and the Miller's fabliau to the Wife of Bath's prologue, the Pardoner's sermon, and the Parson's treatise. Begun c. 1387 and left unfinished at Chaucer's death in 1400.
works.plot: In the General Prologue the narrator joins a company of pilgrims — knight, miller, reeve, wife of Bath, pardoner, summoner, nun's priest, and the rest — each vividly portrayed; Harry Bailly, the Host, proposes the tale-telling game, and the tales that follow answer and quarrel with one another across the whole range of medieval genres, from courtly romance (Knight, Squire, Franklin) through fabliau (Miller, Reeve, Shipman, Merchant) and saint's life (Second Nun, Prioress) to sermon (Pardoner), beast fable (Nun's Priest), and the closing penitential treatise of the Parson.
works.significance: The most influential single work of English literature: its pilgrims, its tales, and its frame established the English tradition of comic realism, dramatic monologue, and narrative irony that runs through Shakespeare to the novel.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of unprecedented flexibility, with rhyme royal, tail-rhyme, and prose for special effects; the decasyllabic line perfected.
works.context: Composed c. 1387–1400 in London, drawing on Boccaccio, Ovid, Boethius, and the estates tradition; the pilgrimage to Becket's shrine at Canterbury supplied the frame; circulated in some eighty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1476–78) and his successors, making it the foundation of the English printed canon.
works.characters: the Narrator; the Host (Harry Bailly); the Knight; the Miller; the Reeve; the Wife of Bath; the Pardoner; the Friar; the Summoner; the Nun's Priest; the Parson; and the other pilgrims
works.structure: A frame narrative (the pilgrimage, the Host's game) enclosing twenty-four tales grouped into ten fragments; the links between tales stage the pilgrims' quarrels and judgments, and the work's unfinished state is part of its design.
works.attributionNotes: Uniquely well attested: Chaucer's authorship of the Tales is not in doubt, though the ordering of the fragments and some links are editorial.

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

works.title: The Cardinal
works.description: Shirley's last tragedy, written in Ireland and performed at the Cockpit in 1641, in which a scheming cardinal forces a marriage that leads to poisoning, madness, and death.
works.plot: The Cardinal, thwarted in his own designs on the Duchess of Pavia, compels her to marry his protégé Columbo; when she loves the soldier Alvarez instead, Columbo kills him, and the Duchess poisons the Cardinal and herself.
works.significance: A late and vigorous Caroline revenge tragedy, notable for its portrait of ecclesiastical ambition and for closing Shirley's career.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Composed during Shirley's Irish period and revived at the Cockpit in 1641, on the eve of the civil wars; printed in Shirley's Six New Plays of 1653.
works.characters: the Cardinal; the Duchess of Pavia; Columbo; Alvarez; Celinde; Hernando
works.structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a catastrophic denouement.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Castle of Health
works.description: Elyot's vernacular treatise on diet and regimen, the first substantial English medical handbook written by a layman for lay readers.
works.plot: The book surveys the four humours and complexions, the properties of foods and drinks, sleep, exercise, and the regimen proper to each age and season, advising the reader how to preserve health through moderation and self-knowledge.
works.significance: A landmark in the vernacularization of medicine and natural knowledge in Tudor England, influential on later dietary literature and a document of humanist attitudes to the body.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the mid-1530s and printed by Thomas Berthelet in 1539 (with editions to 1610); Elyot's attempt to bring learned medicine into English paralleled his linguistic programme in The Governour.
works.structure: Four books of systematic exposition, compiled from Galen, Hippocrates, and the medieval regimen literature.

works.title: The Castle of Perseverance
works.description: The earliest complete English morality play (c. 1400–25, 3,649 lines): the life of Mankind (Humanum Genus) from birth to judgement, staged on the famous circular 'place' with its central castle and five scaffolds, as the virtues and vices battle for his soul through the Seven Ages. The most ambitious play of the English medieval stage.
works.plot: Mankind, born in sin, is led by his Bad Angel through World, Flesh, and the Devil to the seven deadly sins; rescued by Confession, he is garrisoned in the Castle of Perseverance with the virtues; the sins' siege fails, but Covetousness wins him in old age, until Death strikes and the debate of the four daughters of God — Mercy, Peace, Righteousness, Truth — yields his salvation.
works.significance: The foundational English morality: its stage diagram, its allegorical cast, and its theology of mercy set the pattern for the genre through Everyman to the Elizabethan stage.
works.meter: Thirteen-line stanzas (rime couée with wheel), with stage directions prescribing the elaborate fixed staging.
works.context: Composed c. 1400–25 in East Anglia (the manuscript's language is Norfolk), in the milieu of the great fifteenth-century moralities; preserved uniquely in the Macro manuscript (Folger Shakespeare Library, MS V.a.354, c. 1440) with Mankind and Wisdom.
works.characters: Mankind (Humanum Genus); the Bad and Good Angels; World, Flesh, and the Devil; the Seven Deadly Sins; the Seven Virtues; Confession; Death; God; the Four Daughters of God
works.structure: A four-scaffold cosmic drama (God; World; Flesh; Devil) around the central castle, with the banns, the siege, the death scene, and the parliament of heaven as its great movements.

editions.title: The Macro Plays

works.title: The Changeling
works.description: Middleton and Rowley's tragedy of desire and madness: Beatrice-Joanna, betrothed to Alonzo but in love with Alsemero, commissions the ugly servant De Flores to murder her fiancé; his price is her virginity, and the play follows the pair's descent through murder, the bed-trick with the maid Diaphanta, and madness to the final deaths — while the comic sub-plot of the madhouse, where the pretended fools and madmen perform, doubles the theme of 'change'.
works.plot: De Flores kills Alonzo and claims Beatrice-Joanna; the wedding to Alsemero proceeds through the virginity-test and the Diaphanta substitution; the castle catches fire (in the plot), the murders of Diaphanta and the witnesses follow, and the final scene's confessions — Beatrice-Joanna's 'I am that of your blood was taken from you' — end with the lovers' deaths and the madhouse's ironic close.
works.significance: One of the great Jacobean tragedies — the study of complicity and self-loss ('the deed's creature') that T. S. Eliot would single out as the age's masterpiece of moral horror.
works.meter: Middleton's verse in the main plot — swift, ironic, and chilling — against Rowley's prose farce in the madhouse.
works.context: Performed by the Lady Elizabeth's Men in 1622, at court in 1624, and printed in 1653; based on Reynolds's God's Revenge Against Murder (1621).
works.characters: Beatrice-Joanna; De Flores; Alsemero; Alonzo de Piracquo; Tomazo de Piracquo; Vermandero; Diaphanta; Jasperino; the madhouse crew (Alibius, Lollio, Antonio, Franciscus, Isabella)
works.structure: A two-plot structure unique in the canon: the main tragic plot (by Middleton) and the madhouse comedy (by Rowley) run in deliberate counterpoint, never meeting until the thematic rhyme of the final scene.
works.attributionNotes: Middleton (main plot) and William Rowley (madhouse sub-plot) as stated on the title page; the division is uncontested.

editions.title: The Changeling (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Changes
works.description: An early Shirley comedy of romantic change and constancy, in which lovers exchange and re-exchange partners before the final matching; it is Shirley's first play on the theme of inconstancy that would dominate his later work.
works.plot: Two pairs of lovers in London and the country undergo reversals of fortune and affection, and the title's 'changes' resolve into a stable set of marriages.
works.significance: One of Shirley's earliest plays and an example of the Caroline comedy of manners in formation.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed by Queen Henrietta's Men at the Cockpit in 1626; published 1632.
works.characters: Phillipa; Vincentio; Annibell; Clarinda; the Duke of Florence; Antonio
works.structure: Five acts alternating between court and city settings.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Chief Promises of God unto Man
altTitles: A Tragedy or Interlude Manifesting the Chief Promises of God unto Man
works.description: John Bale's interlude of the covenants of God from Adam to Christ, composed c. 1538 and printed at Wesel in 1547; a dramatic sermon on the promises fulfilled in the gospel.
works.plot: God the Father, in seven acts, makes his successive promises to man — to Adam of the woman's seed, to Noah of the rainbow covenant, to Abraham of the blessing of nations, to Moses of the law, to David of the everlasting throne, to Isaiah of the virgin's son, and to John the Baptist of the Lamb of God — each act closing with a prayer or antiphon, the whole demonstrating that the Old Testament is fulfilled in Christ.
works.significance: The most accomplished of Bale's biblical interludes and a model of Reformation dramaturgy: its covenant structure turned the mystery-cycle tradition to doctrinal ends and influenced the biblical drama of the Elizabethan church.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic passages with antiphons
works.context: Written c. 1538 during Bale's service as a Protestant dramatist under Cromwell, and printed at Wesel in 1547 in the collection of Bale's biblical plays; the play embodies the Protestant programme of replacing the old mysteries with doctrinal drama drawn from scripture alone.
works.characters: God the Father (Pater Coelestis); Adam; Noah; Abraham; Moses; David; Isaiah; John the Baptist; Baleus Prolocutor
works.structure: Seven acts, each a dialogue between God the Father (as Pater Coelestis) and a biblical figure, framed by a prologue (Bale as Prolocutor) and an epilogue; the play is a doctrinal pageant of the covenants.

editions.title: The Complete Plays of John Bale, vol. 2

works.title: The City Madam
works.description: Massinger's comedy of a citizen's wife, Lady Frugal, whose ambition to be a lady leads her husband to fake a departure for the Indies and to test her virtue and her daughters' constancy.
works.plot: Sir John Frugal pretends to embark for Virginia; Lady Frugal and her daughters, believing themselves rich, cast off their modest lives; the test exposes their vanity and they are sent to the colonies as punishment.
works.significance: Massinger's fullest treatment of London citizen society and one of the most striking Caroline comedies of female ambition and colonial punishment.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed at the Blackfriars in 1632 and published posthumously in 1658.
works.characters: Sir John Frugal; Lady Frugal; Anne; Mary; Lord Lacy; Sir Maurice Lacy; Ramble; Luke Frugal
works.structure: Five acts of a Jonsonian testing-comedy with a moralising conclusion.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The City Mouse and Country Mouse
altTitles: The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd to the Story of the Country Mouse and the City Mouse
works.description: A burlesque of Dryden's The Hind and the Panther (1687) by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu, retelling Dryden's fable of the mice in mock-heroic terms to ridicule his conversion and his religious argument — a celebrated example of Whig literary mockery and Prior's early wit.
works.plot: Following Aesop's fable (used by Dryden), the country mouse visits the city mouse and, after witnessing the dangers and hypocrisies of town and court, returns to the safety of the country, applied as satire on Dryden's religious and political position.
works.significance: A notable Whig burlesque of Dryden and an early showcase for Prior's wit; it reflects the literary politics of James II's reign and the quarrel over Dryden's conversion.
works.meter: Heroic couplets in a witty, parodic mock-heroic register.
works.context: Written in 1687 by the young Prior and Montagu (later Earl of Halifax) against Dryden's Catholic poem, and published anonymously; it launched Prior's reputation.
works.characters: the City Mouse; the Country Mouse
works.structure: A burlesque verse fable in heroic couplets parodying Dryden's poem.
works.attributionNotes: Collaborative, by Matthew Prior and Charles Montagu; Montagu is not in this database, so only Prior is linked.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Cloud of Unknowing
works.description: The classic English treatise of apophatic contemplation, written in the late fourteenth century by an anonymous master (perhaps a Carthusian or secular priest) for a young disciple: the soul seeking God must enter the 'cloud of unknowing' between itself and God, striking down every thought with the dart of longing love and the 'naked intent' of the single word. The most intellectually rigorous work of the English mystical canon.
works.plot: The author teaches his disciple the work of contemplation: the forgetting of all creatures, the rejection of discursive meditation, the piercing of the darkness with love — and warns throughout against the false mysticism of physical fervour and deluded visions, prescribing the discipline of the single word ('God' or 'love') repeated in the heart.
works.significance: The supreme English expression of the negative way and a work of the first rank in the European contemplative tradition; its psychology of attention and intention has given it a continuing modern readership.
works.meter: Precise, sinewy prose, paradoxically articulate about the ineffable; vivid negative imagery (clouds, darts, nakedness).
works.context: Composed c. 1375–1400, probably in the north-east Midlands, in the orbit of the Carthusian order; it circulated with the author's other works (The Book of Privy Counselling, the translation of pseudo-Dionysius's Mystical Theology) and was read by the English Benedictine revival and by modern contemplatives (Thomas Merton).
works.characters: the author (spiritual director); the young disciple (addressee)
works.structure: Seventy-five short chapters of graduated instruction, in the apophatic tradition of pseudo-Dionysius, with the 'cloud' as its organizing image.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the author is often identified as a Carthusian on grounds of the work's transmission, but the identification is conjectural.

works.title: The Comedy of Errors
works.description: Shakespeare's shortest play and his only pure farce, built on Plautus's Menaechmi: twin masters and twin servants, both pairs named Antipholus and Dromio, are separated by shipwreck and reunited by coincidence in Ephesus, where the confusions of mistaken identity multiply until the family is restored in the recognition scene before the Abbess.
works.plot: Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio arrive in Ephesus, where their long-lost twins live; the day becomes a cascade of wrong beatings, wrong dinners, and wrong arrests, until the Duke's judgment and the Abbess's revelation untangle the knots and reunite husband, wife, and sons.
works.significance: The most technically perfect of the early comedies and Shakespeare's demonstration that classical comedy could be outdone in English.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose for the servants' comedy; the play includes the verse 'discourse' scene between Antipholus of Syracuse and Luciana.
works.context: Probably written for Gray's Inn's Christmas revels of 1594; the frame of Egeon's doom under Ephesian law darkens the farce with the threat of execution.
works.characters: Antipholus of Syracuse; Antipholus of Ephesus; Dromio of Syracuse; Dromio of Ephesus; Adriana; Luciana; Egeon; the Abbess (Emilia); the Duke
works.structure: A single-day, single-city action — the closest Shakespeare came to the classical unities — with the errors compounded scene by scene to the recognition finale.

editions.title: The Riverside Shakespeare, 2nd edition
editions.editor: G. Blakemore Evans (ed.) with J. J. M. Tobin

editions.title: The Oxford Shakespeare: The Complete Works, 2nd edition

works.title: The Comical Revenge; or, Love in a Tub
works.description: George Etherege's first comedy, a witty Restoration intrigue play that alternates heroic verse scenes of courtship with prose scenes of low comedy, and gave the stage its first true Restoration rake in Sir Frederick Frollick.
works.plot: Two brothers love two sisters; Colonel Bruce and the Widow Rich clash in the main plot, while Sir Frederick Frollick pursues the Widow with comic irreverence; all is resolved in marriage.
works.significance: The first of the great Restoration comedies of manners; Sir Frederick Frollick established the type of the gallant-rake that Dorimant would perfect.
works.meter: Rhymed couplets in the high plot and prose in the low comedy.
works.context: Performed by the Duke's Company at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1664; it made Etherege's reputation immediately.
works.characters: Sir Frederick Frollick; the Widow Rich; Colonel Bruce; Graciana; Beaufort; Palmer; Dufoy; Mrs Gudgeon
works.structure: Five acts with three parallel plots of differing social register and metre.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Commonwealth of Oceana
works.description: James Harrington's utopian treatise on the ideal commonwealth, in which he argues that political power follows the distribution of landed property and proposes an elaborate republican constitution with a bicameral legislature and rotation of office.
works.plot: The Archon of Oceana, after the dissolution of the old government, establishes a commonwealth founded on an agrarian law limiting landed property, with a Senate proposing, a popular assembly resolving, and a magistracy executing; the model is Venice and ancient republics rather than monarchy.
works.significance: The most original political theory of the Interregnum; its theory that power follows property influenced Marx, and its constitutional model directly shaped the constitutions of the American colonies and of the early United States.
works.meter: A mixture of narrative and constitutional prose.
works.context: Written during the Protectorate and dedicated to Cromwell, who is said to have suppressed it until Harrington's friends obtained its release; published in 1656.
works.characters: the Archon; Olphaus Megaletor; the Council of Legislators; Parthenia
works.structure: A narrative frame of the founding of Oceana followed by the text of the proposed constitution and the Model of the Commonwealth.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Compleat Angler; or, The Contemplative Man's Recreation
works.description: Izaak Walton's pastoral dialogue on fishing, in which the angler Piscator instructs Venator, combining practical lore on the taking of fish with songs, poems, and reflections on the contemplative life; the fifth edition of 1676 added Charles Cotton's second part.
works.plot: Over five days of dialogue, Piscator teaches Venator and Auceps the arts of angling and defends the quiet life of the angler against the pursuits of the hunter and the falconer.
works.significance: One of the most reprinted books in English (over 400 editions), a founding text of the English pastoral tradition, and the standard expression of the ideal of quiet country retirement.
works.meter: Gentle, conversational prose with interpolated songs and verses.
works.context: First published in 1653, in the Commonwealth, when Walton had withdrawn from public life; revised and expanded in five editions to 1676, when Charles Cotton's part on fly-fishing was added.
works.characters: Piscator (the angler); Venator (the huntsman); Auceps (the falconer); Peter Manwood; Piscator's scholar
works.structure: A pastoral dialogue in five chapters or days, interspersed with songs, verse quotations, and digressions.
works.attributionNotes: Parts I-III by Walton; the 1676 edition adds Part II by Charles Cotton (not in this database), who is named on the title page.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Conquest of Granada
altTitles: The Conquest of Granada by the Spaniards
works.description: Dryden's heroic play in two parts on the Christian conquest of Moorish Granada in 1492, whose overweening hero Almanzor became the type of the Restoration hero of honour and love.
works.plot: Almanzor, a free-lance warrior of boundless ambition, serves first the Moors then the Spaniards, loves Almahide, and is torn between love, honour, and freedom until the fall of Granada and the lovers' final recognition.
works.significance: The supreme example of the English heroic drama and the occasion of the most important Restoration quarrel over the form; Almanzor's rhetoric of boundless will anticipates the eighteenth-century sublime.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets at their most sonorous and rhetorical.
works.context: Performed by the King's Company at the Theatre Royal in December 1670 and January 1671 and dedicated to the Duke of York; it was attacked by Buckingham in The Rehearsal and defended by Dryden in the Defence of the Epilogue.
works.characters: Almanzor; Almahide; Boabdelin; Lyndaraxa; Abdalla; Selin; Ferdinand; Isabella; the Duke of Arcos
works.structure: Two parts of five acts each, with a masque and an epilogue; the plot interweaves the historical siege with the love story.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Constant Couple; or, A Trip to the Jubilee
works.description: Farquhar's second and most popular comedy, in which the gay, generous Sir Harry Wildair returns from Paris and wins the virtuous Angelica; the character became the signature role of Robert Wilks.
works.plot: Sir Harry Wildair, a rake with a good heart, returns to London during the Jubilee year; he is courted by Lady Lurewell and falls for the disguised Angelica; the plot resolves in marriage and reformation without sentimentality.
works.significance: One of the most popular plays of the early eighteenth century and the creation of the good-hearted rake that anticipated the sentimental hero; it marks Farquhar's decisive break with Restoration cynicism.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at Drury Lane in November 1699 and published in 1700; the sequel Sir Harry Wildair followed in 1701.
works.characters: Sir Harry Wildair; Lady Lurewell; Angelica; Standard; Colonel Standard; Vizard; Smuggler; Dapper; Tom Errand
works.structure: Five acts with a double plot of high intrigue and low comic theft.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Countess of Montgomery's Urania
works.description: Lady Mary Wroth's prose romance, the first by an Englishwoman and a continuation of her uncle Sidney's Arcadia: the interlaced adventures of Pamphilia, Amphilanthus, Urania, and their knights and ladies through the courts and islands of the romance world, with the sonnet sequence 'Pamphilia to Amphilanthus' appended — the book whose recognizable court portraits caused a scandal at its publication.
works.plot: The romance follows the loves of Pamphilia (constant) and Amphilanthus (inconstant), the wanderings of Urania and the shepherds, and the enchanted palaces and rival queens of the romance geography; the appended sonnet sequence tells the same story of constancy and betrayal from Pamphilia's side.
works.significance: The first English romance and sonnet sequence by a woman — the foundation of the women's fiction tradition, recovered and canonized by modern scholarship.
works.meter: Prose of the Arcadian school, with the appended sonnets in the Sidneyan form of Wroth's inheritance.
works.context: Published 1621, dedicated to Susan Herbert, Countess of Montgomery; Sir Edward Denny's furious response to his alleged portrait in the book and Wroth's reply are the first documented quarrel of an English woman novelist with her public.
works.characters: Pamphilia; Amphilanthus; Urania; Parselius; the romance's queens, shepherds, and enchanters
works.structure: An interlaced prose romance in the Sidneyan manner, with the sonnet sequence as its lyrical mirror and the author's own family history (the Sidney–Herbert circle) thinly veiled in its portraits.

editions.title: The First Part of The Countess of Montgomery's Urania
editions.publisher: Medieval and Renaissance Texts and Studies

works.title: The Country Wife
works.description: Wycherley's most famous comedy, in which Horner, a rake who pretends to have been unmanned by a surgeon, gains access to the wives and mistresses of the jealous town while the innocent country wife Margery is brought to London.
works.plot: Horner's feigned impotence lets him seduce Lady Fidget, Mrs Squeamish, and others; the country wife Margery Pinchwife is kept under lock and key by her jealous husband, but her innocence defeats his vigilance; Horner's trick is nearly exposed and is saved by the women's complicity.
works.significance: The most performed and most discussed Restoration comedy; its savage exposure of jealousy, hypocrisy, and the marriage market makes it the darkest of the comedies of manners.
works.meter: Prose of great energy, with the famous china scene as the height of comic innuendo.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in January 1675 and published in the same year; it drew on Molière's L'École des femmes and L'École des maris.
works.characters: Horner; Margery Pinchwife; Mr Pinchwife; Lady Fidget; Alithea; Harcourt; Sparkish; Mrs Squeamish; Dorilant; Sir Jaspar Fidget
works.structure: Five acts with two parallel plots — Horner's intrigue and the Pinchwife marriage — and a low comic subplot of Sparkish and Alithea.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Covent Garden Weeded
works.description: Brome's moralising comedy set in the newly built Covent Garden piazza, in which a reformed rake and his companions set out to 'weed' the district of its whores, pimps, and gallants.
works.plot: Arthur Manly, the honest soldier, and his friends undertake to clear the Garden of vice; the plot turns on the rescue of the virtuous Rebecca from the brothel and the exposure of the pimps and gallants.
works.significance: An important document of the social history of Covent Garden and a notable Caroline attempt to moralise the city comedy of Jonson and Middleton.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Salisbury Court in 1632, in the newly developed Covent Garden district designed by Inigo Jones; published in the 1640 collection of Brome's plays.
works.characters: Arthur Manly; Sir Nathaniel; Captain Ironside; Rebecca; Tria; Lady Blanche; the Pimp
works.structure: Five acts with a strong reform plot and a satiric survey of the Garden's inhabitants.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Coverdale Bible
altTitles: Biblia: The Bible Faithfully Translated into English
works.description: Miles Coverdale's translation of the whole Bible into English, printed in 1535 (probably at Antwerp); the first complete printed Bible in English.
works.plot: A complete Bible — Old Testament, Apocrypha, and New Testament — translated 'out of Douche and Latyn' (German and Latin versions) as Coverdale's title page honestly states, with Tyndale's New Testament and Pentateuch incorporated; dedicated to Henry VIII, with a preface defending vernacular scripture.
works.significance: The first complete English Bible in print and the bridge from Tyndale to the authorized versions: its psalter became the Prayer Book psalter of 1662, still sung in Anglican worship, and its title page initiated the tradition of the English Bible as a national book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Printed in 1535, probably at Antwerp (the colophon of some copies points to Cologne); Anne Boleyn's patronage and Cromwell's diplomacy won it royal acceptance, and in 1537 it was licensed for sale in England, making the English Bible legal for the first time.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, chapter summaries, and a dedication to the king.

works.title: The Creed
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious lyric (creedal paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A versification of the Apostles' Creed in 57 lines, expanding each article of the faith — the creation, the Incarnation, the Passion, the harrowing of hell, the Ascension, and the last judgment — into alliterative verse of notable doctrinal clarity.
works.plot: The poem follows the articles of the Creed in order: God the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth; Christ's conception, birth, suffering, death, descent into hell, resurrection, and ascension; and the coming judgment of the living and the dead.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English verse rendering of the Apostles' Creed, valuable for its formulation of Christology and eschatology in the native idiom.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the poem's compact clauses follow the Creed article by article.
works.context: The Creed was taught to all Christians as the summary of the faith and recited in the daily offices; its versification belongs to the same vernacular devotional project as the Lord's Prayer poems.
works.structure: A sequential paraphrase of the Creed's articles, each expanded with traditional doctrinal imagery (the descent into hell, the trumpet of judgment).

works.title: The Defence of Poesy
works.description: Sir Philip Sidney's treatise in defence of poetry, written in answer to Stephen Gosson's attack The School of Abuse (1579): poetry is the first light-giver to ignorance, the sweet food of sweetly uttered knowledge, superior to both philosophy and history, and the English tongue is fully capable of the highest poetic kinds.
works.plot: Sidney answers the charges against poetry one by one, derives its antiquity and dignity from the ancients and the Bible, anatomizes the genres (pastoral, elegy, comedy, tragedy, lyric, epic), diagnoses the current poverty of English drama, and closes with the famous mocking peroration on the poet's power to make men 'not only to know, but to do'.
works.significance: The founding document of English literary criticism, from which the tradition runs through Jonson and Dryden to the Romantics.
works.meter: Prose, in the polished periodic style of the humanist oration.
works.context: Written about 1579–82 amid the Puritan attack on the stage; circulated in manuscript and printed posthumously in 1595 in two editions under its two titles.
works.structure: A classical judicial oration: exordium, narration, proof, refutation of objections, and peroration, salted with anecdote and wit.

editions.title: Miscellaneous Prose of Sir Philip Sidney
editions.editor: Katherine Duncan-Jones and Jan van Dorsten (eds.)

works.title: The Descent into Hell
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.form: religious narrative poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A narrative poem on Christ's descent into hell between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection, his release of the patriarchs and prophets, and the Resurrection itself. It draws on the Gospel of Nicodemus tradition and dramatizes the harrowing as a triumphant act of liberation.
works.plot: Christ descends to hell, breaks its gates, and frees the captive righteous — Adam, the patriarchs, and the prophets — who greet him as their long-awaited redeemer. The poem closes with the women's discovery of the empty tomb and the angel's announcement of the Resurrection.
works.significance: The only surviving Old English poem devoted wholly to the harrowing of hell, and an important witness to the devotional imagination that also produced The Dream of the Rood and Christ III.
works.meter: Alliterative long line with formulaic phrasing; the speeches of the patriarchs are given rhetorical weight through balanced alliterative clauses.
works.context: The harrowing of hell was a central motif of early medieval devotion, represented in art and liturgy as well as poetry; the poem is contemporary with the flourishing of the theme in Anglo-Saxon stone sculpture and homiletic prose.
works.characters: Christ, Adam, the patriarchs and prophets, the women at the tomb
works.structure: A compact narrative in two movements: the harrowing itself (the descent, the breaking of the gates, the speeches of the patriarchs) and the Resurrection morning at the tomb, with typological echoes of the Exodus throughout.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. No attribution has been proposed.

works.title: The Description of a New World, Called The Blazing-World
works.form: utopian fiction; prose romance; science fiction; philosophical dialogue
works.description: Margaret Cavendish's fantastical prose fiction, appended to her Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, in which a young lady is carried to a parallel world at the North Pole inhabited by hybrid animal-men and rules it as empress.
works.plot: A lady is abducted, carried to the Blazing World, and made empress; she converses with the animal-men and with the soul of the Duchess of Newcastle about natural philosophy, then returns to rescue her native world from invasion.
works.significance: The first science fiction by a woman in English, a pioneering work of utopian and speculative fiction, and a philosophical answer to the experimentalists; it has become a canonical text of early modern women's writing.
works.meter: Vigorous, digressive prose of great imaginative freedom.
works.context: Published in 1666 together with Observations upon Experimental Philosophy, as an appendix; Cavendish was living in exile and later visited the Royal Society in 1667, the first woman to do so.
works.characters: the Empress; the Duchess of Newcastle; the Bear-men; the Bird-men; the Fish-men; the Ape-men; the Satyrs; the Worm-men
works.structure: A two-part narrative of travel and philosophical dialogue, combining utopian fiction, romance, and natural philosophy.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Cavendish; the title page names her as the Duchess of Newcastle.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Destruction of Troy
altTitles: The Gest Hystoriale of the Destruction of Troy
works.description: The longest alliterative poem of the revival (over 14,000 lines), translating Guido delle Colonne's Latin Historia destructionis Troiae: the full Trojan story from Jason and the golden fleece to the fall of the city and the homecomings of the Greeks. A work of encyclopedic narrative scope, prized for its battles, storms, and sieges, preserved in a single manuscript.
works.plot: The poem recounts the causes and course of the Trojan war — the Argonauts, the first destruction of Troy, the judgement of Paris and rape of Helen, the ten years' siege with its councils, battles, and single combats, the treachery of the wooden horse, the burning of the city, and the fates of the returning heroes.
works.significance: The fullest Middle English Troy narrative and the summit of alliterative translation; its matter links the revival to Lydgate's Troy Book and the Tudor Troy tradition.
works.meter: The unrhymed alliterative long line sustained over an unprecedented length.
works.context: Composed c. 1385–1400 in the north-west Midlands, translating Guido delle Colonne (1287) with additions; preserved uniquely in Glasgow, Hunterian MS V.2.8 (mid-sixteenth century).
works.characters: Hector; Achilles; Priam; Paris; Helen; Agamemnon; Ulysses; Troilus
works.structure: A continuous chronicle-romance in the Guido tradition, organized by the war's causes, course, and aftermath, with elaborate set-piece descriptions.

works.title: The Diary of John Evelyn
altTitles: Memoirs Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn
works.description: Evelyn's diary, kept intermittently from 1641 until a few days before his death in 1706, recording his European travels, the courts of Charles II and James II, the founding of the Royal Society, and his gardens and experiments at Sayes Court.
works.plot: The diary records Evelyn's journeys in France and Italy, his observations on art, architecture, science, and gardening, the Great Plague and Fire, and the religious and political events of the Restoration.
works.significance: The indispensable companion to Pepys's diary for the history of the Restoration; Evelyn's account of the Great Fire, of the Royal Society, and of English gardening are standard sources.
works.meter: Learned, observational, and sometimes ornate prose, more formal than Pepys's.
works.context: Kept from 1641 to 1706; the manuscripts remained in the family until publication in 1818.
works.characters: John Evelyn; Mary Evelyn; Charles II; Robert Boyle; Samuel Pepys; Christopher Wren; Margaret Blagge
works.structure: A continuous daily and occasional journal over sixty-five years.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Evelyn; the manuscripts are in his own hand.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Diary of Samuel Pepys
works.description: Pepys's private shorthand diary, kept from 1 January 1660 to 31 May 1669, the most detailed and most candid account of daily life in Restoration England ever written, recording the Restoration, the coronation, the Plague, and the Fire of London.
works.plot: The diary records Pepys's work at the Navy Board, his amours, his household, the theatre, music, books, politics, and the great public events, with an unflinching self-portrait of ambition, curiosity, and pleasure.
works.significance: The greatest diary in the English language and the single most important source for the social, political, and cultural history of the 1660s; it invented the modern confessional journal and has never been out of print since 1825.
works.meter: Lively, colloquial, and confidential prose, written in Thomas Shelton's tachygraphy (shorthand) and not intended for publication.
works.context: Kept during Pepys's rise in the naval administration and during the two great catastrophes of the Restoration; the diaries passed to Magdalene College, Cambridge, and were first deciphered and published in 1825.
works.characters: Samuel Pepys; Elizabeth Pepys; Sir William Coventry; the Duke of York; Deb Willet; Mary Knep; Nell Gwyn
works.structure: A daily entry over nine and a half years, interrupted only by illness and the strain of failing eyesight.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Pepys; the manuscripts are in his own shorthand and were deciphered by John Smith in 1819-22.

editions.title: The Diary of Samuel Pepys
editions.publisher: Bell & Hyman / University of California Press

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Dictionary
altTitles: The Dictionary of Syr Thomas Eliot Knyght
works.description: Elyot's Latin–English dictionary, the first classical dictionary of the English language and the basis of the later English lexicographical tradition.
works.plot: A reference work with no argument: Latin headwords with English definitions, drawing on Calepino's Dictionarium and enriched by Elyot's own scholarship, published in a revised edition as Bibliotheca Eliotae in 1542 (revised and enlarged by Thomas Cooper, 1548).
works.significance: The founding work of English lexicography: it made classical learning accessible in the vernacular, standardized English equivalents for Latin terms, and served as the model for all subsequent Latin–English dictionaries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Compiled 1536–38 for Thomas Berthelet, with a dedication to Henry VIII; it was the first Latin–English dictionary intended for the study of classical authors rather than the medieval vocabularies, and Cooper's revisions made it the foundation of Renaissance lexicography in England.
works.structure: Alphabetical dictionary entries.

works.title: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Beautiful Empire of Guiana
works.description: Ralegh's report of his 1595 voyage up the Orinoco in search of the fabled golden empire of El Dorado: the rivers, peoples, and wonders of Guiana described with the eyewitness's precision and the courtier's art, the gold of Manoa promised and half-believed, and the whole offered to Elizabeth I as the instrument of Spain's overthrow.
works.plot: The narrative follows the expedition from Trinidad up the Orinoco's mouths; the Indian peoples, the Spanish depredations, the rumours of Manoa's gold, and the hardships of the return fill the account, which closes with Ralegh's arguments for the conquest of Guiana and his answers to the objections of the envious.
works.significance: The classic English narrative of exploration — the book that fixed El Dorado in the European imagination.
works.meter: Prose of grave, plain magnificence — the Elizabethan traveller's style at its finest.
works.context: Published 1596 after the 1595 voyage; its promise of El Dorado underwrote Ralegh's career, his 1617 return voyage, and his death.
works.characters: Sir Walter Ralegh (the narrator); the Indian peoples of the Orinoco; Topiawari (the aged cacique); the Spanish governor Berreo; the expedition's captains
works.structure: A first-person voyage narrative with the apparatus of argument and apology — the explorer's report fused with the promoter's prospectus.

editions.title: The Discoverie of the Large, Rich and Bewtiful Empyre of Guiana (Revels)

works.title: The Discovery of a World in the Moone; or, A Discourse Tending to Prove That 'Tis Probable There May Be Another Habitable World in That Planet
altTitles: The Discovery of a World in the Moone
works.description: John Wilkins's popular scientific treatise arguing, on Copernican grounds, that the moon is probably a habitable world, with a discussion of the possibility of flight to it; it introduced the new astronomy to a general English readership.
works.plot: Wilkins argues that the earth is a planet, that the moon is an earth, and that it is probable the moon is inhabited; the final proposition considers whether flying to the moon might one day be possible.
works.significance: The first popular English exposition of the plurality of worlds and a major influence on seventeenth-century imaginative literature, including Milton's cosmology and the early science fiction of Cyrano de Bergerac.
works.meter: Clear, persuasive prose for a lay readership.
works.context: Published anonymously in 1638 by the young Wadham College fellow who would become a founder of the Royal Society; it drew on Galileo, Kepler, and Godwin's The Man in the Moone.
works.structure: A series of numbered propositions with arguments and objections answered.
works.attributionNotes: Published anonymously; Wilkins's authorship was acknowledged in the third edition of 1684.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Distichs of Cato (Old English)
altTitles: The Old English Dicts of Cato
works.manuscriptDate: Cambridge, Trinity College MS R.9.17 (c. 1100); also London, British Library, Cotton Julius A.ii and Cotton Vespasian D.xiv
works.description: An Old English prose translation of the Disticha Catonis, the late-antique collection of moral distichs that was the standard first reader of the medieval schoolroom. The translation renders Cato's maxims — on wisdom, speech, friendship, thrift, and the conduct of life — into plain vernacular prose for readers without Latin.
works.plot: The text translates the four books of Cato's moral couplets and the prefatory matter: exhortations to wisdom, prudence in speech, care in friendship, moderation in all things, and the fear of God, each maxim expanded into a clear Old English sentence with occasional explanatory glosses.
works.significance: The first English version of the most influential moral textbook of the Middle Ages, linking the Old English wisdom tradition to the classical curriculum inherited by later English literature.
works.context: The Disticha Catonis was the most widely read school text of the Middle Ages; its translation into Old English shows the vernacular classroom tradition of the reform era extending the standard curriculum to those learning through English, in the same spirit as Ælfric's Grammar and Colloquy.
works.structure: A book-by-book, maxim-by-maxim prose translation following the order of the Latin distichs, with each couplet rendered as one or two vernacular sentences.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous translation; the translator is unknown.

works.title: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce
altTitles: The Doctrine and Discipline of Divorce: Restor'd to the Good of Both Sexes
works.description: Milton's controversial tract arguing that incompatibility, not merely adultery, is grounds for divorce, prompted by his own unhappy marriage to Mary Powell; it defends companionship and 'meet and happy conversation' as the true end of marriage against a rigid scriptural literalism.
works.plot: Milton argues from scripture, reason, and natural law that marriage exists for mutual help and companionship, and that an uncongenial union frustrates its divine purpose, warranting divorce and remarriage.
works.significance: A landmark in the history of marriage and divorce debate and an important document of Milton's radical Protestant individualism; it also occasioned his defence of unlicensed printing.
works.meter: Dense, passionate argumentative prose, at once learned and personal.
works.context: Written in 1643–44 after Mary Powell left Milton; it scandalised the Presbyterians and led directly to Areopagitica when Milton published without a licence, and to his later tract Tetrachordon (1645).
works.structure: A two-book argumentative treatise in prose, with scriptural exegesis and appeals to reason and natural law.

editions.title: The Complete Poetry and Essential Prose of John Milton
editions.editor: William Kerrigan, John Rumrich, and Stephen M. Fallon (eds.)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Double Dealer
works.description: Congreve's second comedy, a tightly plotted intrigue play built around the double-dealing Maskwell, who betrays his patron, his friends, and his mistresses in pursuit of an heiress.
works.plot: Maskwell, the trusted friend of Mellefont, secretly loves Lady Touchwood and conspires to disinherit Mellefont and win Cynthia; the plot is discovered only at the last moment and the lovers are saved.
works.significance: Congreve's most formally rigorous comedy and one of the most intricate plots in English drama; Maskwell is the finest villain of Restoration comedy.
works.meter: Prose.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in November 1693 and published in 1694 with a dedicatory epistle to Charles Montagu, later Earl of Halifax.
works.characters: Maskwell; Mellefont; Lord Touchwood; Lady Touchwood; Cynthia; Lady Froth; Sir Paul Plyant; Careless; Brisk
works.structure: Five acts observing the unities of time and place, a formal experiment in the French manner that made the play less popular than its predecessor.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Doubt of Future Foes
works.description: Queen Elizabeth I's poem on Mary Queen of Scots and the succession: the 'doubt of future foes' — the captive rival queen and her foreign allies — threatens the realm, but the poet's 'wit' and providence shall cut off the 'tops of hope' before they grow; the most famous of the queen's surviving poems, circulated in manuscript from the early 1570s.
works.plot: The poem moves from the menace of the rival and her 'foreign banished wights' to the queen's resolve: the sword of justice and the pruning of ambitions — a lyric of statecraft in the register of the mirror-for-princes tradition.
works.significance: The queen's own voice in the literature of her reign — the poem through which the sovereign entered the lyric tradition she patronized.
works.meter: Fourteeners (rhymed seven-stress couplets), the form of the queen's Protestant poetics.
works.context: Written about 1571, after the Ridolfi plot, when Mary Stuart's captivity and the Catholic powers' intrigues made the succession the realm's danger; it circulated in manuscript and was printed in Puttenham's Art of English Poesy (1589) as the queen's poem.
works.characters: Elizabeth (as speaker); Mary Queen of Scots (the 'future foe', un-named)
works.structure: A single lyric in two movements — the threat, then the answer — in the courtly plain style of the queen's circle.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; printed by Puttenham in 1589 as the Queen's.

editions.title: Elizabeth I: Collected Works
editions.editor: Leah S. Marcus, Janel Mueller, and Mary Beth Rose (eds.)

works.title: The Dream of the Rood
works.description: The greatest religious poem of the Old English period (156 lines): a dream vision in which the Cross itself speaks, recounting the Crucifixion as a heroic battle in which Christ, the young warrior-king, mounts the cross of his own will. Related texts survive on the eighth-century Ruthwell Cross runic inscription and the Brussels Cross.
works.plot: The dreamer sees a wondrous tree shining with gold and gems, stained with blood, and the Rood tells its story: cut down in the forest, it was made the gallows of the young hero who climbed it willingly; it trembled, dared not bow, and with Christ it was pierced with nails and mocked, then buried and later raised up as the honoured sign of salvation. The poem ends with the dreamer's hope of the heavenly homeland and the injunction to seek the tree of victory.
works.significance: The supreme fusion of Germanic heroic form with Christian content in the period; one of the great medieval dream poems.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre, richly figured; the poem's end has been thought to show hypermetric lines.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (Vercelli, Biblioteca Capitolare CXVII, fols. 104v-106r); the Ruthwell Cross (Dumfriesshire, early eighth century) carries an inscribed extract in runes, and the Brussels Cross (c. 1000) a related couplet, evidence of the poem's early circulation.
works.characters: the Dreamer; the Rood (Cross); Christ (the young hero)
works.structure: A frame vision enclosing the Cross's first-person narrative, followed by the dreamer's response and a homiletic conclusion; the Cross is the earliest sustained prosopopoeia in English poetry.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; early attributions to Cædmon or Cynewulf are not accepted.

editions.title: The Dream of the Rood

works.title: The Dreme
altTitles: The Dreme of Schir David Lindsay
works.form: dream vision in couplets and stanzas
works.description: Lindsay's dream vision addressed to the young James V: the poet, transported in sleep to hell, purgatory, and paradise, meets the spirit of the king's ancestors and returns to instruct the king in the duties of rule — an epistle to the sovereign that founds Lindsay's career as the conscience of the Scottish crown.
works.plot: The poet dreams he travels with Dame Remembrance through the three realms, hears the lament of the dead Scots kings over the realm's decay, and wakes to write the 'Exhortation to the King' that closes the poem.
works.significance: The classic Scots poem of princely counsel and the seed of the Satyre of the Thrie Estaitis; its vision of national decay set the tone of the Scottish Reformation's literature.
works.meter: Scots couplets and stanzaic passages in the Makar tradition; plain, forceful didactic verse.
works.context: Written in 1528 as James V escaped the Douglas faction and took personal rule; Lindsay, his childhood companion, speaks as the king's tutor and conscience.
works.characters: the poet; Dame Remembrance; James V (addressed); the dead kings
works.structure: Dream vision with epilogue; the three-realm journey frames the political exhortation, which is the poem's true centre.

works.title: The Duchess of Malfi
works.description: Webster's tragedy of the widowed Duchess who remarries her steward Antonio against her brothers' will: the 'Aragonian brethren' — the twisted Ferdinand and the corrupt Cardinal — pursue her with spies, imprisonment, and madmen's masques until her murder by strangling; the play then turns to the revenges that destroy the brothers, ending with the famous line, 'Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle; she died young'.
works.plot: The Duchess secretly marries Antonio and bears children; Bosola, the malcontent spy, discovers the truth; Ferdinand's fury and the Cardinal's policy drive the persecution — the wax corpses, the madmen, the executioners; the Duchess dies with her dignity ('I am Duchess of Malfi still'); and Bosola's belated revenges kill Ferdinand, the Cardinal, and himself in the final bloodbath.
works.significance: Generally ranked the greatest non-Shakespearean tragedy of the English stage — the supreme study of courage under persecution.
works.meter: The summit of Webster's blank verse — the wooing scene, the prison scene, and the dirges — with the malcontent prose of Bosola as its instrument of irony.
works.context: Based on the story of Giovanna d'Aragona (d. 1510) via Painter's Palace of Pleasure; performed about 1614 by the King's Men at Blackfriars and the Globe; printed in 1623.
works.characters: the Duchess of Malfi; Antonio Bologna; Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria; the Cardinal; Bosola; Delio; Cariola; Julia; Pescara; the Doctor; the madmen
works.structure: A five-act tragedy in two movements — the Duchess's love and martyrdom, then the revengers' self-destruction — with the echo scene and the madmen's masque as its set pieces.

editions.title: The Duchess of Malfi (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Durham Proverbs
works.description: A collection of forty-six Old English proverbs, each paired with a Latin version, written into a Durham cathedral manuscript of Ælfric's Grammar. The proverbs are earthy and practical — about friendship, speech, household management, and the follies of men — and descend from a common European proverb tradition.
works.plot: The proverbs counsel prudence in speech and friendship ('a friend in need is a friend indeed'), household thrift, and wariness of fair words, pairing each English saying with its Latin equivalent in the manner of a bilingual schoolbook.
works.significance: The only substantial surviving Old English proverb collection outside the poetic corpus, and evidence of the international proverb lore that fed later English wisdom literature.
works.meter: The Old English proverbs are rhythmical prose, often with alliterative patterning; they are not verse in the strict metrical sense.
works.context: Copied into a manuscript associated with the reform's school curriculum, the collection shows the continuity between vernacular wisdom literature (Maxims, Precepts) and the bilingual classroom tradition of the eleventh century; several proverbs have parallels in Wulfstan's homilies.
works.structure: A numbered list of proverb pairs (Old English with Latin), without framing narrative; the sayings range from two to six lines.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The proverbs are drawn from common tradition; the compiler is unknown.

works.title: The Dutch Courtesan
works.description: Marston's city comedy of appetite and virtue: the young gallant Freevill, about to marry the chaste Beatrice, casts off his mistress, the Dutch courtesan Franceschina, whose jealousy hires the pander Cocledemoy's 'murder' of him; the counterfeit death, the trial of the innocent Malheureux, and the final act's reversals end with the courtesan whipped and the lovers married — virtue triumphant over the city's flesh-markets.
works.plot: Freevill's engagement and Franceschina's fury set the plot; Malheureux, the would-be virtuous friend, is tempted by the courtesan and trapped; the staged murder, the substitute corpse, and the trial scenes complicate the middle acts; and the final scene, with the 'dead' man's return, sentences Franceschina to the cart and the whip and marries the two honest couples.
works.significance: Marston's best comedy — a satire of appetite whose frankness about sex and money tested the private theatre's licence.
works.meter: Prose for the London scenes and verse for the lovers, in Marston's sharpest comic register.
works.context: Performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels in 1605 and printed the same year; its London scenes answered the city-comedy vogue of 1604–05.
works.characters: Freevill; Malheureux; Franceschina; Beatrice; Crispinella; Cocledemoy; Mulligrub; Mistress Mulligrub; Tysefew; Mary Faugh
works.structure: A five-act comedy of intrigue on the Jonsonian model, with the brothel scenes and the trial as the play's moral poles, and Cocledemoy's prose trickeries as its comic engine.

editions.title: The Dutch Courtesan (Regents Renaissance Drama)

works.title: The Dyetary of Health
altTitles: A Compendyous Regyment or a Dyetary of Helth
works.description: Andrew Boorde's vernacular regimen of health, first printed in 1542; a popular handbook of diet, dwelling, and daily conduct for the English householder.
works.plot: The book advises on diet (meats, drinks, bread, and their digestions), on choosing a healthy dwelling site, on sleep and clothing, and on the management of the body's humours, in a plain and often earthy prose salted with proverbs and personal opinion.
works.significance: One of the most popular health manuals of the sixteenth century and a rich source for Tudor domestic life, diet, and popular medicine; Boorde's colloquial style anticipates the plain-speaking of later popular medical writing.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written by Boorde after his return from his European travels and printed in 1542 (with many later editions to 1630); it belongs to the same vernacular medical movement as Elyot's Castle of Health, aimed at readers without Latin.
works.structure: A systematic handbook in short chapters, arranged by topic from dwelling-place to foodstuffs to regimen.

works.title: The Eclogues (Barclay)
works.description: Barclay's five eclogues, the first English pastoral poetry: three adapted from Mantuan and two from Aeneas Sylvius's De Curialium Miseriis, in which shepherds debate the miseries of courts and the corruption of the clergy, and the city's poverty is set against the country's sufficiency.
works.plot: Shepherds — Coridon, Cornix, Faustus, Amyntas — meet and debate in turn: the woes of courtiers, the pride of churchmen, the pleasures of the country life, and the duties of the rich toward the poor.
works.significance: The first English pastoral, founding the tradition that runs through Spenser's Shepheardes Calender to the great pastoral of the 1590s.
works.meter: Rhyme royal for the pastoral dialogue; the smooth didactic verse of the early Tudor humanists.
works.context: Written in the decade when the court satire was becoming the period's dominant mode; the eclogues import the Mantuan model that every Elizabethan grammar school would memorize.
works.characters: Coridon; Cornix; Faustus; Amyntas; Codrus; Minalcas
works.structure: Five discrete eclogues in the Virgilian-Mantuan manner, each a debate between named shepherds with its moral explicit.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; the eclogues are adaptations of Mantuan and Aeneas Sylvius.

editions.title: The Eclogues of Alexander Barclay

works.title: The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic
works.description: Hobbes's first systematic treatise, circulated in manuscript in 1640 and dedicated to the Earl of Newcastle, which was published without his consent in 1650 in two separately titled parts.
works.plot: Part I ('Human Nature') sets out Hobbes's materialist psychology; part II ('De Corpore Politico') derives the necessity of government from the state of nature and defends absolute sovereignty.
works.significance: The first statement of Hobbes's system and a crucial document of the intellectual origins of the civil-war controversy on sovereignty.
works.meter: Plain argumentative prose.
works.context: Circulated in manuscript in 1640 during the Short Parliament; Hobbes fled to Paris in November 1640 as the treatise's royalism became dangerous.
works.structure: Two parts, each subdivided into chapters; the 1650 printing divided them into separate books.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Hobbes; the manuscript circulated under his name and the 1650 printing was unauthorised.

editions.title: Leviathan: The English and Latin Texts
editions.publisher: Clarendon Press (Clarendon Edition of the Works of Thomas Hobbes)

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Essays
altTitles: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
works.description: Francis Bacon's essays, published in three successively enlarged editions (ten essays in 1597, thirty-eight in 1612, fifty-eight in 1625): counsels civil and moral on studies, truth, death, revenge, marriage, gardens, masques, and the conduct of public life, in the aphoristic prose that made the form an English genre.
works.plot: No plot: each essay is a compact meditation on its subject — the 1625 title calls them 'counsels, civil and moral' — moving from observation through maxim to practical advice, with the famous 'Of Studies' ('Reading maketh a full man') and 'Of Truth' as its touchstones.
works.significance: The book that naturalized the essay in English — the prose counterpart of Bacon's philosophical revolution, and a schoolbook of English style for three centuries.
works.meter: Prose of aphoristic compression — antithesis, balance, and the telling image — deliberately plain and packed.
works.context: The 1597 edition was among the first English essay collections, after Florio's Montaigne was still to come; the 1625 edition, published the year before Bacon's death, is the canonical text and the foundation of the English essay tradition.
works.structure: A collection of fifty-eight numbered essays in the final edition, each a self-contained meditation in the Senecan and Montaignian modes.

editions.title: The Essayes or Counsels, Civill and Morall (Oxford Francis Bacon)

works.title: The Essays of Montaigne
works.description: John Florio's translation of Montaigne's Essays (1603), made from the 1595 French edition: the first complete English Montaigne, in which the Frenchman's scepticism, self-portraiture, and humane wisdom enter English prose in Florio's expansive, inventive idiom — the book Shakespeare read and quarried for The Tempest.
works.plot: No plot: the Essays proceed by subject — custom, cannibals, coaches, friendship, experience — Montaigne's 'I' the matter of the book, and Florio's version enlarging the French into the rich Elizabethan English of the translator's own invention.
works.significance: One of the great translations in the language — the book that gave English thought its sceptical conscience and Shakespeare his New World speech.
works.meter: Prose of Florio's characteristic copiousness — Montaigne's sentences doubled and ornamented into the idiom that Shakespeare knew.
