works.context: Published 1603, dedicated to the Countess of Bedford and others; Shakespeare's Gonzalo in The Tempest paraphrases 'Of Cannibals' from this translation, the most famous borrowing in English drama.
works.characters: Michel de Montaigne (as speaker); his friend La Boétie (in 'Of Friendship'); the cannibals; the ancients quoted throughout
works.structure: Three books of essays in the 1595 arrangement, with Florio's dedicatory epistles, his preface 'To the Reader', and his appendix of the author's life.
works.attributionNotes: Translation by John Florio from the 1595 French text; uncontested.

editions.title: Shakespeare's Montaigne: The Florio Translation of the Essays, A Selection
editions.editor: Stephen Greenblatt and Peter G. Platt (eds.)

works.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
altTitles: The First Examination of Anne Askew
The Latter Examination of Anne Askew
works.description: Anne Askew's first-person accounts of her two examinations for heresy before the ecclesiastical authorities, printed in 1546 and 1547 with prefaces by John Bale; the most important English text written by a woman in the first half of the sixteenth century.
works.plot: Askew narrates her arrest and first examination before the bishop's chancellor (March 1545) and the second, harsher examination before Bishop Bonner, Bishop Gardiner, Wriothesley, and the privy council (1545–46), recording her scriptural answers on the eucharist, her refusal to name her fellow evangelicals, and her racking in the Tower — 'I answered that I would not deny my master and my God'; the account ends with her condemnation, the burning following on 16 July 1546.
works.significance: The first sustained autobiographical narrative by an English woman in print and the founding text of the English martyr tradition; Askew's scriptural self-defence under torture made her a model of the speaking female subject for later centuries.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in prison in 1545–46, smuggled out, and printed by Bale at Wesel in 1546 (first examination) and 1547 (latter examination) as Protestant propaganda against the Henrician church; John Foxe incorporated the Examinations into the Book of Martyrs, making Askew the most famous of the Henrician women martyrs.
works.characters: Anne Askew (narrator); Bishop Edmund Bonner; Bishop Stephen Gardiner; Thomas Wriothesley; Christopher Dare; John Bale (editor)
works.structure: A first-person testimonial narrative in two parts, with Bale's framing prefaces and his 'elucidations' printed alongside; the latter examination includes the exchange with the council and the account of the rack.
works.attributionNotes: The text is Askew's own account, edited (and heavily framed) by John Bale; the record attributes authorship to Askew, with Bale's role as editor noted.

editions.title: The Examinations of Anne Askew
editions.publisher: Oxford University Press (Women Writers in English 1350–1850)

works.title: The Example of Virtue
works.description: Hawes's first major poem, an allegory of the soul's life: Youth, guided by Discretion, journeys through the world and learns virtue's lessons from Lady Sapience, marries Cleanness, and passes through Age to the vision of Eternity. Printed by Wynkyn de Worde about 1504.
works.plot: Youth, counselled by Discretion, crosses the sea of the world, defeats the dragon of vice, and is led by Sapience and Fortune's lessons to the marriage with Cleanness; Age overtakes him, and the soul enters Eternity.
works.significance: A minor but characteristic example of the late medieval moral allegory, showing the tradition Spenser was to transform.
works.meter: Rhyme royal in the Lydgatian manner, with aureate vocabulary.
works.context: Written early in the reign of Henry VII, when the court still sustained the allegorical tradition of the fifteenth century.
works.characters: Youth; Discretion; Lady Sapience; Cleanness; Fortune; Age; Eternity
works.structure: A moral allegory in the pilgrimage form, moving from instruction through trial to the vision of eternity.

works.title: The Exeter Book Riddles
works.description: A collection of some ninety-five riddles in the Exeter Book, ranging from the majestic (the swan, the iceberg, the storm, the bookworm) to the bawdy double entendres (the onion, the key, the churn), all spoken in the first person by their subjects — the largest surviving body of riddles in any early medieval vernacular.
works.plot: Each riddle presents an oblique first-person self-description — 'I am a wonderful creature...' — inviting the reader to name the hidden subject; subjects include weapons, tools, animals, natural forces, writing, and domestic objects, with several deliberately suggestive 'obscene' solutions masking innocent ones.
works.significance: The cornerstone of the English riddle tradition; a unique window onto the everyday and the marvellous in Anglo-Saxon imagination.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the riddles vary from four lines to over a hundred.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 101a-115a and elsewhere); the genre descends from the Latin enigmata of Symphosius and Aldhelm.
works.characters: the speaking objects (swan, iceberg, bookworm, onion, key, etc.)
works.structure: A sequence of independent enigmas, likely arranged by the compiler in thematic groups; the collection ends with a famous series of double-entendre riddles.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the collection may include compositions by several poets over centuries.

editions.title: The Old English Riddles of the Exeter Book

works.title: The Faerie Queene
works.description: Spenser's unfinished national epic and allegorical romance: twelve projected books of the adventures of knights who embody the private virtues, of which six were completed — Holiness (Redcrosse), Temperance (Guyon), Chastity (Britomart), Friendship (Cambell and Triamond), Justice (Artegall), and Courtesy (Calidore) — together with the fragmentary Mutabilitie Cantos (printed 1609), all moving through the fairyland that shadows Elizabeth's England and court.
works.plot: In each book a knight-errant undertakes a quest under the commission of the Faerie Queene (Gloriana): Redcrosse defeats the dragon and wins Una; Guyon destroys the Bower of Bliss; Britomart seeks Artegall through her founding vision of Britain; Artegall dispenses justice against Grantorto; Calidore wins Pastorella; the whole is shadowed by the giants, enchanters, and false knights of moral and political evil.
works.significance: The supreme poem of the English Renaissance and the fountain of English romantic narrative; Milton, Keats, and Tennyson all took their bearings from it.
works.meter: The Spenserian stanza: nine lines, eight of iambic pentameter and a final alexandrine, rhyming ababbcbcc.
works.context: Composed across the Armada decade; dedicated to Elizabeth I, with Books I–III printed in 1590 and IV–VI in 1596 during Spenser's service in Ireland; its allegories address the Reformation, the conquest of Ireland, and the cult of the Queen.
works.characters: Gloriana (the Faerie Queene); Prince Arthur; Redcrosse; Una; Guyon; Britomart; Artegall; Talus; Calidore; Archimago; Duessa; Acrasia
works.structure: Six completed books of twelve cantos each in interlaced romance structure, unified by the figure of Arthur, Prince of Britain, and by the allegorical design announced in the Letter to Ralegh.

editions.title: The Faerie Queene
editions.editor: A. C. Hamilton (ed.), text by Hiroshi Yamashita and Toshiyuki Suzuki

works.title: The Fair Jilt; or, The Amours of Prince Tarquin and Sister Henrietta
works.description: Behn's short prose fiction based on the real scandal of Sister Henrietta of the Convent of the Holy Sepulchre at Antwerp, who was tried for attempting to murder her sister; Behn, who sat on the jury, presents her as a beautiful and irresistible temptress.
works.plot: The beautiful Henrietta, forced into a convent, is pursued by the friar Tarquin; her intrigues with a nobleman and her attempt to murder her sister lead to her trial, and she is finally reconciled to the church.
works.significance: An important example of the Restoration scandal narrative and of Behn's exploitation of the boundary between reportage and fiction.
works.meter: Restoration prose of the scandal-chronicle type.
works.context: Published in 1688; Behn claimed to have witnessed the events while in the Spanish Netherlands in the 1680s.
works.characters: Sister Henrietta; Prince Tarquin; the Prince of Antwerp; the Prioress
works.structure: A short prose narrative with a documentary frame, presented as a true history.

editions.title: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Works of Aphra Behn
editions.publisher: William Pickering / Ohio State University Press

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery
works.description: Thomas Southerne's most successful tragedy, an adaptation of two of Behn's novellas, in which Isabella, believing her husband Alonzo dead, remarries and is destroyed when the first husband returns.
works.plot: Isabella, in poverty, believes Alonzo dead and marries Biron; Alonzo returns; Isabella, unable to bear the guilt, kills Biron's brother and then herself.
works.significance: The most popular she-tragedy of the 1690s and an important adaptation of Behn's prose fiction for the stage.
works.meter: Blank verse.
works.context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1694 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's Isabella was one of the great performances of the age, and the play held the stage into the nineteenth century.
works.characters: Isabella; Alonzo; Biron; Baldwin; Carlos; Anne
works.structure: Five acts in blank verse with a subordinate comic plot.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Southerne; he acknowledges the debt to Behn in the dedication.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Fates of the Apostles
works.form: religious catalogue poem in alliterative verse
works.description: A poem of 122 lines cataloguing the deaths and missionary fields of the twelve apostles, signed by Cynewulf in a runic acrostic that spells his name. The catalogue frame encloses a meditation on the poet's own need for grace, the best-known of the four Cynewulfian signatures.
works.plot: The poet, speaking as a weary traveller, enumerates the apostles in order — where each preached and how each died (Peter crucified, Paul beheaded, Andrew in Achaia, John at Ephesus, and so on) — then turns to himself: begging the prayers of the reader, weaving the runes of his name into a meditation on the gifts of God and the terror of judgment.
works.significance: The earliest signature of an English poet in his own verse; a key document for the Cynewulf canon.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre; the runic acrostic spells CYNEWULF.
works.context: Preserved in the Vercelli Book (fols. 52v-54r) and in the same collection as Andreas and the homilies.
works.characters: the twelve apostles; the poet (Cynewulf)
works.structure: A thula-like catalogue of the apostles followed by the runic signature passage, which modulates from report to prayer.
works.attributionNotes: Signed by Cynewulf in runes; accepted as authentic.
themes: Slavery, empire, and the Atlantic world

works.title: The Finnsburh Fragment
works.manuscriptDate: lost; preserved in an early eighteenth-century transcript
works.description: A fragment of about 48 lines of an older heroic lay describing the night attack on the hall of Finn, king of the Frisians, in which the Danish prince Hnæf and his men defend the doors for five days. The story — later told allusively in Beowulf's 'Finnsburg episode' — is one of the great Germanic tales of feud and loyalty.
works.plot: A watchman sees the gleam of weapons as Finn's men attack the hall by night; Hnæf's Danes hold the doors, and the fight lasts five days without a man falling, until the fragment breaks off. The fuller story, reconstructed from Beowulf and other sources, involves the peace-pledge of Hildeburh, the death of Hnæf and Finn's son, and Finn's eventual slaying by the Danes.
works.significance: The sole surviving example, alongside Beowulf, of the heroic hall-fight; indispensable for reconstructing the legend and the older lay tradition.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre of an archaic, compressed kind.
works.context: The story belongs to the fifth-century Germanic migrations; the text survives only in the transcript made by George Hickes for his Thesaurus (1705) of a manuscript leaf (Lambeth Palace MS 487) now lost.
works.characters: Hnæf; Finn; Hildeburh; Hengest; Sigeferth; Garulf; Guðlaf; Ordlaf
works.structure: A single vivid scene of hall-fighting, extended by speeches (the door-defenders Garulf and Guðere, the veteran Sigeferth); the poem's brevity and compression suggest the style of the older lays behind Beowulf.
sources: The Cambridge History of Medieval English Literature

works.title: The Forc'd Marriage; or, A Night's Intrigue
works.description: Aphra Behn's first play, a tragicomedy of forced marriage and intrigue in which Alcander is compelled to marry Erminia while loving another, and the complications are resolved in a set of marriages.
works.plot: The King forces Erminia to marry Alcander, who loves Aminta; disguises and mistaken identities lead to a night of intrigue, and the plot ends with the rightful pairings.
works.significance: The first play by a woman to be performed on the English public stage, marking the beginning of professional female authorship in English drama.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in December 1670 and published in 1671; it ran for six nights, a modest but respectable success for a first play, and by a woman.
works.characters: Alcander; Erminia; Aminta; Cleontius; Lisander; the King; Galliard
works.structure: Five acts of heroic tragicomedy.

editions.title: Kissing the Rod: An Anthology of Seventeenth-Century Women's Verse
editions.editor: Germaine Greer, Susan Hastings, Jeslyn Medoff, and Melinda Sansone (eds.)

editions.title: The Works of Aphra Behn
editions.publisher: William Pickering / Ohio State University Press

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Forest
works.description: Jonson's collection of fifteen poems printed in the 1616 Folio, including the country-house poem 'To Penshurst', the odes 'To Celia' and 'To Heaven', the song 'That Women Are but Men's Shadows', and the epistle 'To Sir Robert Wroth' — the volume that made the estate, the court, and the virtuous life the matter of English lyric.
works.plot: No plot: the poems move from the celebration of Penshurst's hospitality and Sidneyan estate-life, through the songs and odes of love and devotion, to the epistles and epitaphs that map Jonson's moral world of patrons and friends.
works.significance: Home of the English country-house poem and of Jonson's most enduring lyrics — the classical counterweight to the metaphysical fashion.
works.meter: Couplets, odes, and songs of classical restraint, including the famous lyric 'Drink to me only with thine eyes' (a cento from Philostratus).
works.context: Collected for the 1616 Folio; 'To Penshurst' (c. 1612) founded the country-house poem that Lanyer, Carew, and Marvell would continue.
works.characters: the poet; the Sidney family (at Penshurst); Celia; Sir Robert Wroth; the Countess of Bedford
works.structure: A miscellany of fifteen poems organized by theme — place, love, virtue, mortality — with 'To Penshurst' as its opening masterpiece.

editions.title: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, 7 vols.
editions.editor: David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (gen. eds.)

works.title: The Form of Living
works.description: Richard Rolle's English epistle of spiritual guidance, written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, the anchoress of Ainderby, and the most influential of his English works: a rule of the devout life in twelve chapters, from the love of God and the practice of prayer through the discernment of true contemplation to the joy of the heavenly song. It became the classic handbook of English anchoresses after Ancrene Wisse.
works.plot: Addressed to Margaret 'in the form of living', the epistle teaches the love of God above all things, the exercise of prayer and meditation on the Passion, the temptations and consolations of the solitary life, and the discernment of the true 'song' of contemplation from delusion.
works.significance: The bridge between Ancrene Wisse and the fifteenth-century devotional manuals, and the classic of the Rolle tradition in English.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose of the Rolle school.
works.context: Written c. 1348 for Margaret Kirkby, recluse of Ainderby, in the last year of Rolle's life; the most widely copied of his English writings, it circulated into the fifteenth century and was printed by Wynkyn de Worde.
works.characters: Rolle (writer); Margaret Kirkby (addressee)
works.structure: Twelve short chapters of practical and mystical instruction, in the epistle form of the Rolle canon.

works.title: The Forme of Cury
works.description: The earliest English cookery collection: some 200 recipes compiled c. 1390 by the master cooks of King Richard II, from potages and roasted meats to the subtleties and spiced dishes of the royal table, including the first English recipe for pasta ('macrows') and dishes with olive oil. It is the foundation document of English culinary literature.
works.plot: The collection proceeds from the 'furmenty' and potages through flesh and fish days to the elaborate final courses, with the spices of the East (saffron, cloves, mace) and the French culinary vocabulary of the court marking the recipes' royal provenance.
works.significance: The first English cookbook and the classic document of medieval English courtly cuisine; its recipes are still cooked by food historians today.
works.meter: Prose: terse, practical recipe English with French technical terms.
works.context: Compiled c. 1390 by the chief master cooks of Richard II, and preserved in the manuscript BL Additional MS 5016 (with the closely related manuscripts of the Curye on Inglysch group); first printed by Samuel Pegge (1780).
works.characters: none (recipe collection)
works.structure: A recipe collection in the medieval cookbook tradition, organized by course and occasion, with the royal headnote claiming its authority.

works.title: The Fortunes of Men
works.description: A poem of 98 lines cataloguing the fates that befall men — one dies young, one by the sword, one from a fall, one on the gallows; the hawk dies, the wolf mourns, the singer is praised — closing with the assurance that God apportions all gifts. A companion to The Gifts of Men.
works.plot: The poem surveys the deaths and destinies of men (and, in an admired passage, of a hawk), then turns to the arts — one man learns song, one harp, one the law — and concludes that the Measurer shapes each man's lot, bestowing craft, wealth, and wisdom as he will.
works.significance: A finely crafted example of the catalogue poem and of the period's providential view of human diversity.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book (fols. 87a-88b), following Widsith.
works.characters: none
works.structure: A double catalogue (fates, then gifts) closed by a doxological gnome on divine providence.

works.title: The Four Elements
altTitles: A New Interlude and a Mery, of the Nature of the Four Elements
works.description: John Rastell's pedagogical interlude on the four elements and the new geography, printed by the author c. 1520; the first English play designed to teach natural science.
works.plot: Humanity, instructed by Nature and Studious Desire, is taught the four elements, the roundness of the earth, and the new-found lands of America; he is then tempted by Sensual Appetite into the tavern, where he wastes his learning in drinking, and the fragment (the play survives incomplete) breaks off with Experience promising his restoration.
works.significance: The first English play to teach science and geography, and a pioneering attempt to harness the stage to the new learning; it documents the arrival of the Age of Discovery in English popular culture.
works.meter: Couplets and stanzaic songs
works.context: Printed c. 1520 by Rastell, More's brother-in-law, who had himself attempted a voyage to the New World in 1517; the play's geography lesson celebrates the discovery of America, and its music survives in the unique fragment (British Library).
works.characters: Nature; Humanity; Studious Desire; Sensual Appetite; Experience; Ignorance; The Taverner
works.structure: A morality framework used for instruction: a series of lectures on cosmology and geography alternating with scenes of temptation and fall, with songs (including one with music) and a dance.

works.title: The Four PP
altTitles: The Play Called the Four PP
works.description: John Heywood's best-known farce, a lying contest among a Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, and a Pedlar; the earliest surviving edition is that of William Middleton, c. 1544.
works.plot: A Palmer, Pardoner, and Pothecary each boast of his trade and its profits, and the Pedlar proposes a contest: whoever tells the greatest lie wins the wager. The Pothecary's tale of a marvellous cure and the Pardoner's account of a soul released from hell's pains — capped by the Palmer's claim that he has met a woman patient and uncomplaining — end the contest, the Palmer winning the palm and the company concluding in good fellowship.
works.significance: The most famous of the Tudor interludes and the classic English stage farce before Shakespeare; its tale of the woman patient in all things circulated into later jest-books and remains the play by which Heywood is chiefly remembered.
works.meter: Couplets
works.context: Composed c. 1520–30 in Heywood's period as a court entertainer and virginal player to Henry VIII; the lying contest reworks the fabliau tradition (the tale of the patient wife appears in Boccaccio) and the satire of pardons and relics reflects pre-Reformation criticism of popular piety.
works.characters: The Palmer; The Pardoner; The Pothecary; The Pedlar
works.structure: A single-scene farce built of successive set-piece tales, with the Pedlar as proposer and judge of the wager.

editions.title: The Plays of John Heywood

works.title: The Fox and the Wolf
works.description: The earliest English beast fable, a comic tale of some 300 lines in which the fox, trapped in a bucket down a well, persuades the gullible wolf that he is in paradise, and escapes by the wolf's folly. It inaugurates the English Reynardian tradition that runs to Caxton's Reynard the Fox.
works.plot: The thirsty fox climbs into one well-bucket and is stranded; when the wolf asks what he does there, the fox claims the well is paradise, induces the wolf to descend in the other bucket, and is drawn up as the wolf goes down.
works.significance: The beginning of the English Reynard tradition and the earliest English fabliau-fable; an essential witness to the continental debts of early Middle English narrative.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with lively dialogue.
works.context: Composed c. 1250–75, adapted from the French Roman de Renart; preserved in the late thirteenth-century Digby MS 86 (Bodleian Library).
works.characters: the Fox; the Wolf
works.structure: A single comic episode built on the trickster's persuasive lie and the dupe's comeuppance.

works.title: The Garden
works.description: Marvell's meditation on the pleasures of a garden and the withdrawal from worldly ambition and sensual love into contemplative solitude, culminating in the famous image of the mind as a sea that 'Annihilates all that's made / To a green thought in a green shade'.
works.plot: The poem rejects the vain pursuits of ambition and the grosser pleasures of love for the superior delight of the garden, then rises to a Platonic vision of the soul's meditation and the paradise of the solitary, innocent mind.
works.significance: A central poem of retirement and contemplation in English, admired for its wit, its green imagery, and its metaphysical meditation on the mind.
works.meter: Iambic tetrameter quatrains with a serene, meditative wit and paradox.
works.context: Composed probably in the 1650s, published in Miscellaneous Poems (1681); it reflects the Neoplatonic and Epicurean ideal of retirement valued by Marvell and his contemporaries.
works.characters: the poet; the soul
works.structure: A nine-stanza lyric meditation moving from satire of worldly pursuits to celebration of the garden to visionary contemplation.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; there is a Latin companion poem 'Hortus' by Marvell.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Poems of Andrew Marvell
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Garden of Cyrus
altTitles: The Garden of Cyrus: Discourse on the Quincunx
works.description: The companion piece to Hydriotaphia, a learned and increasingly mystical discourse on the quincunx — the five-point arrangement — as it appears in the gardens of Cyrus, in nature, and in art, and as an emblem of cosmic order.
works.plot: Browne traces the quincunx from the Hanging Gardens of Cyrus through Roman military formations, botanical patterns, and the arrangement of the stars, arguing that the figure reveals a divine geometrical order in creation.
works.significance: A unique experiment in emblematic natural philosophy and one of the strangest and most beautiful works of English prose; it has been a touchstone for critics interested in the seventeenth-century imagination.
works.meter: Dense, incantatory prose; the concluding 'night-piece' is famous for its drowsy cadences.
works.context: Published in 1658 together with Hydriotaphia and dedicated to Nicholas Bacon.
works.structure: Five chapters of accumulating pattern and digression, ending in a nocturnal vision.

editions.title: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Garland of Laurel
works.form: dream vision in rhyme royal and Skeltonics
works.description: Skelton's self-crowning dream vision: the poet, wandering in a forest, is brought before Queen Fame and the assembled court of the Countess of Surrey at Sheriff Hutton, where Pallas and the ladies of the court intercede for him and Fame grants him the laurel — the poem including a catalogue of his own works that is the first English poet's bibliography.
works.plot: The dreamer debates with Occupation and Fame whether he deserves the laurel; the ladies of the court, led by the Countess of Surrey, petition on his behalf; Fame crowns him, and the poet wakes to compose the envoy of praise.
works.significance: The first English poem to canonize its own author, with a bibliography of his works; a unique document of the poet's self-understanding at the Tudor court.
works.meter: Mixed rhyme royal and Skeltonic passages; the courtly and the demotic styles deliberately alternated.
works.context: Written at Sheriff Hutton in Yorkshire, in the household of the Countess of Surrey, in 1523, when Skelton's laureate claims needed the court's support against Wolsey.
works.characters: the poet; Queen Fame; Pallas; the Countess of Surrey; Occupation
works.structure: Dream vision with debate and pageant; the catalogue of the poet's works embedded in the intercession of the court ladies.

works.title: The Gentle Craft
works.description: Deloney's fiction of the shoemakers' craft: the legendary origins of the 'gentle craft' in the saints and heroes who took up shoemaking — St Hugh, St Crispin and Crispianus, Sir Simon Eyre the shoemaker Lord Mayor, and the apprentice who married a king's daughter — the book that gave Dekker his Shoemaker's Holiday and the trade its mythology.
works.plot: The frame of the shoemakers' feast encloses the tales: Hugh's love for the king's daughter Winifred and his martyrdom; Crispin and Crispianus serving the king in disguise; Simon Eyre's rise to the mayoralty; and the apprentice Tom Drum's wooing of a great lady — each tale proving the craft's gentility and the shoemaker's wit.
works.significance: The classic of the craft romance — the book that made the shoemaker's bench a seat of English legend.
works.meter: Prose of Deloney's popular register, with songs and the frame's festive setting.
works.context: Published about 1597–98; its Eyre story supplied the plot of Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday (1599), and its craft-patriotism answered the decade's civic pride.
works.characters: St Hugh; Winifred; St Crispin; Crispianus; Simon Eyre; Tom Drum; the master shoemakers and their guests
works.structure: A frame-tale collection in the manner of the Decameron, with each story a romance or jest of the craft's legends.

editions.title: The Works of Thomas Deloney

works.title: The Gentleman Dancing-Master
works.description: Wycherley's second comedy, a satire on affectation of French and Spanish manners, in which a would-be Spanish grandee is fooled by his daughter's suitor disguised as a dancing master.
works.plot: Monsieur de Parelle, an affecter of foreign fashions, is outwitted by St Jago, who courts his daughter Hippolita by posing as her dancing master; the plot exposes the emptiness of the gentleman's pretensions.
works.significance: An important link between Wycherley's first comedy and his two masterpieces, notable for its satire on cultural affectation.
works.meter: Prose dominant.
works.context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1672 and published in 1673.
works.characters: Monsieur de Parelle; Hippolita; St Jago; Madame Caution; Don Diego; Mrs Flareit
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy with a strong comic central figure.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Gifts of Men
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990
works.description: A catalogue poem of 113 lines celebrating the diversity of human talents as gifts of God: one man is strong, another wise, another skilled in song, hunting, navigation, smithing, or counsel. The poem's theme is that every gift comes from the Lord and none should be despised.
works.plot: The poet enumerates the many endowments distributed among mankind — physical strength, beauty, eloquence, song, learning, craftsmanship, skill in the hunt, the sea, the harp, and the council — and concludes that God, the giver of all gifts, has so ordered the world that no one possesses everything and each talent has its place.
works.significance: A major statement of the Old English wisdom tradition's social vision, and a companion piece to The Fortunes of Men; both poems treat the same theme of distributed human destiny.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the catalogue form is carried by parallel clauses of the 'sum... sum...' (one... another...) type characteristic of Old English gnomic verse.
works.context: The poem belongs to the Exeter Book wisdom tradition alongside Maxims I and II and The Fortunes of Men, with which it is often compared; it reflects the Anglo-Saxon conviction that society is knit together by complementary gifts under divine providence.
works.structure: A sustained catalogue organized by successive human activities and skills, framed by an opening assertion of God's generosity and a closing meditation on the ordered distribution of gifts.

works.title: The Golden Legend
works.description: William Caxton's translation of Jacobus de Voragine's Legenda Aurea, printed at Westminster in 1483: the great medieval collection of saints' lives and feasts of the church year, in nearly 450 leaves and the first English printing of the work. It became the standard English legendary for a century, reprinted repeatedly into the 1520s.
works.plot: Following the church year, the collection narrates the lives and martyrdoms of the saints — from St Andrew through the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins — with the great feasts (Advent, Christmas, Passiontide) expounded and the legends moralized for the reader's instruction.
works.significance: The great bestseller of Caxton's press and the principal English channel of the Legenda Aurea; its saints' lives nourished English devotional reading into the sixteenth century.
works.meter: Prose: Caxton's mature plain style at its most ample.
works.context: Translated by Caxton from French and Latin sources and printed at Westminster in 1483, in the orthodox devotional market of pre-Reformation England; nine editions appeared by 1527, before the Reformation ended the cult of the saints it served.
works.characters: the saints of the calendar
works.structure: A calendrical legendary in the Voragine tradition, with Caxton's additions (including lives of English saints) and his prologue explaining the work's purpose.
works.attributionNotes: Caxton's translation is documented in his own prologue.

editions.title: Caxton's Golden Legend
editions.editor: Mayumi Taguchi, John Scahill, and Satoko Katsumata (eds.)

works.title: The Great Bible
works.description: The first authorized English Bible, a revision of Matthew's Bible (itself based on Tyndale and Coverdale) carried out by Miles Coverdale and printed in Paris and London in 1539 under Thomas Cromwell's patronage; the Bible ordered to be set up in every parish church.
works.plot: A complete Bible in large folio format, with the title page by Hans Holbein showing Henry VIII handing the Word to Cranmer and Cromwell; the text revises the Matthew Bible's Old Testament against the Hebrew and Latin, and its 1540 second edition carried Cranmer's preface, giving the book its later name.
works.significance: The Bible that made the English Bible a public institution: chained in the churches, read aloud to the people, it established the vernacular scriptures at the centre of English religious life and supplied the psalter of the Prayer Book.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Commissioned by Cromwell and begun in Paris (the French printing was seized by the Inquisition, and the presses moved to London), the Great Bible of 1539 was ordered by the injunctions of 1538 to be placed in every parish church; its psalter entered the Prayer Book tradition, and it remained the standard English Bible until the Bishops' Bible of 1568.
works.structure: The full biblical canon with prologues, summaries, and the famous illustrated title page.
works.attributionNotes: The revision is Coverdale's, on the basis of the Matthew Bible (edited by John Rogers from Tyndale and Coverdale); the record attributes the work to Coverdale as revising editor, following standard usage.

works.title: The Harley Lyrics
works.description: A collection of some forty secular and religious lyrics preserved in the Ludlow scribe's anthology, BL Harley MS 2253 (c. 1340), the richest single manuscript of early Middle English lyric: love songs, laments, satires, and devotional poems in French, Latin, and English, including such masterpieces as 'Alysoun', 'Wynter wakeneth al my care', and 'Blow, northerne wynd'.
works.plot: The poems range across the lyric repertoire: the lover's springtime longing and complaint, the satire of corrupt clergy and unjust lords, the meditation on death and the Passion, and the praise of the Virgin.
works.significance: The indispensable witness to the early Middle English lyric tradition at its best, and the principal source of the poems that bridge early and Ricardian poetry.
works.meter: A remarkable variety: tail-rhyme stanzas, alliterative long lines, and French-derived stanza forms, often with refrains.
works.context: Copied c. 1340 by a professional scribe working near Ludlow, Herefordshire, for a gentry household, from materials of the later thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries.
works.characters: the lovers and speakers of the lyrics
works.structure: An anthology, not a sequence: the manuscript's trilingual arrangement (with English poems often paired with their French and Latin analogues) supplies the order.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; the poems are the work of many hands, assembled by the scribe.

works.title: The Hind and the Panther
altTitles: The Hind and the Panther: A Poem in Three Parts
works.description: Dryden's great beast-fable of religious controversy, written after his conversion to Roman Catholicism: the milk-white Hind (the Roman Church) is pursued and slandered by the Panther (the Church of England) and the other beasts of the English sects.
works.plot: The Hind, immortal and unafathed, seeks her lost children; she debates authority and interpretation with the Panther, recounts her own conversion, and the poem ends with the fable of the Swallows and the Martins.
works.significance: The longest and most serious of Dryden's poems and the fullest statement of his Catholic apologetic; a masterpiece of sustained argumentative verse that influenced Pope's Essay on Man.
works.meter: Heroic couplets of sustained eloquence, with the most complex syntax of Dryden's verse.
works.context: Published in April 1687 under the Declaration of Indulgence, when James II's policy of toleration for Catholics briefly encouraged open Catholic argument; it was parodied within weeks by Montagu and Prior in The Hind and the Panther Transvers'd.
works.characters: the Hind (the Roman Catholic Church); the Panther (the Church of England); the Bear (Independents); the Hare (Quakers); the Wolf (Presbyterians); the Ape (Freethinkers); the Swallow (Titus Oates)
works.structure: Three parts: the characters of the beasts, the theological debate at the Hind's house, and the concluding fable; framed by an extended address to the poem itself.

editions.title: Metaphysical Lyrics and Poems of the Seventeenth Century: Donne to Butler
The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of King Richard III
altTitles: History of King Richard the Third
works.description: More's unfinished prose history of the rise and fall of Richard III, composed in parallel English and Latin versions; the English text was first printed in a corrupt form in Hardyng's Chronicle (1543) and the definitive version appeared in Rastell's edition of More's English Works (1557).
works.plot: The narrative traces Richard's path to the throne: the death of Edward IV, Richard's seizure of power as Protector, the removal of the princes, Buckingham's rebellion, and Richard's coronation and brief reign, breaking off during Morton's embassy to France. It portrays Richard as a dissembling tyrant whose deformity mirrors his moral deformity.
works.significance: The first great work of English prose history and the fountainhead of the Tudor myth of Richard III; its psychological portraiture and dramatic irony made it a major source for Shakespeare and for sixteenth-century historiography.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written during More's second period of public service, probably 1513–1518, drawing on oral testimony from Morton's household where More was raised; the work circulated in manuscript and shaped the Tudor 'black legend' of Richard III long before Shakespeare used Hall's chronicle (which incorporated More's account) for his play.
works.characters: Richard III; Edward IV; Elizabeth Woodville; Henry Stafford, Duke of Buckingham; John Morton; Lord Hastings; Edward V; Richard, Duke of York
works.structure: Unfinished chronicle in five books, driven by dramatic set-piece speeches (Buckingham's oration, Elizabeth Woodville's lament) and a Tacitean focus on character and motive rather than providential design.

editions.title: The History of King Richard III (The Yale Edition of the Complete Works of St. Thomas More, vol. 2)

works.title: The History of the Reformation of the Church of England
works.description: Gilbert Burnet's monumental church history in three volumes (1679, 1681, 1714), which gave the Church of England an authoritative narrative of its separation from Rome and became the standard Protestant account of the Reformation.
works.plot: Burnet narrates the reigns of Henry VIII, Edward VI, and Elizabeth I, using original documents, to show the Reformation as a lawful and providential return to primitive Christianity.
works.significance: The standard English history of the Reformation for two centuries and a principal source for the Anglican identity of the Church of England.
works.meter: Clear, vigorous, plain historical prose.
works.context: Volume I published in 1679 and rewarded with a doctorate of divinity by Oxford; volume II in 1681 and volume III, posthumously, in 1714.
works.characters: Henry VIII; Thomas Cranmer; Edward VI; Elizabeth I; Thomas Cromwell; Thomas More
works.structure: Three volumes of narrative history with collections of documents appended.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of the Royal-Society of London for Improving of Natural Knowledge
works.description: Thomas Sprat's official history of the Royal Society, commissioned by the Society itself, which defends the new experimental philosophy against its critics and sets out the ideal of a plain, unadorned prose suited to the reporting of fact.
works.plot: Part I surveys the history of learning and the corruption of philosophy; part II describes the Society's constitution, methods, and achievements; part III answers the objections of the schools, the wits, and the clergy.
works.significance: The principal source for the early history of the Royal Society and the classic statement of the ideal of plain prose that dominated English non-fiction for a century; it has been a touchstone in the history of scientific writing.
works.meter: Elegant but plain prose; the famous passage on the Society's resolution to reject 'swelling of style' and to use 'a close, naked, natural way of speaking' became the manifesto of the plain style.
works.context: Published in 1667, five years after the Society's charter; Sprat was a chaplain and Fellow who had access to the Society's records and to Evelyn and Wren.
works.characters: Francis Bacon; Charles II; the Fellows of the Royal Society
works.structure: Three parts in a continuous history and defence.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Sprat; the work was commissioned and corrected by the Society.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The History of the World
works.description: Ralegh's great history, written during his imprisonment in the Tower: the story of the world from the Creation to the end of the Macedonian empire, told as the record of God's providence over kingdoms — with the famous preface's meditation on death ('O eloquent, just, and mighty Death!') and the running argument that the wise man serves God, not fortune.
works.plot: The five books move from the Creation and the patriarchs through Egypt, Assyria, and Persia to Greece and Alexander; the rise and fall of each empire demonstrates the providence that raises and casts down; and the closing books and the preface frame the whole as counsel to princes and consolation to the prisoner.
works.significance: The great English history of the Renaissance — the prisoner's summa of providence and power that Milton and Cromwell's generation read as scripture of state.
works.meter: Prose of grave sententiousness — the prison's composure in every period.
works.context: Written 1603–14 in the Tower, dedicated to Prince Henry, and published in 1614; James I is said to have disliked it as 'too saucy in censuring princes', and the book was suppressed after Ralegh's fall.
works.characters: Adam; Noah; Moses; the kings of Egypt, Assyria, and Persia; Alexander the Great; the historical actors of the five books
works.structure: A universal chronicle in the classical and biblical tradition, organized by empire, with the author's moral reflections interlacing the narrative.

editions.title: Sir Walter Ralegh: The History of the World

works.title: The History of the Worthies of England
works.description: Fuller's great county-by-county biographical and antiquarian survey of the notable men and women of England, with descriptions of each county's natural resources, wonders, and families; it was published posthumously in 1662.
works.plot: Each county is treated in a uniform sequence: its natural commodities, manufactures, wonders, battles, families, and memorable persons, with biographical notices of its 'worthies'.
works.significance: A foundational work of English local history and biography, and the source for countless later antiquarians; it remains in use as a biographical reference.
works.meter: Fuller's characteristically digressive, witty, and compressed prose.
works.context: Written during the Commonwealth and published in 1662, after Fuller's death in 1661; it is the first systematic topographical and biographical dictionary of England.
works.structure: An alphabetical arrangement by county with a general introduction.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Holy State and the Profane State
works.description: Thomas Fuller's most popular work, a book of 'characters' describing the ideal states of the church, the family, the court, and the commonwealth, followed by the contrary vices of the profane state.
works.plot: The first part describes the good parson, the good husband, the good magistrate, the good soldier, and the like; the second part describes their profane opposites; the third part gives the history of the Church from the creation.
works.significance: The most influential English collection of characters after Earle and the principal model of the pithy, aphoristic prose style that Johnson imitated.
works.meter: Fuller's characteristic pithy, epigrammatic, punning prose.
works.context: Published in 1642, on the eve of the civil wars, and dedicated to the Lady Montagu; it was reprinted throughout the century.
works.characters: the good parson; the good husband; the good magistrate; the good soldier; the good merchant; their profane opposites
works.structure: A series of short character-pieces followed by a historical narrative.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Holy War Made by Shaddai upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World
works.description: Bunyan's second great allegory, a military and spiritual epic of the town of Mansoul, built by Shaddai, captured by Diabolus, and recovered by his son Emmanuel; it is a complex allegory of the soul's fall and redemption.
works.plot: Shaddai builds Mansoul and gives it law; Diabolus besieges and takes it; Emmanuel, Shaddai's son, wages war to recover it, captures and pardons the town, and appoints officers; Diabolus returns by stealth and the town must be continually defended.
works.significance: Bunyan's most ambitious and most learned allegory, and a major work of Puritan theology in narrative form; it has been judged more complex but less popular than The Pilgrim's Progress.
works.meter: Plain prose with an elaborate allegorical nomenclature and occasional verses.
works.context: Published in 1682 with a copperplate frontispiece, four years after Part I of The Pilgrim's Progress, and dedicated to the reader in an allegorical address.
works.characters: Shaddai; Emmanuel; Diabolus; the Lord Secretary; Captain Credence; Mr Conscience; Mr Recorder; the captains Boanerges; the towns of Mansoul
works.structure: A prose epic in four parts with an allegorical cast of named officers, captains, and townspeople.

editions.title: The Pilgrim's Progress
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Honest Whore, Part 1
works.description: Dekker and Middleton's comedy of conversion: the courtesan Bellafront, courted by all Milan, is converted to virtue by the grief of her rejected suitor Hippolito; the madhouse of Bethlehem, where her father Anselmo feigns madness to save her, supplies the play's great scene; and the play ends with her marriage to the patient Matheo — the first part of the diptych continued in Part 2 (c. 1605).
works.plot: Bellafront plies her trade until Hippolito's lament and her father's disguise break her heart; her conversion, the testing of her suitors, and the schemes of the pander and the courtiers follow; the scene in Bedlam, with the madmen's pageant of the city's vices, is the play's moral centre; and the final act restores Bellafront to marriage and her father to peace.
works.significance: The great Elizabethan-Jacobean comedy of conversion — the play that made the 'honest whore' a type of the English stage's moral theatre.
works.meter: Prose and verse in the two authors' distinct registers, with the madmen's speeches as the play's most quoted passages.
works.context: Performed by Prince Henry's Men in 1604 and printed the same year; the Bedlam scene answered the vogue for madhouse shows, and the play's reform of the whore answered the city's moralists.
works.characters: Bellafront; Hippolito; Matheo; Anselmo (disguised as the madman); Candido the linen-draper; the Duke of Milan; Infelice; Fluello; Castruccio; Pioratto; the madmen of Bedlam
works.structure: A five-act comedy of conversion built on the two great set pieces — the madhouse and the conversion — with the Duke's disguised progress through the city as frame.
works.attributionNotes: By Dekker and Middleton jointly, as printed; the division of scenes is debated.

editions.title: The Dramatic Works of Thomas Dekker, 4 vols.

works.title: The House of Fame
works.description: Chaucer's comic dream vision of fame and rumour (2,158 lines in octosyllabic couplets, unfinished): the dreamer is carried by a talkative eagle through the heavens to the House of Fame, where the goddess dispenses reputation with sublime arbitrariness, and on to the whirling House of Rumour where every report, true and false, takes wing. A poem about poetry, authority, and the instability of language itself.
works.plot: The dreamer, pondering the causes of dreams and the nature of fame, finds himself in a temple of Venus adorned with the story of the Aeneid; an eagle (comically garrulous, in the Dantean manner) snatches him up and lectures him on sound, air, and the physics of speech; before the House of Fame he sees the petitioners — great and small — receive arbitrary reward or oblivion; and in the twig-built, whirling House of Rumour every tiding breeds and flies; the poem breaks off as 'a man of gret auctorite' appears.
works.significance: The most brilliant medieval English poem about poetry, fame, and the circulation of language; its self-reflexive comedy anticipates the metacritical concerns of modern literature.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets with colloquial verve; the eagle's lecture burlesques the didactic mode.
works.context: Composed c. 1378–80, during Chaucer's Italian-inspired middle period, drawing on Dante, Virgil, Ovid, and Boethius; the invocation promises tidings 'of love or such thinges glade' — a tease never fulfilled.
works.characters: the Dreamer (Geffrey); the Eagle; Fame; Aeolus; the suitors of Fame; the 'man of great authority'
works.structure: Three movements (the temple of Venus; the eagle's flight and lecture; the houses of Fame and Rumour), with the Aeneid and the physics of sound as its digressive armature.

editions.title: The Riverside Chaucer

works.title: The Husband's Message
works.description: An elegiac poem of 54 lines in which a wooden rune-stave, carved with a message, speaks on behalf of an exiled lord to the woman he loves, recalling their former vows and summoning her to join him across the sea.
works.plot: The stave tells how its lord was forced into exile by a feud, how he longs for his lady, and how he now sends word that he has wealth and a hall prepared for her; the poem closes with a runic passage (often solved as 'sige', 'rad', and other rune-names) promising their reunion and the renewal of their vows.
works.significance: An early and sophisticated use of the speaking-object device and of runic writing as poetic material.
works.meter: Alliterative accentual metre.
works.context: Preserved in the Exeter Book, following the riddles; often paired with The Wife's Lament as complementary perspectives on exile and separated love.
works.characters: the rune-stave (speaker); the lord; the lady
works.structure: A speaking object (prosopopoeia) delivers the lord's message; the closing runic riddle has prompted attempts to read the poem as part of a composite sequence with the riddles that follow it in the manuscript.
movements: The AB Language Group (West Midlands Devotional Prose)
sources: English Historical Documents, Volume I: c. 500–1042

works.title: The Indian Queen
works.description: The first full English heroic play in rhymed couplets, set in the conquest of Mexico, written by Dryden in collaboration with his brother-in-law Sir Robert Howard.
works.plot: The Aztec prince Acacis and the Indian hero Zempoalla are caught between love and ambition in the war against the Spaniards; Zempoalla's usurpation, the sacrifice of the captives, and the intervention of the gods lead to a final resolution.
works.significance: The founding work of the English heroic drama, and the occasion of the Dryden-Howard controversy over rhyme that led to An Essay of Dramatic Poesy.
works.meter: Rhymed heroic couplets in iambic pentameter.
works.context: Performed by the King's Company at the Theatre in Lincoln's Inn Fields in January 1664 with music by Henry Purcell's teacher John Banister; the collaboration quarrel is recorded in the prefaces.
works.characters: Zempoalla; Acacis; Zempalla's son Amexia; Montezuma; Traxalla; Garrucca; the High Priest of the Sun
works.structure: Five acts with masque-like spectacle, songs, and machinery.
works.attributionNotes: The 1664 quarto names Dryden and Howard jointly; modern attribution assigns the bulk to Dryden.

editions.title: The Poems and Fables of John Dryden
The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Introduction of Knowledge
altTitles: The Fyrst Boke of the Introduction of Knowledge
works.description: Andrew Boorde's popular geography and travel book of 1547, the first English printed book to describe the nations of Europe in verse and prose for the general reader.
works.plot: The book presents each nation of Europe (and beyond) through a woodcut portrait of a native in national dress, a verse dialogue spoken by the figure, and a prose description of the country's customs, currency, and distances — a compendium of travel knowledge for merchants and pilgrims.
works.significance: The first printed English survey of European nations and an early document of English ethnographic description; its woodcut national portraits founded a visual tradition that lasted into the seventeenth century.
works.meter: Prose with verse interludes
works.context: Compiled from Boorde's European travels of the 1530s and printed in 1547 by William Copland; Boorde, physician and Carthusian, had been licensed to travel by Thomas Cromwell, and the book reflects the expansion of English geographical curiosity in the mid-Tudor period.
works.structure: Thirty-nine chapters, one per nation, each combining woodcut, verse self-description, and prose itinerary.

works.title: The Itinerary
works.description: John Leland's topographical survey of England and Wales, the record of his itineraries undertaken with a royal commission from Henry VIII to search the libraries of the monasteries, compiled c. 1535–43 and first printed by Thomas Hearne in 1710–12.
works.plot: The Itinerary is a county-by-county record of Leland's travels: towns, rivers, bridges, castles, churches, and the antiquities of each place, noted in terse first-person entries that document the landscape of England on the eve of the dissolution of the monasteries.
works.significance: The founding text of English antiquarianism and topography; it inaugurated the tradition of the county survey that runs through Camden, Aubrey, and the eighteenth-century antiquaries, and its value as an eyewitness record of pre-dissolution England is irreplaceable.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Leland held a commission from Henry VIII (1533) to search the monastic and collegiate libraries; his itineraries of c. 1535–43 covered most of England and Wales, and his notes preserve records of books, inscriptions, and buildings later destroyed in the dissolution and after.
works.structure: Topographical notes arranged by county, preserved in autograph notebooks; the printed text of 1710–12 follows Hearne's edition of the surviving manuscripts.

works.title: The Jew of Malta
works.description: Marlowe's black comedy of Machiavellian revenge: the merchant Barabas, his wealth seized to pay Malta's tribute to the Turks, revenges himself on the Christian state by intrigue and poison, betrays the island to the Turks, and is finally caught in his own engine — the cauldron prepared for his enemies — in a play whose prologue is spoken by 'Machevill' himself.
works.plot: Barabas is stripped of his estate; through his daughter Abigail he recovers his hidden gold and buys the deaths of the governor's son and suitor; Abigail's conversion and death, his purchase of the slave Ithamore, and the double poisonings follow; made governor by the Turks, he plots the city's destruction, but the falling floor delivers him to the cauldron and the Christians' triumph.
works.significance: The most corrosive of the Elizabethan revenge plays — a satire of Christian, Jew, and Turk alike that Shakespeare answered in Shylock.
works.meter: Blank verse for Barabas's great soliloquies of gold ('infinite riches in a little room') against the prose of the play's farcical intrigues.
works.context: Performed from 1592, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and the Marrano anxieties of the 1590s; not printed until 1633, when it was revived with prologues by Heywood.
works.characters: Barabas; Abigail; Ithamore; Ferneze, governor of Malta; Lodowick; Mathias; Calymath; Bellamira; Pilia-Borza; the two Friars (Jacomo and Bernardine); Machevill (the Prologue)
works.structure: A five-act intrigue of escalating double-dealing, alternating the prologue's sardonic commentary with farcical villainy, and ending in the spectacular engine of the cauldron.

editions.title: Christopher Marlowe: The Complete Plays

works.title: The Judgement Day I and II
works.manuscriptDate: Exeter Book (Exeter Cathedral Library MS 3501), c. 960-990 (Judgement Day I); Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 201 (Judgement Day II)
works.description: Two independent eschatological poems on the last judgment. Judgement Day I (119 lines) describes the cosmic terrors of doomsday and the soul's reckoning; Judgement Day II (306 lines), based on Bede's De die iudicii, is a sustained meditation on sin, penance, and the judgment, addressed to the individual soul.
works.plot: Judgement Day I depicts the universal conflagration, the trumpets, and the assembly of all souls before the judge, contrasting the fate of the blessed and the damned. Judgement Day II urges the penitent soul to recall its sins now, while confession is still possible, painting the terrors of judgment in images of fire, darkness, and weeping, and closes with hope for those who repent.
works.significance: The fullest Old English verse treatments of the last judgment, and (in Judgement Day II) an important vernacular witness to the reception of Bede's Latin eschatological poetry.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; Judgement Day II's sustained length and homiletic urgency make it the most ambitious of the Exeter/CCCC 201 eschatological poems.
works.context: The judgment was the master-image of Anglo-Saxon homiletics, from the Blickling and Vercelli homilies to Wulfstan's Sermo Lupi; the poems belong to that culture of penitential fear and are the verse counterpart of the homilists' doomsday rhetoric.
works.structure: Both poems move from description of the cosmic catastrophe to exhortation; Judgement Day II is organized as a sequence of meditations on sin, the hour of death, the judgment, and the possibility of mercy through penance.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous. The two poems are independent compositions; Judgement Day II is an adaptation of Bede's De die iudicii, not by Bede himself.

works.title: The Katherine Group
altTitles: The Lives of St Katherine, St Margaret, and St Juliana
works.description: Three prose lives of virgin martyrs — St Katherine of Alexandria, St Margaret of Antioch, and St Juliana of Nicomedia — written in the same West Midlands 'AB language' as Ancrene Wisse for a female religious audience. They are the classic Middle English saints' lives: rhetorically elaborate, vivid in their debates and torments, and fervent in their celebration of virginity.
works.plot: Each saint refuses a pagan suitor and judge, defeats her learned or demonic adversaries in debate, endures spectacular torments, and wins a martyr's crown, with Christ or angels as her comforters.
works.significance: The founding texts of the AB language group and the model for Middle English hagiography in the thirteenth century and after.
works.meter: Rhythmical alliterative prose with the characteristic AB-language vocabulary and spelling.
works.context: Composed c. 1190–1225 in the same Herefordshire milieu as Ancrene Wisse; preserved in Bodleian MS Bodley 34 and BL Royal MS 17 A.xxvii.
works.characters: St Katherine; St Margaret; St Juliana; the tyrant-judges (Maxentius, Olibrius, Eleusius); the demons
works.structure: Conventional martyr-act structure (arraignment, debate, torture, death) enriched by long speeches and prayers; Juliana includes the saint's dialogue with a demon.
works.attributionNotes: Anonymous; grouped with Ancrene Wisse and the Wooing Group by dialect and manuscript kinship.

works.title: The Kentish Hymn
works.manuscriptDate: London, British Library, Cotton Vespasian D.vi, fol. 69 (tenth century)
works.form: religious lyric (liturgical paraphrase) in alliterative verse
works.description: A 43-line paraphrase of the Gloria in excelsis in the Kentish dialect, the only substantial Old English poem preserved in that dialect. It praises the Trinity, Christ the Lamb, and the Holy Spirit, and prays for the mercy of the Lord.
works.plot: The poem renders the Greater Doxology clause by clause: praise of God the Father, the Lamb of God who takes away sin, the Holy Spirit with Father and Son, and a closing petition for the Lord's mercy and protection.
works.significance: A rare dialectal witness to Old English religious verse and an early example of the Gloria rendered in English verse.
works.meter: Alliterative long line; the Kentish forms of the text are among the few dialectally marked verse survivals outside West Saxon.
works.context: The hymn was added to a manuscript otherwise containing Kentish glosses and documents; it attests the spread of vernacular liturgical paraphrase beyond the West Saxon heartland of the literary standard.
works.structure: A direct liturgical paraphrase following the order of the Gloria; the doxological clauses are expanded with brief devotional glosses.

works.title: The Kingis Quair
works.description: The dream vision traditionally attributed to James I of Scotland, written c. 1424 after his eighteen years of captivity in England: the imprisoned narrator, sleepless with love, reads Boethius, sees his lady from the tower window, and is taught by the goddesses of Love, Fortune, and Wisdom in a vision that reconciles him to his fate. The fountainhead of the Scottish Chaucerian tradition.
works.plot: The sleepless captive, turning the pages of Boethius, hears the bell of matins and falls into a dream; guided by the goddesses, he ascends to the sphere of Venus, where his love for the lady seen from the tower is confirmed and fortune's wheel is explained; waking, a dove brings him the message of hope, and he ends his book in praise of love and his lady.
works.significance: The fountainhead of the makars' tradition: the first great poem in the Scottish Chaucerian line and the model for the royal and courtly poetry of the Stewart century.
works.meter: Rhyme royal stanzas of Chaucerian fluency, in Older Scots.
works.context: Composed c. 1424, on the eve of James's release, celebrating his love for Joan Beaufort, whom he married in February 1424; preserved uniquely in the Selden manuscript (Bodleian Arch. Selden. B.24, c. 1488).
works.characters: the captive narrator (James I); the lady (Joan Beaufort); Venus; Minerva; Fortune; the dove
works.structure: A single dream vision in the Chaucerian-Boethian manner: reading, waking complaint, dream ascent, counsel of the goddesses, and waking resolution.
works.attributionNotes: The attribution to James I rests on the poem's autobiographical frame and manuscript tradition; it is widely but not universally accepted.

editions.title: The Kingis Quair and Other Prison Poems
editions.editor: Linne R. Mooney and Mary-Jo Arn (eds.)

works.title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle
works.description: Beaumont's mock-romance of the citizen audience: a grocer and his wife, watching the play 'The London Merchant', demand that their apprentice Rafe act the part of a knight errant; the 'Knight of the Burning Pestle' then rides his adventures through Waltham Forest and the giant Barbaroso's barber shop, while the merchant play and the citizens' interruptions double and parody each other to the final, multiple endings.
works.plot: The Citizen and his Wife interrupt the Prologue and hijack the play; Rafe's quests — the dainty damsel, the giants, the adventure of the barber — alternate with the merchant comedy of Venturewell, Jasper, and Luce; the plots collide at the mock-death of Rafe ('for the honor of Knights') and the play ends with the citizens' epilogue and the players' revenge on their audience.
works.significance: The first great English theatrical burlesque — the ancestor of Sheridan's Critic and of every later play about the audience's power over the stage.
works.meter: Mixed verse and prose, with the ballad metres of Rafe's adventures and the songs of old Merrythought ('Nose, nose, jolly red nose') as its parodic instruments.
works.context: First performed by the Children of the Revels at Blackfriars about 1607, where it failed; revived by the Queen's Revels boys and printed in 1613; it mocks the citizen taste that The Shoemaker's Holiday had flattered.
works.characters: the Citizen; his Wife; Rafe (the Knight of the Burning Pestle); George (the apprentice); Venturewell; Jasper; Luce; Humphrey; Merrythought; Mistress Merrythought; Barbaroso the barber; the players
works.structure: A play-within-a-play satire in which the audience is on stage from the start — the first burlesque of the English theatre's own conventions, including the romance, the city comedy, and the 'lamentable' death scene.
works.attributionNotes: Generally assigned to Beaumont alone (perhaps with Fletcher's help); the 1613 title page names only Beaumont.

editions.title: The Knight of the Burning Pestle (Revels Plays)

works.title: The Lady of May
works.description: Sidney's pastoral entertainment, written for a royal visit to Wanstead (probably that of 1578 or 1579): a May Lady must choose between the shepherd Espilus and the forester Therion, while the clownish schoolmaster Rombus and the Queen herself referee the debate between the contemplative and active lives.
works.plot: The Lady of May is courted by the shepherd Espilus and the forester Therion; Rombus presents the case for each; the suitors debate in verse and prose, and the Lady — after a comic intervention by Rixus the pedant — gives her hand to one of them, with Elizabeth I invited to judge the dispute.
works.significance: The earliest English pastoral entertainment of the great age and a document of Sidney's courtly politics; it established the genre that Jonson's masques would crown.
works.meter: Mixed prose and verse, including singing parts.
works.context: Performed for Elizabeth I during her progress to Wanstead, probably in 1578 or 1579, when Leicester (Sidney's uncle) was pressing Sidney toward the Anjou marriage policy.
works.characters: the Lady of May; Espilus the shepherd; Therion the forester; Rombus the schoolmaster; Queen Elizabeth (as judge)
works.structure: A short masque-like entertainment in prose and verse, built on the debate form and ending with the Queen's judgment.
works.attributionNotes: Uncontested; first printed in the 1598 folio of the Arcadia.

editions.title: Miscellaneous Prose of Sir Philip Sidney
editions.editor: Katherine Duncan-Jones and Jan van Dorsten (eds.)

works.title: The Lady of Pleasure
works.description: Shirley's most admired comedy, contrasting the extravagant, pleasure-seeking Lady Ariola Bornwell with the prudent and reformed Mistress Constance; it is the sharpest Caroline critique of conspicuous consumption and fashionable vice.
works.plot: Sir Thomas Bornwell, disgusted by his wife's extravagance, pretends to leave her, while the virtuous Lord Lacywoth courts Constance; the Lady is finally shamed into reform and the couples are properly matched.
works.significance: Long regarded as Shirley's masterpiece and the finest comedy of manners before Etherege; its treatment of the extravagant lady anticipates Restoration social comedy.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed at the Cockpit in 1635, at the height of the fashionable London society that Shirley depicts and satirises.
works.characters: Lady Ariola Bornwell; Sir Thomas Bornwell; Constance; Lord Lacywoth; Celestina; Littleworth; Decoy
works.structure: Five acts with two parallel domestic plots of contrasted moral temperaments.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Lady's Trial
works.description: Ford's last surviving play, a tragicomedy in which Aurelio tests his wife Spinella's chastity, is deceived by the malicious Amoretto, and the trial is resolved by the intervention of Spinella's sister Castanna and the reformed Benatzi.
works.plot: Aurelio's test of Spinella, engineered by the villain Amoretto, appears to confirm her unfaithfulness; the truth emerges when Castanna's own constancy is proved and Amoretto's imposture is exposed.
works.significance: Ford's final play and a mature example of Caroline tragicomedy; its concern with the testing of female chastity connects it to the tradition from Boccaccio to Shakespeare's Cymbeline.
works.meter: Blank verse with prose.
works.context: Performed at the Cockpit in 1636 and published in 1639.
works.characters: Aurelio; Spinella; Castanna; Amoretto; Benatzi; Fulgoso; Adurni
works.structure: Five acts of intrigue with a tragicomic resolution.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ford on the 1639 title page; authorship undisputed.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Lamentation of a Sinner
works.description: Catherine Parr's spiritual autobiography and treatise on justification by faith, published posthumously in 1547; the fullest statement of the queen's evangelical faith.
works.plot: Parr confesses her former life 'in superstition and ignorance', recounts her awakening to the doctrine of justification by faith through the reading of scripture, and expounds the gospel of free grace against the reliance on works, ending with a meditation on the passion and an exhortation to trust wholly in Christ's merits.
works.significance: The first spiritual autobiography by an English queen and an important document of the Reformation's inward turn; it shows the queen — the only woman whose books were printed in her lifetime in Tudor England — articulating the doctrine of faith in her own voice.
works.meter: Prose
works.context: Written in the last years of Henry VIII's reign, when Parr's evangelical circle faced persecution (Askew was burned in July 1546), and published by William Cecil (later Lord Burghley) in 1547 after the king's death; the book became a manual of Edwardian Protestant piety.
works.characters: Catherine Parr (narrator)
works.structure: A two-part work: a first-person confession and conversion narrative, followed by a doctrinal exposition of faith, grace, and the law.

editions.title: Katherine Parr: Complete Works and Correspondence

works.title: The Land of Cokaygne
works.description: A rollicking satire of some 190 lines on the fantasy land of Cokaygne, a paradise of food, sleep, and license reached by a week in a sow's belly, whose abbey of gluttonous monks is described with anti-monastic glee. It is the earliest English example of the European Cockaigne tradition and a masterpiece of clerical self-satire.
works.plot: The poet describes the geography of Cokaygne — roast geese flying, rivers of oil and wine, the fountain of youth — and dwells lovingly on the abbey where the monks, fattened without labour, fly about at their pleasure with the abbess.
works.significance: The first English Cockaigne poem and the liveliest anti-clerical satire before Langland; a favourite of modern anthologies for its comic invention.
works.meter: Octosyllabic couplets of comic energy, in an Irish-influenced Middle English.
works.context: Composed c. 1300, perhaps in Ireland (the sole manuscript is the Kildare miscellany, BL Harley MS 913, c. 1330), where the Cockaigne tradition flourished among the friars.
works.characters: the monks of Cokaygne; the abbess
works.structure: A catalogue-description of the dream land, closing with the burlesque of the monastic abbey.

works.title: The Law of Freedom in a Platform; or, True Magistracy Restored
works.description: Winstanley's mature political programme, addressed to Cromwell, in which he sets out the constitution of a free commonwealth without buying, selling, or private land, and with an elected magistracy and universal education.
works.plot: Winstanley proposes a commonwealth in which the earth is a common treasury, labour is organised communally, the clergy of the old order are abolished, magistrates are elected annually by the people, and laws are short, plain, and enforced by storehouses and officers.
works.significance: The fullest statement of English Digger communism and one of the most original political documents of the seventeenth century; it anticipates socialist and anarchist thought and has been a touchstone for the radical tradition.
works.meter: Prophetic, plain, biblical prose of the radical sects.
works.context: Published in 1652, three years after the Diggers' experiment on St George's Hill (1649), and dedicated to Cromwell, whose commonwealth Winstanley urged to go further.
works.structure: Six chapters with a dedicatory epistle to Cromwell and a proposed code of laws.

editions.title: The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 10th edition, Volume C: Restoration and the Eighteenth Century

works.title: The Laws of Cnut
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The comprehensive law code of King Cnut (r. 1016-1035), drafted by Archbishop Wulfstan: the most elaborate legislation of the Anglo-Saxon period, combining royal law, ecclesiastical regulation, and Wulfstan's characteristic moral exhortation into a grand statement of a Christian commonwealth.
works.plot: The two parts of the code regulate the church (tithes, sanctuary, feast days, the clergy's conduct), the king's peace, legal procedure (ordeals, oaths, hundred courts), the ranks and dues of society, theft, homicide, and the punishment of the faithless; framed by Wulfstan's homiletic prologues exhorting all men to love God and keep the law.
works.significance: The summit of Anglo-Saxon legislation and the last great royal code in English before the Norman period.
works.meter: Old English prose with Wulfstan's rhythmical cadences.
works.context: Promulgated in the councils of 1020-1023 after Cnut's accession; preserved in later eleventh- and twelfth-century legal manuscripts.
works.characters: Cnut (legislator); Wulfstan (draftsman)
works.structure: A systematic code in two parts, with homiletic prologues and perorations.
works.attributionNotes: Drafted by Wulfstan for Cnut; Wulfstan's authorship is established on stylistic grounds.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Christopher Marlowe

works.title: The Laws of Ine
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The law code of King Ine of Wessex (688-726), preserved as an appendix to Alfred's law book: the earliest West Saxon legislation, covering church dues, theft, the status of the Welsh, land law, and the mutual obligations of lords and men.
works.plot: The code's seventy-six clauses regulate church dues and oaths, theft and its pursuit, the wer and wergild of each rank (including the Welsh), land tenure and the duties of gesiths and ceorls, and the penalties for harbouring fugitives.
works.significance: The earliest surviving West Saxon law and a major source for early English social structure.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued c. 688-694; preserved in the earliest manuscript of Alfred's laws (Cambridge, Corpus Christi College MS 173), to which Alfred appended it.
works.characters: Ine (legislator); his counsellors (the prologue names his father Cenred and bishops Hædde and Eorcenwald)
works.structure: A clause-by-clause royal code.
works.attributionNotes: Attributed to Ine in the code's prologue.
sources: The Cambridge Companion to Shakespeare

works.title: The Laws of Æthelberht
works.form: law code in Old English prose
works.description: The law code of King Æthelberht of Kent, the earliest written English law and the oldest surviving document in the English language: a tariff of compensations for injuries, from homicide through wounding to the loss of a toe or a fingernail, with provisions protecting the Church and its property.
works.plot: The code opens with compensations for offences against the Church's property and peace, then proceeds by descending tariff through the body — head, hair, ear, eye, nose, teeth, fingers, nails, feet — assigning a fixed bot (compensation) for each injury according to the victim's rank.
works.significance: The earliest English law and the first extended document in the English language.
works.meter: Old English prose.
works.context: Issued by Æthelberht of Kent c. 602/3, shortly after the arrival of Augustine's mission (597); preserved only in the Textus Roffensis (Rochester, Cathedral Library, MS A.3.5, c. 1120).
works.characters: Æthelberht (legislator)
works.structure: A list of ninety clauses in the Germanic tariff style.
